_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely a "hidden" gem!Pacing feels good, written narrative is surprisingly interesting to follow and the general mood of the game is relaxing and captivating at the same time. Even though the combat is turn-based, there are certain aspects that force you to make quick decisions in some encounters, so the game strikes a nice balance between calculating your actions and having to think on your feet.Backtracking sometimes feels like a chore, even though longer distances are travelled automatically. It would be nice if we could skip going through each screen again, though there is a certain atmospheric mood to traveling with the animals, so perhaps the slow travel can almost be justified.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo, enjoyed the gameplay and thought "I'll probably skip the dialogue as usual" and boy was I wrong. The story is very enticing, I found myself playing not only because I enjoyed the gameplay, which is fun on it's own, but also because I wanted to know what happens next.Also, i've only done one run so far, but it seems like the game has branching paths and some moral choices aren't presented as moral choices,the game simply asks you "what do you want to do?" and you must deal with the consequences. It feels so much better than the mass effect approach of "good or bad decision"
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Criminally underplayed. Ever since Flamberge was abandoned, I've been waiting for this kind of tactical gameplay again. It's charming as hell and has very cool combat, with an excellent soundtrack. If you're a fan of simultaneous action turn-based tactical games, you should really give this a try.Edit: The story and characters just keep getting better. The world is unique and engaging with a sort of understated mythical feel to it. The dialogue is entertaining and genuinely funny at times.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Really refreshing to play a game with an original combat system, and I think it lands well! The ghosts help give it almost a blend of turn based and real time combat feel. The vibe of the game is perfect with the music really helping the imagination fill in the pixel art visuals. I haven't finished the story to see where it goes, but it has me intrigued in act 3. I really think, especially at the price point, the game is worth giving a go.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the greatest indies Ive played recently. I am not someone who is typically interested in turn based rpgs and while Ive followed the artist for their pixel art for most of this games development I was hesitant to buy it due to its price and my typical interests. However after just over 2.5 hours of play I can promise this game is worth the purchase and more. And according to the dev, thats about how much the free demo is. give it a try I promise it wont be a waste of time. art direction: Incrediblemusic: wonderfulStory: still early but the world feels very deep due to the random interactions and how they impact your play. More of world building aspect but it feels good to walk around and interact.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: The combat drew me in because it reminded me of similar tactics seen in into the breach and FTL with telegraphed enemy moves and time freezes, but wow... the story ended me. The writing and dialogue is concise  but uses every word to pack a punch and really get you attached to the world. All I can say is I hope we see move projects like this from the devs. Absolute proof that writing and game mechanics are all you need for an absolute banger. this game punches WAY above its price tag and easily in my top 5 games of all time on story quality alone.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun little tactics rpg with beautiful pixel art, an interesting setting, choices that matter without feeling like the end of the world, and a weird little combat system with just enough timing mechanics sprinkled in to make turn based combat feel fresh. Just watching your characters ride llamas around the gorgeous landscape is a great time.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Arco is an action RPG with a deep story and multiple intertwined mechanics. The trailer is very detailed and does an excellent job introducing it, so check it out to help your buying decision. Here are my three thoughts:1. There is a LOT of story, and it's delivered through short conversations and action scenes. Very "show, don't tell".2. Combat is complex and challenging. Think Slay the Spire meets action. The designers did a great job adding elements like dodging into a turn-based game. It's also quite hard, which I found delightful.3. Your story decisions matter. No spoilers, but whatever you do and how you communicate with characters influence where the game goes.I greatly enjoyed the game and wholeheartedly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Great gameplay, really cool skill trees.Interesting setting, interesting characters. The story itself is a little hit or miss. The whole "journey of revenge" thing felt a little over played imo, but it hit best in Act 4 and 5 for me (act 4 was my fav). Also it's uh. Really heavy. For almost the entire thing. So I found that a bit hard to play through when I wasn't always in the mood for heavy. There's also lighter funnier bits that I enjoyed, but they feel pretty far and few in between.Honestly, I really want a roguelike version of this game were you slap together your rag-tag crew of 2-3 ppl and go take on the big bad ala sts map traversal. Would happily pay another $10 for that.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Cute art, fantastic OST, nice story and fresh gameplay, was really enjoyable throughout and it has a pretty unique personality. Would've liked a bit of a longer closure but I'm probably too spoiled there. Took ~12h for me but don't make the same mistake of hoarding items and cash as I have.Seems potentially fairly replayable, might give it a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Arco is intriguing so far!I'm only in the middle of Act III, but I'm enjoying Arco immensely. The soundtrack is fantastic, the writing and world building grabs your interest, and the combat is a refreshing take on a turn-based RPG system. The guilt system is neat and I should probably stop killing folks because the sins of my actions weigh heavy on my characters' minds!Will update my review when I finishEdit: I finished Arco and I loved it. It's story and characters were fascinating all the way to the end! Some fights were pretty tough but the game encourages you to change your skills and items when failing, so it was enjoyable to solve. If you're looking for a fresh turn-based RPG experience, Arco is for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Engaging story and thought provoking choices that actually feel like they mean something. The turn based combat feels different but in a good way. its a very fresh and fun way to manage fights. Please give this a try if you're interested, the writing is fun and the world building is great and easy to understand and get into. Play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: I'm partway through Act III, but this is one of the best indie games I've played in a while. The combat is satisfying, and may take a little bit to figure out (the amount of time i dodge rolled bullets that hadn't been fired yet, only to die to them is embarrassing) but when you get a feel for it is truly fluid. It's a perfect combination of turn based and real time, which did had me sceptical but now is something I'd love to see in more games!! So if that is worrying you, just go for it - I had a blast  Aside from that, the story and writing is incredibly compelling, and I'm a big fan of the humour. The soundtrack WILL NOT EXIT MY HEAD IT GOES SO HARD. Not to mention the art and character designs, its incredible (i am just a sucker for pixel art tho).Only encountered small 1 bug, and has been said it will be patched. So the polish is extremely highOverall, highly recommend
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Feels wonderfully unique to play — in many ways it reminds me of a modernized take on CRPGS like Fallout 2. Their take on turn-based combat is pretty inventive! NPCs and player characters share plan and execution phases, but certain things like projectiles take multiple turns to complete so you have to do a bit more planning ahead than you might expect. The systems feel good so far (somewhat into Act 2), and the story has felt compelling enough to make me want to explore and talk to characters outside of just progression-oriented dialogue.It’s a special game, and I really hope more folks pick it up!
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: The combat system is totally unique, and I love the art and setting. I think there are a few wrinkles that could be ironed out- some areas are a little odd to explore if you enter from the east for the first time, for example. Despite some rough edges, the passion at the core really shines through! Highly recommend :)
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: So I'm two hours into my second playthrough and this Game is Just pure Magic, Getting to 1000+Gold was also fun while abusing the Trader lmao.Awesome Game, amazing Music, Neat Story, effective Skilltrees with enough variety (pls more gun abilities DEVS PLS <3), Choices U are allowed to make are cute and Spice it Up Sometimes, straight Up banger Game.Thank you for this Gem
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: A game so nice I finished it in two days, realized I'd been so excited to see everything that I'd inadvertently skipped a lot of side stuff, and so immediately started it up again. It's incredible to me how fresh, exciting, and dynamic it feels even while playing it for an immediate second go around. The fighting is a fun, turn-based strategy style that I'm not good at by nature but really enjoy the challenge of; I can't speak for how someone with actual skills at that may enjoy it, but I love it. I could recognize a genuine improvement arc in myself--not just my characters--as I played the game and really began to learn, understand it, and get more clever about how to use the mechanics, which I really enjoyed. But what to say about the story? I love the story. A lot. The characters are endearing, the world is enchanting, it feels full of love and potential and passion. This is a kind-hearted game with something important to say. I'm trained as a history teacher and did my senior thesis (and most of my undergrad/grad research in general) on the intersection between ecological disruption and european-style imperialism. Arco deals with this topic in a way that is engaging and impactful, and offers players the rare opportunity to explore it through a strictly indigenous perspective. It's rare to find fiction on this topic that doesn't inevitably crumple to a white savior complex or stumbling over itself to assuage a white audience's guilt. The protagonists all experience this world and react to it in their own ways, having unique stories that eventually are woven together by common threads. The themes of guilt and grief tied into the revenge plots are phenomenal, giving the player incentive to think about what they do before they do it and also feel the weight of their character's conscience as they barrel through the world. The senses of love, grief, hope, loss, family, and anger all bleeding through the story are something really special to me. It's a game I wish I could reach into and touch. It's a sentimental experience with a fantastic gameplay loop that makes it equal parts introspective and exciting. The art style is both adorable and breath taking, a combination that's hard to nail. The music is so good my friends listening to me play kept asking for the song names (and thankfully, the soundtrack is already up on spotify! <3) This is a game that feels cared for. I want more of this world. I want more South American fantasy in general. I love spending time with this game and these characters. I really hope to see more from these devs!
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: This game is immaculate. It's just the perfect mixture of "difficult but fair". It's not perfect, there are some typos, there are some quirks...but you'll be enthralled by the surprising depth of the story, the compelling character narratives....it's really, really great. I'm 30+ hours in the game and that's only on my first play through heading towards the 5th chapter.....and I feel like I might even give it another go after that to see how the story changes.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games where the makers put their heart and soul into it, and knew what they were doing. This game is among the best RPGs I've ever played and certainly earned a place at the table of greatest pixely combat RPGs ever.The story is dark and immersive but the visuals are cute and pleasing that creates a juxtaposition unlike any game I've ever seen.Everything is so fighty and detailed and i love it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: This is an RPG with a nice atmosphere. The battle system is a bit unconventional but that's something I enjoy here except for battles with more than one character to control. Those are a bit stressful and at least until now for me not worth the hassle. I also didn't find out how to heal my companions, so they tend to immediately go down. Anyway, get it, play it and see for yourself.Edit: You can switch to the other characters in the inventory screen by clicking on their names.I finished it. Wow, what an atmosphere this game has. Play it, fall into it, fall in love with the story! Buy this!
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: A couple hours in this game is phenomenal. Tight, refined Battle mechanics. Clever storytelling both in raw prose and in interactive structuring. It feels like the game is flirting with the player, training them to embrace the story with their heart rather than raw mechanical expectations. Great stuff!
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game with rewarding turn based combat mechanics and exploration. I'm engrossed in the narrative of the game as well, one has to be careful of the choices they make in the game because the actually have appropriate consequences. Can't recommend this enough to anyone who's into tactics or turn based strategy games, it's well worth your money.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Arco really caught me off guard in the best way possible. I was expecting a fairly casual play-through but ended up getting hooked by the story. The dialogue options feel incredibly meaningful, and there are plenty of secrets to discover that keep you wanting more.The music is another standout—these tracks are just beautiful and really set the mood for the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible atmospheric experience with an open, beat by beat tactical combat system that feels as if it could be expanded upon indefinitely.  Expect hypothetical sequels and mods of this game to keep you engaged for hours post credits.  Special shout-out goes to the color palette and musical score for matching the mood spectacularly.Has some stuttering and bugs in the late game, but nothing that will ruin your experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: I find this game super unique for its kind. I'm kind of really enjoying it so far. I love where its going. If I had to nitpick and complain about something, I am SO ANNOYED at the fact that when you are picking movements, it allows you to run right off a cliff. In the game if you want to move the option will grey out if you try to move to somewhere that you cant. BUT if you pick a place too far past a cliff it will drop you right off. If its too far or if you can prove past it, grey it out.OTHERWISE, pretty sick game so far. I'm liking it.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Arco gives me the feeling of returning to the original fallout games in the best way possible. The combat and the world are really interesting, and the writing is light touch and ever so slightly memey in a way that works for the game. The optional route I've stumbled on is insane- I have no idea where the story is going, but things have gotten out of hand in a fascinating way and I'm along for the ride.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Gorgeous pixel art and music, an emotional story, a compelling combat system and many secrets to discover - what more could you want? I'd wholeheartedly recommed this game if any of these points seem interesting to you.The game can drag a little bit towards the end with the amount of combats and some less exciting story phases, but it doesn't overstay its welcome by any means. I took ~2 hours of break time and then dived right into a replay to search for more secrets, experiment with different skill builds and explore how other story choices play out.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: This game will get you tearing up pretty early. The gameplay is fun, but story is even more fun! I'm on chapter 3 and Oh man, I did absolutely everything I was not supposed to do. The game, doesn't punish you too severely for making those dreadful choices. Has it's own humor and very sad parts. The game so far is outstanding!
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: This is a special game - Excellent game play mechanics, music, story, and heart. It is difficult, each encounter being a puzzle to solve but the restart button is free and generous. I failed many battles many times but I was always close so I tried again. The ending really affected me , I'm sure I'll play again some day and make different choices.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute gem. Stunning pixel art, gorgeous music, addictive fighting and a story that gives you the same righteous anger as the protagonists.Do not play this game without headphones. There’s no voice acting but the music is not to be missedThere are still glitches and optimizations that need to be made, this game is not perfect and may crash occasionally. Still, it is absolutely worth every second you play
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so good. I could gush about semi-coherently for hours if someone let me. However, I must restrain myself.Arco is a game about revenge set in a Mesoamerican-inspired fantasy world. Even though it sits squarely in the Western genre, the world of Arco still feels unique. This great setting is boosted by the wonderful art and music, which is simplified while still feeling real and visceral. All the characters you meet feel like real people, and the cultures are not stereotypes or "planets of funny hats". The devs could have stopped with this. I would be happy for a game with such an awesome world, even if its gameplay was mediocre. But the gameplay isn't mediocre. The gameplay is AWESOME. The turn-based tactical combat hits the right balance between simple enough to grasp but complex enough to have fun playing with. You will never feel as much like an action hero as when you dodge between bullets and punching someone in the face. Each ability has a clear-cut, unique role to play, and you can customize your skills to your play style. Want to shower the enemy with a hail of arrows? You can do that. Want to get up close and personal with the enemy? You can do that too.Finally, the story is very well-written. I would highly suggest going into it blind. You will not be dissappointed.10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: So far so very good!My favorite thing about Arco is how blisteringly fast its combat is compared to most TBS/tactics games or JRPGs. I get the impression the developers respect my time, not only in that the game progresses quickly, BUT ALSO because it's so fast, Arco can ratchet up the challenge for free (and it does so). Failing a mission in FFT or Battle for Wesnoth can be exhausting or frustrating. But ARCO expects you to die like Dark Souls and Hollow Knight expect you to die. Fights are short and brutal, and you can retry them instantly without condescension.If that sounds scary, well, it also seems the greatest difficulties in this game are optional, self-imposed. You're given ample opportunity to prepare yourself for mandatory story fights, via the RPG mechanics in the game.Also the music and sound design help you settle into into Arco's rhythmic and moody combat. It's very satisfying.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Came for the pixel art, stayed for the gameplay. I've been following the development of ARCO for months now and, despite knowing almost nothing about its gameplay or story, I was planning to buy it on release mainly because of the art style. Was not dissappointed at all: graphics are beatiful, animations are fluid and sounds, music and VFX turn this into a very solid game.The biggest surprise came with the gameplay, the combat system and the story. Challenging but fair turn based combat with a twist - I am still on the second chapter and I already discovered several ways to approach every battle. The plot of the game is very mature, your choices affect the outcome in certain parts of the story, you definitely root for ARCO's characters...Will update this review as I finish the game but so far I cannot stress how good this game is. Very much recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: A new spin on turn based strategy with nostalgic pixel art and a breezy story about revenge and retribution. It's a lot of fun and easy to pick up. There are plenty of choices you can make and I'm curious to see how they affect the story and replayability. There are also various builds for each character, so you should have enough to explore and try out for a second playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: I was initially drawn to this game by its captivating pixel art and strategic combat. However, my heart was taken away with the music, the writing, and the story. Arco is an adventure brimming with wonder and depth, where each character’s journey feels profoundly real. The struggles they face and the evocative sounds of this world linger long after you close the game. Both the narrative and the combat system shine as they tread on unfamiliar territories, remixing ideas from tactical RPG's but making choices both in combat and out, really change the course of the game.I've played the game from start to finish, I've enjoyed every fight and story arc. The combat is hard yet once you get the hang of it (also very easy to restart lost fights) you feel like coordinating a western standoff in real time. Don't miss this game if you like tactical combat. Few games have tied mechanics like this, and you will be happily surprised.This indie gem is a treasure, offering a full game experience that resonates on a deeply emotional and aesthetic level. My sincere congratulations to the team for creating something that feels genuinely fresh.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

_childDocuments_.review: Enter the breathtaking world of Arco, a dynamic tactical RPG where your decisions shape the story. Three tales forged in bloodshed, laced with magic, and united by revenge.
_childDocuments_.name: Arco

name: Thank Goodness You're Here!
short_description: Thank Goodness You're Here! is an absurd comedy slapformer set in the bizarre Northern English town of Barnsworth. As a traveling salesman, take the time to see the sights and meet the locals, who are very eager to give you a series of increasingly odd jobs…

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to come right out and say this straight away: Thank Goodness You're Here is one of the funniest games I've ever played. I can't remember the last time I laughed out loud *this* often doing anything. The visuals are endlessly charming, the voice acting is perfection, the music is great and it's just so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ funny.Now - big asterisk - I am English. Half Northern, half Midlander. Much of what's funny about Thank Goodness is based in very specific references and vibes from Northern English culture from the last forty or so years. I may have been bordering on tears seeing a shop called "Price Shaggers" and the hilariously named products contained within, but I do wonder if this game might just make an American's head explode. That's what I love most about Thank Goodness though. It absolutely refuses to compromise in its depiction of the Yorkshire essence. It may only be a small subset of gamers who can fully enjoy the game, but by god will that group of people love it. It's obvious just how much love is in the developers for this county, dialect and cultural reference point. Despite some often grotesque or unflattering imagery, it never feels mean-spirited. Instead, Thank Goodness depicts a people and place with honesty and a wry humour that is more respectful than if they'd avoided anything potentially offensive. It's akin to when your best mate takes the piss out of you. From the outside, it looks cruel, but between the two of you, it's the truest expression of affection.The game is definitely on the shorter side, only taking me two hours (and I was really dragging my feet trying to see everything) but it's so jam-packed with jokes, weird dialogue and unique animations that I could have sworn it was more like four or five hours. The gameplay itself is fairly rote and is just there to facilitate as many jokes as possible, and the structure of the game can feel aimless as you loop through the same four or five areas over and over. Each return visit does see the area changed, with background characters advancing jokes or new sub-areas to explore, but it can be a little discouraging to go through the same bits over and over. Ultimately though, the devs turn this flaw into part of its big meta-joke on the relentless busywork that's prolific in so many games, so it's hard to really criticise the game for a flaw that can't really be remedied without losing so much of what makes it special.If you've ever lived above the middle of England, it's basically law that you have to play Thank Goodness You're Here!. A shining example of surrealist comedy that manages some surprisingly emotionally affective moments, this is a sublime experience that I can do nothing but recommend. I can't wait to forget as much of it as possible so I can play it again.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: In the , Deus Ex creator Warren Spector famously stated that his dream project would be a game taking place entirely within a single, expertly crafted city block, where you`d go aroud interacting with its people and their stories.In , a stranger will relentlessly offer you sausages through a fence hole in Coal Supper`s "" - a game where you assume the role a lil' british goblin-manchild, who goes about solving the problems of the jolly townsfolk of Barnsworth entirely by means of slap.It is beautiful, it is aggressively Northern England and it just might be the funniest game I`ve played. Buy this.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: Usually, I'll review with deadpan one-liners, but for this absolute gem, I'm going to stuff a bit more meat in the pie. I first caught the reveal trailer on Friday morning and spent the whole day itching to get back home to play it.I live abroad now but grew up in England—alright, the south, but still—this game made me incredibly nostalgic for the warm vibes of the old stomping grounds. As a kid, I lived for the British absurdist comedies of the 2000s—The IT Crowd, The Mighty Boosh, and Garth Marenghi's Darkplace—and Thank Goodness You're Here captured that spice and had me laughing out loud again and again.With that said, I don't want to alienate or imply that anyone who didn't have the same childhood wouldn't find this a joy. The devs even diegetically added the option of having 'English' subtitles as opposed to 'Dialect'. The absurd running jokes in a cozy Yorkshire town really were the milk in the tea. Speaking of, it's absolutely recommended to mash a Yorkshire brew on the side to top it all off, so pop the kettle on and I'll go through some spoiler-free stuff in the meantime:You control a nameless businessman with, for the most part, three inputs: move, jump, and slap. The slap, hilarious as it is, doubles up as how you interact with the world. In this sense, it's a simple, relaxing break if you're coming from fast-paced action games, and a great next play if you're used to point and click, visual novels, and the like. Perfect to kick back and play from the sofa with a controller.The art style and feel of the game are reminiscent of 90s/00s British comics and illustrated books, you know, the kind where there's a bunch of stuff happening in one massive picture, and the thrill comes from scanning your eyes over the entire page to catch everything. With punchy and quirky animations adding to the charm, this is spot on. A genuine joy to play.Though it's around 2-4 hours for a single playthrough, the shorter time shouldn't put you off. They've packed so much personality into this that it’s well worth it. I wrapped it up in a couple of nights, so it’s ideal if you enjoy shorter experiences. I found myself wanting to knock on every door and check every corner for smaller gags, and I'm pretty sure there's more for me to go back and find on a second playthrough. I wasn't disappointed with what I'd found so far. It's tempting to give examples, but please just check it out yourselves.Oh yeah, Matt Berry's in it as well.Thank you, James, Will, and the rest of the team at Coal Supper! I had a lot of fun <3
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: I usually don't bother writing reviews for games because I'm just an average Joe who plays games and I don't have anything insightful to say. However, Thank Goodness You're Here has probably been the best $20 I've spent on a game in a long time. It has a great art style, great humor, and good music and really makes me want to explore this little town that is filled to the brim with personality from top to bottom. PLEASE do not watch anything about this game before going in, just dive in and have a great time!
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge person on watching people play games, and if they seem good or funny enough, trying them out myself. I didn't make it a full five minutes into someone's gameplay when I desperately wanted to try this game out for myself and I'm so glad I did. As someone who was born in America, some of the english language or words were extremely funny, especially out of context. I had no idea what some of the people said but I didn't need to!This game is a perfect mix of funny and weird and it's right on the border where I loved it. Some of the scenes left me speechless in a good way. I was actually surprised at how much effort went into this game, there was quite a lot of interactions that changed over time and it made it so much funnier. My favorite were the two neighbors with the trashcan, that was gold!
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: What a strange and original production. It's very funny and very British (especially the accents), satirising elements of "culture" we don't see in American games, like Greggs pasty shops, Victorian chimney-sweeps, and chavs at the chippie. It's also extremely surreal, recalling quirky Brit media like '90s TV news parody "The Day Today" or David Firth's darkly weird "Salad Fingers".Gameplay is somewhat linear, and easy throughout — you explore different sections of the town and occasionally do a platforming or collect-'em-up section — and replay value will be very limited. You could plough through it in a few hours if you were so inclined, but then you'd miss a lot of hidden treats and eavesdropping on the townsfolk's wacky conversations. I saw it as more of an interactive short film, and a very entertaining one.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: Thank Goodness You're Here is a pretty short comedy game, but what it lacks in length it more than makes up for in humor. The gameplay is very basic and boils down to "hit all the things until something progresses", but every single thing you hit will either make you giggle or piss your pants laughing. It takes 2-3 hrs to beat, but I plan on replaying once or twice and inviting my friends to watch and experience the humor. As an example, it starts out with some random question that I assume someone from Northern England would understand, and when you say "What?" it turns on subtitles with translations.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: 100% yes. Fun jokes, great voice, music, animation and awesome stories to follow. If you take it slow, you can enjoy different scenes as time goes by- the neighbors with their bins, the lady with the driving instructor, the burnt steak etc. Best part, is that there is no hint but the game is made in a way that certain paths are blocked at specific scenes to help you understanding where you need to go, plus the dialogues will let you know roughly what you need to go. Bought this game when it's on sale- it's worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure I understand what I just played.Thank Goodness You're Here is an interactive cartoon where you play a silent gentleman trying to see a Mayor about a business proposal. Since the mayor's in a meeting, you can either wait quietly for him to finish, or explore the town. Exploring the town opens you up to a world of linear requests that take you from one whacky scenario to the next across a very British, very insulated little community.There is very little challenge here; when I was stuck I just kept meandering until I found an open path. But the joy of the game isn't really in the challenge, it's in just seeing and hearing the people interact. Your character helps move things along with them but I almost get the feeling that they would do their own thing without you. It's not a bad thing, mind you. But, considering the $20 price tag, there will be some people who find it too expensive for what you get.I paid $17 for it but I think it's more worth $15 when you take into account the animation and voice acting involved. It is a very short experience--three hours for me with a few moments where I didn't know what to do. With that in mind, my recommendation is to wait for it to go on sale.I wouldn't skip the experience, though; it is an entertaining one. I should also point out that although it is animated, it is not for children. There is a lot of language and inuendo in the game and at one point, you do see a man who is naked from the waist down. It's not a huge deal, but I thought I'd point it out.

_childDocuments_.review: All I could think of ever since I've played the demo was: Slap slap slap —Slap slap slap Slap slap slap Must. Slap. Everything. Every. Thing.(and everyone, for that matter)All. The. Time.A first look:That being said, this game is hilarious. It's funny, absurd, weird, fascinating and above all creative. Thank the lord for subtitles, too, because I would be a tad lost sometimes without them; I love the accents. It's stellar voice work, and I'm here for it. The play on words you often come across is glorious, too. I'm still laughing over tits—the birds, of course. Someone will have to explain 'threepence' to me, though. I should stalk my UK friend this evening…My only pet peeve, but that is more on me than the game, is that I'm so eager to explore and discover everything that I sometimes rush through too fast and miss some conversations. When I turn back to tune in, the conversation stops or is without subtitles. Yet it didn't pass by me that there are fun little details like things written on the wall or ground, the employee of the month pictures above the window at the very beginning, the market stalls,… Accompanied by cartoonesque visuals and great music, it just comes together. Everything feels right, which leads to a real vibe while playing, and I love that. I'm just laid-back exploring and slapping, lots and lots of slapping. I… I just can't help it. I'm not even ashamed of it!So, it's a big yes for me, with a big thumbs up and a smile. You can tell how much dedication, love, labour, etc, that went into this game.I even would like to ask when "thank goodness you're still here" will be released. I would love to see more of this odd 'slapformer', which I didn't know I needed so badly in my life!

_childDocuments_.review: My guess would be around 4 to 5 hours if you know what to do. Or if you follow a guide it might be shorter as you won't miss out on an achievement, so you don't have to replay the game.  2/10 1,1 but probably 2,1... why the decimal number you ask... because there is an ending you can reach within under 20 minutes.  not yet. , but it is still missing a few achievements.  No Yes, many! No No No No No No difficulty option NoWhat the heck did I just play? I expected something funny and strange.. but I wasn't prepared for this amount of strangeness going on in this game. To be upfront, my rating for this game might be a bit lower than some others because it turned out the humor in this game wasn't my style. There were funny moments, but also quite a lot of moments that didn't do anything to me. In Thank Goodness You're Here! you play as a little guy who goes to visit the small town Barnsworth. The reason why... I'm not exactly sure. Your boss asks you to go there and don't miss the bus. So the good employee you're... you jump out of the window to not miss the bus! There you have an appointment with the Major, but he is busy the moment you arrive. So you have a choice... wait for the appointment, or explore the town. If you choose to explore the town.. you'll enter the wildest fever dream you'll have without having a fever or without dreaming. You'll make multiple runs through town to help out the people, or sometimes make their life miserable. The story on its own is wild and I would recommend playing the first playthrough without a guide and using a second playthrough to mop up the missing achievements. At this moment achievements don't unlock if you start a new playthrough directly after your first one. You have to restart the game for the achievements to work on a second or third playthrough. Thank Goodness You're Here! has many missable achievements. a whole bunch you'll just unlock out or curiosity and some by just following the story, but there are many where you have to do something specific. Like: listening to two potatoes talking before you chop them down to make fries or find all the singing mice. I think that the main story can be beaten in 1,5/2 hours, so a second playthrough to mop up what you missed isn't the worst. I hope that someone will end up writing a complete achievement guide. I tried to make a start but wasn't sure about everything and also had no clue about a few of them, so I gave up writing one. I'm looking forward to coming back to this game after a guide is available to mop up those last few achievements I'm missing. I give Thank Goodness You're Here! 3 out of 5 stars.

_childDocuments_.review: A slapstick comedy puzzle game set in fictional 1980's Britain, filled with more dry wit than you'll know what to do with. There isn't much in the way of gameplay—it's more like a tool for dispensing jokes rather than something to challenge the player—but the writing's more than good enough to make up for it. I just wish it was a little bit longer, because you're only looking at around a 2-3 hour runtime even if you go out of your way to try and see everything it has to offer.  is a comedy game where you, a nameless and inexplicably tiny salesman, get roped into a series of increasingly odd jobs in the fictional Northern English town of Barnsworth. At its core, it's a puzzle game revolving around the simple game mechanic of slapping things—seriously, like 95% of what you do is just walk up to things and push a button to slap them and see what happens. People, animals, public infrastructure, private property—you name it, you can slap it, and doing so will probably end up solving your problems for some reason or another.The basic gameplay loop is finding a resident that needs help with something, then exploring the much-more-literal loop that is the streets of Barnsworth to find whatever will help them with their request. It kind of gives me point-and-click adventure vibes at times, especially since you can slap almost everything for a silly reaction just like the old Humongous Entertainment games. These puzzles aren't exactly hard, but you'll need to pay close attention to what each character says so you know what you should be doing, because they typically won't repeat their instructions twice.Navigating the town can be a puzzle in and of itself, though not always the fun kind of puzzle. Barnsworth only has a few streets you're allowed to access, and you'll need to visit each one multiple times throughout your playthrough; but the catch is that when you cross into a new street, the path back is blocked and the path forward changes on every visit, so you might find yourself beating your head (or slapping your hand, I guess) against everything to find the new exit since it's not always obvious. The mild annoyance of this mechanic is offset by the fact that each return trip to a street brings new characters and new dialogue so it keeps this loop from feeling quite as monotonous.Those character interactions are where you'll find much of the game's charm as well as most of the jokes. Each one has their own unique personality, full voice acting, and simple but expressive design that feel like they could've been pulled right out of a kid's cartoon. Make no mistake, though: this is  a family-friendly game. There's a fair share of what they call "general mature content", like swearing and copious amounts of pub beer (two of UK's biggest exports, I believe); as well as a few, more egregious things like the crude depictions of one man's haddock and another man's pork and beans, so to speak. It's not exactly  or anything, but maybe don't give it to your kid without vetting it yourself first.The writing involves a lot of cultural references that might get lost on players that didn't grow up in the rather specific time and region this game loosely depicts, so you might miss out on some of the jokes if you can't relate. That said, there's still plenty to laugh at, as much of the comedy revolves around slapstick gags mixed with a healthy dose of dry wit. No matter how absurd a situation may get, there's this jovial but deadpan delivery to it all, as if the ridiculous stuff you're seeing is actually quite normal and you're the weird one for thinking otherwise. That juxtaposition is funny from start to finish, and it's not long before you'll be rolling with the punches like everyone else.Beating the game will probably take you around 2-3 hours, but you're encouraged to explore and interact with as much of Barnsworth as possible to extend your stay, with plenty of optional achievements to help incentivize you to do so. If you fancy yourself an achievement hunter, note that any you miss will require you to replay the game from the beginning to acquire them; and most of them are easy to miss if you don't already know what you're looking for. Just be diligent about interacting with everything and you should be able to find most of them; and don't be afraid to open the hidden achievements to view their descriptions if needed—I promise it won't spoil any big story events for you.Overall, I got about four hours out of it: three on my initial playthrough and an additional hour getting the last few achievements I missed the first time. I wish I could've gotten a bit more time out of it, but at least I can say that time was well spent.

_childDocuments_.review: Many people have compared this game to Untitled Goose Game however, whilst the settings are relatively similar, UGG was a quirky take on the stealth genre with some relatively interesting puzzles. I can't say the same for Thank Goodness You're Here. TGYH has little to no gameplay. You simply walk around a town 5 times slapping things to interact and initiate comedy scenes. There's no puzzles. No game. It's more of a loosely interactive movie. Overall it took me about 150mins to complete from start to finish - including unlocking a ton of secret scenes most players have missed. If you want an interactive movie experience with humour similar to something like Smiling Friends or Don't Hug Me I'm Scared it provides a nice little experience. If you want a something reminiscent of Untitled Goose Game I'd recommend giving it a miss.

_childDocuments_.review: "Thank Goodness You're Here!" is a delightful and quirky adventure that offers a fresh and humorous experience. Set in the peculiar Northern English town of Barnsworth, you play as a traveling salesman navigating a series of increasingly odd tasks assigned by the eccentric locals. The game's unique art style and witty dialogue create a charming atmosphere that keeps you engaged throughout. While the game is relatively short, with many players completing it in under two hours, its originality and humor make it worth the experience. If you're looking for something different and enjoy a good laugh, this game is a must-try.

_childDocuments_.review: Very much a bri'ish cartoon episode of a game, but that is what I want sooo thank you very much. Oodles of tiny quirks and references to it's island (See it, smell it, sorted) bring a local & regional charm to it - a glimpse of an absurdist depiction of living in some northern town, somewhere in the UK. Adoring the fat mono outlines & bold colors as your circle through Barnsworth as this little/tiny/quite suprisingly average-sized fella through scene to scene as call-backs occur, gags continue on or scenes turn to surreal crazyness. It is with these repeated visits that I kind of adore the game - the jokey writing on the wall, revisiting the oddball cast interacting with one another and seeing the devs comitting to every bit they start - gotta respect the jokster for using the rule of threes whenever they can. The DHMIS-esque crescendo of a song a perfect goodbye-wave to the grinning flavor of a game that is Thank Goodness You're Here.

_childDocuments_.review: Not for many years have I ever been so compelled to leave a recommendation for a game so early into its playthrough, but Thank Goodness You're Here! breaks the cycle. TGYH! is a short comedy adventure game with platforming elements, and many visual gags in styles reminiscent of classic British humour.With so many little details present in the world, such as a "Piss Poor" food hygiene rating for a restaurant, or Today's Special for the pub being "Drinks", I've had an amazingly entertaining few hours while playing this through on my Steam Deck.Incredible voice talent is featured across the title, featuring the likes of Matt Berry and many others, including the game devs themselves! There are so many charming characters to come across throughout the game, with elements of progression with things like ongoing dialogues, which adapt and evolve over the course of the game.The game runs brilliantly too, with no issues aside from some delayed subtitles during the cutscenes. A consistent 90fps from start to finish when playing through on my Steam Deck, with a wide variety of resolutions to pick from. I enjoyed the language options between British English and true Northern slang too!If you've a yearning for British deadpan comedy, and multiple subtle visual gags, then Thank Goodness You're Here! won't let you down. While not as long as other people may expect, this casual comedy is an easy 10/10 from me.

_childDocuments_.review: Why don't more games like this exist. Such a neat and fun experience. _childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is full of life. Every detail in "Thank Goodness You're Here!" is immaculately thought out as it invites everyone to fully and authentically join the fun - I don't think I've ever laughed so much while playing a game. Every character has something unique to offer to the inter-weaving stories, whether it's a visual gag, play on words or bizarre revelation. As a person who grew up in a Yorkshire town not too dissimilar to the fictional Barnsworth, there is an additional layer of nods, winks and cultural references to that corner of the world which made me very happy. As well as the characters, setting, gameplay, soundtrack and story all being excellent, the voice acting deserves a special mention. While it boasts an appearance from the multi-talented Matt Berry, the entire voice cast is on top form, delivering lines with perfect comedic timing. "Thank Goodness You're Here!" is a true joy to experience and an ode to cosy, British silliness.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: very novel in presentation and specific but solid in its sense of humor! i love to be the smallest ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dude in the world. gets a little weird at some points but not in a way i didn't expect after having played good time garden, a prior work from this dev. at the time when i first heard about this game, it was during gamescom 2023. i had been kind of exhausted by that point in the conference and not a lot of the trailers for new things had interested me at all, and the trailer for this came in as the second-to-last thing of the particular conference i was watching. the trailer delighted me enough to more than make up for the boredom that had set in, and the game lived up to the expectation that set. lovely game!

_childDocuments_.review: As a Lancastrian, the hapless folk of Yorkshire are, of course, my rightful ancestral foes. It was therefore with a mixture of horror and disgust that I saw this game appear, and I think it only fair to give my entirely fair and impartial view.As expected, the game is puerile, absolutely full of innuendo, entirely ridiculous, packed full of absurd dialect, features a cast of ludicrous simpletons with preposterous and almost completely pointless things to ask you to do, and everywhere you look there is some form of reference, pun or sight gag that the devs clearly believe to be funny. I simply cannot properly express how much I resent that they are absolutely right because it is very very funny indeed, this game is brilliant and I am enjoying it immensely. It is frankly a crime against nature that I should be so entertained by something that is so Yorkshire, and I am now in hiding from the Lancastrian authorities who I fear will now strip me of my Red Rose and my George Formby collection. Curse you, Coal Supper, I fear I will now have to monitor all of your future output to ensure you never do anything like this again.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game specifically because it was mentioned by Lucy on the “Friends per second“ podcast. I’ve never been to the UK, but I am pretty open-minded when it comes to comedy. I still had an absolute BLAST running through this glorious morsel of a game.The jokes, both verbal and visual, Will probably land with more impact if you are a UK native, but I found myself laughing out loud and grinning with delight At the unfortunate series of events that follow the protagonist from the second they leave their office to the roll of the credits. My significant other Couldn’t help but join in the spectacle as she ordered Me to slap every trash bin and pigeon around town, both of us surprised by the amount of variety that can be packed into these few short hours. I absolutely recommend this game if you are looking for something lighthearted, low stakes, low brow, and highly British.  We need games like this to remind us that the industry is not all about million dollar AAA safe bets that push out mostly the same experience year after year. COAL SUPPER likely knew that this game would not be for the majority of gamers. This is something crafted for a niche audience. A specific experience that will mean a lot to a small group of people, and they still chose to develop and publish a game like this. these guys should be praised and supported long into the future. Long live Indies. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: What do you get when you try to make Viz comic-meets-'Don't Hug Me I'm Scared' but fail? This game. I went in knowing nothing bar the title and some positive buzz, having been kindly gifted the game by a friend. I wanted to like it. I was ready to like it. I played it all the way through. I admired the technical skill and artistic craft that went into the game. I appreciated the archive footage of a Britain I just about remember, the place so perfectly parodied in the Scarfolk books. I went into the game ready to eagerly engage.And I hated it. I laughed - well, grunted - three times, and smiled four throughout the whole experience. By the 2 hour mark I was begging the game to end. TGYH is *very* convinced of its own hilarity and will yell it in your face. It's got comedy music! It's got a cast entirely made of grotesques! 'LOL so random' humour! Animal whimsy! Imagine a papercraft The League Of Gentlemen but with the edgier jokes removed! If the prospect of that causes you to develop a low-level tension headache, you have an idea of how this game may make you feel. It took me about 10 minutes for a weary dismay to set in that wouldn't leave me until the end credits. A whole bunch of the voice acting is horribly overdone in a way I haven't experienced in a game since the atrocious 'Candace DeBebe's Incredibly Trick Lifestyle', and it kills the gag every time. It's the "funny" voice, a kind of strained semi-shout that reeks of comedy stillbirth Bo Selecta. The jokes would have landed better if they'd just got some locals from Ossett or Goole to read the lines straight.Save yourself some time and money and play Untitled Goose Game instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like quirky, cozy little games with an outstanding, cheeky sense of humor? Because that's exactly what you'll get with Thank Goodness You're Here.While the game itself is only a few hours long, it's absolutely worth the price of entry. I couldn't stop laughing as I played through. Not to mention the fantastic job the game does both introducing the various characters around town, and showing their absurd exploits as you progress through the game. The voice acting is fantastic as well.I would absolutely recommend this game to just about anyone, and hope to see more from the developers in the future! Seriously, try it today!
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: it feels more like an interactive story book than a game. as in the humour is not tied to HOW you interact with the game but WHEN you interact with it and thus the only thing you're actively changing is the pace of the game.an important question comes to mind, does this really need to be a game? i would argue absolutely not. i feel like the humour is not in the interacting but rather the watching. i would have very much preferred to just watch this because half the time it was me wasting time not knowing where to go next. it made me so bored because theres nothing enticing in those moments between jokes that invite me to explore. the game does it feel like you're interacting with the world, but rather just looking for the next silly thing to happen while you aimlessly wander around hitting stuff. it's barebones interaction, you're not really doing much besides observing. like zoo, or an art gallery, but for jokes! i think hitting stuff has so much potential to be funny but most of the time it's just a way to provide dialogue or to just be ocd and hit everything in the world, rather than to set up for a laugh. like i'm genuinely hitting everything just in case i'm missing out on a joke or something, and 99% of the time there is no joke to be told and i'm just hitting stuff for no reason.at the start i was giddy just walking around and hope to do something funny or cool, or to explore and go on little side quests for the townsfolk at my own pace, or to be a nuisance and just hit everyone for no reason other than it's funny and for the townsfolk to have funny reactions; only to realise it's not all there and you can only laugh when the game decides it's time for you to laugh... i think thats a deal breaker for me.however, i really REALLY love the style of the game, using real life imagery to contrast with the cute/silly art-style. it's a fun little experience of doing the mundane and it all wraps up really nicely at the end with the hilarity and absurdity of it all in a song and dance, perfectly encapsulating this fun little ruckus.some of the jokes are hilarious and british humour will always be funny no matter what
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a game. This is more of an interactive animation. It takes anywhere from 2.5 - 3.5 hours to complete. I would not say it is very replayable - I am missing 7 achievements and am not interested in going back for them simply because there is no chapter system or way to go about it without replaying the entire thing. The only reason I could see going back through would be to explore the dialogue/subtitle options, because the devs really poke fun at it. All that said, I really enjoyed the time I spent with Thank Goodness You're Here. I am from the US and I'm sure that I missed a lot of the subtle nuance, but there was enough there for me to consistently laugh and chuckle to myself throughout. You essentially play as a little yellow man completing various mundane tasks for the locals. You have maybe a dozen-ish separate  areas you will repeatedly loop through while completing and picking up these tasks. You have a jump button and a slap button, along with the left stick to control movement and that's it. It's pretty on-rails but every time you loop through, something will be different, whether it's the dialogue, new NPC, or new opening to explore or pass through. If you are here for an actual GAME in the traditional sense, you will probably get bored and/or frustrated by this. But if you are ready to enjoy some good British humor and comedic timing of each set piece then you will be in for a treat. I really can't compare it to anything else, which is exactly why I am happy with it. If, as an American, you enjoy the kind of dry deadpan humor associated with shows like The IT Crowd, Absolutely Fabulous, Taskmaster, The Vicar of Dibley, Doc Martin, Peep Show, The Mighty Boosh, etc.. then you can expect the same from Thank Goodness You're Here, and can judge whether or not you think it's worth $20 to you. The Devs also have a free-to-play game called The Good Time Garden. Played entirely on Steam Deck and worked great with no fiddling.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: A true piece of art, Thank Goodness You're Here is exemplary is every way:- Gameplay is simple, but engaging.- The art is characterful, detailed and well-made.- Sound design is unmatched (Not to mention they somehow bagged Matt Berry as a voice actor).- Writing is witty, but subtle. Some punchlines only hit me while watching my friends play.Every second of this game has had care and devotion poured into it.

_childDocuments_.review: Thank Goodness You're Here is a short but fun game that takes place in an imaginary northern town in 1980s England. It wears its national character on its sleeve and really soaks in the setting, from everything costing 10 bob to missions involving making pies and fish and chips. Despite its cartoon visuals looking like an interactive version of Mr Men, this game is not for kids! It contains adult humour and even some brief (and in my opinion, unnecessary) cartoon nudity. The actual gameplay is very basic. You run, you jump and you smack things. That is all you can do and the majority of the game involves running around smacking everything to see what happens. This sounds boring but the game is bizarre enough and funny enough that just seeing what everyone does when you smack them is worth a go around. My biggest gripe is that the story involves a fair amount of backtracking - there are a few different locations and the route to get to them is linear, so you'll end up circling around the same few screens several times by the end of the game. Things do get shaken up each time you go around with new characters and situations but it is overall a very linear game with minimal replay value. Once you've seen everything there's little reason to do it again.Definitely worth picking up for cheap; it'll only last a handful of hours but if you like off the wall British humour then Thank Goodness You're Here! is worth your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: I normally don't like "LOL so random" type games, but the Northern British absurdity of this, combined with the art style had me laughing throughout. Adding these would go a long way.There are a lot of missable achievements as well!  Be warned.

_childDocuments_.review: As I get older, gain more responsibilities, and lose more of my brain cells to the impending memory loss from excessive alcohol consumption, it becomes in my best interest to enjoy games that are not thirty-hour, blockbuster spectacles. Most games I start that have long "run-times", my adult-diagnosed ADHD throws a spanner in the works, and I get distracted by the next shiny thing that comes my way.Thank Goodness You're Here! took me less than three hours to complete, and yet it was worth every bob I spent on the yoke. The game is a love letter to northern and midlands England, but even if you have little to no connection to the area, you'll still enjoy the quaint romp through Barnsworth. If you're a dumb yank like me, you might miss out on a few bits here and there, but it's otherwise one of the funniest games I've played. The banter between character, along with their voice acting, is top class. Animation is fluid, and disguises it's video game medium fantastically. Each character is unique, memorable, and adds to the lived-in atmosphere of the town. Cut-scenes are slapstick and brilliant. Gameplay is incredibly simple, and some might call it the game's downside, though I would disagree. If you deconstruct the game at it's most basic elements, it is a "walking simulator" mixed with "light puzzle" themes. Though the city is multi-sectional and is "open-world", the game places plot points and obstacles in your way to lead you on a linear narrative. For some, you could argue that the price-point might be steep if the gameplay is "press X to slap", and it only lasts three hours.But here's the thing: . It's absolutely perfect for me. The entire time, I was entertained, howling in laughter, and enjoying my short amount of free time available to me. I was sitting on the couch, with my Steam Deck, sipping a cuppa, taking in the bants and colorful atmosphere. I was locked in. My stupid short-form-video-scroll-induced attention span was taken away to another world, even for just an afternoon. I could have spent that same money for a takeaway, ore even a film at the cinema that would cost more.And lads, at the end of the day, that's the craic.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: So I wasn’t sure I was going to want this game. I’m from and still live in Yorkshire and I felt this game might be too northern even for me. But my friend got me it for my birthday so I thought I might as well.I absolutely loved it!The humour works really well and the Yorkshire-yness plays well with the absurdism of this game. It is also weird hearing a home town reference being made by a worm but I’m here for it!The gameplay is something similar to Untitled Goose Game but I found this to be more obvious with directing you to where you needed to go, I never felt lost at any point and it gave the game a really nice pace.I highly recommend this game if you want to chill, not commit to anything and have a laugh then it’s one for you… but maybe be privy to Yorkshire just a bit, it really does go deep with the slang/dialect at times.

_childDocuments_.review: “Thank Goodness You’re Here!” – A Proper Comedy GemAh, brace yourselves, chaps and chapettes! Gather 'round the digital hearth, for I’ve got a tale to spin – a yarn as British as a soggy crumpet on a drizzly afternoon. And what’s this? A video game set in Yorkshire? Well, I’ll be a monkey’s uncle! Let’s dive into the delightful absurdity of “Thank Goodness You’re Here!”The Heroic Quest: Picture yourself – a nameless fellow of indeterminate age and wilfully inconsistent height. You’re dispatched to the fictitious Northern England town of Barnsworth. Why? No one knows, old bean. But fear not! The adventure kicks off with a bang – or rather, a leap out of the boss’ office window. Because doors are for amateurs, right?Barnsworth Bliss: Now, Barnsworth – it’s a proper masterpiece. A hand-drawn fever dream of a town, complete with ♥♥♥-strewn market squares, oozing riverbanks, and more sight gags than a Monty Python sketch. Spiders boing on lampposts, ants shimmy up walls, and scruffy pigeons flutter about. Oh, and the children? They merrily beat each other with sticks. Jolly good fun!Surreal Whimsy: Brace yourselves, mates. This game is sillier than a tea cozy at a royal garden party. From the first “Thank goodness you’re here!” (and trust me, there’ll be many), it’s a relentless barrage of absurdity. But it’s the way it dances with form – manipulating comedy rhythms like a tipsy Morris dancer – that truly shines. Takes a bit to unravel, mind you, but oh, the payoff!Peans and Marrow Songs: Ever heard of Peans? Not quite peas, not quite beans – something delicious in betweens. And the Marrow Song? A bawdy ditty that’ll have you tapping your crumpet spoon. It’s all part of the madcap journey through Barnsworth, where logic takes a holiday and whimsy reigns supreme.Verdict: So, my dear gaming comrades, “Thank Goodness You’re Here!” is a gem – a comedy gem polished with Yorkshire wit. It won’t suit everyone’s taste, mind you. But if you fancy a pint of absurdity, served with a side of chuckles, this game’s your cup of Earl Grey. Pip pip, tally-ho, and all that!

_childDocuments_.review: This is an interactive movie game in the vein of something akin to Kids and Plug & Play. I personally think the developers could've been ambitious and incorporated the occasional WarioWare-esque microgame, as it would suit the absurd slapstick personality. But there's enough simple interactivity here to keep it more engaging than just watching on YouTube; plus, it's genuinely well-designed in that the player retains control as much as possible. Fantastic presentation all around, unironically puts other cinematic games to shame. I normally don't like the bean (or pean) mouths and general flatness of modern digital cartoons, but I can't think of a better art style for this game, and of course the animation itself is fluid and great. Highly quotable dialogue from funny voice actors, and wonderful music. Maybe I like British people now.

_childDocuments_.review: Recently, I was scrolling through my YouTube notifications to see what had been uploaded. I saw that Stumpt had posted a video for a new game called . After watching the video and cracking up, I knew I had to check the game out for myself.Taking on the role of a small traveling salesman, we’re tasked with heading to the strange Northern English town of Barnsworth to meet with the local mayor. But we have to wait to see him. So, we decide to explore the town and meet the locals. However, they ask us to do some tasks all around town for them. That shouldn’t be too hard, right? Now, if only these jobs were regular ones…Even after watching the one video from Stumpt, I still didn’t know what I was getting myself into by playing this and had no real expectations. But I am so glad I went into this generally blind. From start to finish, this game was exceptional and made me laugh so much. The comedy throughout ranges from recurring gags (the man who continually has to clean soot from his living room comes to mind) to more wordplay, wisecracks, and much more (“Reggie’s wife could learn a thing or two”). I don’t know if everyone will get this game’s type of humor. Still, you may like it if you enjoy things like ,  (the wackiness of this reminded me of the show), or other old British sitcoms. In general, the game is pretty straightforward and linear, as things around the town only change once a job has been completed. There was some backtracking to finish tasks, but I didn’t find it too annoying as I had so much fun.One aspect I really liked about this game was the fact that it was fully voice-acted. I especially enjoyed seeing Matt Berry pop up; his voice is so recognizable, and I was surprised to hear him. I also really liked the cartoony art style that the developers went with here. It works perfectly for a game like this. In all honesty, I don’t really have any critiques. Everything that was done for this, the art, gags, voice acting, the writing, all of it, was wonderful.In my humble opinion,  is an instant classic that I recommend in all its absurdity!

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute banger. Packed with gags - slapstick, surrealism, visuals, great characters -  and properly funny dialogue. The juxtaposition between the bright artwork and the sometimes dark, often mucky humour is ace. They’ve captured that Vic and Bob, Bottom, League of Gentleman strain of British humour. Humour is tricky to pull off in a videogame given how important things like timing are, but they’ve actually used the medium to make the jokes. The comedy’s in the game itself, not just the cutscenes. Avoiding spoilers - humours much better in context than typed into a review - but even the very first interaction you have as a character shows the humour the creators can generate from player interaction, visuals and character. TGYH’s design encourages mischief at every turn. Unlike other games where the central verbs might be "stab" or "parry," here it’s "slap." You interact with everything and everyone with a slap, including dialogue interactions. If you think you can slap it - NPC’s, bin bags, meat -  you can. If you’ve ever bounced off the visual novel genre, consider how much more fun it could be if you constantly had the option to slap. The art and animation style is a perfect match for the game’s daft story and characters, just an exquisite vibe. Bizarre scenarios contrast the mundane aspects of small-town life. The music, from parping trumpet to gently plucked  guitars, and the sound effects are exceptional. TGYH doesn’t hold your hand—there are no quest journals or glowing HUD elements telling you where to go next —but figuring out what to do is never difficult and always fun. And if you do get lost for a moment, you’ll probably find another joke you might have missed. The game’s tightly designed and the lack of explicit direction is testament to that, discovering all the quirky details Barnsworth has to offer rules.At a few hours to run through the story, the lengths is bang on for its content. Feels like bingeing a season of an amazing cartoon. It keeps things pacey and the humour and novelty stay fresh from start to finish, leaving you wanting more rather than overstaying its welcome. It's also dense as a premium pie, packed full of weirdo characters and unique visuals. Massive respect to Coal Supper for crafting such a cohesive, polished and joyously weird experience.

_childDocuments_.review: My mother nation was ruled by the British Empire, and its cultural legacy lives on in so many ways that we continue to see it with a mixture of both resentment and awe. Those of us with a historical bent might treat a visit to England as a kind of fairtytale come alive.This game gives us a similar deep insight into a certain cross-section of England, and helps us truly understand how these fine people were able to rule us for hundreds of years. One could see the protagonist as a metaphor for Great Britain itself - a blobby homunculus who, through the power of gratuitous violence, bends the huge world around him to his will.Posterity will see this as a work of profound cultural significance. I am enlightened and I think I need a ciggie.

_childDocuments_.review: A Quirky and Beautifully Crafted Short AdventureRating: ★★★★☆"Thank Goodness You're Here!" delivers a unique experience, despite its short length. The game's whimsical, hand-drawn art style alone makes it worth the purchase, offering a vibrant and offbeat world that draws you in from the start. Every scene is filled with quirky details that give the game its unmistakable charm.I finished the game in about two hours and went back for another playthrough to grab more achievements. The captivating visuals and humor made it easy to enjoy exploring the surreal world again. While the experience is brief, the artistry and atmosphere made those hours feel fully worthwhile.Though I don't see myself returning for another round, I’m happy with the time I spent in this odd and delightful universe. If you enjoy distinctive art styles and quirky humor, "Thank Goodness You're Here!" is a memorable gem that is well worth playing, even if only for a couple of sessions.Edit: I did not refund the game. No idea why Steam thinks I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Thank Goodness You're Here!: A Yorkshire DiamondThank Goodness You're Here! is a right corker of a game, a proper Yorkshire diamond, if you ask me. You'll be chuckling your socks off as you navigate the town's peculiar folk and their unusual requests. It's like a pint of ale on a sunny day, a real treat. * Nonlinear gameplay: The game's open-ended structure lets players explore Barnsworth at their own pace and discover hidden gems. It encourages experimentation and replayability. It's a bit like exploring the Yorkshire Dales, you never know what you'll find. * Engaging characters: The residents of Barnsworth are a colorful bunch, each with their own distinct personalities and quirks. Their interactions with the protagonist are both entertaining and heartwarming. It's like having a pint with your mates at the local pub, a real pleasure. * Beautiful art style: The game's hand-drawn art style is visually appealing and complements the quirky tone of the narrative. Its concise length makes it a perfect choice for players who want a quick and enjoyable gaming session. It's like a quick pint after work, just what you need.Overall, Thank Goodness You're Here! is a must-play for fans of quirky indie games and British humor. Its unique blend of comedy, exploration, and engaging characters make it a truly memorable experience. It's a proper Yorkshire gem, a right diamond in the rough.

_childDocuments_.review: Cute, funny, and full of personality, Thank Goodness You're Here lies somewhere between Untitled Yorkshire Game and point-and-spank adventure game.While there is great humor in the game's objectives - from escaping a pint of beer to visiting a chippy on behalf of a sick cow - much of the game's comedy comes from the eccentric townsfolk and their absurd reactions to the chaos that we create along the way. Without being in the business of tiny pies, I can't confidently say I would react any differently than Tiny Tom to the prospect of a giant one. But I'd hope my response would give others the same hearty chuckle I got on his behalf.Thank Goodness You're Here reinforces its comedy through a clear awareness of the fourth wall. By keeping our protagonist ambiguously small, and inserting Barnsworth commercials seamlessly into what's on screen, the game's scenes are organized like an interactive cartoon. Sometimes you wander into the next scene and catch the tail-end of an amusing conversation, where the ridiculous punchline implies an equally preposterous setup. Backgrounds are filled with jokes that many players won't even notice during their playthrough.The game is short, yet exactly the right size for this type of experience. Its length keeps all the jokes fresh, and makes a great game for a weekend. I'd rather explore the next Barnsworth than keep gu'in in a game that already feels so finished.I look forward to their next game; I'd gladly pay 10 bob.
_childDocuments_.name: Thank Goodness You're Here!

_childDocuments_.review: Within the first few seconds of loading this game up (mind you, it asks you a very important question going in), I knew it would be a life-changing experience. You're this little adorable man that goes around helping folks. That's the basic gist of it and yet there's so much more involved. Here are my pros and cons: THE BEST STUFF: Thank you for this comedic genius. - my response to the developers. Timing was on point, I sometimes couldn't even differentiate if I was supposed to be playing or if I was watching a cut-scene. This alone was a perfect setup for the laughs that ensued and I won't spoil it because the ending is a prime example of this. So, yes, humor was sublime, some of the best dialogue I've ever heard and I'm so excited to play this over to get more achievements. EVEN BETTER? The artwork. With each silly or funny thing said I contribute a lot of my laughs to the expressions of these whimsical and amazing characters that I can't forget. Also WOW the innuendos in this were subtle to downright "HERE WE GO." Loved it. AN ANNOYANCE? Honestly nothing really annoyed me, except a bit of the repetition, but it's also integrated into the main story of well "yup, this is where you are." So, kudos it's part of what you have to go through. That's hilarious in itself. Honestly, great game. SCORE: 10/10 - would do again.

_childDocuments_.review: This game could have been a cheap pastiche of northern england and still gotten passable review scores, but it is so much more than that. There are many jokes in this game that stand up on their own merits without needing to lean on reference humour, which helps prevent the slice-of-life humour that is there from getting stale for the game's 3 hour run time. It also helps that in addition to the directly presented jokes, there are recurring "joke motifs" that weave their way through the town and help the humour to build into something more substantial, like the way a stand-up comedian will lead the audience on a journey through the course of a set. Stuff like the big pie vs small pie rivalry has so many tiny influences across the game that you can't even tell what the "original" joke is and what is a spin off. It's like joke worldbuilding.The little gameplay there is is frictionless, the platforming is intuitive, and all the object interactions are snappy and satisfying. The only critique I have is that I wish the camera was a little zoomed out, it could feel cramped at times. I loved this game.
