_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon: Gaiden- The Man Who Erased His Name is the kind of storytelling that all series' choosing to begin a new era should strive for. Kazuma Kiryu, now operating under the codename Joryu, is at his best in what series director Masayoshi Yokoyama implied would be the last game with Kiryu as the leading character. With a dynamic soundtrack, beautiful art direction, memorable characters, and smooth gameplay, Like a Dragon: Gaiden easily cements itself as one of my favorite games- not just in Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio's library, but of all time.The game takes place after Yakuza 6, during Yakuza: Like a Dragon (7) and before Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth (8) yet still manages to only be around 12 hours in story length. This short amount of time allows the writers to satisfyingly propel the player from the game where Kiryu was last playable, Yakuza 6, into his seemingly-final playable role in Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth, all while explaining his whereabouts in Yakuza: Like a Dragon. Convoluted, right? This is because Gaiden works best after playing every mainline entry in the series. Ignore the tempting claims from Ryu Ga Gotoku Studios' social media pages- Like a Dragon: Gaiden is not a jumping off point. The game fully expects the players to understand the emotional weight of Kiryu's journey thus far, and uses these expectations to tell an incredibly impactful story. In just 12 hours, I found myself to love the entire cast and get enthralled in the rich settings- both old and new.I'm speaking as if 12 hours is some foreign length for the franchise, but this game's length is admittedly more of a return to the series roots. It felt like its been forever since there was an adventure in this franchise that didn't at least hit 30 hours, but Gaiden's length is perfect for the story its trying to tell. The game hits all the story beats of the other games in a way that makes you forget it was supposed to be a 30 minute add-on to next year's Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth. The ending is Takaya Kuroda's best performance as Kiryu by far, a heavily emotional melancholy ending where you can't help but feel Kiryu's sadness along with him. The story's boss is also very satisfying. While they aren't my favorite character or boss, I still think they're worthy of being put alongside other greats in Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio's history. This story is still a very post-Kiryu Saga narrative. I never felt that the writers were regressing from the promise that Like a Dragon's Kasuga Ichiban would be leading in Kiryu's place from here on out, which is how it should be! Gaiden perfectly delivers Kiryu's narrative without making him feel like the center of the universe, something a lot of series fail to capture when it comes time to get rid of a legacy protagonist. Gameplay wise, Gaiden is honestly pretty hard, I probably died more in this game than I did in most of the other ones combined. It utilizes the improved combat systems from RGG's Judgment franchise mixed with the same ol' Kiryu gameplay  style we've had since the beginning in Yakuza Style, contrasting by the new and bizarre Agent Style that lets former-Yakuza member Kiryu essentially become James Bond. The Agent Style is tricky, but with practice, it becomes very satisfying to pull off.I haven't gotten a proper chance to listen to Gaiden's in-game soundtrack very much, but the credit song, Fading Away, is easily my favorite credits theme in the franchise. And what's more beautiful than ending the credits with where we began all the way back in 2005- Amazing Grace.Despite being advertised and presented as a "mini game" bridging the gap between the 7th and 8th Like a Dragon games, Like a Dragon: Gaiden- The Man Who Erased His Name chooses to go above and beyond to deliver a more than Game of the Year worthy product. If this is what RGG considers a mini game, then I'm excited to see all the content that Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth has in store.

_childDocuments_.review: A GREAT KIRYU COMEBACK AND FAN SERVICEI am a big fan of the Like A Dragon series and although initially excited, was also skeptical of this game since LAD Gaiden follows a more different structure than other mainline games and follows similarly, according to some developer interviews, to The Kaito Files, a special DLC for Lost Judgment. I actually like these shorter Like A Dragon experiences since the mainline LAD games, even the old ones, are very lengthy and have so much stuff to do. So this is a nice break and spin of the usual formula and opens more potential for more stories that can be told in the LAD universe if the devs wishes to do some.Like A Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name is a LAD game that focuses on an undercover Kiryu Kazuma being an agent of the Daidoji faction, assuming the name Joryu. This game being a Gaiden (side-story) tells a fun and simple and somewhat interesting tale about this new side of Kiryu Kazuma. Being an agent means he will always fight and do combat (as he always do) and enables him to have a very new and unique style which is Agent Style that gives him alot of spy tools and gadgets.The story is okay and simple but I will say my criticisms for the story is that there are really no stakes. This is mainly because the game takes place at the same time as Yakuza 7 and the whole goal of Gaiden's story is to reach a crucial moment that will impact the overall story in Yakuza 7. So any moments where Kiryu and his friends are in danger, never really feel like actual danger since they all are in Yakuza 7. Another criticism I'll give is on a certain antagonist that I was kinda hyped due to how much backstory he has but ultimately, he's just another generic villain that is evil.I will say that this is the most chill Yakuza or Like A Dragon game. Kiryu in this game is somehow the best he has ever been. Kiryu Kazuma has always been a very interesting and very well-written character starting from Yakuza 1 to Yakuza 6 with the sixth game being tying a neat bow to Kiryu's saga. That's why I was skeptical towards this game's release since for me Kiryu's tale is already done, but fortunately Kiryu has a great comeback and he comes hard. While there's daddy Kiryu in Yakuza 3, depressed Kiryu in Yakuza 5, and angery Kiryu in Yakuza 6, LAD Gaiden has peak, Dragon of the Dojima Kiryu Kazuma.In some way it is brilliant to have Kiryu being an agent to showcase his pure intelligence, raw skill, talent and charisma, that really presents why Kiryu is the Dragon of Dojima since in the past games, there was never really a moment of that part of Kiryu's life other than being mentioned and told by characters countless times. Even Yakuza 0, the prequel that shows his origins, only presents the period before his tenure as the Dragon of Dojima. All the characters in LAD Gaiden are likable as there always banter between Kiryu and them. I really love the more quiet moments where they are just chilling out eating, or just complimenting each other, or just..... talking. Although Kiryu and his peers are mostly out of the norm, being a Yakuza and all, the writing and the dialogue makes them all very grounded and very relatable.Combatwise, it is okay. I am still getting used to Agent Style and found myself using it when fighting larger crowds, but ultimately all the tools you use as an agent like whips are very fun and crazy as they always been. Kiryu has two fighting styles with the other being Yakuza Style which is the classic traditional Kiryu combat from past games. There's also the juggling system from Lost Judgment so Kiryu can finally juggle enemies too. I'm not an expert when it comes to Like A Dragon combat but I've lot of fun with it here.Being a shorter Like A Dragon game like Kaito Files, this game is obviously short. I finished the main story in 20 hours and there are two big side-content which are the classic substories (but in a unique spin) and the fighting arena (which also has unique spin). My only criticism is only on the substories with the gang related substories being very repetitive and tedious as hell. But that's just my only main complaint since the other substories are bangers as all things should be.Music for me is also kinda okay. There some bangers that kinda mixed in with not so banger ones. Some of the not so bangers are kinda generic, trailer musicish, but the banger ones are great like Deadly Struggle, Un Altro Appasionato, and the Yakuza Style theme.When comparing between Kaito Files and LAD Gaiden, I ultimately prefer Kaito Files first mainly because of how high the stakes are there. Not to the discredit how high the stakes can be in LAD Gaiden, but LAD Gaiden is also a fun time with Kiryu and I'm kinda glad he's somehow back. Comparing to the mainline games isn't really fair since this is a much smaller game and different direction, but LAD Gaiden does takes elements from mainly the Kiryu Saga games and offers abit of homage to them.I recommend those who have played the Yakuza games to play this. For newcomers are also welcome since this game is great at recapping some aspects but mostly in Kiryu's backstory.Overall, a solid and short Like A Dragon experience.4/5

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start the review by saying that this game is not worth sixty dollars. However, with that being stated! I still would recommend you play this game because it's a fantastic installment to the Like A Dragon franchise and gives some real emotional payoff that has been in the making for seven installments with our remarkable stoic protagonist Kazuma Kiryu. This game is best consumed after playing Yakuza 7: Like A Dragon. With all that being said my biggest complaint with this game is how incredibly short it is compared to other games in the franchise. I completed the story in about eleven hours and got the final achievement right at the eighteenth hour mark. The basic plot summary for this game without getting into many details is that after faking his death at the end of Yakuza 6: Song of Life, Kiryu is roped up into a plot to protect the people he cares about most, while some shady individuals try to reign control of the Dragon of Dojima to benefit themselves.Outside of the main story you can partake in many side activities that are not forced. There is a collection of accomplishments you can do if that sort of thing strikes your fancy. You can also partake in little side missions to help people's issues that just give a cute little slice-of-life feel to break up the pace of the story if you like. However, within this game, the big chunk of your time outside of the side missions that you get through this woman named Akane is that of the coliseum. The introduction to this game's gimmick that being the Hell Team Rumble was very enjoyable for what it was and I wish there was more to it. The game is beyond beautiful, runs perfectly on my computer, and sound quality is great! The change of just two fighting styles instead of just the Dragon of Dojima style we got used to over the course of the games is a nice change of pace. Agent style is stupidly not balanced, but! Balance isn't really an issue in this single-player experience because the combat is utter perfection. With that! I would recommend you buy this game, maybe at a discount if you can... However, if you're willing to spend 60 on a 12 hour game go ahead, you'll have a fantastic time. PS: Make Amon great again...

_childDocuments_.review: Gaiden's events happen alongside the events of Yakuza Like a Dragon, here telling the story of a Kazuma Kiryu trying to erase his name under the codename of Joryu. Gaiden relies a lot on Kiryu's past, so a little bit of warning it has all sorts of minor and major spoilers from many games, and also spoilers of the one that happens alongside with it, so do be aware of that. WIth all that said, I was not ready at all for how hard this story would go, main story doesn't beat any longer than maybe 10-12-ish hours but they still manage to pack a whole lot of drama and feelings into this one small package, all of the new characters are memorable, and obviously some good old Kiryu coolness as we love itCombat throws back to the hack'n slash formula, bringing Kiryu a bit of Judgment influence which is great. Agent style is nimble and tactical, full of gadgets and technical combat, and the Yakuza style brings back the street fighting dragon, full of heavy power and strong strikes. You can't go wrong with either style honestly, both have their unique shine in the right time, combos feel awesomeSide content also goes hard, the Coliseum is the big attraction of this game and the main moneymaker, spending time here experimenting with teams and even playing other characters is mighty fun. Akame Network is quite bulky and important to upgrade abilities, the return of Pocket Circuit is a welcome funsies add, show your charm for the girls in the Cabaret Clubs (this time in live action), visit the Boutique to customize Kiryu's clothes and face, and of course all the usual gambling and sports minigames are present as well. Also, big props for bringing an arcade of Sega Racing Classic 2 (renamed out of Daytona USA 2 due to licensing), that's a first ever PC/console release for that game and I was really excited for itDragon Engine had great graphical ugprades, more specifically to lighting, reflections and colors, everything is so much more atmospheric and colorful I love it, and once you have a taste of the Infinite Wealth demo you can tell they meticulously upgraded these departments thinking of this game to deliver a very lively and colorful Honolulu, definitely the peak in graphics for the seriesAnd speaking of, Like a Dragon Infinite Wealth Special Trial is an extra gift you earn after beating the main story of Gaiden, packing a short story demo and an exploration demo, it's similar to the same event demo you've seen a few times on youtube but here with even more content and no time restrictions (thankfully!). Needless to say this game is looking and feeling awesome, I could fill another half-review with how many cool details it has but you've read a lot of text at this point already. Can't wait for it now, fueled my hype that was already skyrocketedGaiden only has one DLC. Not a huge impact in this one it's more for fanservice funsies, you get three legendary yakuza for the coliseum, obviously they're awesome and strong but if you want to spare some money it's okay, not that much to be lost in terms of contentAfter you beat the game you can still enjoy Premium Adventure as you always do in the series, but Gaiden unexplainably lacks New Game+ for you to replay the story carrying over your abilities. My theory is that it maybe just maybe could have to do with how Akame Network works, but it's just a silly little theory of mine we never really got word on why's NG+ just missing, but yeah that has to be my only big complaint about this game

_childDocuments_.review: The Man Who Erased His Name is another entry in the long running Like a Dragon / Yakuza series of third person action games. This is a sequel to Yakuza 6, and features a new playable character called Joryu.When a powerful Yakuza clan believes that Joryu’s true identity is actually the legendary Dragon of Dojima, Kazuma Kiryu (despite the fact that Joryu wears glasses, while Kiryu doesn’t wear glasses, and he’s definitely not the same guy wearing a terrible disguise), Joryu is drawn into a plan which could define the future of the Yakuza.•	Writing is good, and contains the usual dramatic scenes, twists, and betrayals that the series is known for. This is also a story about how much someone will sacrifice to protect their family.•	TMWEHN also connects to the later chapters of Ichiban Kasuga’s story in Like a Dragon, which means we already know how this part of the story ends, however we do learn more about Joryu’s role in those events.•	I really like Joryu, so I hope we see him again as the main character in another game. There are also a few other interesting characters, including government agents and Yakuza members who want to use Joryu for their own agendas, and a young woman called Akame, who runs a network which takes requests to help homeless people.•	Cutscenes are cinematic and have good graphical quality.•	I played with the Japanese voice acting, which has good quality, but only the cutscenes are voiced, with in engine conversations during both the main quest and substories, being text only. Yakuza 6 was fully voiced (I can’t remember if this was also the case with Like a Dragon), so this is a backwards step.•	Most of the action takes place in two main locations, Sotenbori (previously seen in Yakuza 0, 2 and 5), and an amusement park for the rich, known as the Castle.•	Fight against gangs of Yakuza and other thugs in real time combat, using a combination of punches, kicks, and various melee weapons, while building up your heat meter to perform powerful finishing moves.•	Joryu has a new “agent” fighting style which allows him to use various gadgets during combat. The spider can trap enemies in webs, but I didn’t find the others that useful, so I preferred to use the classic Yakuza style.•	Boss fights are fun, mainly thanks to the responsiveness of Joryu’s dodge move allowing him to quickly evade their attacks, while also setting up opportunities for a powerful counter attack. I was actually able to win most fights through skill, instead of relying on drinking the drug store’s entire stock of toughness z’s to stay alive like in some of the older games.•	Besides the main quest, there are various activities to keep you busy.•	Akame Network involves stopping groups of thugs from beating up civilians, and simple fetch quests (mainly to buy food or medicine from shops). This is basic copy and pasted content similar to what Ubisoft fill their open world games with, but they do reward you with cash which can be used to buy ability upgrades.•	Substories – the best one features a cameo appearance from a familiar character, but unfortunately most of them lack the wacky tone of the previous games, and can also feel a bit repetitive, for example three of the substories ask you to defeat gangs of thugs, but each gang involves the exact same sequence of 6 fights.•	Fight in the Castle’s coliseum against single opponents or larger groups for huge cash rewards. Many of the substories allow you to recruit allies into Joryu’s clan, which can take part in team fights. However, I don’t like the time limits, especially at platinum level, where you have to fight 15-20 enemies who all have massive health bars. Winning is less about skill, and more about how much money you’ve spent upgrading your damage to KO enemies quickly.•	When you want to take a break from the action, there’s also the usual wide selection of minigames, including darts, pool, golf, karaoke, sega arcade, pocket circuit racing, poker, blackjack, mahjong and shogi.•	It took me just under 30 hours to complete the story and most substories and coliseum fights, which is a decent amount of content, but still shorter than most games in the series.•	Controls worked great on my xbox 360 controller.•	I didn’t have any problems with bugs, crashes or framerate.•	I recommend using DLSS to clear up some distracting edge flickering, which can be particularly noticeable on Joryu’s glasses.Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name is a good game which existing fans of the series should enjoy. While the gameplay feels like just another Yakuza game, its definitely worth playing to continue the story. However I would advise waiting for a sale due to this being a shorter game.As the story directly follows the events of Yakuza 6, this wouldn’t be a good place for new players to join the series. I would advise starting with Yakuza 0, or the Judgment spinoffs which have similar gameplay but a separate story.

You have gadgets that actually are fun to use against crowds. Drones suck and useless, explosive cigs are fun and chaotic. Yakuza style is okay, but i didn't like that you can evade only when you're locked on an enemy. And i couldn't figure out how to switch targets. Also switching styles was completely inconsistent and unresponsive. _childDocuments_.review: Folks: it's over. There will never be game in the series to top Yakuza Kiwami 2. This game is maybe 10 % as good as that one. It has less reason to keep existing than Yakuza 3 AKA Blockuza. Sure it has tons of references to the previous games, though all of it feels hollow and the new stuff seems silly (Akame network, live video hostess segments, etc.)I used a taxi for the first time and the game crashed to desktop. That is the level of cobbled-together quality this game represents.50 to 75 % of the gameplay is loading screens. This is not like Kiwami 2 where you could seemlessly enter everywhere and have reasonable loading screens. Even when entering small interior sections, the game loads minutes on end for a relatively minimal environment. It is like Yakuza 0 in that it trashes all data and even minor changes in the location make it re-load the whole thing, costing minutes every couple of minutes. This game is really short and you can beat it in 90 minutes if you have good computer with an SSD drive. If you don't, it is likely to take 8 hours because of the loading times. Even the cutscenes have sizable loading times that can last for minutes on end.Gameplay-wise, this feels worse than Yakuza 6 and that game was partially incomplete. This game has a stupider plot than Yakuza 3. The conclusion is that he beats some new Omi guys you will never have time or the preceding story build-up to care about and you are likely to forget the whole game.The fighting system is still the same irritating one where you either slide wildly around or feel like your feet turn into immovable concrete every time you do a move as if you were proposing for marriage. Reacting is super clunky and often delayed. There is also the arbitrary input buffering that can confuse you about how many of the inputted moves are still waiting to be executed before the character can accept new ones. You feel more trapped than in control.The plot is a weird back-and-forth thing much like the gameplay. A lot of the main quest is about thinly-veiled minigame tutorials late into the game. There is a golf center tie in after the halfway point of the game. It is also so badly paced Chapter 2 is longer than the rest of the game.Bottom-line, if you cannot segment your game to keep the loading times reasonable, do not make a 98-gigabyte game. This game is both technically and content-wise undesirable.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly floored by how much I enjoyed this game. It's a short one, well for a game in this series, only having a small handful of chapters and a fair bit of side content. The combat in this game is fun. The Agent Style adds quicker moves together with gadgets that are fun to use in certain fights when you've figured out how to control your opponents with them. The Yakuza style is probably the most fun Kiryu has been to play in a non RPG game in a good while. Overall the usage of these two styles together can make fights with enemies and bosses alike interesting if you use them in fun ways. A fair bit of the side content is related to The Coliseum which gives you your standard 1 V 1 fights of past games, vs groups of enemies and the new mode where you have a team you assembled face off against an enemy team. This mode is fun when figuring out how to best support your team to make sure they don't get eliminated whilst fighting everyone although leveling up said team mates does feel a bit tedious and time consuming unless you have a lot of money on hand already. That being said, when your team is the appropriate level it's a fun side mode to figure out how to handle battles. You can also play as the fighters you recruit although they have a limited moveset so Kiryu is usually who I stuck with.The story and music is some of the best the series has had. Almost all of these tracks are amazing and the composers of them went above and beyond! The story is genuinely something I did not expect to hook me as it is a side story that seems like lead up to Infinite Wealth but oh how I was wrong. This story goes from a small steady thing to one of the most engaging bits of story this series has ever had. I am honestly amazed with how they hooked me so good towards the end. This is a must play experience for fans of Kiryu's story. Beyond that this game has side activities you would expect from the series. Golf, mahjong, gambling, cabaret clubs, side stories, pocket circuit, locker keys, Master System games, arcade games, claw games, pool, shogi and darts. This is a game that is worth it for long time series fans and if you are new to the series start with Yakuza 0 or the first game on PS2, otherwise this game will probably not do as much for you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is outright amazing.Not only does it have the most polished version of the combat style we've seen Kiryu use since the old days, and not only is the story very well crafted (what else would you expect from RGG?), but it really delivers for the money. There is SO MUCH content to do, the substories are really entertaining, there are dozens of minigames, and more minigames within minigames (take the SEGA arcade for example), and fighting for fun has never been more true. The spy gadgets also are also a hella fun addition, and you can use them in most Coliseum battles (which are also the best iteration of the Coliseum to date).I don't care what anyone says, I preordered the deluxe edition of this game and I feel like I got my money's worth. DEFINITELY A 10/10 GAME!P.S: This is arguably the easiest entry in the series to 100%

_childDocuments_.review: A nice side game in the Yakuza/LaD series. Enjoyable game even if the main story is quite short, 5 chapters for 10 hours if you only play that, the gameplay part, the story and some subquests are still very good. There are no new minigames on this title but 2 returning ones : the pocket circuit, which is harder than Y0 and you'll need to cap your fps to 30 for some circuits, and the colliseum with the new "team" category.On a side note, you need to have played the 'old" Yakuza games to enjoy the game on the best way possible. There are a lot of references to previous games in this one.If you're a completionist, the trophies are more accessible in this game than previous ones because you don't need to do every content to the fullest, looking at you mahjong.The game optimisation is fine with a lot of graphics options and some recents ones like DLSS/FSR/XeSS. It's the "Dragon Engine" so it will strungle when there are a lot of action going on.It took me approx 35 hours to complete it with all achievements and a bit of messing around.Overall score : 7/10.Good points :-One new combat style, the agent. It's a very quick style with a lot of AoE attack, it's original, for the series, and fun to use.-Good story with a strong and emotional finale.-Appealing new characters.-One of the best colisseum in the series.-You can customise Kiryu appearance.Bad points :-Boring Akame's "Stroll n' Patrol" quests, they are open-world types fetch quests.-Some subquests weren't that interresting.-The new colisseum "Tag team" is a mess visually, sound-wise and is poorly optimised.-The minigames and activities feels very "deja vu", nothing really new if you played the previous entries.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of the games but this one is just shallow and left me unsatisfied. TLDR I do not recommend it for current price (50$) and would recommend waiting for sale . Can easily recommend it for 30$. It just feels like a dlc turned standalone game and reminds me a lot of current COD MW3 situation- There's only one city (Osaka) and it's reused from Kiwami 2/LAD , the first chapter does feature yokohoma for like few scenes and goes unused for the rest of the game. I was expecting them to have 3 cities (Yokohoma, Kamarucho and Sotenbori) but only one goes used.- The minigames suck for the most part. Pocket circuit racing (I seriously don't get people hype behind it) is just reused from Y0/kiwami with barely any changes and just overall reusing minigames in Like a dragon games IMO is bad idea since most of them are "oh that's cool" things that overstay their welcome in the same games they featured in. This includes pocket circuit racing and it's annoying enough that they are mostly tied to substories and you have to play and beat them for Amon fight. I think if you reuse minigames, reusing it more than one time makes it extremely boring and just lazy. One thing I will say that they did good job on is hostess club. The fact they using FMV add to the experience and also they made it not grindy at all like in past titles. Don't even get me started on another fighting ring that's again is boring as hell and has substories tied to it so you must do it.- The main story is extremely short. Even though my play hours said 20h, 4 h was actual story content while rest was filled with grindy boring minigames. The overall story also felt relatively weak, it did had some good characters but yeah.- The substories are extremely boring and uninspiring. Again, there are very few good ones but most of them are "THERES THIS GANG AROUND TOWN, BEAT THEM UP" and then after you do that "THERES ANOTHER RIVAL GANG, BEAT THEM UP" and that's like legit 75% of substories, just pure filler.- Amon fight sucked ass, but atleast it wasn't as bad as InshinI don't know if this is true or not, but to me, this feels like it was made by the same B team that made Inshin remake and it shows. Again, fine if it's on sale and if you are a fan of series, but this is not a good "entry point for a franchise" like SEGA is promoting it and honestly, I would skip this one unless you're a fan or wait for sale. I can't justify 50$ for it and probably the second like a dragon game that left me unsatisfied and I just did not enjoy fully (first being inshin)

_childDocuments_.review: Very welcome entry to the series, it covers what Kiryu was up to from the end of 6 to the beginning of 8. While it is kind of a spin-off and by far the shortest game of the series, I would consider this to be up there with the best LaD games. The combat uses the styles mechanic from 0, 1 and 2, which in my opinion is a more fun and dynamic feature than the single combat style we have (for Kiryu at least) in Y3-6. There are two very distinct styles and both of them feel satisfying and fun to use.Story and characters are great, the OST is a banger, the coliseum is a blast and the mini games are still very fun, I'll highlight pocket circuit making a very welcome return.I highly recommend this if you liked the rest of the series. Definitely don't start with this one though, it's pretty much LaD 7.5, so it spoils every game so far.

_childDocuments_.review: This game perfectly fills in the gap in Kiryu's story between The Song of Life and Yakuza: Like a Dragon. The new dragon engine combat feels fleshed out and allows us to experience Kiryu's combat prowess at its peak with a mix between his more restrained agent style and his more brutal Dragon of Dojima style with both styles being perfectly suited for different combat encounters. The final boss also suits the end of Kiryu being the main protagonist in this series by having a character who mirrors him and gives us a glimpse of how Kiryu may of turned out if he had only focused on his strength instead of his honour. The environmental story telling in the final fight is also beautiful with each of the boss stage transitions adding more weight to the final encounter.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a considerably shorter title than other titles in this franchise, but considerably longer than the Kaito Files expansion for Lost Judgement.Both fighting styles available to the player are fantastic and gradually become more fun to use the deeper into the game you get. Agent is the style that the game is definitely pushing harder than the Yakuza style, as it has all the new goofy mechanics and gizmos that were advertised as a selling point for this game. Oh, and Tiger Drop is an ability you can use in combat as well.The soundtrack is, as expected of a title of this series, great. My favorite track has to be Cold Fire.The story... I have feelings about it. It takes place after Yakuza 6, and leads up to the halfway point of Yakuza 7/Like A Dragon. Playing both titles before this is absolutely required, I think; there are flashbacks and references to events of both games that spoil their respective titles. For the sake of not spoiling anyone who has yet to play it, I will not say anything further. There's a lot of side content available in this title, and a little somethin' somethin' for the Judge Eyes/Lost Judgement fans as well! The game also includes a special trial version of Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth available right away from the main menu upon launch.For 50 dollars, and with how much extra time you get out of the side content in these titles, that's well worth your money. I powered through the story mode and it took me ~22 hours, with a bit of grinding on the side for abilities. Give it a go.

But the story offers a great perspective that fans like myself have been wondering in between the events of Y6 and LaD. Not only that, but certain moments, seeing certain characters let their emotional guard down as much as they did after everything they’ve been through really tied a bow on their story for me. _childDocuments_.review: Kiryu's Last Stand? Unveiling the Shadows in Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name! (ฅ'ω'ฅ)In the gritty underworld of yakuza lore, the latest addition to the saga, Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name, brings back the legendary Kazuma Kiryu for what might be his final dance. Developed by RGG Studios, this side entry offers a fresh take on the familiar Yakuza formula, introducing the enigmatic Agent style and weaving a tale that unfolds between Yakuza 6 and Like a Dragon.The game's engine, presumably the same one powering the upcoming mainline entry, Infinite Wealth, showcases remarkable graphical improvements. Faces, especially those of significant characters, are meticulously detailed, and the enhanced lighting contributes to a visually stunning experience. Performance-wise, the game runs smoothly at 4k60fps, a commendable feat considering the performance struggles seen in some recent releases.Gameplay innovations come in the form of Kiryu's newfound agility and the introduction of the Agent style. The combat system, though reminiscent of the classic Yakuza beat-em-up style, brings a new layer with the Agent style's high-tech gadgets. However, a few players note that the combat doesn't flow as seamlessly as in previous titles, and there are concerns about potential rushed development, with typos, localization errors, and lingering elements from Lost Judgment.The narrative, set under the pseudonym Joryu, thrusts Kiryu into a gripping action narrative, navigating a web of intrigue created by a mysterious figure attempting to draw him out of hiding. For devoted fans of the Yakuza series, the game provides a satisfying continuation, filled with callbacks to previous events and characters. However, newcomers may find themselves lost amidst the intricate web of Yakuza lore.The game's length and pricing have stirred mixed reactions among players. While some praise the approximately 35 hours of content as enjoyable and worth the price, others feel it falls short in side content compared to previous entries. The storyline itself is lauded for its entertainment value, provided players are deeply invested in the Yakuza franchise.One notable downside is the English voice acting, with criticisms aimed at the performance of one of the characters, Yong Yea, for his portrayal of Kiryu. While some see it as a minor flaw in an otherwise excellent game, others find it distracting, urging players to switch to subtitles for a more immersive experience.In conclusion, Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name is a worthy addition to the Yakuza universe, offering a blend of familiar elements and fresh gameplay dynamics. Its graphical prowess, engaging narrative, and nods to the franchise's rich history make it a must-play for Yakuza enthusiasts. However, the game is not without its flaws, with concerns about rushed development and the English voice acting providing a few blemishes on an otherwise compelling experience.Interested in discovering great Steam games? _childDocuments_.review: it's hard to compare this game's plot with other games in the series because it was created to be a short, contained story between two mainline games. however, the plot of gaiden was fairly straightforward and was relatively tame. it definitely did its purpose in introducing where kiryu has been and those who want to disrupt his life, and wraps it up in a nice bow at the end, also adding some needed family elements and emotional beats. it's filled with fanservice which i'm not complaining about in the slightest, and was short but sweet. a fun time! oh just simply amazing -- every character introduced was absolutely perfect for what their role is relative to the story, and they're somewhat complex for such a short runtime. you like the characters you like, and hate the ones you hate (with some outliers of course). shishido was a standout for me personally, and i'd love to see akame come back from rgg jail please yokoyama  not much, but that was expected. i didn't jive with the interactive cabaret club, or the short street missions but the minigames that reappear from other games are improved upon in the new engine. the coliseum was a blast to playthrough, definitely improved from past games with a fun twist. being able to dress up kiryu not only just around town but also the outfits being featured in cutscenes was some of my favorite parts of the game.  it's pretty custom for an rgg game to have amazing voice acting, but this game really didn't hold back. kuroda kills it as always, and deserves some sort of trophy for best delivery on some of these lines, especially near the end of the game. not a single voice actor let me down!!!  genuinely one of my favorite osts out of the entire series. its more slow and emotional songs are standout to me, and fading away is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the catchiest song of all time. i loved all of the bosses' themes, especially the leadup to the final boss. not a single track that disappointed me.  absolutely stunning visuals and shadows!! everything was very fluid and very sleek looking, which is welcomed considering the spy-esque theme of this game. needing to use both akame points and yen to buy skill upgrades was definitely a choice, but whatever makes the boys upstairs happy i guess. i really had no complaints about the way the game ran at all.  it feels so good to fight in this game i swear!!! it's second best in terms of combat feel (first being lost judgment) and the two styles is such a fun balance of play style. agent style is so refreshing with it's goofy gadgets and methodical punches, while yakuza style is rough and powerful. juggling is beyond easy in this one, and each punch is base boosted with the loudest thud so you really feel the impact. not to mention, heat mode is super overpowered and was almost outright comical at times, and i love it.  this was truly such a fun time with lots of peak moments. i still think about some scenes in my daily life, just because it was that impactful for me. i cried harder at this ending than i did at 8's ending, if that tells you anything.  this is basically a yakuza fan's wet dream!!! if you're already a fan, definitely play this and go have fun, but if you're new to the series DO NOT!!! play this one until you played the rest of the series. its best moments are based on important events in the past games, and would genuinely make no sense without context. such a great game, shame everyone seems to be changing their opinion about it after infinite wealth's release.

_childDocuments_.review: When  was announced back in 2016, it was described as . And sure enough, a new protagonist, Ichiban Kasuga, would take over as the new face of the franchise during the next game, . But as it turns out, Kazuma Kiryu’s story wasn’t quite over after all, as he even went on to re-appear as a protagonist during . To bridge the story gaps between his (re)appearances,  was released - a spin-off that’s also offering a return to the real-time action combat of the older  games.Bluntly speaking,  is a game with a clear target audience in mind: Players who’ve played through all mainline  games before – or at least the most recent ones. It’s not meant as a character introduction of Kazuma Kiryu for newcomers to the franchise, who might’ve started with . I can’t stress this enough:  features heavy spoilers for  and , as it assumes that the player is familiar with the events that conspire in these games. If you’ve yet to play these games (you should!), don’t start with  until you’ve done so!As for the actual game,  is a surprisingly short entry in the franchise. If you’re just going for the main story, you’ll spend about 12 hours finishing the game, though a completionist playthrough clocks in around 32h according to . If we’re only going by a main story-focused playthrough, this actually makes  the . While I don’t the game being shorter as it leads to a more focused story, I do feel like the current asking price (49,99€) might be a little steep for what’s on offer here and I highly recommend waiting for a sale instead.That’s not to say that  is a bad game but despite it’s shorter length, it also uses it’s ties to the recent  games as an excuse to recycle quite a lot of content as well as locations. Now, reusing old content is hardly new for the franchise and not necessarily a bad thing. But as the game , it’s fair to say that the content recycling went even a bit further here than what we’re normally used to. There’s only one new (small) location in the game and there are only 34 substories to complete – and while the story is obviously new, a lot of the remaining parts of the game are minigames you’ve all seen before. Again, these minigames are just as much fun as they were in  for example, but it does not really make the 49.99€ price-tag seem good.Still a lot of fun is the return of real-time action combat. This time, Kiryu got access to two fighting styles: “Agent” and “Yakuza”. The latter one is focused on slower, heavy hitting strikes and consists of moves you might’ve seen in past  games (e.g. a “breakdance kick” once fallen to the ground). The “Agent” playstyle is focused on gadgets instead, like flying drones or a combat wire, which can be upgraded separately. Personally, I stuck to the “Yakuza” style through almost the entire game since it seems to fit Kiryu more, though I was sad to see that the amount of heat actions including objects are quite limited – most of them resort in the same animation (Kiryu bashing his victim’s face in with the object he’s currently holding) and only very few objects received the special animation treatment (e.g. pliers).But generally speaking, beating dozens of enemies up is still as fun as it ever was, no matter the fighting style you might choose. As usual, you can purchase different upgrades, which either increase your stats or allow you to perform new moves in combat. A good way to earn money is the “Akame Network”, a level system that’s basically tied to almost all side content – do side content, level up the network, which results in new side content. Almost all substories in  are unlocked this way instead of encountering them on the streets like in previous  games.Thankfully, levelling up the Akame Network isn’t required for the story after the initial introduction, which means you can just play through the story without any grinding roadblocks (like the 3 million yen story requirement in ) in your way, if you want to. And considering the story does quite a good job of showcasing Kiryu’s new situation and his mental state, I can understand not wanting to stop for billiard of golf.A few of the plot points might come up a little too often but generally speaking,  is one of the better paced story in the franchise that offers the usual mix of twists and turns one can expect by now. Thankfully, due to a smaller cast of characters, the story is also quite easy to follow and doesn’t become as convoluted as some of the other  games did. But while some of the events that happen are quite foreseeable thanks to the intersection with , it was the bittersweet ending that really took me by surprise and made me shed more than a few tears. Without spoiling anything, if you’ve been on the journey with Kiryu as long as I’ve been, you really don’t want to miss the two final cutscenes of this game.Concluding,  can best be described as a bite-sized  experience. It got everything one expects from the franchise, from the flow of combat to silly minigames and even sillier substories, and does give players a better understanding of the new chapter in Kiryu’s life. However, it’s also a shorter game with a lot of recycled content that can’t really justify the high price-tag of the game, since it doesn’t really bring anything new to the table. It’s quite clear that it was originally conceived as DLC but as long as you don’t expect anything else, you can’t go wrong with this game if you’ve enjoyed what came before.

_childDocuments_.review: The best way to describe Gaiden is that it's a greatest-hits compilation celebrating Kiryu Kazuma, the Dragon of Dojima.While it's a rather short game, only comprising 5 chapters – it's a fun little jaunt that put you back into his shoes and reminds you just how great of a character Kiryu is. Great callbacks, with Takaya Kuroda's incredible voice acting really showcasing just how much Kiryu has changed over the past 7 games.Combat-wise, it's not as great as Lost Judgment. I'd put it slightly above the first Judgment, but it's still fun to beat up random dudes. This game shines in it's side-content, where I've spent majority of my playtime doing. That's not something I usually do in a Yakuza title, as I greatly enjoy the story content more, but Gaiden incentivizes you greatly for checking off that list, and I couldn't help but continuously support the Akame Network.I'd rate it a solid 8/10. My only downside would be the humungous file size. I hope RGG puts out a patch to reduce the storage taken up by the Cabaret Club FMVs, and also consider making the LAD8 demo a separate download / DLC install. 98GB is too much space for a 15-30 hour bite-sized Like a Dragon game. I'm certain that Infinite Wealth will be much smaller than this when it comes out in January.

_childDocuments_.review: First off I wanna start off with the positives of the game before I talk about whats bad about it. On my account I have played all yakuza games but not 7 (I don't really enjoy turn-based combat) so take this with a grain of salt.Pros:-Despite its shortness, a brilliant story that is told surprisingly well.-I love that they copied a few things from Lost Judgment (the best combat in the franchise) like the mortal reversals.-Coliseum being back is great again (although it has its issues).-Amazing action scenes, martial arts is on point and it really sets a new standard.-Villains were brilliant probably the best even though the story couldn't show them off more.-Great references to characters from previous games except missing Y3 and Y4 which is upsetting because Y3 had a lot of good characters that they had to throw away due to the old quality of the game which deterred people.-Side stories were funny as usual and did not miss.Now the flaws...-HEAVILY downgraded combat from LJ. It is still quite good standard but on professional difficulty the gameplay was sometimes an utter chore. The AI was tweaked differently in order to balance Agent Style but giving enraged enemies ultra instinct and bosses a mountain of hyper-armour while making yakuza style slow af was definitely annoying. Whoever decided to make story bosses get enraged, I hate you with a passion. Heat builds up way too slow that it came a little close to giving me yakuza 3 flashbacks. Extreme heat was given less emphasis yet they gave it lots of extra moves but then it comes with having to pick extreme heat mode for extra moves rather than for heat actions and vice versa which just doesn't feel right, AND heat drains way too quickly its annoying. I don't know how much time RGG had with this game but they could've at least added some kind of hidden arts. Agent style is both good and bad, its rush combo is overly long making it hard to utilise without being hit from bum♥♥♥♥ nowhere and the combo being abruptly ended. Lock-on was actually a bit strange and didn't lock onto the enemies I wanted to, I have no idea if its just me but I have no idea how RGG (again) broke something that was already established in LJ. I hate that the gameplay was tailored more to casual players who just mash the attack button than the OG fans who love the combat because they can't find it anywhere else. Its a case of RGG fixing a lot of what isn't broken (all they had to was copy and paste Lost Judgment combat).-Missing character development between a few characters. Sometimes I felt that Kiryu (Joryu) kind of needed more time or backstory of why he is good buddies with certain characters. This is only just a minor nitpick not a deal-breaker.-Story should've been a bit longer. Paying £10 less for such a cut in story length doesn't really seem like a good deal. Obviously I would've preferred not being side-tracked to do fetch quests or whatever but maybe something to fill the gaps as it is fairly short.-Quality seemed to be worse than its other dragon engine games, must be due to its short development time but RGG should've delayed the release to polish up on its looks. I must note that characters have more jagged edges and enemies look especially bad when they pull off their mortal attacks.-Game kept freezing in odd parts, it might be my computer on my end but I have never had any freezing issue with any RGG game ever. My specs are also quite good so it cannot be that.-Reusing old assets like enemy movesets from LJ (they sucked because kiryu literally has barely anything to work with), pocket circuit racing (im kind of glad its back but at the same time it is blatantly lazy). But also they forgot to reuse other things like the ally movests for coliseum which makes no sense. Why give enemy AI a full expanded moveset but then proceed to take away all of its features when the player uses them (Kaito was a ♥♥♥♥♥ to fight in particular even though he is basically the same from Judgment, goes to show that judgment's combat is better despite being 4.5 years old).-Coliseum being time based than skill based (crowd pleasers) shoes the devs attitude to the combat. Having a set time means that the devs mainly wanted damage output to fix all the flaws the game has so battles don't drag out long and aren't difficult which I think is stupid. I try to play with no damage upgrades to make the game challenging and fun as it pushes me to style on enemies rather than mash one button or heat action spam. However the coliseum makes it almost impossible as damage output at base level is just not enough to keep up. I don't think any yakuza game has made it timed before and when its timed its for ultimate battle so it makes perfect sense.In conclusion maybe get this game if you are a yakuza fan, IT IS GOOD but I am leaving a thumbs-down as RGG shouldn't EVER use this game as an example for brawler combat in future it is bad. I do regret pre-ordering and I must emphasise to get this game at a heavy discount as its not really worth its high price. Really? £45 for a rushed RGG game. (Anyone who disagrees with my opinion on the combat probably think that ishin's combat is good).

_childDocuments_.review: First of all I want to say that I don't recommend this game to someone that hasn't played all the previous games or atleast 6 and 7. Even though the game tries explain some things that occurred so far I still recommend to go play those games because the plot can get a little complex in these game and you might get confused, also you will miss all the fan service stuff. Alright now that we got that out of the way time to talk about the game. Kiryu returns as the protagonist in this one and at first I was a little skeptical about this after the great send off that Yakuza 6 gave him. To my surprise however after completing the game I would say that this was a much needed storybit that had to be added not only to tie any lose ends to the Yakuza 7 story but to Kiryu's character and relationships also. I won't get into spoiler territory but trust me this game is really emotional (it made me cry like 2 times). The new characters are also quite good, the antagonists really stole the show for me and like every yakuza game there's a twist you might not see coming. Now for the gameplay part of the review I think we all agree that this is the best Dragon Engine Kiryu. His Yakuza style contains his classic moves from the other games with some new ones added and overall better balanced. Now his new style is called Agent and I FREAKING LOVE IT! They gave him so many gadgets that if he had a cape and a mask he could be batman and I know that doesn't sound like the aproach rgg usually takes with styles but trust it is really fun. I mean how can a game where a japanese middle-aged man uses his wire from his watch and freaking cigarette bombs not be fun. Honestly my only complains about the game are that you acquire heat much slower than the other games and that there's a bit of padding in the story to make the game longer that I think could be removed (it's some substories that you must do in order to progress the story). Overall this game offers so many different and fun expierences in the different minigames, combat scenarios and story missions that I recommend it to every yakuza fan out there

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly this is a DLC quality game being charged at nearly full game pricing.  While the story itself is good and it can keep you entertained for a while, I cannot in good faith recommend this to anyone but hardcore Yakuza fans at the current pricing and even then its with the caveat that its story really feels like there was about 5 additional hours potently cut to make the game available before LAD8 releases.  I just dont understand why RGG would decide to charge 50 bucks that you can beat in around 5-6 hours when the Kaito Files is 30 bucks for a very similar length experience.And that's the key phrase i will use here.  the Experience is the same as almost any other RGG game just compacted into the most bizarrely paced story imagineable.  there's periods where it feels like the story is barely crawling and then periods where everything happens all at once at the same time.  Its all over the place and frankly while the ending was a great catharsis, I cant get over the story told up to that point.  Even a key plot point is barely talked about and is seemingly swept under the rug late in the game, almost as if it was just dropped to give long time fans of the franchise something to discuss and freak out about while having almost zero relevance to the actual story.Combat feels so pointless too even playing at the profesional difficulty.  Agent style is borderline useless outside of 1 or 2 spots in the story and requires skills (which are gated by 2 different currencies) to actually feel where Yakuza style actually starts at.  Most encounters feel reletively non-threatening as money is plentiful and health items are cheap, and boss encounters feel more like a QTE to land Tiger Drop once you have unlocked it.In short, if your a Yakuza/LAD diehard who loves the franchise, this is more of the same that you love but in a condensed form that left me wanting much more for the price.  I honestly cant recommend it to newer people to the franchise because this isn't representative of the usual length and story telling that RGG usually does.

_childDocuments_.review: Gaiden is Gaiden. A short spinoff you can call Yakuza 6.5. Its a very short game, only 5 chapters, but those 5 chapters are pretty solid. The mini games are pretty good, many returning from 0.Gameplay feels like Judgment with two fight styles. Dragon, and Agent.I dont need to explain Dragon to you, so lets talk about agent.Agent is very fun, a very fast swan like style. It comes with much fun abilities like holding square to throw bomb cigerattes, holding X to dash around and run over people with rocket shoes, holding triangle to send in drones that attack people over time and circle you while blocking, and of course the string which you can use to pull enemies, items hidden around the map, and weapons to you. It was a very fun style to pair with THE DRAGON STYLE. The unlock system is money based like 0.The core side missions are little missions you take on for an intel woman. This woman provides many pretty good mini games from what I have played. you will unlock points for her, which allows you to get awards, upgrade your abilities. Not a huge fan they tied this into the upgrades, but fair enough. The upgrade screen is very similar to Judgments also.THE CASTLE. What a grand and amazingly crafted location that is beautiful to see. Its a major plot point of the game and holds many gambling mini games and the wonderful coliseum you fight in. The coliseum mode is pretty awesome. You can fight as many different characters you recruit into your team, among some being very prominent characters from past games if you got the dlc preorder, as well as a suprise Judgment reference if you accomplish a certain side quest. I thought it was fighting arena done best its ever been done in the series, so if you like that you will like this. There is team battles, your team vs others, 1v1s, 1vgroups, and SPECIAL battles that usually involve weapons and special fights like certain types of bosses.So, the only downside to this game is its incredibly short, as I said the campaign is 5 hours long. The only thing holding this game back. Idk if its fully worth 50 dollars. I would say more 30 or 40. It definitely shouldve got cut in half Id say. The story was pretty solid and well done despite how very short it was, with an incredible tie back to the moment (you know the one) in Yakuza 7 where kiryu shows up. The story ties it all up in a bow for 8 coming out the beginning of next year, and it was a pretty good experience despite how small the game is. It had a very beautiful end and truly made it feel like this is the last game Kiryu is the main protagonist in.8/10 - JIRYU WICK.

_childDocuments_.review: After finishing this game I can say that this was more than just an after thought for Kiryu and his story after 6, it feels like this was genuinely made to be from the start of 3. The amount of references to many of the games in the series along with meeting certain people from a certain similar series, shows that they really wanted to solidify this game into the series.I highly recommend playing this only if you've experienced the game Yakuza: Like a Dragon and the games before, since many of the events that take place in this are related to key events of that game.The combat feels more polished than what Kiryu was left with in 6, making him feel the best he's been since Yakuza Kiwami. Agent Style adds a new feel to the game, akin to hack and slashes with the way Kiryu mows through crowds of enemies using his new Spider gadget. Yakuza Style felt like a lite version of Kiryu's iconic Dragon style, which isn't bad since it is taking the backseat for Agent Style.The game definitely feels like one you should complete in one playthrough, since the length isn't as long as the other titles in the series. The game starts off with many cutscenes, but you'll start to see more and more things unlock as it goes on. You'll be doing yourself a disservice if you rush through the game, as you won't get the most bang for your buck. The game has so much to offer with it's coliseum mode. It gives us a chance to experience the game outside of the main Yakuza cast. Not to mention if you beat the game, you can play the trial of the next game in the series.Overall, the story alone was enough to keep me involved, but the substories and the new content kept me wanting to play more. Real Yakuza play Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name

_childDocuments_.review: Relatively short for a Yakuza game (hence the Gaiden in the title); probably 1/3 the length of Yakuza 8 (also known as Yakuza: Like a Dragon). However, it's almost all killer, no filler. The ending sequence had me in tears. 10/10I liked the return to the traditional Yakuza combat; I didn't mind 8's turn-based combat as much as some die-hard fans but it was definitely a slog at times. It definitely fits the more standard Yakuza theme of "Kiryu keeps punching things until the world is as it should be" that this game has.My only complaint is that there is a specific fight that overlaps in this and 8 () that I would have love to have played from Kiryu's perspective, but that was just shown in flashback form at the end. I was really looking forward to it, and was bummed it wasn't there. Not a huge deal though, as the rest of the game is fantastic.One thing that I liked / disliked was the Akame requests system. I do like that it was really easy to find and complete all the substories without wandering around looking for the triggers or relying on a guide, but it also felt less "Yakuza-y", in that there wasn't an equivalent of, for example, randomly getting roped into a Michael Jackson music video. It certainly streamlined things though.All in all, it's a great game, and whets the appetite for Infinite Wealth without burning you out on the formula.

_childDocuments_.review: As a reminder: This game is a conclusion of all the Yakuza games released to this day. Playing this first would be the same as watching the final Season of Attack on Titan or any other good series before Season 1-4. You would ruin your experience.Now for the review:Kazuma Kiryu is back, for better or worse, depending on how you see it, but on a technical level, this game takes everything that made Yakuza 6 and Kiwami 2 amazing and improves it quite a bit:Kiryu keeps his Dragon of Dojima style, which is now called the Yakuza style, but it’s slightly nerved in comparison to Y6 and K2. They made it slightly slower and took away two of the side-steps, you can only do one now (and you get a roll upgrade later) otherwise the moveset is mostly unchanged.The star of the show is the new Agent style. It’s mixture of Yagamis Crane and Kiryus old rush style with some new gadgets, which are really fun to use.Gameplay wise Agent style is superior, especially on harder difficulties, due the nerving of Yakuza style and it generally being faster.One of the biggest changes in terms of combat is the number of enemies you can fight at once. Some battles (mostly in the Colliseum) makes you fight up to 20 enemies at once. After this game, One Man Army Kiryu definitely deserves his title.The main story might be shorter but in terms of minigames and side content, Gaiden has almost as much content as a normal Yakuza game:Additionally, something, that doesn’t really fit into any of the Subcategories: Some outfits from older games return or you can just dress him up as a clown, and it will affect almost every cutscene!Now for the most important part of the game:In terms of story writing, it's kind of amazing to think that the entire situation of Kiryu, where everything started to go downhill for him, begun in Yakuza 5 or more specifically it's ending.Before that, all Yakuza games had it's of own concluded stories without any big impact for it's successors, but with Yakuza 5 and successor Yakuza 6, everything changed:The entirety of Yakuza 6 and Gaiden could have been prevented, if Kiryu would have been there to protect Haruka. The decision Kiryu made at the end of Yakuza 5 to go into prison were the trigger for everything that took place afterwards. You could even go further back and say that Kiryus decision to let Haruka pursue her dream of becoming an Idol let to all of this, which is impressive to think about.You could say, that this is all an one big arc and it's still ongoing for 11/12 years now.If the writers of Yakuza, or Like a Dragon, how it’s called now, planned this from the start, it’s actually really good story writing. Now we will have to see how it continues in Like a Dragon Infinite WealthThe sum it up, without spoiling the game, this game has definitely the most emotional scene in the entire franchise with one of the best voice acting pieces I’ve ever heard, which would even make the toughest Yakuza cry.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game overall that'll appeal to anyone who has been following the Yakuza series but a few downsides that are unique to this one. On the good side, the combat feels so much smoother and fast paced than previous titles. There's essentially two stances - Agent mode and Dragon. Agent mode is a mixture of gadgets and fast paced moves from Kiryu that aren't "light" attacks by any means. It feels fantastic and I did most fights in this stance because you could quickly evade and follow up which was something I felt lacked in past games. Dragon stance is more of the older approach of brute forcing attacks with block penetration and immediate counters. Overall both are great. The gadgets are more of a gimmick than anything so 90% of your damage will come from actual attacks. Downside is the path this game takes to get you from start to finish. There's a huge block that comes in the middle of the game that forces you to do sub stories and arena battles. In other games, these were totally optional and at no point did I ever feel forced to do a bunch of sub stories that I wasn't interested in. It's not the case here and I'd say half of my playtime was being forced to grind through them with a relatively short main story line. The story itself was alright. It ties into the other yakuza games by portraying yakuza in general as degrading into a bunch of common criminals exploiting regular people who are being phased out from society. It runs largely parallel with LAD with Ichiban so unless you've played that you might not know what's going on. There's a montage that tries to inform people who haven't played it, but I thought it was way too fast and insufficient if I hadn't already played that.Overall, worth a buy if you have time. I think this might be the last game we get with someone stoic like Kiryu running as the lead--I'm not a fan of the naive/energetic Ichiban who seems to be the new lead of the franchise. It's a little darker than the other games, but I actually liked that part and felt it fit well. I just wasn't a fan of the substory grind, but I could get over that.

_childDocuments_.review: Another AWESOME Yakuza game. While the RPG formula and slower pace of the now mainstay series grew on me to the point I prefer it, it was nice to get this on the side. An old-school, simpler game, with an interesting story, where you again run around and beat a lot of people up. Sure, the game is much shorter and smaller in scope, there's no XP, no working vending machines, no elaborate sub-stories or mini-games (though the "homeless HQ" half of the story attempts to make up for it), but the game plays great, looks great, and the story is captivating and characters interesting. In some ways, it feels like an elaborate Yakuza 6 DLC in a super-modern engine with all the bells and whistles, with simplified mechanics, but a cool and unique alternate fighting style. It also answers a lot of interesting and previously mysterious questions. Overall, I'm having as much fun playing this as I did playing Yakuza 6. _childDocuments_.review: A great story with a lot of fan service and a brilliant combat system.I played Judgment and Yakuza 0 before this game and can definitely say that the combat feels much nicer and crispier. The only annoying thing is the ragdoll stun attacks that just force you to wait a few seconds to recover. The problem is so much worse with pistol enemies who just stun spam you. Also surprisingly there is no quick select of items like there was in Judgments. That just makes it more annoying to heal as you need to go through the menus every time.In terms of story, it is engaging right from the start and I am glad that you do not need to play all the yakuza games to understand what is going. The only game I would say you need to play before this one is Yakuza Like a Dragon as the story would make a lot more sense if you do. One minor complaint I have about the game is that there are a few times where the story is locked behind progression in the open world. The grind is not too bad and it honestly never affected me as I was already doing the side objectives anyway but I still find this game design annoying.The fact that this game is shorter than others in the series actually plays in its favour as it picks up much faster and the story is just overall lean. That is especially praiseworthy as these yakuza games tend to be a bit bloaty and consistently run about 8 hours too long. Here the story is to the point.Overall a great game and a nice change of pace to have a brawler as a bridge between two huge 60+ hour turn based rpgs.

_childDocuments_.review: [Y6 spoilers]This is probably one of the most refined Yakuza experiences you can get. They trimmed the fat majorly, and it's to the game's benefit.  Minimal padding, fun and exciting combat and a story that'll hook you despite its smaller scale than the numbered sequels of the series.  I would recommend buying this if it's on sale, as the game is pretty short. I clocked in at 12 hours on Professional Difficulty. I paid £25 and for that, I'd say it's worth it, especially if you liked 0, Kiwami 2 and 6.  The final boss alone feels like an apology for how much of a pushover Iwami was at the end of 6. Likeable characters, memorable soundtrack, pulse-pounding combat and fun minigames are abound in this DLC-sized entry, and I'm sure you could extend the playtime even further if you went for all the sub stories on offer. Performance-wise, this runs like a dream. On my RX 7800XT I was running 1440p at 120FPS with no drops, even during set pieces with dozens of enemies. An exemplary PC port, if ever there was one.

_childDocuments_.review: Released on November 08, 2023, Like a Dragon Gaiden successfully continues the Yakuza saga with a captivating plot that serves as an epilogue to Yakuza 6. The narrative seamlessly connects with new protagonists, Ichiban Kasuga and Takayuki Yagami, while maintaining a strong link to the beloved Kazuma Kiryu.Strengths:    • Accessible for Newcomers and Appealing to Veterans: The game strikes a balance, making it accessible for newcomers with thorough explanations and Portuguese subtitles, while also catering to series veterans who can relish the return of Kiryu. The central characters are charismatic, revealing a more sentimental side of Kazuma Kiryu, providing a well-rounded experience for players of varying familiarity with the franchise.    • Engaging Setting and Activities: Set in the Sotembori district, the game offers a visually stunning and lively environment with diverse activities such as karaoke, game rooms, and casinos. The Coliseum, now known as the Castle, provides exciting challenges, adding depth to the gaming experience. The district's visuals, especially in the Coliseum, shine with impressive graphics, even on older generation consoles.    • Innovative Combat System: Like a Dragon Gaiden introduces a fresh combat system for Kazuma Kiryu, departing from the traditional stances and incorporating modern gadgets inspired by Eastern culture. The game maintains an engaging combat experience with improved gameplay, making combos more accessible and adding new strategic elements, such as using gadgets for unique effects.Bugs/Weaknesses:    • Short Duration: Unlike previous titles in the Yakuza series, Like a Dragon Gaiden has a considerably shorter completion time, with the main journey lasting around 15 to 20 hours. While this may cater to players with limited time, it may disappoint fans accustomed to the longer gameplay experiences offered by previous Yakuza titles.    • Potential for Expansion: The game's brevity, coupled with its narrative starting immediately after Yakuza 6, may make it feel more like a DLC than a standalone installment. While it serves as a joyous reunion with Kiryu for longtime players, it also raises questions about the potential for a deeper, more expansive experience.    • Distinctive but Separate: Despite its connection to Yakuza 6, Like a Dragon Gaiden's journey with Joryu feels somewhat detached from the core Yakuza narrative. This separation, while providing a fresh perspective, might leave players feeling that the iconic character of Kiryu deserves a more integral role rather than a side story.In summary, Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name excels in storytelling, accessibility, setting, and combat innovation, but its brevity and potential for expansion may leave players with mixed feelings, particularly those expecting a more extended and integral installment in the Yakuza series.

_childDocuments_.review: Even though Gaiden is a side game with a main story and side contents roughly half the size of the usual RGG games, it still delivers on pretty much most of it. The biggest strength in Gaiden is how it bridges between Yakuza 6, 7 and upcoming Like A Dragon Infinite Wealth. The story revolving about Tojo and Omi's dissolution and how the aftermath of 6 made Kiryu a Daidoji Agent are handled really well. Even with short runtime, all the major characters are well written and have their own story arcs. The final boss symbolizes perfectly well about how the dissolution won't be easy for lots of the yakuza, how times are changing and some of them are desperately clinging to their old way of life. It's tragic but also handled with an intense and cathartic action sequences that is both entertaining to play through and make you feel for the characters.And then the ending, one of the, if not the saddest moment in the series. It's moments like this that make Kiryu feel believable throughout the games. Beneath his stoic demeanor hides an overwhelmingly warm heart to his family. Gaiden is ultimately a direct continuation of Yakuza 6 and that feeling of parenthood and sacrifice echoes throughout the game and especially in the ending. Combat in Gaiden feels great and the more aggressive enemies make for more challenging fights. It just feel and play incredibly well in every situations. The side contents, although small in variety, still manages to entertain. Some substories are among the best in the series and tackle Kiryu's past events, some are about current technological dilemma and some are just really funny. The live action cabaret hostess minigame is actually enjoyable, even if it's shorter than the previous games and lack depth that Yakuza 6 had. The fact that you can't ask them out for Karaoke is also a bummer but the live action videos itself are acted well enough, some are sweet, some are seductive and some are funny to watch. Pocket Circuit is back, still great as ever and it does have a callback to previous Pocket Circuit. The Boutique is great, although a bit barebones compared to other games with similar feature. The Castle Coliseum is the best version of the series coliseum to date, it can be challenging, chaotic and just really fun to fight.Gaiden is mostly about quality than quantity. It comes with smaller package than the previous games but still manages to be one of the best RGG games, especially for longtime fans. Coupled with varieties of great soundtrack, the updated gorgeous visual, the beautiful locations and its attention to details and generally just how much optimized the game is, it's made in less than a year  but still a quality game through and through.A perfect bridge between previous games and Infinite Wealth that not only concludes one of the series' story arc in a beautiful way but also genuinely telling an engrossing and emotional story.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name is an outstanding addition to the series, offering a fresh yet familiar journey for longtime fans. The combat system has evolved with new mechanics and fighting styles, delivering intense battles that keep you on your toes. The world is beautifully detailed, packed with side quests and minigames that add layers to the experience. It’s a perfect blend of storytelling and gameplay that will resonate with anyone who has followed Kiryu’s journey from the beginning. Like a Dragon Gaiden is a must-play for those who want to continue exploring the legend of the Dragon of Dojima.
