_childDocuments_.review: Story (no spoilers):Definitely conscious of the character. This game does justice to Kazuma Kiryu's past, ideals, burdens and history.It does an excellent job at feeling as a perfect focus for him, with its occasional callbacks to past games, with it not being too little, but not too much either as not to feel like complete fan service rather than a well founded game. So yeah, if you want a game, even if short (5 chapters in lenght only) that gives a gives a more proper send off to Kiryu, this is a entry you shouldn't skip by any means. (Why would you want to skip it, anyways?) Kiryu has much more attitude than in many previous games, too. The ending made me drop tears of both sadness and joy.Gameplay: The gameplay is, to put it simple, fun. Agent, the new fighting style, is presented as a more tactical one, being able to overwhelm hordes of enemies. However, as you progress through the game, it becomes less than that to become more of a quick, easy way around finishing fights. And no, it's not because the character being bound to get stronger as the game progresses, but rather than it not being as tactical as presented, but more of a silly mix up of gadgets that justify the name of the fighting style, some of which are of quick and of more slow use, but all of them being able to finish the battle in a minute, or 8 seconds in most cases. It doesn't mean it's not fun, because it's the complete opposite, but it's definitely not a before and an after when it comes to battles styles in the series either. Kiryu's signature Yakuza fighting style (now being the fighting style that you unlock as you progress a little further into the story) has some minimal changes that might not be for the convenience of the player too, like it being powerful at the price of being slow, and the beloved ¨finishing hold¨ move being stuck behind Heat Mode. Even so, this is the most fun it has been playing with Kiryu in the Dragon Engine so far, to say the least.Duration and side stuff: The main story is around 12 hours, but that was no relevant for me because of how the side content of the game does a wonderful job at stretching the game to around 30 hours. Side missions. Customizable clothes. Minigames. Immersive hostesses. Pocket Circuit Races. Colisseum fights and the entirety of the Castle. Even being able to play as any of the characters you recruit to join your side at the colisseum.All of that felt like a fitting part of the main story as I went through it. What I'm trying to say, if you want the game to be longer and more enjoyable than what only 5 chapters sound like for a Like a Dragon/Yakuza game, all you need to go is to go out of your way and have fun. I cleared all of the colisseum fights with a S Grade and reached rank 30 in the Akame missions, and it was like having a buffet served in front of me that left me with a smile and conversations topics for the future.DLC: Owning the Legendary Fighter Pack DLC is fun, but definitely not a must to overcome the colisseum. In case you think it will be defining to your enjoyement of the game if you don't own it because of how the characters there are some of the glorified cameos of the series. (Looking at Majima still spinning as the fight ends is fun, though).Conclusion: Akame is very cute. Having the game's duration in mind might help you savor and enjoy the game and its events more. Buy the game on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: This is meant to be just a short game, to fill in the gap between 6 and 7 in regards to Kiryu, and i expected to finish it in just one or two evenings, but i found this game has a lot more to offer.LEGACY:It pays proper homage to previous entries with mini-games and substories. Fans of the series will appreciate numerous easter eggs dropped in the form of text or quests. Those subquests are bite-sized but i wouldn't say they are short, it's definitely not "bump into a scammer" sort of thing. They explore some topics that never got much attention in previous games which i love.COMBAT:Absolutely fantastic, with TWO GLARING FLAWS(more later), but still i never get tired of it. This game makes you feel extremely powerful and gives quite a bit of exploitable abilities and playstyles, but at the same time it can be quite challenging(at least in the arena but we'll get to it). My favorite has been using the payback ring and indra's amulet to blast through arena bosses as quickly as i can. The GLARING FLOW i was talking about, however, is related to the juggling limit. When you bounce an enemy off the ground, much like in Lost Judgment, you can keep them in the air by dealing damage and thus creating combos. The problem is that this game limits HOW LONG YOU CAN KEEP IN THE AIR. A completely unnecessary limitation, coupled with inability to quick-cancel out of Agent Style finishers, despite it being supposedly a faster, more evasive style than Yakuza Style. It is quite difficult to play evasively in this game in general because of how slow Kiryu's attacks are, and Agent Style could have been his saving grace, but alas. Another thing is i was hoping that you'd bring back wall-bounds. It seems you have something similar where the enemy can be pushed into a wall with a finisher, prompting them to bounce off of it, but nothing else can be done about it. It's not a flaw, but i wish you could bring back this mechanic from Yakuza 3 and Yakuza 4.PLOT:I don't want to spoil much, it stays true to its original vision, while also freshing things up. I've never seen Kiryu this expressive before, much of it is thanks to Kuroda Takaya's stellar performance as his voice actor. And while the story is not very long, it is extremely rich with events, 1 chapter may feel like 2 or 3 chapters! And the side activities help you thin it out and be prepared for the next emotional rollercoaster.DLC CONTENT:This i feel deserves a special section because i was very let down by the special fighters Majima Goro, Saejima Taiga and Dojima Daigo in the arena. They don't have even half of their moves from previous games, it's fun to play as them for a bit...But nothing more. It's a shame, because i was really looking forward to it.OVERALL:I feel like this game is well worth its price. I know it could have been a lot better, but for a short game this is an amazing result and i hope they do even more Gaiden games, so we can play as our other favorite characters someday. If you feel hesitant, then i implore you to give this game a try!

_childDocuments_.review: In the Yakuza series, this episode is much shorter story-wise than average; I'd say it's about a third of the usual does of content. However, I did not see that as a disadvantage. A more concise story not only felt more personal for the MC, but it also game me more room to spend time on minigames, making this the first time in the series that I bothered to 100% all side-quests and extra content.The main storyline isn't particularly engaging, and I was disappointed in how certain primary characters were underutilized. It does lead to a very emotional conclusion, and fun crossovers with Like a Dragon plot, though. Furthermore, where screenplay lacks, the excellent direction and VA work make up for it.A solid entry in the series, particularly from the technical standpoint, just expect to spend more time playing Pocket Circuit, darts and Coliseum than in the main story.PS. Don't even think about starting your Yakuza adventure from this game.

_childDocuments_.review: If this is your first Yakuza Game (Like a Dragon is the name of the series in Japan), have fun! Though this game is primarily a brawler-style game, it throws our favorite karaoke singer Joryu into a wide variety of activities besides the street combat you'll find in the rest of the series. You could spend a lot of time on recreational activites Joryu himself may do, such as golf, board games, gambling, pit fighting (best way to grind cash in this game hint hint), and my personal favorite, singing Baka Mitai at the bar.For those who have played Yakuza games before, this game uses the same engine as Yakuza 6 and Yakuza 2 Kiwami, making for seamless transitions between combat on the streets and roaming Sotenbori. The game devs allow you to progress the story at your pace, and they will give you ample warning when you are going to a long brawling segment (except for the Chapter 1 gauntlet, watch out), so you can either take time to do some other activities or prepare for the long battle. I would recommend doing the side activities, not only because they are fun and provide comedic relief to an otherwise dark story, but because you'll need them to strengthen Joryu's stats and abilities since the upgrade tree requires the currency the side content provides. I had a fun time with this game and made it through the story on Normal mode in 33 hours. Keep in mind that I did not go for 100% completion so this number could vary for you if you decide to pick the game up for yourself. PS: Start the game with Japanese VA's. The English VA for Joryu ... let's say that it leaves a lot to be desired.

_childDocuments_.review: 100% Steam achievements with 38 hours clocked. I had a great time with Gaiden and loved almost everything about it but I just wanted to quickly highlight the very few things that I didn't like:1) Akame is a great character but ranking up her network often felt like boring busywork which was clearly designed to pad out the runtime of what is a fairly short game. This is especially true of the requests that require you to run all over the map talking to various NPC's placed on opposite ends of the map or fighting groups of gangs scattered across town. These were definitely a chore to get through and they frankly don't do anything for the overall experience. The substories were great though.2) I wasn't a fan of the live-action hostesses at the cabaret clubs. They felt awkward and forced and frankly unsettling. I had to power through those by skipping through every scene. Fingers crossed they never bring that back.3) JUSTICE - the Third King bossfight found in the Colosseum - is completely scuffed. Anyone here who has fought him knows exactly what I mean. Not even Amon comes close to the level of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and unfairness found in this fight, almost to the point where I can't quite believe it was intended to be this way. I guess time will tell. In any case, this was the lowest point of the game for me and the only time when I felt frustrated and angry while playing Gaiden. Other than that I universally loved everything else. The game is short by RGG standards but by every means sweet and the story is up there with the best this studio have made. I'm more excited than ever for Infinite Wealth and I'm desperately hoping that Kiryu gets the ending we all know he deserves to have.

_childDocuments_.review: 9,5/10 Wonderful game!I had so many questions when I played Yakuza: Like a Dragon. Like "What was Kiryu doing before chapter 12?", "Where was he?", "Is he okay?", etc.Most of my questions are solved with this game. It's a wonderful spin-off game that takes place after Yakuza 6 and during Yakuza 7. It also offers a preview of Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth (e.g. why the story takes place in Hawaii).The story is just as emotional as the last Yakuza games. The graphics look almost realistic. And I love the gameplay. Finally we get the good ol' beat 'em up game that almost feels like a Dynasty Warriors game. XDThe only thing I don't like about this game is that the game is too short compared to older Yakuza games. Only 5 chapters. You can play through the game in 10-12 hours. Therefore, I would advise you not to buy the game for the full price. It's only worth it if the game costs less than 20 euros. Unless you really want to experience the story of Kiryu and not watch it on YouTube. Then you can get it. Overall:To sum up, I can tell you that the game is very good. However, it feels like a DLC for Yakuza: Like a Dragon. You can also play the demo version of Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth, which is also interesting. If you don't want to have the demo version on your PC because it takes up too much disk space (25 GB, iirc), you should delete the Runtime2 folder in the game's installation folder. I look forward to playing more of your older games. ^^

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon Gaiden is an enjoyable experience that acts as a homage to past Yakuza titles as well as a bridge between the end of Yakuza 6 and the beginning of Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth. This makes it a must-play for long-time fans of the franchise despite being short-lived in terms of story length. New fans will probably need to play or be familiar with the major events of Yakuza: Like a Dragon beforehand, as the story of LaD Gaiden's plot revolves around some major spoilers for it. Some knowledge about core events of Yakuza 0-6 pertaining to the main protagonist are recommended as well.Completing all story and side activities will take roughly about 40+ hours or less (minus idle time). If you played and enjoyed any of the Beat'em games made by RGG Studio previously or simply a fan of story-driven action games, then this is definitely for you.  :)* The good old beat'em up styles of game protagonist Kazuma Kiryu (from Yakuza 0?) got remixed into two distinct fighting styles. One of which includes the use of spy gadgets to add a new flavor to the combat, and each style has its advantages depending on the situation* Adequate amount of sub-stories that does not feel bloated, and plenty of mini games that can keep you hooked for a good while* Grinding level is pretty adequate compared to some of the past titles in the franchise, and 100% completion is not required for full Steam achievements (more like 80%, and you can actually skip Mahjong and/or Shogi if you're bad at them and still get all achievements :D)* Customizable character appearance that persists even during cut-scenes after it becomes available (except for Karaoke scenes)* Inclusion of graphical settings like DLSS that boost overall fps for smoother experience* A trial version of the upcoming sequel "Like a Dragon: Infinite" is included with the game for players to get a feel for the game* Certain mini games can be a hit or miss with the players, in my opinion* Certain Coliseum fights can be ridiculous in difficulty even at full personal and team upgrades, and some races in Pocket Circuit mini game feel dependent on RNG to win* While not a con, the game finale fights may feel too underwhelming (that is, enemies are as weak as paper) if the player has fully unlocked & upgraded all abilities :DStory: 9/10Gameplay: 10/10Visuals: 10/10Soundtracks: 9/10Overall Score: 9.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon Gaiden is the first mainline "mini-game" in the Yakuza/LAD series, taking place right before and during the events of Yakuza: Like a Dragon. Starring Kazuma Kiryu, who hasn't been playable since Yakuza 6 back in 2016, masquerading as Joryu as we get a peek into his life as a Daidoji operative after his supposed "death".Getting some of the obvious out of the way, this is not a full experience Yakuza game. Only sporting a total of 5 chapters, where most other Yakuza games boast an average of about 13, rushing through the story won't give you as much mileage as before. Alongside this, this mainly takes place on two of the smallest free roam maps in the series: Sotenbori, which has very little new areas to explore, and the Castle which is essentially just Purgatory 2.0. Don't expect a full series game out of this, but there is still fun to be had.From a gameplay perspective Kiryu's styles seem to take a page from Judgment. Agent, the new style tempered around fast attacks and crowd control, ends up feeling underwhelming outside of extreme heat mode and it feels significantly weaker than Yakuza, the slower single target style that focuses on single target damage. While Agent is fun, especially with how much crowd control gadgets have, it feels significantly weaker than Yakuza style outside of extreme heat mode, which mainly powers up the gadgets to an insane degree where you can just nuke enemies without much thought. Alongside these changes are the re-introduction of deadly attacks, press dodge to counter them before they hit for a large amount of damage. This mechanic was copied and pasted from Judgment/Lost Judgment, but with the added caveat that enemies cannot be killed until their attack ends, meaning you're better just waiting the attack out to counter than to beat them to the punch, adding this weird combat pace at times where you'll wail on someone, they'll almost go down, but then they deadly attack and you have to wait for a short time. Then, onto sidestory content. This game's sidestory is Coliseum where we get a return and improvement on the Kiryu Clan/Majima Construction minigames with Hell Team Rumble. You choose a character to lead, either being Kiryu or another character that's part of your group, and build a formation where you go head to head with AI. Unlike in their previous renditions, you actually have a hand in the fight outside of just pointing out where your troops go, making it feel more natural for a Yakuza game. Pair this up with how insane the fights can get, Hell Team Rumble is a huge highlight of the game that I hope comes back in some capacity in a future game. Coliseum outside of Hell Team Rumble is still very fun as well, as it actually pays out well and has progression that doesn't require a massive amount of grinding. To top this off, you can only go into certain VIP areas after completing a certain amount of fights, so you're encouraged to complete these to open up the Castle further. Pocket Circuit also makes a return, but is just more of the same, with the only difference being that most parts can no longer be bought outright for cash and has to be earned with Circuit Points that come from finishing a race, completing a time trial, or beating a rival. Hostess clubs make a return as well, but this time somewhat downgraded. This time it incorporates FMV instead of in-game models, which feels very bizarre and takes me out of the game, despite in-game most of the NPCs state it's "Immersive". Alongside this, Hostess affection is harder to get, and major details about them are actually missable due to the new question structure. In other games, Hostesses will ask you questions that relate to their personality and substories, and anything that's important to their substory is unmissable. In Gaiden however, you can choose between three different questions, but some of them have no bearing on their personality and don't help towards learning their interests, especially since now the final question events to up their affinity can have wrong answers that, while neutral and doesn't lose any meter, will require you to re-visit them. Their max affinity dates are also underwhelming as since there's no in-game model, we just get dialogue over screenshots until we reach an unskippable FMV of the hostesses trying to be sexy. Hostess club was tedious before, especially if you were aiming for Amon, but now it's made worse due to odd structuring.Story wise, it's so compacted that saying anything past Chapter 1 is a pretty big spoiler. It's quite good and is fairly standard for a Yakuza story. He really is the man who erased his name.Now for everything else: Soundtrack is pretty good, feels like a mix between Like A Dragon's more dubstep style and a blend of some of Lost Judgment's themes. Graphically the game looks great, especially with the lighting in the Castle. Voice acting is also top tier as usual.TL;DR A good, but short Yakuza game that could have used a little more polish for combat, but is still very fun.8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: This game really feels like the twilight of Kiryu's life and it does it in a way that doesn't overstay it's welcome. The game doesn't overstay it's welcome with an artificially extended play time. This game feeds you the story that brings Kiryu between LAD 6 and 7 and sets him up for his story in 8 (which I suspect will truly be his last as a fairly literal passing of the torch). You go back to all of the best minigames. You get callbacks and references to some of the best highlights of the games prior. It really feels like the entire game is Kiryu looking back at his life and experiences and taking it all in one last time. I'd recommend it even without prior LAD experience, but like. If you played the others, this one is a must. It really does feel like a love letter from RGG to the franchise that made them what they are today.

_childDocuments_.review: Loved the game, bought it on sales. Would 100% wait for the sale. In terms of a reboot, it's clever, fun and feels more like a teaser rather than a full fledged Yakuza game. I would say that the MSQ is probably 7-8h. The rest is substories, grinding the "Castle" which has a Coliseum, which in itself is not new aspect but like each Yakuza game, there's some level of mini game that makes you stupid rich. It's the prettied Coliseum of most Yakuza game in my opinion. You can use the taxi to get on it, which I felt was breaking my immersion that it's a boat in international waters. The critique I've read so far is that you can play with other character in the Coliseum but their moves/fluidity is far from being fleshed out and is by far a let down.As for the story, I feel it's pretty good, this feels like a kind of "Multverse" where Kiryu looks not older than 35 yo but this appears to be set in the future when the kids from the orphanage are in their early 20's. The vilains are mid, the overall dept of the Yakuza line of story is not good. Well to be fair, it's still pretty fresh, I like that Kiryu works as Joryu a covert agent which works for some covert government agency also collaborating with the CIA... Kind of sexy spy who get in to leave the life of crime, protect is children while pretending to be dead. (an absolute easy card pulled each time in Yakuza).So overall the structure of the game is good. The fluidity of the fighting system - the way it's been kind of dumb down is still very fun. The gadgets are super fun and OP AF. The levelling can be pretty much fully done by chapter 4. Which is 2/3 into the game. Doing all the substories unlock some nice stuff including the 2nd point system needed to level up. So they are kind of extremely important. Like every Yakuza game, we are in extremely familiar territory. The mini-game are stale and basically feels like a copy-paste of all the universe and feels lazy.  It's a plus and a con. The pocket circuit comes back and it's a blast! The datacom/SEGA console old games are ok but when I play Yakuza I'll admit, I'm not interested in that. The Karaoke is also not scalable (no difficulty level adjustment); I suck at it! Still enjoyable. The Cabaret is ok. It's a film cutscene of JAV actress, which is OK I guess. Like in every Yakuza game, you have a side partner which here it's Akame who was a ok new addition but didn't felt like a mark in the Franchise. Meaning, I wouldn't care if she's not in the next game. She share a drink with you, she talks about why she's doing what she does. There's an attempt to build a rapport, but only feels like a tick in a box to achieve a level of narration, rather than an ally that's actually OP (like all past close allies usually are in Yakuza game) that you find either funny, interesting or add tons of fun to the game. By the time you're ready to do the final chapter and you've completed S rank all of the coliseum, gotten all the sexy expensive gear, you've filled up in potions and food. You've had some fun challenges in the Coliseum, you're thinking, Let's freaking go!! Last Boss, Last chapter, action pact +100 low level yakuza, with 30 mini boss and 5-6 big boss fight... Right? Nope! It's OK but it's just not good enough, In fact after you're done with it and you're like... Oh... Ok. There's No New Game + , much MUCH shorter than other games. The added features are mid and overall the polishing of the scenes and the custscene as still very good.  It's a solid 6, low 7/10 - Still pretty ok

_childDocuments_.review: Heads up, I will spoil some gameplay related stuff, I won't talk about what happens in the story itself. - is one of the shortest games in the series that's more of a setup for an upcoming adventure while showing stuff that happened in 7th entry off screen along the way. Despite being advertised as a bite sized RGG title and having a good time all the way through, I still can't help but feel like I've been overcharged considering the amount of content this game provides. I am not talking about the story length, that was to be expected to be short, but I was hoping they'd make up for it by having a decent amount of side stuff and extras. This game does not have NG+, Legend difficulty, or any sort of Gauntlet/Climax Battle challenge mode, so once I was done with all side stuff I could possibly do, I can't find a good reason to ever return to it. So what unique modes are there?Yeah its not really a unique game mode, but the gimmick of this one is that you have group fights, your teams and you can play as a whole bunch of characters. That sounds all well and good until you realize majority of characters just kinda suck to play as. Even characters that used to have hype move sets have been bastardized, and I will never forgive RGG for what they did to Higashi from Judgment series in this game. Kaito is also there, but you bet he's nowhere near as good as he was in Kaito Files DLC for Lost Judgment. Sugiura is there too, and unfortunately, Yagami is too expensive so he's completely absent.When you finish the game, you will be granted access to the upcoming LAD 8 demo, This demo is fairly lengthy and lets you explore a lot more than I'd normally expect with a side story or two being available. This is cool and all, but in the future I doubt there'd be a reason to ever look at it for what it is so.... enjoy it until the real thing's out I guess?If I could give it a mixed rating I would, I did have fun with it but its not an easy recommendation unless you're really into the series. I am sure I'd be way, WAY more forgiving if the damn thing didn't take 100GB of space, but as it stands, I see no reason to not uninstall it now.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the most well-tuned brawler produced by RGG using the Dragon engine I have personally seen. Runs exceptionally well on AMD hardware. The emotional beats are on point as always. It is very much a Like a Dragon game for Like a Dragon fans.Special mention to go the music. Whether it is the 007 style jazz for "Agent Style", the amazing karaoke tracks (both old and new) or the creeping 80s synth when Kiryu wanders the neon streets of Sotenbori, the soundtrack lives up to the bar raised by its predecessors. While if you are new I would recommend playing the other titles first in order to appreciate the full story of this game, if you are familiar or especially a fan, both young or old, Like a Dragon Gaiden is a masterful chapter in the saga of Kazuma Kiryu.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably one of my favorite RGG games. There's caveats but I think the whole package is fantastic overall. I'd highly recommend as a Yakuza/Like a Dragon fan. I don't know if I'd recommend to newcomers but only because the game is one made to fill gaps and bridge the gaps between 6, 7, and 8. You could probably enjoy it either way but I'd recommend 6 or Y:LAD(7) before this, personally. It's a much better conclusion to Kiryu's time as sole & main protagonist than 6 was and the story itself was great. Having a smaller, more centralized cast of characters did wonders for them all. Production values on the non-CG and non-animated(hard to describe the disction between regular animated cutscene and the ones that are for lack of a better term, rendered in game with canned animations and where you can skip individual bits of dialogue instead of the entire scene) are great. The game runs better than previous Dragon Engine offerings like Yakuza Like a Dragon(7) or 6.Combat isn't on par with Lost Judgment but it's definitely better than K2 and 6. Side content is great, or at least the coliseum is! Best coliseum/combat arena in the series, by a high margin. Being able to play group fights, team fights, gimmick matches, and 1v1s at your leisure is a much needed improvement over prior offerings. Alternative characters are hit or miss but some are able to carry their weight and make the option of having multiple characters worth it. Music is definitely a highlight among the franchise. Probably one of the only times the cutscene music impressed me and stuck out positively. The combat themes, the coliseum ones in particular, are amazing.

_childDocuments_.review: Additional Info:Once again, we slip into the suit of Kazuma Kiryu, the former Dragon of Dojima. In an attempt to protect himself and his past, he faked his own death and went into hiding under the alias Joryu. In true Superagent style, he hides his true face behind a pair of glasses and earns his yen in Sotenbori as a henchman for the local Daidoji gang. Naturally, though, Kiryu—er, Joryu—can't escape his skin either and soon finds himself entangled in another conflict once again. Ultimately, the incidents create unrest across the yakuza as a whole.Right now, I don't want to reveal too much. In the spin-off, a young all-around player named Akame is introduced as the new sidekick. With the aid of the local homeless, she has amassed an information network. She is not just a client but also a vital point of contact for Joryu, providing him with direct access to the underground. Like A Dragon Gaiden relies on bigger, freely accessible sections rather than a true open world. Since Sotenbori is where we spend a significant portion of the game at first, there are plenty of eateries, shops, and places to relax and build strength in addition to an entertainment district and leisure areas.The streets are crowded with people and have vivid colors that give off a typical Japanese flare. But here, too, the issues are apparent and, more importantly, visible. We frequently encounter homeless people on the streets, as well as wandering gangs who we would gladly punch. Then there's the castle itself, a massive cargo ship used by the underworld as a home for chaos, the expression of evil forces, and bizarre dreams. The Colosseum, a significant new game element, adds a nostalgic touch to this otherwise amusement park-like location. We can establish ourselves as prize fighters here, move up the ranks, and get large paychecks. We have the option of fighting as a team or as individuals. This allows us to enlist additional teammates and use them in our squad through side missions.Akame's talents advance as we acquire network experience, allowing us to hold tournaments with progressively larger awards. The Hell Team Rumble competitions offer chaotic combat entertainment. We can choose the fighters starting positions and the order in which they will compete using the team screen. Though, to be honest, this strategy quickly evaporates in the chaos, group activities and intense fights make for an enjoyable game.Like A Dragon Gaiden Is a well-bred action game with a strong emphasis on the intuitive battle system. With just a button push, we can switch between our two available styles whenever we want. We can use a variety of technical aids as agents, such as the spider, an electromagnetic lasso that we can use to bind or throw opponents. In true James Bond fashion, we can even call in drones to assault our targets and set off a device akin to a cigarette that explodes. We can also turn on a tiny jet engine beneath Joryu's shoes and use it to surf around rather than running. As an agent, we often hit targets more quickly and precisely, but our single hits deal less damage.This mode's opposite is the red-colored Yakuza mode. We deal greatly more damage in close quarters and during charge-up assaults when we're in this state. You learn new moves as you advance in skill and with various Heat Actions; however, you must hold down a specific button to use the Agent devices. It can be irksome when, as it frequently happened in my case, I created a Heat Action in place of using an Agent device. Control and overview are frequently lost because the camera is unable to keep up with the fast-paced action. The intense fight scenes elevate the Yakuza series despite these flaws. The addition of weapons and items adds to the appeal of punches and kicks, which feel incredibly forceful. We can build up heat energy through effective attacks and counters, which we can then release in a sort of fury mode. Joryu is less vulnerable to hits and does damage very swiftly during this phase.The game allows for some free time in between all the fighting and gory killing. And as anyone who has watched the Yakuza series will attest, hilarity and seriousness go hand in hand. This is also the case in this spin-off, where we practice golf, play darts or pool, and complete laps in pocket circuit racing. Alternatively, we have the option to play renowned classics like Fighting Vipers 2, Virtua Fighter 2.1, and Sega Racing Classic on nearby Sega Mega Drive systems and at arcades. We also comb vending machines for adorable plush toys, and these can then be given as presents to the local nightclub's hostesses. The interactions between the scantily clad ladies are presented by the developers with subtly obtrusive live-action footage. However, despite their humorous sound, the flirting attempts are actually pretty unsettling. The unflattering camgirl attractiveness of the scene is accentuated by the easily identifiable ring light reflection in the woman's eyes, which regrettably creates a weird lasting memory.Following the original series, the spin-off also doesn't take itself or its characters too seriously. In my opinion, the peculiar and distinctively Japanese humor could have been somewhat more prominent and exerted a more significant influence on the adversary design. The criminal adventure occasionally becomes bogged down in monotonous ranked bouts and the required elevation within the Akame network, despite the thrilling plot and intriguing characters. To put it simply, this means that we must finish the side missions and engage in combat in the Colosseum whether we want to or not. There are a few notable exceptions, but there are nine (!) substories alone that only feature gang battles, hence why I would have preferred more variation in the missions itself. At the end of the day, all of the missions are ultimately about brawls, sometimes bigger and sometimes smaller.Like A Dragon Gaiden took only six months to develop and was initially intended to be a DLC for the upcoming Infinite Wealth which even suprises me more. It possesses all of the series hallmark qualities, including an engrossing plot, peculiar comedy, a ton of side activities (even though they're somewhat repetitive), and a ton of minor surprises to discover. The only catch is that you must be familiar with the series in order to really enjoy this game. For those who are unfamiliar with the series, Like A Dragon, Judgement, or Yakuza 0 would be a better choice. Nevertheless, I can heartily recommend this espionage spin-off to enthusiasts. Particularly for fans of the Yakuza: I swear, the conclusion will make you cry.

_childDocuments_.review: Like A Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name, or Yakuza 7.5 is a pretty good game; though, it sticks true to its name of being half of a game. The game has a total of 5 chapters compared to a regualar yakuza games 12 chapters.Yakuza Gaiden's combat is more akin to Judgement's combat rather than Lost Judgement. Like Judgement, Kiryu has 2 styles now, being Agent Style (More Defensive, and Gimmick related), and DOD/Yakzua Style, also sadly Kiryu does not have the power of Tekken to Juggle. Extreme heat is also back, and it increases the amount of Agent Style's Gadgets Kiryu can use; while for DOD/Yakuza Style, it enhances the physical capabilities of it (More damage, and a new light attack combo after the 6th? light attack where Kiryu uses that one heat action but it isn't now). Agent Style has 4 gadgets being a long-range web slinger (Spider), a drone (Hornet), a explosive cigar (Firefly), and a pair of thrusters for the shoes (Serpent). Spider, Hornet, and Firefly's upgrades just increases the number Kiryu can use it, while Serpent's upgrades just increase the duration of the boots. The gadgets are mostly just crowd control gizmos, with Hornet being a distraction for bosses, or enemies. Agent Style's normal attacks are rather lackluster, but Kiryu can dish out more than 7 light attacks. Personally Agent Style is more used for defensive or crowd control situations, but its still a decent style.The Dragon of Dojima style (Yakuza 6 version) is back, and its rather good. There is really nothing to say about this style other than the addition of having an ability to have Triple Finishers (One of the finishers is the Famous Kick), and that the style is rather pretty great.The game's story right off of Yakuza 6, and also runs parallels with Yakuza 7. At the start, Kiryu makes a deal with the Daidoji. Under this deal Kiryu is "Dead", and works with the Daidoji. A new life outside the Yakuza underworld, and a new life under the Daidoji. Daidoji is an organization of elite skilled agents who do contracts from certain other organizations (like the CIA). I would classify the Daidoji faction as a shadow organization since no one really knows it, and the HQ is a temple. Kiryu lives under the new name of Joryu, and is trained in martial arts (Agent Style), and was given gadgets by other Daidoji affiliates. One of Joryu's major tasks refers him to a dockyard where Joryu waits for a truck of gold; however, this turns out to be a trap. Soon Joryu goes to Yokohama (Literally only appears in one chapter), where Joryu investigates the Omi which is also a trap and Joryu's handler, Hanwwa (I don't know how to spell his name; however, its something like that), is kidnapped by two Omi Members Tsueno, and Shishido. The Daidoji does not care about a single member of their team getting kidnapped; however, Joryu cares about him, and the Daidoji does not allow him to leave. Soon Joryu discovers the truth of the kidnapping, and the plot of the Watase Family.To be written... probably trust me.Most of Yokohama is locked out, and its literally only available for the first chapter, and premium adventure. It has nothing to note apart from a reference to Yakuza 7 when Namba found Ichiban.Sotenbori is the main map of LAD:Gaiden, and it added back the park that was removed from Sotenbori in Yakuza Kiwami 2. The map is still the same Sotenbori, apart from the removal of certain businesses, and the addition of others.Pocket Circuit Race returns within Sotenbori; however, Kiryu's favorite buddy, Pocket Circuit Fighter, is sadly not present.The Castle is the "second" map you have access to throughout the game (Yokohama is only available for one chapter and then you're locked out lol). There are two main attractions within the Castle, and those are the gambling hall/Casino, and the coliseum. Not much people gamble within the Yakuza fan base, and instead they just play mahj-, so the coliseum is just the main attraction. Anything else notable? Yes.Like a Dragon Gaiden is a rather good game; however, Yakuza Gaiden is a half of a game, and because of that it is rather short. The Combat follows judgement rather than Lost Judgement, which means no juggling or attack cancelling. The Story is very interesting (Not on any of the Judgement series story's level though), and I can't wait for LAD:IW to come out and continue Kiryu's story in Hawaii. Overall this game is okay, will I recommend it? Eh kind of if you want to see Kiryu's story in Yakuza 7.

_childDocuments_.review: This stems from playing Yakuza 0, Yakuza Kiwami 1, Yakuza Kiwami 2 and Yakuza: Like a Dragon.As far as story telling goes, it not very exciting. It really doesnt get exciting until Chapter 4 (out of 5). Of the games in the series I have played, this really felt like a DLC - A Colosseum game with quests and a lot larger gambling space really is what this game sums up to be. Youre mainly stuck in Sotenbori. Have little to nothing to do in Ijinjo and you dont even get to touch Kamurocho. They do tie in their Yakuza Like a Dragon game and the upcoming games in the series and it does cover the tiny interaction Kiryu had with Kasuga and thats it. They bring back some of the  references and players from their previous titles which kind of gets me engaged just a little more, but the face value it brings falls below my expectation. In perspective, I spent more time finishing the Cyberpunk DLC alone at 100% achievement than this game also at 100% achievements. Ill get more into the game details towards the end. Fighting feels a little sloppy. Im glad they brought back the button mashing brawl way of fighting. He doesnt really reach to hit the next enemy so there is a lot of air combat. You get 2 fighting modes: Agent mode where you can use your weapon arsenal which is great to use for anyone who is not a boss. Then you have Yakuza mode that is good for bosses which is pretty much it. As far as using or finding weapons, you cannot keep or equip any weapon. The weapon you use in that fight only last until the end of the battle scene, until you use a heat action or until you are knocked down. \Unlike other Yakuza games, you can stack similar items and have compounding stacks. Here, you cannot. They got rid of the food combos for more effective healing and they also removed item sets for boosted stats. When youre swapping out gear, the equipment screen does not tells you what stats the current item gives, but it will indicate what stats will change when you swap it out. They dont show duplicates which makes equipping gear much simpler and easier, but its also very limited and shrunken down. Im so glad that the golf mini game has gotten so much better to play. The golf mini game is actually fun to play and enjoyable. The Karaoke game feels like an actual rhythm game now because the buttons match the beats but you can only sing with Akame- no one else.The achievements are realistic to accomplish. Unlike the Kiwami versions of the game, the achievements are impossible feats of perfection. This one at least, you dont have to play the game up to a certain level to be able to get the achievement to pop. Its cool that there are quests you can do depending on the outfit youre wearing. I would like to see more of this in future titles, but make it where you can change your outfit in your home base or even use your Colosseum outfit out in the open like a regular costume. It also shows the change of outfit during the cutscenes. This game only allows you to change outfit in one place, and its troublesome to access sometimes.POCKET RACING - even with guides, you really have to work for your wins and you do really have to utilize your boosts and stabilize abilities at the right times. Its so much more fun. They did try to do something unique with their cabaret club interaction where they make it more like an interactive movie instead of the usual game graphics. Its unique; like the photography studio sidequest on Yakuza Kiwami 1. As for the overall game, the writers did a great job with the ending. It portrayed very strong emotions and does tie in Kiryu (in this case, Joryu) with the whole reason he had his name erased in the first place. Its just THAT ending scene alone is what makes playing thru feel a little rewarding. Still, all things considered, I still felt more disappointed than satisfied (or even just ok) with this game as a whole. its really difficult to justify paying for this game at full price. Its fun, but it just felt lacking - unfinished even. Im really hoping that they get to add perks in the next game for people who bought this one because it really doesnt feel worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: So, getting this out of the way at the top, this game is probably not worth a 50 dollar asking price. Taking the game out of context, there is a lot of game here, but it has little to offer people who aren't already significantly invested in the series, and people who are already significantly invested in the series will find this a very paltry offering compared to RGG studios' normal offerings. Yakuza 0 costs 20 dollars right now and offers easily three times as much content. So, if you're not someone who already desperately wants to know what Kiryu was up to between the events of Yakuza 6 and Yakuza: Like a Dragon, or someone who just wants more Kiryu wherever you can get it, this is not a good investment.For invested fans of the series (which, despite some attempts to make the game accessible and interesting to anyone) Gaiden does offer a great and emotionally gratifying experience. The game is certainly short for a Yakuza/LaD title, as it was originally envisioned as a standalone DLC, and there's only a few notable additions to the formula, but what is there is solid, and the story is on point. The port is also well done, and performs great on my aging hardware while looking beautiful.In short, it's a game that will only appeal to fans of the franchise and might feel a little lacking to its target audience, but it delivers where it counts enough to be well worth fans picking up.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like a dash of Judgment in your Yakuza(/LAD) and that's not a bad thing (such as the strong enemy attacks you can interrupt and follow up with hard-hitting counters and bleeding from bladed weapons). The game is short (by comparison) if you're looking for the usual Yakuza experience but if you are invested in the story of the games, if you want some more context behind a certain character's arrival in Like A Dragon, if you are invested in Kiryu and what he has gone through in his life then this story is really, really good. The ending tore my soul apart in the best way. It really is a must for fans.You will find a some fun references to Yakuza 2 as well as one or two Yakuza 0 callbacks and while it is easy to become overpowered in combat it does, at least, make clearing the street trash rather quick. There are some fun attacks that combine with the agent style but you will find yourself feeling familiar with the style if you've played Judgment (it is not outright copied but has the same tight feel as Yagami's tiger style). Among some incredible cameos I won't spoil, there is a Judgment character who shows up in a really great sub-story. In fact, I'd say the sub-stories in this game are almost all fantastic and worth the time.The arena allows you to play as many different characters (including three from Judgment). The coliseum really does feel like the big showpiece of the game and it's a really is a spectacle to be introduced to. Akame, a new character, is also a fun addition to the cast.Problems:Your mileage may vary but I found the hostess stuff absolutely weird and uncomfortable (but if you're a fan of Kson, that might be different?), two of the four gadgets feel as if you really could just ignore them outright. While there are many options to fight as in the coliseum there is, unfortunately, no real contest between Kiryu's strength and playing as someone like Daigo, Majima, or Saejima (which, while fun, does lack the upgrades Kiryu has). While the group battles in the coliseum are really fun it does bring out a bit of a grind to level your team which might extend gameplay for some but was not quite for me. I also found the omission of some classic heat actions from Kiryu's Yakuza style to be a disappointment. Also, if you happen to be a fan of grappling attacks in combat you can expect to be frustrated as almost all enemies but the weakest will quickly break free. While the agent style does have a fun way to snatch weapons from enemies or the ground there is something lost in not being able to actually carry weapons on your person like previous titles (though you will be familiar with this if you have played the Judgment games).Conclusion:All in all, if you're a Yakuza fan (and have played Yakuza 0 and Yakuza 2 or Judgment) you will find a lot here to like. There are some really great moments where you finally see Kiryu losing his composure and usual cool with where his choices in life have left him and the pain it is putting him through. It's a must for following the Dragon of Dojima and his story and leads into an explanation as to why Kiryu will be found in Infinite Wealth. While it might not be worth full retail price right now, the english dub might be enough to warrant it (if you prefer not to deal with subtitles) but I don't think it will hurt to try and get this game at around 40 or so. If you love the Yakuza storyline, however, the price of admission is worth seeing the emotional ride Kiryu goes through in this title.Quick edit: As for long-time Yakuza fans? You can FINALLY WEAR DIFFERENT OUTFITS WITHOUT HAVING TO BE IN PREMIUM ADVENTURE!

_childDocuments_.review: This game originally was going to be DLC, but it ended up becoming its own stand alone title. You can honestly finish this whole game in 12 hours if you just rush the story. So the game is obviously in the short side but I really think this is one of the best games in the franchise gameplay wise. Story itself without going into spoiler territory is a bit slow at first however it then kicks into high gear in the later chapters. Normally I would have a problem with that style of story telling (Kingdom Hearts 3 left a sour taste in my mouth) but considering the length of the game, it's not horrible to deal with. Side content there's a shocking amount of stuff to do. Substories wise they're a treat as usual with some great fan service. The Colosseum is easily the best it's ever been with the ability to also play as every single ally you recruit into your team is also really awesome, despite the lack of heat actions for them. Gameplay as I mentioned is really REALLY good, It's Lost Judgement combat with even more juggling, and the style switching for juggle combos are really smooth. I'm not claiming to be the sauciest or best gamer in the universe, however I hit some saucy ass combos on some bosses and it felt really satisfying. Agent is a really sick new style and the gadgets are pretty funny to mess around with, and the traditional Dragon Style feels at its absolute best in this game, really shows RGG is improving the combat with every new game they make. TLDR tho, I would honestly still wait for a sale, despite all the praise I've given this game. cuz you're paying for a 12 hour game featuring a demo of Infinite Wealth.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a Dragon Gaiden feels to me like the perfect distillation of the best parts of modern Yakuza games, compressed down into a package that's much more compact than other recent entries while still providing the same mix of compelling story, incredible combat, and wildly varied mini-games and side content. As a companion to Yakuza 7, it provides a wonderful feeling of familiarity, and as a standalone entry in the franchise, it stands tall among the better entries in the series.By nature, Gaiden is a much shorter game than 7 or either of the Judgment games - it's designed as a side-story, returning to Kiryu to fill in the gaps in his narrative between his exit in Yakuza 6 and his small side-role in Yakuza 7. Despite clearly being a shorter narrative, though, I found that it felt plenty meaty, moreso than several of the pre-5 entries in the series. I think a big part of this is that its story is split across just five chapters, making each of those chapters quite long compared to how these games are usually structured. The end result is that the narrative has very little downtime, with only a few periods where the story gives you the time to poke around and do whatever you want for a little while. The story is typically split between serious, heavily-written drama and absurdity, centering Kiryu's struggle to continue on in a life that, in his perception, no longer has meaning, and this narrative thread carries him through to where he seems to end up in Infinite Wealth. It's well-written and feels like it does Kiryu much more justice than 6 did, while setting him up for a potentially perfect true departure from the franchise with the next game.The combat is not quite peak Dragon Engine combat - Yakuza Style still feels weird and retread-y even with the tweaks to combat borrowed from the Judgment games, but Agent Style is an absolute revelation and completely justifies the weird narrative framework of the Daidoji faction. Seeing Kiryu shoot out Spider-Man webs and whip people around relentlessly, zip around on rocket boots, summon literally fifty drones to irritate every enemy in sight, and blow people up with explosive cigarettes is both hysterical and deeply satisfying. The group/1v1 split in the styles is still clear, with Agent ideal for clearing out large groups of enemies and Yakuza best suited to one-on-one showdowns, but it often felt like a necessity to switch to Yakuza rather than a choice I was glad to make. On the whole, though, it's still modern Yakuza combat, and it still just feels great.On the whole, Gaiden is another worthy entry in the Yakuza franchise, far more essential than its side-story nature suggests. As a brawler-style palate cleanser between the turn-based 7 and 8, it's extremely fun, and it provides a great mix of connective tissue between the games and standalone entertainment and intrigue. Pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely loved this game. Its events occur at the same time as Like a Dragon's, so it's quite a self-contained game story-wise, but it still took me 20+hr to beat the game and side content (notably, substories and arena, didn't quite never got into Pocket Circuit racing).As Kiryu's last dance approaches (presumably), we get to see him in action again from the ending of Y6 until the ending of Like a Dragon. This time around, Kiryu's some kind of secret agent with gadgets and all, which give some variety to the combat gameplay. First few hours of combat fell a bit stale and lack options, but variety quickly grows and combat gets funnier very soon as you start unlocking new moves.We get the same old Yakuza Style, and the brand new Agent Style, which is a more swift, agile combat approach in which you can use Kiryu's gadgets. Some of them felt pretty useless (cigar and drones), but thread and rocket-powered shoes felt like they added variety and added some strategical options, so a nice change of pace. It's not like fights are very difficult anyway, specially since this game allows us to unlock Tiger Drop as early as chapter 1...Music and voice acting are top tier as usual and the graphics are the same formula as ever: gorgeous for main character models, more modest in environments, and some PS3 sprinkle for NPCs...If anything, I would complain that unlike in Y6 or LaD, Gaiden's new characters didn't really leave a mark on me. Kiryu and the old dogs steal the show, really. Though I would like to see Akame back, she seems qualified to take over as a new kind of Florist of Sai.All in all, if Like a Dragon franchise is the kind of game you enjoy, this is close to the greater ones, so don't hesitate to give it a try. Solid 8-8.5 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Overview:Depending on how you look at it, this is either a low-effort dlc-into-full-game spinoff or part of a proper send-off of the Kiryu Era or objectively both.Part of the reason why some would buy this game is that it is possible RGG will move on from  the older Yakuza action games  as they continue onwards in the Ichiban era, but moving on seems hard for both the developer and the players.Supporting this game might send a message they should do more action spinoffs like this and Judgment now that turn-based is the MAIN game.Regardless - the point of this game is that it is intended as a final sendoff for those who were invested into the older games and an excuse to make people pay for Kiryu. You get backstory of Kiryu addressing events from Yakuza 6 and Y:LAD and a linkage + demo to Infinite Wealth.Spoiler Advisory for old and new players:To be clear, this is game for the fans from the Kiryu era. It is heavy on references that need most players to play those game to appreciate them.If you are new, ensure you played at least Yakuza: Like a Dragon before you play this game to avoid spoiling yourself. Knowledge of Yakuza 6 is recommended but not optional.While you should play this game before Infinite Wealth, but it isn't *strictly necessary* based on the story I seen for myself. Not everything about Kiryu in IW is addressed in this game but if you love Kiryu anyway, just play this game before IW if you can.Why you should play this game (slight spoilers):- You are a big RGG/Kiryu fan like me- A lot of references to older games. Probably most of all the Kiryu Y0-Y6 games.- You enjoy the fan service, familiar minigames and familiar 4-king-something subplots- You enjoy dressing up Kiryu- You think live-action girls cabaret is awesome (meh)- And you think it's cool to play as an Agent (it's a little absurd and tech superhero-like)- You want to see the latest Sotenbori (it's the ONLY main map in this game. the rest don't really count)- You want to try the Infinite Wealth demo (unlocks after completing game)- You are okay with the pricingWhy you should wait for a sale or skip for Infinite Wealth (again, slight spoilers):- You expect new and fresh things. There's not much 'new things' aside from agent style and cabaret. The main driving point of this game is just narrative and sentimentalism. No new minigames, just a reboot of Pocket Circuit. And a Coliseum.- It's quite obvious this game was indeed finished in 6 months. Most of the stuff here are carried from older games. Some parts feel abit unpolished. Just adjust your expectations accordingly.- There's only one completely new karaoke song. Horrifying!- There's half of the side stories, and only 1/4 of them is interesting (imho). I never really liked the four-king subplot but here it is, occupying 2/5 of the substories.- It's too expensive for half the content of any Yakuza game- You aren't interested in the minigames, sidestories, coliseum, challenges, etc. Then you probably will get even less value of this and probably can finish the game in 2-3 days.Also the Judgment crossover is one of the bigger sidestories. But it has no dedicated voiced lines for story, just recycled grunting. Google yourself to find out more.I love crossovers but this one just feels abit meh. Consider it as bait.Side note on Difficulty:Dev tries to make the game more accessible through 'action assist' and a 'combat tip' that show things that the game think is helpful. The video is ok (abit annoying) and can be toggled off, but the action assist doesn't work very well, trigger things without your consent and makes you unable to learn the combat, manage your heat bar or fight unpredictably.Recommend most people to just play normal mode at start. The economics of this game is easy enough for you to eat regularly and prep enough heals.TLDR: Only Real Yakuza/Kiryu Fans should buy this game. Everyone else should wait for a sale or play any or the older games, or just invest in Infinite Wealth. That game is likely to be rad based on the demo I played.

_childDocuments_.review: *Some Minor Spoilers*Like A Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name is a conclusion to a Saga that should have definitively ended in 2016's Yakuza 6: The Song of Life.Yakuza 6 is by all means not a “bad” game and definitely not a terrible conclusion to Kazuma Kiryu's story. Instead, it is remembered as a game that didn't have the proverbial guts to end the Dragon of Dojima’s seven game journey. Yakuza 6 did numerous things correctly by establishing Kiryu as a grandfather and introducing us to a new cast of supporting characters in Onomichi, Hiroshima.  Unfortunately, The game seemed allergic to using legacy characters in the Saga and relegated most of them to the wayside in favor of a new supporting cast.  In consequence, Kiryu's final game feels smaller and intimate, for better or worse. If this truly was the end of Kiryu's story, then Yakuza 6 should have been a celebration of the same. Instead, The end product was just another mainline Yakuza game and not the emotional climax of the journey. As we watch Kiryu walk down that street, fans are instead teased for more. The Dragon never dies. And the tease bore fruit. Kiryu returns as the sole playable protagonist of Like A Dragon Gaiden. Once again described as Kiryu's send off, Gaiden is set with the task of providing its audience with a smaller, intimate, and emotionally satisfying ending for one of gaming's greatest protagonists and it does so successfully.Gaiden's story places Kiryu in an interesting setting, practically divorced from his legendary life and past relationships. Over the course of the game, Kiryu forges new bonds, fights against a new bunch of baddies, and eventually enters an ideological battle for the future of the Yakuza. In the midst of all this crime ridden chaos, Kiryu's emotional journey remains at the forefront even if it doesn't seem obvious. Kiryu doesn't show a lot of emotions in the story, the logic of its plot makes it necessary to do so. But when Kiryu's stoic veil falls, the writers really make it count.Takaya Kuroda brings his performance of Kazuma Kiryu to new heights, delivering a beautifully human performance for a historically stoic character. For the first time in years, the writing truly allows Kiryu to become incredibly vulnerable, giving Kuroda a chance to show us a side of Kiryu never seen before. At one point, I was convinced that there were no stories left to tell with this character until Takaya Kuroda proved me wrong. There is much to tell with this character, even if this is the final stretch. It's one of the greatest voice acting performances in the video game canon and leaves its ending as the best in the series. Kudos to the facial animations as well, the emotional scenes would have been hollow without the fantastic work behind them.Speaking of the ending, I can definitely say that the final chapter is an all time great experience. Upon its arrival, the game fires on all cylinders to deliver a climactic and emotionally resonant experience filled to the brim with fist fights, team ups, hype moments, climatic showdowns, and a greater degree of emotional vulnerability for Kiryu. It’s seemingly the end of a Saga until Infinite Wealth finds a way to top it. While I cannot say much about the ending, what I can say is that it is a fantastic ending. An explosion of emotions built up over several games. Jacob Geller in his "The Best Games of 2023" video, once called the final hours a “transcendent experience.” I am inclined to agree. This is amazing stuff and they saved the best for last.If it's not obvious by now, the characters are the biggest strength of The Man Who Erased His Name. All of them are memorable in their own right, even if some are more developed than others.  Within the short runtime, the story is able to develop its cast of new characters with varying degrees of success. Characters like Akame and Shishido are standouts and have already become fan favorites. This is thanks to the lovely character writing and great acting from their voice actors, delivering the human qualities this franchise is known for.However, other characters such as Hanawa are written in a strange way. Hanawa typically doesn't show much emotion, but he does reveal some humanity in rare and interesting moments. Upon further examination, this is by design. But you would have to play the game to see it yourself. Despite the interesting writing and time spent, it was hard to fully invest into Hanawa. A true shame as the character makes a substantial appearance in Infinite Wealth.Unfortunately, Gaiden has pacing issues in the story. The game mandates the player to engage with the game's side content such as The Akame Network and the Coliseum before moving onto the main story throughout the various chapters. This results in an inorganic and frustrating introduction to side content that takes away the narrative momentum of the story.The strangely slow pacing is saved by the fun of Gaiden’s combat that I absolutely loved. This is the best brawler combat the franchise has ever done. It’s smooth, responsive, and incredibly fun to play. The game provides the player two fighting styles to toy around with. The first is the Agent style, which turns Kiryu into a methodical and elegant fighter and provides him with gadgets such as Flying drones and the Spider rope. His movement is swift and can transform a battle from a brawl to a fluid dance if done right. A far cry from the destructive, forceful, and familiar Dragon of Dojima fighting style that is also provided as the second fighting style in the game. The fighting styles serve to show Kiryu’s development as a character, that he has become refined and patient as shown with the Agent Style.While some of its plot elements remain underdeveloped, some characters aren’t that interesting, and its pacing is somewhat of a mixed bag, the story of The Man Who Erased His Name remains to be a good and rewarding experience. The focus on Kiryu pays off spectacularly and the Saga is capped off nicely.  The gameplay may be typically “Yakuza”, but it remains fun and polished to play. 8/10

I never had an issue with getting enough , though I did have an issue getting money as that is also used to get upgrades. However, there are ways to get money - it’s just that I ran out most of the time getting upgrades and buying healing items.As mentioned before, The  has a few side quests for you to complete that will earn you money and . There are also  missions for you to complete that will give you the same rewards. This can raise your  and the higher it is, your rank will go up in the , which is a secret area you can visit that has a colosseum for you to fight other people.However, I do have one issue with the gameplay and that is with the  style; it’s underwhelming. The issue comes with the fact that the  style is better for taking out enemies as a whole. While the  is useful for crowd control and there are upgrades to grab more enemies with it, that also has an issue. To use any of the gadgets you have to hold down the button. So, for example, if I want to use the , I will have to hold the B button on my controller and this applies to the other ones as well. To get them out is a bit slow and you are kind of a sitting duck while doing so.Except for the  gadget, that one makes you move and it seems to be quick to activate. I wish I could have used  more but besides the delay of holding X and the time it takes for the smoke to explode, it's not worth it as sometimes it will be out of range of enemies and can hurt you and your allies.The graphics for the game are honestly beautiful with some of the scenes being simply breathtaking, all backed up with a fantastic soundtrack.I tested the game on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 3GB, AMD Ryzen 5 1500X Quad-Core Processor 3.50, and 16 GB of RAM. I experienced no issues while I was playing, and the game ran fine for me. Although there were some drops in my frames a few times that may be due to the fact I need new PC parts, only time will tell if I can run the next game.I had a ton of fun with , but I need to mention that if you are someone who is starting out with the series, I'd avoid this game for now, as you won’t understand the story of this game all that well. Also, the game is only 6-7 hours long. There is a lot of side content but that only brings it up to about 20-40 hours in length. _childDocuments_.review: Set between 7 and 8, a conclusion to a certain bodyguard's story. The main story is very short relative to past games, so it is very obvious it is being padded out with Akame side content to slow down the progress. During the early parts it does not affect the pacing that much, but during late game the point requirements forces the player to do all the substories and minigames for points, on top of grinding for stupid amount of money in the Castle, to upgrade abilities.The battle system is  like Judgement(two styles), one for solo and another for group. Classic battle style is good from the get go but Agent requires a lot of investment in abilities to become usable and eventually very fun. Suzuki Taichi's basic moves are greatly simplified in this entry so being able to call 20 drones to do the fighting instead is great to have. On the topic of fights, from a pure game play pov there are no memorable fights nor bosses in the mainline quest, maybe in a longer game there will be more time for character developments to hype things up, but boss fights are shockingly plain. Past entries you have some random guy that bust out the door with machine guns, and chainsaws, and some other . In this entry the most interesting boss is a dude wielding a tanto that gets knocked out before he can even show anything.....Perhaps the most praiseworthy aspect of Y7.5 is the graphics. On a mid range set up I can max out every graphic setting and still run the game stable at 60fps. The lighting, assets, special effects and detailed character models looks amazing in most environment. Compared to Y7, it felt like there is a greater emphasis on uping the saturation and contrasts to make cut-scenes more dramatic, sometimes it gets too dark to see any details on default gamma settings.Overall: Amazing teaser for Y8, play it.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven’t played many of the yakuza games. I have all of the main ones (aside from 6, judgement and ishin), but I have never played them. I was a couple chapters into zero, but I stopped and got burnt out. This game is a master piece. The ending genuinely brought tears to my eyes and don’t know much about the prior story.In this yakuza game, there is only two styles. If my knowledge from playing zero is consistent, there’s usually more. However this isn’t to say they aren’t varied. The agent style and all of its gadgets are absolutely amazing and allow for some great combinations. The yakuza style is also great and has that impact. Due to having only two styles, it’s extremely easy to swap to a different style. This allows for an amazing chain of heavy yakuza attacks and utilising the agents gadgets. This honestly makes this one of the most creative combat I have seen in gaming. This really links back to a core ideal that is shown throughout the game that combat its self is art. The fact that the combat parallels so well with the story itself is amazing.The story of Like a dragon gaiden: the man who erased his name is not your typical mob story. It’s intricate, it shows the dynamics of honour and what it truly means for someone to go underground and lose everything that had meaning to them. It also shows that there are two ways to go about it. You can rise up and keep on going or you can just give up. I don’t want to go into too many details to avoid spoilers, but the ending was perfect  is just so endearing to see that such a stoic figure can such deep and intricate emotion.The minigames, as with any yakuza game, are heavily prevalent. Every game is fun. I will admit, I didn’t try nearly enough, but the karaoke was amazing and the pool was fun. Not to mention the cabaret clubs were… fun to say the least ;) . All of these things packed into the small map is amazing and really makes it feel so good. Speaking of the small area, I actually got to memorise the place and I didn’t have to use the map at all at one point. I knew where ashibata park was and I knew where shokofuchu street was.Like a dragon: gaiden is truly amazing. I am ashamed it didn’t win any awards this year, but that doesn’t change the testament that this is an amazing game. I am happy I played through it the way I have been doing prior games at just one game at a time. I truly must recommend this to anyone who wants to get into the yakuza/like a dragon series.

_childDocuments_.review: So - yes, I recommend it with hesitance.  I got it on a very steep discount.It's a decently good story - if you ignore the final sequence before the ending.   It's a bit difficult to follow what's going on, because it assumes that you are intimately following the story from all the way back to Yakuza 0.  There's even an intersection with Yakuza 7 (the first Like a Dragon), all the way to a specific set of cutscenes, and it'd been so long since I played that game I didn't remember the segment was there too until I looked it up on Wikipedia.  I did remember the homeless camp where Ichiban goes after he gets injured, but that's all I'd remembered. That's not to say it's a bad story, it's just that the subsequent games don't do a good enough job of revisiting older segments.  There's too much assumption about how closely you follow this stuff.Final Fantasy X did so good of a job with its world building that by the time you played X-2 that came out years later, everything was 100% recognizable; that's how it should have been done here but wasn't.What I REALLY liked though?  This fight engine is how Street Fighter should be like.  I absolutely loved pulling off counters and neutralizing baddies with a smoothness that I've never experienced in any game before or since.  It's also a generally visually impressive looking game over all (lip sync is a bit questionable, but don't really care about that).But...- Akame should have been a love interest.  Period.  She came across like just a helper, and that's nowhere close to what she really is/was.- The excessive "stab with knife, cut with sword, smash with bricks" mantra only to have guys constantly come back over and over and keep on fighting (via cutscene).  I would say more, but it would spoil things.  Bottom line: it suffers from the "Kingdom Hearts" syndrome.- This is an EXTREMELY short game.  The core gameplay itself - with no side content - can't be more than 10 hours.  My playtime is rushing and purposely watching the full cutscenes when they played; the cutscenes have to be half of the playtime.  It's ridiculous (and I LOVE cutscenes).So I recommend it...but NOT at full price.  It's a generally fun game, but it's simply not a $60-70 game.

_childDocuments_.review: For a smaller-scale game, this is an extremely comprehensive Yakuza package; it easily triumphs many of the mainline games in all around quality. These games are so great, and I hope RGG continues to work their magic until the day I die.I had soured on Like a Dragon Gaiden a lot since its initial release. The way its narrative is treated in Infinite Wealth did not mix well with the fact I found myself decently disillusioned with the two action-based Yakuza-adjacent games I've played most recently. Upon a spontaneous second playthrough, I have learnt that my hindsight had failed me. This game is great, nay more than great!The combat in this game is so much fun. Both styles are infinitely expressive and are smooth as I am after my bi-weekly full body wax. Most older Yakuza games have combat that would not feel out of place in the worst sort of licensed game, but, subtly, they've sharpened their craft quite a bit over the years. The music goes crazy style, with subtle melodic call-backs to some of the series' greatest tunes. I'm no (D)Anthony Fantano, but to me this soundtrack is scientifically divine. The narrative also fervently owns. It may have several lulls, but I believe it to be a well written and exciting drama. In particular, the final scene in this game is a masterclass in the type of soapbox storytelling Yakuza games aspire to. It made me cry a lot more this playthrough than I did the first time around. I did not expect that.These games have slowly found their own little pocket within my heart, and I now think it's fair to say this series means a lot to me. I love Kazuma Kiryu. I love the Yakuza games. Often I throw about the word love carelessly when writing about videogames, but I use it here in the most emotional and the most affectionate way. They will remain a part of me forever, and will always push me forwards. For that, I am appreciative. And when searching for a word to describe this appreciation, I find that love is the only one that fits. This game is good. You should play it. Thanks for reading.There is a hefty chunk of other stuff in this game which I did not talk about, as I skipped through it! There is a free trial for this game on Steam right now. You can play the game for a whopping 4 hours! I can now confirm that if you put the game on easy mode and skip through all the cutscenes (apart from the ones you really like) you can beat this entire game within this time constraint. You can even play the Infinite Wealth demo for a bit! Pardon my French, but that is pretty swell!!

_childDocuments_.review: This game does not at all let you know it was made in the span of 6 months in parallel with 2 other games from the studio.    As a Like A Dragon entry, it's well paced and punches way above its weight with a very cohesive narrative that still has its classic mood swing charms, yet it avoids the messy plot webs of the PS3 era games that might make it too nauseating for less committed fans. Kiryu's characterization is even stronger than it was in the previous games, but it still finds time to explore and discuss the formerly-titular organisations that this franchise is actually about.    As a standalone game, it is one of the shiny gems of 2023 with a characteristically strong desire to make an enjoyable product and tell a compelling story. The downside i can see in playing this game as a person unfamiliar with the series, however, is that structurally, Gaiden is heavily reliant on callbacks and references to at least 4 previous titles, from characters that are mentioned to events that are retold, which can leave a new player with gaps in the understanding of the overall story.    The $50 price tag, though, might just be a bit too steep for a game with about half the playtime of a mainline title, especially considering that most of the secondary content is reused from previous titles.    Overall, this is one of the best entries of the franchise, and its a fairly high bar.
