_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: Ultros is one of the most intriguing games ever, not only from a narrative perspective but also in terms of gameplay and how the two are intertwined. Completing it 100% is only for the select few but in my opinion Ultros is a must play for metroidvania lovers, atleast up to the first ending. As many of the reviews point out though this may vary depending on the person. Reason being the sort of reset mechanic that happens several times throughout the game. This initially worried me greatly so i sorta rushed the start to get a feel for this mechanic within the 2 hour refund window. In hindsight it is not that bad at all, especially because by the 3rd loop you know when and more specifically where a reset happens. . The fun thing about this is that the game opens up new pathways every loop so it really doesn't feel that samey as people make it out to be. These new paths do a good job of guiding you through the game's substantial map, which features a set of varied and unique biomes. Most areas play pretty differently so there's a lot of variety in that regard. You can discover most of said biomes on your first pass through but like any good metroidvania there's some stuff for later. Level design is pretty solid in general so exploring each area is pretty fun the first time. On loop resets your map discovery is kept, but unfortunately broken barriers also reset. This is the one thing i would have loved to see handled differently as it's a bit of a headache sometimes. There are other things that do persist though mainly the things that you plant. Because other than a metroidvania with roguelite elements this game is also a farming game??!This caught me pretty of guard initially but by the 3rd loop it became clear how much this would change the map in future loops which is super unique and also kinda fun (for the most part). It also ties into the games' narrative and symbolism super well so i must say that it worked for this game. The unfortunate thing though is that seeds get lost upon resets but luckily there's always the right ones nearby. These plants play a MUCH bigger role in the post game to get the true ending but at this point the mechanic becomes very convoluted as it's no longer as straight forward which plant to put where. There's tons of soil patches, 10 different plant types and the matter of composting it or not. To save yourself a headache i'd suggest using a guide after you get the first ending as that's still possible at this point if you're interested in getting the proper ending.I got about halfway this true ending when i decided that i was no longer enjoying the mechanic. Even with the proper plants in place there's still some fiddling about with your gardening tools and i felt like i was fighting the controls a bit. Up till this point the controls had been super smooth though, not only for the platforming but also in combat. The platforming is a bit basic but the environments add fun obstacles like scaled that tip or jumping pads. In combat it also responds quickly and while combat as a whole is rather quite easy there's still enough going on to be engaging. Bosses were fun and unique too, although not as hard as most other MV's. You can make it easier yet by spending points in the talent tree. You unlock these by eating your enemies' remains, with cleaner kills (using different moves rather than button mashing) yielding better spoils.These upgrades also get lost upon reset, except for when you use a special collectible item to lock these memories. These as well as lore bits are the games' true collectibles and finding enough of them to lock the whole skilltree was one of my primary motivators to progress in the game. Other than exploring the map and unveiling the story ofcourse! Said story is just impeccable. The way it ties the central mechanic into it as well as the environmental storytelling on display is just amazing. Your starting location tells something the game never explicitly mentions but which the eagle eyed players will soon pick up on. Most metroidvania's go light on story but this one i'd say it's the focussing point. And they nailed it, not only in the overal story but also the backstory of each character/zone.Speaking of zones the visual variety is great, you have gardens, luxury districts, living quarters, temples and even a distillery. The overal game is just beautiful but that's something nearly every person agrees on and is apparant from the very first time you see a screenshot or boot up the game. What you don't see initially but will hear soon enough is just how utterly INCREDIBLE the soundtrack is. The song 'broken promise' which plays in the rotten orchard especially is just downright beautiful. I'm picking up a copy of the game's OST which i'm listening to as i'm writing this and will continue listening to for a long time. In some ways i'm even happier i played the game because it introduced me to the OST so even if you don't plan on playing this game, do yourself a favor and give it a listen.Finally there's performance which at this point was spotless. I also had no bugs, like at all... I'm actually suprised about this given how many systems the game has to keep track off in terms of physics and all the different plants. At first i thought these were static in their growth but with the later tools you can manipulate these quite a bit so the fact that it worked as well as it did was suprising to me. I had no crashes either or any other technical hickups and loading times were super fast. So technically the game is incredibly polished. It's a super unique experience that is super enjoyable untill the first ending. After this engaging with the more finnicky gardening mechanics became more of a chore but not enough to leave a sour taste. I'm perfectly happy where i left it off and may revisit this title some day to finish it up.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: Every time I shut down this game, I need an hour or so to touch the ground again, and uhh... I am trying to write a review after having finished it.This game is extremely unique. I love the bizarre and ethereal music, the beautiful and alien art, the central concept of connection and gentleness, and just, this amazing and intriguing world teeming with life. Trying to make a Metroidvania with new ideas is a gargantuan challenge, and I honestly believe that the gardening system in this game is one of freshest, most brilliant puzzle mechanics I have seen in several years. Initial impressions can be confusing, but rest assured, there is an answer to everything if you keep pressing forward. There is a surprising number of combat moves, which makes sense given how the game's hunting system works. However, the combat challenge is actually very, very low for the genre - and that is okayI have no complaints worth making about the game itself. I did experience some programming bugs that hindered progression (ie. soft-locking because I entered a save capsule and the game didn't load the menu, or doing so because it can't load the next screen for some reason). I also don't appreciate that the frame limiter doesn't kick in until you get in-game, nor do I appreciate the game turning my DS4's light green or yellow for some reason.This game is something truly special, and it is absolutely worth picking up if you are interested in Metroidvanias, psychedelic imagery, or planting gardens. You won't find the next Hollow Knight in here, but you will find whispers of a future we have yet to attain
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: A psychedelic surrealist metroidvania that tries to do a lot of new things in combination with a stark and vivid art style. While I was initially excited to delve into the game I quickly found myself bouncing off it.The art style is probably what stands out most about the game and granted it is beautiful, with vivid colours and creative animations all blending biology with technology. Unfortunately the game lacks an understanding of contrast. There is so much detail and colour that it's difficult to tell what is foreground vs. background. Interactive vs. inert. The visual language games have - colours that communicate qualities and mechanics, sparkles and particles that denote interactivity - all become lost in this haze of overwhelming colour and movement.The combat itself is trying to stand apart in a few ways. Your first sword has very short reach and you are encouraged to pull off a combo with minimal repeated moves - though it doesn't specify what actions count as repetitive, and this early on I only have two attacks so it seems obtuse to demand variety. Equally the combat is very rigid with a dodge-and-counter approach that requires you to learn to 'dance' with each foe - learning the patterns in a very structured way that feels at odds with the ultra natural and flowing world. The limitations end up feeling like enemies have a 'correct' way to be killed in spite of your options.The skill tree also feels very messy. Killing enemies rewards food items (portions of their body) and the quality depends if you killed it 'elegantly' or not. Food items fill some amount of the four bars that represent your nutrition, and these bars can be emptied to learn new skills. It's a nice idea albeit convoluted, with quantities being very imprecise so you can't plan ahead (maybe I'm being too rigid now). In the first hour I unlocked maybe 5-10 of these upgrades but they were for small granular things I hardly noticed or for features I hadn't even learned to use a 'normal' way yet so my choices didn't feel very impactful or meaningful. Not that the upgrade tree seems to have any coherent structure either.In the same way my first hour of play didn't feel like I was really accomplishing anything. Part of this is contrast again - the signal to noise ratio on all of the dialogue is mixed. Everything is intentionally obtuse and seems to be style at the expense of substance, you just vaguely understand that someone needs to be killed because they're preventing you from leaving. Even item descriptions are surrealist contradictory nonsense - things 'taste of time' and 'smell of Elysium'. Part of my attraction to the game was that it seemed to have a detailed and cohesive alien world to learn about, but it feels more like everything is being made up as the artist goes. The detail is there because it looks cool not because it's functional, the writing is flowery nonsense because it sounds cool, not because it means anything.In conclusion, I get the feeling Ultros is a result of inexperience. Not that it isn't an impressive looking game - but the level of presentation betrays a lack of fundamentals. There are essential game design elements that are missing or roughly hewn, it's not unplayable but certainly sets up some expectations that miss the mark. I'm sure some folks will get everything out of this they want, but for me it just hit all the wrong buttons unfortunately.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: I'm quite mixed on this one. This game has an interesting take on the metroidvania genre, but it suffers from requiring a lot of patience in order to be able to do actions most metroidvanias already have given you.Experimenting with plants is a brilliant concept, even more interesting when they can be used to create new platforms, allows wall running, or going to a higher areas by attaching a plant head that launches you far away on a tall tree. There are so many things you can do, granted if you have a lot of patience and plant seeds in your disposal to experiment with, and this is where the issue lies.Some plant seeds are located at remote areas, and due to the game's time loop nature, if you forgot to use those seeds, you have to go back collecting them at their respective areas. Some walls are only breakable from plants, but the question is, what plant should you use? You have to consider the geography when choosing the plant; which requires you to understand how the plant works and interacts with the environment, and these requires a lot of patience and experimentation. The one I hate the most is in Greggamoja Refinery, where you have to use a spray ability to bend the stem of a plant so they grow along the flow of water, and it becomes tedious when the gimmick of this region is doing this across the entire region.Other mechanics that require you to use plants are unlocking mechanical doors and allowing current save point to be fast-travel-able. A lot of areas don't have any soil to begin with, but you can feed the enemies so they can tender the soil or even generate new soil in that location. You have to do a lot of work just to be able to fast travel, which is insane really. Games usually reward you with fast travel so you can backtrack for collectibles, but in this game you backtrack to unlock fast travel primarily, then the collectibles.I can see the whole focus of this game is about the nature; hence why a lot of mechanics in this game are tied to the plants. The story is also related to the nature, where you become one with them. You care for the soil, and the nature will reward you. It is an idea that I really liked, but perhaps done too much to the point the gameplay hampers down my enjoyment towards the whole narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: It took a little getting used to post-demo, but I dig it a lot. The gardening mechanic is very cool, but I will be honest that I was a bit put off the first time I got time looped (if you played the demo, it's directly after the end of the demo).Disregard the reviews with one hour of game time pegging this as a rogue-lite. It surely is not.There is a re-birthing time loop mechanic, but it is not on death, and the progression is not rogue-lite esque. It IS a metroidvania with some unique twists- and it is possible that not everyone will like all of them. But if you only gave it an hour, you didn't give it a chance. Your map and exploration, as well as your gardening, is persistent between loops.With that said, you do need to re-learn skills that you've unlocked- done by hunting and harvesting the enemies for different flavors of experience. It is quick to do, and fairly fun. It was a bit off-putting to me at first, but you can 'lock' favorite skills before you time loop, thus increasing your ability to explore and fight each time.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: It took me a while to get into it as it starts slow and unimpressive, not taking into account the dazzling colours. This game is honestly one of the most vibrant visual feasts out there. I wasn't a fun of the it being yet another exercise in loops and rogue mechanics, but good news is, it's short and sweet, therefore, you don't get a chance to get tired of it.When it comes to combat, there's not a lot of it as the variety of enemies is low. It's the bosses where it gets fun. It's surprising as you get a big variety of attacks, but you'll find out why in due time. The controls are responsive, but the aerial combat is hit and miss... mostly miss.As with most roguelikes, there are plenty abilities to unlock and lose an hour later. Thankfully, if you look around, you find a way to memorise them. Very soon losing them is not a bother. Some I never used as I didn't fully use the mechanic to grow food. I can imagine it's essential for the full experience though. Eating is how you regain health and unlock abilities, as each plant has different nutritional values. It's a neat idea.Metroidvania shows it's face by introducing you to an expansive map full of secrets and hidden passages. Exploration is, therefore, a big part of this game. That and platforming. Ultros generally balances multiple genres well and presents some unique an wacky ideas. It's little shocking it seems not that many people finished it.Last thing I want to mention is the music. Simply amazing and different then anything else. When it goes full on jazz at some point, I'm not sure why I'm still surprised.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game. At first glance and for the first couple hours it seems great, but once you've made it through the first couple cycles the glaring flaws start to show. The devs made some serious design flaws when making this game that really hold it back. For example having to do the combat training sequence every new cycle if you go through the area, which you don't even get to until your third cycle anyway. Why would you have to do a tutorial every new cycle? Being cut off from previous areas with no apparent reason why. The skill tree is 50% useless skills/perks you will never use. And the bosses are extremely ez. I'm on cycle 5 and I've died once. Game is very easy especially if you've played a lot of Metroidvanias.The worst thing about this game though is the exploration. That's one of the best qualities of a gear Metroidvania. In Ultros, all areas look more or less the same with the same color scheme and aesthetic making it really annoying to trying to remember if you've been somewhere or not. You pretty much just have to memorize the layouts or go off landmarks.Hate to give this a thumbs down because it could have been a good game, but due to some severe design flaws I can't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: Ultros has plenty of charm and interesting things going on compared to your typical metroidvania.  It’s a fairly good game with a bit of a niche.  Being underground exploring and dealing with plant life vaguely reminded me of an adventure/exploration game from 2012 called . The first few hours of my playthrough had me quite confused.  I was concerned that I’d find various aspects of the game frustrating, but I just went with what Ultros was throwing at me and things progressed very smoothly.  I’d start each new loop with no idea as to what I should be doing, but the way that the game pushed me in different directions despite me feeling kind of lost was quite clever.  The sound/art is nice, I really dig the colours and art style.  I didn’t find it difficult to distinguish backgrounds from foregrounds and enemies, nor did I have any difficulty tracking my character amongst it all.For better or worse, combat is on the easier side of things. For the most part you just time a dodge (feels like timing a parry in other games), and attack with X + direction, kinda like in Smash Bros.The game wants you to use different attacks on every enemy to be rewarded properly for killing them.  Fortunately you can pretty much do that just by pressing X + a different direction each time.   Bosses look nice enough, but they are total pushovers.  This isn't a game that you play for the combat.As far as the concern from players that hate roguelites (And yes, I'm aware that this game isn't one!), the looping didn't feel repetitive in the way that a roguelite sometimes can. I didn't feel as though I was repeating the same stages over and over.  I felt like I was going in new directions in a persistent world, the feeling is far more what you'd expect from metroidvanias. When I started a new loop, I didn't feel as though I was enduring a great deal of repetition in order to find new ways.As well as acquiring a set of metroidvania abilities, killing enemies nets you plants which you can eat to unlock skills from the skill tree.  ..It is a very small and basic tree.  I think of it as some extra sauce, and not as anything too important.  After the first couple of loops you’ll pretty much have this maxed most of the time without needing to give it much thought.  When you start a new loop, you won’t lose many skills that you care about because you’ll have locked them in with your.. ‘brain thingies’.  You probably won’t have enough ‘brain thingies’ to do that for the first loop or two, but you quickly pick up so many enemy parts to reacquire your lost skills that it hardly matters.  Also on a new loop, and separate from these skills, the main metroidvania abilities need to be reacquired from a specific room on the map, which isn’t much of a hike and didn’t bother me in the slightest.The gardening is an interesting part to this metroidvania, overshadowing the combat and platforming.  You'll grow various plants that can open up paths to new areas.  Each plant is a little bit different, some sturdy ones acting as platforms, others as vines that you can swing on, and so on.  Unfortunately your metroidvania abilities are mostly gardening tools to aid with this.     In the later parts of the game the gardening becomes kind of a finicky puzzle.  You'll need to work out which plants you can manipulate to expand across the map further. It’s tricky to differentiate the plants from one another as they look pretty similar in your inventory.  It actually became too much of a nuisance for 100% completion for my tastes, so i stopped after getting the first ending. _childDocuments_.review: I don't recommend this game but that doesn't mean it's not necessarily a good game. For me, the visuals are a bit over the top for me and make it actually challenging to play to a degree. You can get used to it over time so it's not impossible, but it is a lot - borderline overstimulating, though I do admire the ambitious art.For me, the reason I don't recommend it is because I thought this was going to be a nice metroidvania but it's a roguelike + metroidvania with loops of death and redoing stuff from scratch and replaying the same parts over and over to progress the story. I just am not in any way, shape, or form, interested in these roguelike formats that make you live in a time loop to stretch gameplay and as soon as I realized, after just under an hour, that this was going to be a game where you're reborn and retrace your steps, I was done and refunded it. _childDocuments_.review: Overall, it feels like the combat system would've been incredible if the dev didn't try to force variety down the player's throat. Giving a ton of combat options and letting people experiment with what they prefer (with no penalty) is almost always the best option.I truly wanted to like this game. Despite my short list of good traits, the game really seemed promising, but it fell flat on the most important aspects: the gameplay. A flawed game with beautiful graphics isn't a good game. A game with poor graphics and excellent mechanics will get people hooked. I unfortunately didn't even launch the game until two weeks after purchase, so by the time i tried out the game and realized its shortcomings, I was outside the refund window. _childDocuments_.review: Ultros is not the easiest game to explain. Not only because it takes its psychedelic identity to heart, even during the few crumbs of exposition; the gameplay is similarly baffling at first glance. You might not get it in the opening hour. Is this a metroidvania? Okay, makes sense. The skill tree is a bit quirky, but interesting. Oh, here's an upgrade. I think I'm getting the gist of it.And it resets. All of your stuff, gone. And that's puzzling, because not only the game is most definitely not a roguelike, it also keeps pulling the rug from under you in terms of gameplay. The loops aren't identical. New mechanics keep getting introduced, upgrades you had on previous loops are given to you earlier or in different locations, and it might take quite a few loops for you to finally start finding your footing on what the game is, what it expects you to do, and how it's all going to play out. Oh, and then it introduces another huge mechanic that will slowly change the way you go about the game.And frankly, as frustrating as it might sound (and is), it's part of the beauty of Ultros. It's a puzzling game. I like puzzling games, sometimes. Especially when they have beautiful artwork and soundtrack as this one does, together with a vision for what it wants to be. How it presents itself, the story it tries to tell, all of it is coherent and alluring in equal measure. And I have to say, the ending is nothing short of beautiful.But it also has to be said that Ultros is not the most tactile game I've ever played. Inputs often feel less than tight, and plenty of its mechanics require a precision that borders on frustrating. The skill tree is reductive and, due to the loop gameplay (and upgrades that let you keep the skills between them) are so easy to unlock it becomes almost a small inconvenience.The major mechanic of Ultros involves planting seeds and waiting for them to sprout. This is important both for traversal and for another gimmick that gets introduced later in the game. This, while innovative and (to me) kind of addictive, can be extremely frustrating because first, you need to have the seed you want in your inventory, and second, you need to use the correct one (or a good enough one) and fertilize it if need be. This will have you running around the map for seeds, resetting loops, working towards making garden spots appear and sometimes wild guessing on what could work in this particular spot. Busy work.This can be satisfying, but if all you want is a relaxing metroidvania with regular incremental upgrades to give you that dopamine rush, Ultros is not it. Ultros is demanding, taxing and sometimes monotonous. You know, like gardening.And like gardening, if you put in the time, you'll see it bloom. There is something amazing about the way it subtly, but definitely, makes the player change the way they play the game. It's not forced on you; it evolves naturally from understanding it. Mindlessly beating the flora and fauna to a pulp is never the best option, as the game looting system demonstrates from the get-go; but eventually, violence itself will be a last resort. You'll find yourself much more concerned with more peaceful endeavors, something that beautifully echoes the message of the game.I heartily recommend Ultros. It is a game you'll remember, if you have the patience for it. Just be prepared for less than satisfying gameplay and more than satisfying most everything else.

_childDocuments_.review: I was absolutely enchanted by this one. The orchestral soundtrack, the vivid colors, and the cosmic mystery provided a unparalled, captivating experience. While there were many QOL and mechanical frustrations, I navigated past those thorns to enjoy the delicious fruit at the center of this game. The best video game ecology I have experienced by far.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: It is with a heavy heart that I give this a thumbs down. It's absolutely gorgeous and has some truly inventive ideas, but they never really jell into a complete experience.Combat is fussy and unsatisfying. You've got a huge arsenal of moves to learn, but enemies are either practically or actually immune to all but a handful of them. I never felt masterful, but I also never felt outmatched; fights have a kind of graceless, flailing quality to them. You fight less and less as the game advances, and enemy spawns can even be removed from future loops with the right tool, allowing you to remove combat entirely. Managing nutrition was interesting and clever, but with the mycelium I could just save my favorites and not have to worry about picking them up again. This whole constellation of systems feels vestigial, like the game used to have a bigger focus on battles but didn't have the heart to remove them as the focus changed.Gardening is a fascinating idea, but fiddly in its execution, and it comes too late in the game to feel like the core part of the experience it wants to be. Plants and flowers don't always grow in ways you expect them to. Compost to grow them further is a limited resource and can't be recovered if you find that it doesn't fix your problem. Grafting and bending is incredibly slow and tedious. I wish that these mechanics were available closer to the start of the game and more central to the gameplay; relegating so many interesting mechanics to late-game completionism is a truly tragic waste.I admire the craft that went into the visuals and sounds. The illustrations are unique and compelling, and the live orchestrations set the mood flawlessly. There isn't another game out there that FEELS like this one. Unfortunately, the half-baked gameplay got in the way of appreciating the art for the whole time I was with it. I can't even recommend that you just buy it and try it because the experience you'll have in your first 2 hours is completely different than your experience at the end of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game more than I did.I'm a big-time Metroidvania player, so this game held a lot of appeal to me because it offered some unique takes to the genre.  The beginning of the game is the strongest aspect - it has a certain focus while encouraging exploration, sort of like a Castlevania game. As metroidvanias go, the early combat is tame, almost relaxing. But... as this game goes on, the combat becomes entirely de-emphasized, and exploring becomes more and more convoluted and aimless. The idea of connecting a network of trees is unique and cool; but, the execution is less than I'd have wanted. I got about 10 hours into the game before I got so bored that I just quit playing. I wish I could've stuck through it, but frankly, I just didn't have fun.Pros:+ Great and unique artwork+ Great soundtrack, it sets the atmosphere perfectly Cons:+ Lacking focus, changing genres essentially once you hit the mid-point of the game+ Connecting the network becomes a tedious chore+ Combat can be clunky, but is generally overly easy+ Doesn't quite feel like a true Metroidvania
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the coolest things I've ever seen. The art direction is pure genius in every aspect - visuals, writing, sound design. The art is just absolutely stunning, the writing is a word salad of technobabble that usually means nothing at all and somehow that just *works*. There's plenty of unique and interesting concepts in the game design as well, from how you level up by consuming nutrients you get from food harvested from enemies, how that food degrades in quality from hitting the same enemy with the same attack more than once, how the back-tracking inherent to a metroidvania is rephrased as a loop mechanic... I think this is an instant classic, it's amazing, and I honestly can't wait for people to start speedrunning it.

_childDocuments_.review: I HIGHLY RECOMMEND ULTROS.DO NOT i repeat DO NOT listen to any 1 hour reviews of the game claiming its a rogue lite/rogue like. the art is absolutely breath taking and yes, it has SOME features that are common in rogue lites but this is a metroidvania through and through. exploration, is fun and unique because of the loop system, every loop opens up much more of the map, and if you pick the correct upgrades you can even explore places you wouldnt be able to without otherwise mandatory abilities.  fun game, dont listen to uninformed reviewers.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: The demo was great. The second loop was not great. Exploration is directionless and every room feels the same. I have no idea what to plant in any particular spot and the game isn't giving me any clues, environmental or otherwise. This is a problem when there are limited resources. Combat is poorly implemented. Dodge windows are very inconsistent and there aren't nearly enough combat options to justify the "variety" system. The game gives you no feedback on whether your attacks are varied enough until the enemy is dead. I wish the devs had leaned into the gardening aspect and skipped combat entirely. There are so many ideas here that it feels like five games jammed together, but none of the concepts are fleshed out enough to be compelling.

_childDocuments_.review: While Ultros’ visuals are beautiful and music outstanding, the gameplay didn’t hook me. The games combat is satisfying, but the lack of difficulty and enemy diversity doesn’t sell me on it. This issue compounds as the story requires you to loop over and over, going through the same areas and fighting the same enemies, and re-earning the same abilities/perks. To try make up for this they have a farming activity, where you find seeds that grow various different plants, each plant opening up possibilities for shortcuts upon every repeat. However if you plant the wrong seed, you can’t dig it up until later in the game, meaning early game you’ll find yourself wasting these seeds over and over. The farming system feels tedious in design. You can also lock in a small portion of your abilities/perks (to keep them on reset), but neither this nor the farming system mitigates the tedium of restarting. Backtracking/re-exploring feels even worse due to the movement system; there isn’t really any fast way to move through the map, with sprinting tied to continuous running, and all momentum being stopped as soon as you bump into anything, or roll. It’s not even strong as a platformer, with little to no environmental hazards (none that I’ve see so far).None of this is to say Ultros is a bad game, just that it’s not for me. If you’re going in expecting something akin to Blasphemous or Hollow Knight, you’d be sorely disappointed. The movement/combat in those games feels a lot tighter, and there is more emphasis on platforming. Ultros feels more akin to an experience, as you take in the music, atmosphere, world and its unique visuals, and is best treated as a casual game. If that appeals to you, I heavily recommend it, it’s just not for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: Metroidvanias are one of my favourite game genres. Roguelikes have never really appealed to me as I don't like the idea of restarting over and over again. Ultros, however, piqued my interest due to the visuals, the good reviews, and the rogueLITE element, which I thought could be a good middle-ground for someone like me who loves metroidvanias, but has never played a roguelike.Unfortunately, this game just wasn't for me. I did power through and complete the game up until the credits rolled (took me around 11 hours), but I just can't recommend it for those who like metroidvanias, but don't like roguelike/roguelites.First the positives. The visuals are soooo good! The trippy colourful world is so fun to move through. The plant life pops and the changes to the world that slowly happen every 'cycle' are always fun to notice. The score in certain areas and during certain boss fights can be really cool too. I did like the overall idea for the story, even if it was a little confusing and not amazingly executed in the end.So on to what I didn't like. Part of the issue is that it's not reeeeally a true metroidvania in my opinion. It definitely has metroidvania elements - progress, get something new, unlock new area etc - but it's only a metroidvania in that very basic sense. There aren't really abilities to unlock that make game play more interesting, or traversal more fun, or make you want to backtrack to find new things. There are unlockable 'talents' but these are very basic in nature and make very little difference to the overall game as a whole. There are also no in-depth choice mechanics like charms/gems to alter game play or upgrades to weapons/skills so generally feels pretty shallow. In addition, the lack of things to collect makes it feel like there's no benefit to exploring.The game is also very repetitive in premise. There's a central area where Ultros is located, and your objective is to destroy 7 incubators throughout the world and return to Ultros after destroying each. Every time you destroy an incubator you gain something that usually unlocks the next area/incubator, however you need to return to Ultros first, and every time you do it 'resets the cycle' (basically turns back time) and you effectively restart the game and lose all your items and abilities. You then need to return along the same starting areas, fighting the same enemies, regaining the same abilities... it just feels very tedious. The 'resetting' mechanic, whilst making sense for the story being told, really adds nothing to the game in terms of fun or interest.The main issue of this for me is that it just felt hard to get invested in character progression when every 1-1.5 hours your character gets a hard reset.There's also a major mechanic of the game when you need to plant seeds to grow plants. The type of plant that grows is dependant on the seed you plant and you need specific plants to overcome certain obstacles or progress in certain areas. These seeds however are not always readily available, meaning you may need to do a lot of backtracking and searching, especially since you lose these seeds every cycle. You may also need to use compost on these plants for them to grow better and some take more than one cycle to grow. It's just very tedious and in the end I just couldn't be bothered with them, only doing what was absolutely necessary to progress. I just didn't enjoy this mechanic at all.Combat is very basic too. There a sort of interesting mechanic, where if you kill an enemy with different combos they drop better loot/items, but after a while you just ignore it and hack your way to victory spamming the same button - it makes minimal difference - meaning combat leaves a lot to be desired. It's also compounded by the fact that the enemies are far and few between with no real interesting mechanics to counter or adapt to.Anyway that's my two cents. If you're in the same boat as me - you love metroidvanias, but aren't a fan of roguelikes/roguelites - then this won't change that and I can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Lisa Frank fever dream that forces you to lose all your abilities and retread old ground on the regular. _childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: Ultros gives me the same eerie vibe that Scorn had given me last year, except that the former is covered in weird alien plantlife instead of grey flesh. Everything about it is weird, in a good way. The bold usage of colors catches my eyes. The art style walks the thin line between hauntingly beautiful and disturbing. The unorthodox way this metroidvania provides may be a downer at first, but eventually I am fascinated by its design. Now I need to clarify: this game by no means is a roguelite game. There is no random level generator and no starting from scratch after death. There is a time-loop gimmick that resets you, but this is done for the sake of plot progression. Ultros is, without a doubt, a metroidvania that tries something new to differentiate itself from others. And for me, it has done a great job.There are actually two parts of "gating abilities": Extractors and Plant Seeds. Extractors are the usual gating abilities that are given to players after defeating bosses or completing trials. Things like double jump and thruster are easy to understand, but trimmer, sprayer, and splicer? Those won't make sense to you until you combine them with the other part: Plant Seeds. In Ultros, Plant Seeds are the secondary "gating abilities". Players can plant seeds into specific glowing soils and watch them grow. Different seeds yield various results, and their full-grown counterparts can help you traverse to places previously inaccessible: trees can be used as extra platforms in case double jump cannot make it; ceiling moss allows you to swing to places when double jump isn't available; space wheat field even gives you speed boost and special gravity trick which allows you to run up-side-down. What's more interesting is that you can use those extractors to further customize the plants you grow. You can trim them to the right size, spray them to guide them to the right place, and graft different plants together to create the weirdest alien flora ever. The last part is especially helpful because there is a mechanic in mid-to-late-game that want you to re-link the spiritual link through flowers. With grafting, you can guide the spiritual link to most barren lands.→The art style is really something to behold.→Lots of secrets to uncover.→The garden system is weirdly relaxing and exciting at the same time.→: Personally I kinda like the time-loop design simply because it ties to the plant growth. Every time I enter a new cycle, I am excited to see how my plant has grown and how I can properly use them in exploration. Time-loop in Ultros isn't just a hard reset. It also serves as a plot progression tool. Some locations are only unlocked after reaching certain cycles, and NPCs will appear in different locations for new interactions.→: But I can totally see why people can be discouraged by this design easily. Time-loop resets our protagonist's inventory and powers, powers obtained by consuming four different nutrients. You can only get nutrients by eating various enemy parts or fruits. Players need to re-grind the food source and re-apply the powers. This process can be tedious because you won't immediately have your extractor(double jump).I know combat isn't the main feature of this game, but it still doesn't feel decent either. Attack feels floaty. You cannot mix-up each attack smoothly until you complete the whole combo. Airborne attack is severely lacking. Juggling seems to be the focus, except that enemies floats around randomly. The game encourages you to use various combo to carve the best meat from any enemies, but the condition is vague and confusing. Sometimes I get prime meat by spamming normal attacks, yet sometimes I pull out the backstab-into-launcher combo and I still got meat pulp.→You cannot roll through enemies unless they are attacking.→Those elbow blades are really just for show, huh?中文小簡評→有著和Scorn類似美術設計的類銀河系惡魔城。→詭異的外星植生遺跡配上大膽用色令人震撼。→商店頁面有Roguelite標籤，但只是沾點邊而已，這款是有著時空輪迴的類銀河系惡魔城。→技能除了二段跳及推進器外，其他能力都與植物有關。對的位置種對的植物能夠有效幫助你探索更多區域，運用修剪、滋補劑和接枝能夠創造出更多有趣的組合。→關卡內藏了許多秘密，值得運用手中的植物取得。→種植與等待期成長的過程令人放鬆及興奮。→個人是覺得時空輪迴的設定沒那麼糟，NPC會因為不同次數輪迴有不同互動，一些地區也會因輪迴解鎖。→最大的問題是角色能力會重製，之前取得的角色能力需要重新攝食營養素來升級、重要技能需要到地圖中心取回抽取器，過程難免煩躁。→戰鬥雖並非亮點，然而連基本操作都覺得不及格。攻擊回饋不好、連技無法用其他攻擊中斷、空中攻擊非常雞肋，遊戲還想鼓勵玩家多用不同連擊取得高級食物，然而達成條件十分隱晦。→只有在敵人攻擊時你才能滾過敵人。→手肘上的刀刃只是裝飾用。

_childDocuments_.review: *Mild gameplay spoilersThe good:-Great atmosphere and sense of dread/isolation that very few metroidvanias manage to truly achieve.-Artwork is super unique and generally beautiful to look at. I would recommend turning saturation down a bit cause it can give you eye fatigue though.-Living network mechanic is one of the most unique and satisfying mechanics I've played with in theory, execution can get tedious but the potential here is limitless.-Awesome music.-Liked the looping mechanic, it rewards strategic upgrading and it's not super annoying to get your abilities back, especially after a certain point you basically get them back instantly.The bad:-Controls are... Pretty bad. Especially on some perks and abilities.-Walljump is hot garbo.-Hitboxes are hanky sometimes.-Pretty buggy. Most isn't game breaking but just annoying.-Combat tried to be strategic but falls flat. There isn't enough attacks to make it feel free flow and satisfying to get "perfect variety".-Some áreas/level designs are just terrible.The reason I'm recommending it is because if the Devs learn from all the execution flaws they had in this first game, and expand upon all the original and amazing ideas they brought, they could make a sequel (Ultros 2) that would rival the likes of Hollow Knight.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that I've been wanting to see for a very long time - a game which delivers on the appeal of learning to interact with an alien ecology. Early on, your main interaction with the environment is combat, like many metroidvanias. However, as the game progresses, you get more and more ways to interact with the flora and fauna of the game, to the point where combat becomes a rare side-activity to gameplay about manipulating the environment to access new areas and develop the environments of the space station.Interacting with plants in the environment is often not a smooth or elegant process, which might put some people off, but I think it makes for an experience where growing plants and feeding animals can be just as interesting as the combat gameplay. The only real issue I have with this system is that it can be quite buggy, at one point, I encountered an issue that caused my player movement to bug out until I reloaded my save. I think it was inevitable with an experimental gameplay system from a small team, but it still impacted my experience in a noticeable way.
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: I'm giving up on this one about halfway through. The art and soundtrack are beautiful, and the concept of creating a "living network" of plant life is cool. Unfortunately, the game doesn't play as well as it looks and sounds. Exploration just didn't gel with me, and world traversal became tedious and frustrating as I became increasingly more clueless about what to do next. The game is too vague about how some mechanics work, and certain things that were supposed to jump out at me on-screen just weren't that noticeable. By the time I quit, I was looking up a guide every 15 minutes or so, a sure sign I'm just trying to push through and not actually enjoying myself. I usually finish every game I play whether I love it or not, but this one just isn't worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: At the February Steam Next Fest I was able to try a variety of very interesting and promising demos, such as movement shooters, survivals, and even some Metroidvania. Among them I played ULTROS, just before its release, and I was captivated thanks to entertaining gameplay, colorful visuals, and an enigmatic and psychedelic setting. And I must say that its trial version was a small fraction of what I was really expecting, as ULTROS managed to exceed my expectations on more than one occasion, with creative mechanics that are unlocked little by little, linked to the effects of a time loop. Hand in hand with these systems goes a strange and somewhat convoluted story, reactive combat, farming?! And many mysteries to unravel.We'll explore the "sarcophagus", a gigantic space structure which is also referred to as the "uterus", and which houses a sleeping entity: ULTROS. We'll take the role of a character who wakes up without memories or knowledge of her whereabouts, and we'll have to discover our role in the story as we progress. On our journey, we'll find different inhabitants of the sarcophagus, with whom we can talk to follow the plot, and there are also several "memories" hidden along the corridors, which provide us with information about both the structure and the aforementioned NPCs.Honestly, it's a very mystical, spiritual hallucinogenic delirium, but even if what I’m going to say  sounds strange, I think it suits it wonderfully thanks to the enigmatic atmosphere it radiates, and lets one make their own conclusions. I liked it a lot, especially for the participation of Gärdner, the best character in the game! You’ll see if you play it.Beyond the story, the visuals are undoubtedly what grabbed my attention in the first instance. The art in ULTROS is gorgeous, and paints a very sci-fi landscape, from living terrain, forgotten technology, and even spaceship-like rooms, all with vibrant colors. Not only the environments are beautiful, but also the character designs, both humanoid and insect-like enemies (mostly), and the few but important bosses that reside in the sarcophagus. The map is gigantic, too! In addition to this, the soundtrack is fantastic. It has a large number of songs that vary from gentle to catchy; the atmosphere that is created between the two sections is magnificent, and greatly enriched my experience. The gameplay is very deceptive at first glance, hiding remarkable depth and creativity that is discovered as the game progresses. Starting with our character, we'll have a very classic skill tree, but to make use of it we'll have to feed and nourish ourselves. Nutrients are obtained from plants or enemy remains, and fall into four categories, and the skills we can unlock depend on different nutrients. Basically, if you need red and blue nutrients, you have to eat something that gives you that, very simple. ULTROS features a time loop aspect, where we'll have to start over from the beginning when we reach certain points in the game. This implies losing all our skills and resources, and it may seem a bit hopeless, but it is solved with the use of items that can “pin” the skills into place, in order to not lose them in a future cycle. These objects are usually hidden, some more than others, so get to exploring!As for combat, in my opinion it doesn't present much of a challenge, but it is fun thanks to incentivising combos. Because attacking enemies with the same attack over and over again is detrimental, since it causes food dropped by creatures to be in worse condition, giving us less nutrients when consuming it. But combat can be optional, in most cases, as we can also tame the critters by feeding them, and it's even funny that some creatures like one food better than others.Taming the beasts in ULTROS has its purpose, and that is to help create plots to plant. Yes, you read that right, planting, this game is a farm simulator disguised as a Metroidvania, I assure you. Throughout the game we'll find seeds that we can grow, initially in specific locations, and then also where our little creatures have tiled the land. The plants that grow from these seeds come in various colors and sizes, with their own unique uses, like one that lets you create platforms for example; and their growth is affected both by the soil, the passing of the cycles, and as well as with compost that we can find around the sarcophagus.Related to this, we'll have an artifact called the extractor. This gadget will not only allow us to obtain the mythical double jump, but it can also be loaded with additional modules as we progress through the story. From cutting plants with a saw, to being able to dig a seed out of the ground to replant it in another place. It goes hand in hand with the "gardening" theme, and we'll eventually make use of these mechanics to make our way through the sarcophagus, and our creativity will be put to the test. There are a variety of puzzles that are solved using plants, both by themselves and by combining them, creating gardens that can cover a multitude of rooms. It's strange to say, but I had a very relaxing time playing with these mechanics, connecting rooms with plants in this unique Metroidvania. I think it is the strongest and most entertaining point of the game, and the complexity of this system left me fascinated; and I didn’t mention the living network, which is something I’d rather others discover by themselves. ULTROS offers a very unique experience, the exploration feels very good, and the audiovisual area leaves nothing to be desired. It’s a most unusual adventure, which I found even cathartic. So far I found two endings, and I feel that I’ve left a lot undiscovered, so even as I write I feel anxious to get back to playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Ultros is a pretty awesome neon drenched sci-fi adventure.  The first thing you notice is the art direction, and I will admit, when I first saw screenshots I didn't love it and wasn't sure it would appeal to me.  However, in motion it is magical, a lush, vivid, beautiful mix of technology and biology.  It's breathtaking.  You wake up in a pod on some sort of space station, and even after running into some other beings and having some chats... you still have very little idea of what is going on.  It works though, everything is cryptic and strange and alien.  At first, besides the strangeness, everything is standard metroidvania, you move through the 2d world, noticing parts you can't access yet etc.  As you play more though, you discover the two things that really set Ultros apart; gardening and looping.  Whenever you complete one of your main objectives, the game loops, and you start over and lose most of your abilities, but, there are patches of soil where you can plant seeds, and when you loop, time passes and the plants grow.  You can use these plants to access platforms you couldn't reach before, or break through barriers, and do many other things.  It is different and interesting, but also sometimes frustrating.  It's not always clear what plant is needed in what situation, or in what directions the plant is going to grow, etc.   I not only enjoyed the act of moving through the areas and fighting enemies and bosses, but I enjoyed piecing together what was going on, both in the narrative and the gameplay systems.  I sort of finished the game but did not get the "true" ending.  The quest you have to undertake in order to do so is really interesting, and I did a bunch of it... but some parts require extreme plant growing and experimentation and I just didn't have it in me.  I doubt I will return to it, but I enjoyed my time with the game and would still recommend it for sure, as it just so beautiful and interesting. 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Ultros

_childDocuments_.review: - Some may find it a bit excessive, but I love how this game looks. Until playing through Ultros, I didn't realize my tastes were inclined towards the "Lisa Frank tries DMT" aesthetic, but I enjoyed what I was looking at the entire time. The pitch black foregrounds really make the wildly colored hand-drawn backgrounds and characters really pop- The main inspiration (also cited in the credits) is Moebius. While that's evident in some of the characters and set pieces, the use of color is cranked to 11, as is the presence of organic shapes and lines- While not the most fluid I've ever seen, I did like the attention to detail apparent in the various running, jumping, and attacking animations. I've noticed that this aspect of otherwise visually stunning platformers is often overlooked, so I appreciated the effort to make the game look good in motion too- Your enjoyment of the soundtrack sort of depends on how much you like ambient electronic music and noise. I personally found the mix of strange and anxious synth, occasional woodwinds and percussion, and rain forest sounds to be pretty intriguing- The circularity of death and rebirth is a pretty common theme in metroidvanias, but Ultros, raises the conceptual stakes by placing the game within a time loop where the world is continually ending, but a failsafe restores it to its previous state immediately. Welcome to the strange confines of The Sarcophagus- Quick disclaimer: there is a ton of lore in Ultros to string together, and I didn't find all of it. But from the bits I did manage to locate, here's what I gathered about the setup for the narrative. The Berians were the architects of The Sarcophagus and the dead race that sets the plot in motion. Among their other technological accomplishments, they figured out a way to extract negative emotions from themselves and transfer them to residents known as Shamasals. Unfortunately, all this negative energy causes them to wither and die eventually- Out of nowhere, a being merely called The Entity descends upon the Berians, offering to handle all those nasty emotions and impulses for them in exchange for a temple where he can be worshipped (The Sarcophagus). Unfortunately, the negative energy corrupts The Entity as well, but not before the Berians can put a failsafe in place to prevent the end of their world- The game starts with our protagonist waking up on the psychedelic world without any knowledge of where they are. They'll meet a lot of interesting characters there for their own motivations (greed, knowledge, adventure), but there's only one Berian left. I never did find the lore explaining where they all went- With all the high-concept plot ideas that you'll see if you're the type of player who doesn't smash A/X/Space bar every time a game puts words in front of their eyeballs, it feels weird to say that Ultros is all vibes at the end of the day. The narrative is split up and well hidden (talk to characters multiple times), so it takes some effort to string it all together. What you'll really be noticing are the gorgeous visuals and hypnotic music in an exploration-heavy game- I really, really respect all the risk Ultros takes in its game design. It's sort of a mixed bag, but it was refreshing to get to try out something original in the metroidvania space- The primary big new idea is how the time loop central to the game's plot influences upgrade and exploration mechanics. I'll bring it up when relevant- Like any metroidvania, progression and exploration are gated by equipment or abilities you get as a reward for defeating bosses or platforming around the large, interconnected map. In Ultros, these mobility skills usually come in the form of upgrades to The Extractor, a piece of equipment you'll be tracking down every loop so you can do things like double jump or dig through walls again- You'll also get a few movement options via your skill tree, but you'll primarily find stat upgrades, utility options, and attack skills there. Eating the monsters you kill and plants you find or cultivate grant you upgrade materials in differing proportions, so you'll need a diverse diet to start improving yourself- Unfortunately, you lose all of your upgrades every time you complete a loop (triggered by defeating a boss). I've seen some people talk about Ultros having roguelike elements, and this is what they're referring to. Luckily, you can track down your Extractor pretty quickly every loop (this becomes much simpler after your forth or fifth go around), and careful exploration will reward you special items that can be used to lock-in your upgrade permanently so they stick around between loops- Combat in Ultros is not one of its strong points. Much if the upgrade tree feels truly wasted when none of the enemies are hard enough to necessitate a lot of the more advanced dodge and combat skills. Simply improving your combo length and damage is more than sufficient to defeat any foe the game puts in front of you. Regular enemies are mostly a cakewalk, and the bosses don't pose much challenge either. There where multiple occasions where I was left thinking, "Wait, it's already over?"- Ultros has another optional exploration mechanic that I barely scrached the depth of in my playthrough: gardening. You'll find various seeds that, when planted, will provide climbable platforms, jump pads, wall-dissolving moss, etc. that can open up new paths. Some won't fully grow into the next loop- This planting mechanic ramps up considerably once you bring the Living Network, the organic network providing power and connectivity to The Sarcophogus' machinery. You'll need to plant seeds, fertilize saplings, create new plots by feeding enemies if you want to open up the whole map and find all the lore- I don't know if I'll every replay Ultros, but I may come back someday to finish the Living Network so I can see the true ending- As much as I liked the loop mechanic, I found myself really annoyed having to go get the Extractor and my sword at the start of every loop. It added a lot of unnecessary time retreading the same path as before I could start exploring again. I liked the way this worked for the skill tree (providing a way to preview upgrades before locking them in for future loops was smart), though. Keep the extractor near the loop spawn point, and I immediately like this game better- I also disliked how much content is locked behind the Living Network completion. Completing it is a complex and open ended puzzle that apparently takes dozens of hours to finish. I liked the game pretty well, but not enough to commit to that sort of pensive gameplay. Some of Ultros' mysteries are going to remain unsolved for me- The game ran extremely well on the Steam Deck- . I appreciate a game that takes risks and looks good while doing it. This game is really close to being amazing. With a bit less backtracking and a way to take the looping out of the Living Network grand puzzle, this would be stellar game. As is, it's a quite good, but still notably flawed experience that's better suited to patient gamers

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure how to make a review for this game. It's certainly I think much more a chill game then it comes off to be. Farming sim dipped in a candy shell of metroidvania-lite. Stay away if you're expecting rpg / stats / leveling up. Come if you're expecting exploration, map completion, and plant planing. Beautiful visuals, art design, and music. Tedious backtracking probably being it's lowest low. The biggest flaw with the game is the pacing. The beginning is nice and linear, but as soon as you're given freedom you're bound to wander off the desired path. You end up finding tutorials well after they are useful. A little bit of insinuated correct path would go a long way here.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, well. It looks like we have a  here.Or is it not?Just take a look at the store images to know that this is one of those with such an omnipresent sense of aesthetics that every frame of the game will look like a work of art that could be hung on your wall.A psychedelic dance saturated with colors and details. Perpetually engaging, somber music enveloping a strangely introspective, relaxing, and peaceful(?) experience, with spiritual and philosophical connotations sprouting from every piece of the screen in a surreal, majestic and strange colorful nightmare.As if that wasn’t enough, the quality of the animations is excellent and perfectly functional for a game like this.Even the dialogue balloons are beautiful!It’s a game made with vision; you can see it in the first few minutes.But, unfortunately, this is where the praises end.Despite the strong and captivating artistic identity, the game that accompanies it and develops from it is not very interesting. It is regrettably mediocre.To begin with, its greatest quality ends up being one of the biggest detriments to the game's world design. The density of details in the scenery, combined with repetitive and generic layouts to navigate, essentially makes it almost impossible to identify isolated areas and removes any notion of physicality from the exploration.You don’t feel like you’re progressing. You walk through spaces that seem homogeneous and interchangeable, and simply reach the next one, virtually indistinguishable in terms of gameplay and atmosphere.Exceptions are so rare that they become irrelevant. As a rule, I could hardly get anywhere purely by orienting myself through the scenery. Even after walking through some of them several times.It’s not that the game doesn’t have enough variety to be memorable. Everything is SO VARIED that nothing stands out. It’s the inverse problem.Finding your way, mapping it mentally, identifying rooms you’ve been to without the help of the map is simply dreadful. I can only imagine the pain it would be if you couldn’t see where the main targets are. The abysmal time you would waste getting lost, with no idea how to progress.There is no problem with the game having a simpler and more accessible execution, but given the modest amount of movement and combat mechanics, I expected something a bit more elaborate.The game sells a stylish, sharp, and brutal combat system, rewarding precision and variety in the execution of your moves, but rarely demanding anything real from the player. It feels like the character you control and the threats you have to face are out of sync. With you always having options, but with almost no incentive or need (besides looking like a ninja) to use them. The game demands no degree of mechanical competence from the player. And the combat is basically trivialized by the possibility of loading up on healing items with the greatest ease, even after investing in upgrades.In an analogy that a friend of mine likes to use: It’s like killing a cockroach with a bazooka.You may make it look pretty on the screen, but any fun you could have derived from the mechanical execution of these moves practically evaporates when the game doesn’t match what you’re doing. The enemies are not fun to face, and the encounter design of this game is laughable. You very, very rarely feel any pressure from the opposite side.The only exception is the bosses (who are also not the best), as long as you decide, by self-imposition, not to use healing items, because otherwise, winning by attrition, playing completely awkwardly, is more than viable, even at the peak of the most "demanding challenges”.I didn’t expect spectacular exploration or combat, given that the overwhelming majority of metroidvanias are weak in at least one of these aspects. But I also didn’t expect everything to be so uninspired to the point of reminding me of games like Sundered.It seems strangely purposeful to frustrate the player's expectations by giving them combat mechanics when the combat itself is just an incipient part of the experience. It doesn’t feel like you’re walking through dangerous areas with carefully positioned enemies, but rather that you’re exploring a strange place that happens to have some threats. .The cycles that resemble roguelite loops, the seeds that serve as improvised platforms and resource generators, and the dexterity in enemy executions, seem to be just gimmicks, which, although justified by the "narrative" and interconnected mechanically in a masterful way, seem to exist only to fill the hole of the game’s lack of substance.Losing your abilities in each cycle means almost nothing, as you can recover them with the greatest ease (and lock the most important ones), and there are no different builds to be created, essentially making the process just unnecessary and not an opportunity to explore new play styles.But since you want to recover them despite this, you are forced to face enemies who, in turn, preferably should be eliminated in the most diverse way possible to yield the highest amounts of experience, forcing you not to go straight to the point and take longer than necessary to dispatch all sorts of trash you encounter along the way.It seems like they thought a bit of visual spectacle was a substitute for execution. You can eliminate anything with the most basic attacks. They knew this, so to fill the hole of a good dynamic, they created an excuse to force you to “play good” hoping the player would have fun with just that. And then they created another excuse (losing everything in every cycle) to discourage you from avoiding it.It’s not like this process robs that feeling of a power progression, characteristic of the genre, of starting with a weak character and a basic moveset and evolving them throughout the game into something relentless, capable of facing equally more dangerous threats.By the way, remember that feeling when you find a new upgrade in these games and you immediately feel like the world got bigger? With dozens of new exploration opportunities popping into your head? Do you remember the sublime feeling of that the world is expanding, becoming more interconnected, that the “physical space” of that experience is unfolding into something much more mysterious and alluring?Well, you can use seeds to creatively increase the number of places you can go and use attacks to extend your air time and access more distant platforms, but that feeling I described above simply does not exist here.I really wish I had better things to say. Ultros has all the tools; they are even interconnected competently, but they are not used in any interesting way. The game leaves it to the atmosphere projected by the art direction, music, and “narrative” (a cryptic and fragmented philosophical mess) to carry the experience on its back.And it works. Only because at least the game is undemanding… And they gave you a map.I liked the game. But in good conscience, I could never deny how mediocre the elements that make up the experience are. Credit where credit is due: The vibe is great, but the food has no flavor.What I enjoyed most was wandering around, casually, trying to establish the “connections” from one end of the map to the other, like in a glorified game of connect-the-dots.Certainly, I have no desire to play it again. It’s not a core experience that appeals to me. But it's ok.It’s not a terrible game; it’s just surprisingly average.
