_childDocuments_.review: I adore this game; every single aspect of it is fun and exciting in almost every way. I won't go into a huge amount of detail because I'm sure that there are other reviews that achieve that for me. Instead, I'm looking at this from a very casual viewpoint. For starters, lets talk about the positives:-Game runs amazing. I do have a beefy computer (Intel I7 I think over 3 GHz, 16 GB of ram, and a Nvidia 1060) so it runs great on it. No frame rate drops at all and the graphics look great. I honestly do not know how well this game will run on lower end PCs but I believe it to be well optimized so you shouldn't have a problem with it. -Extremely fun. Right from the start I was having a blast playing this, from free-running around the city and slums, to bashing zombies' heads in, to running from them at night, everything I did was a blast, even the fetch quests were fun-Story is awesome. It's nothing award winning, but it is still a good story nonetheless. Will try to get you emotionally attached to certain characters, but because of the nature of the game, it's rather hard to. -Actually is terrifying in some points. Techland does a great job on making the zombies look and act scary. There were multiple moments where I was yelling because something jumped out at me, or I was being chased by a pack of zombies.-Nice weapon varity. Yes, you'll be using the weapons in roughly the same way, bashing zombies. But each class of weapons behaves differently. A giant fireaxe hits harder and slower than a crowbar, while the crowbar has more knockback power than the knife, while the knife hits faster than all of them. Regardless, each weapon class feels unique and forces me to adjust my tactics depending on what I am using. Even the guns, bows, and crossbows feel different, mostly to their one hit kill power. Be careful though, because guns tend to attract even more zombies! -Freerunning is great. Most games that have freerunning tend to be either hit or miss, with most falling into the miss category. Dying Light however is a sure hit; the free running is fun and exciting. The controls are okay, but I'll get to that in a second. Overall however, the freerunning is a solid addition to the game. This is great and all, but nothing is perfect. I have my fair share of issues with this game. -The controls. Yes, the controls are tight, but they tend to not behave how I want them to, leading to a lot of deaths. Sometimes I don't grab a ledge when I should, or other times I get stuck and can't move out of a group of zombies, as in I'm mashing buttons and nothing happens. NOW, I could very well just suck at this game, I admit, so take that one with a grain of salt. However, I do believe that you'll encounter some issues. -The missions and side quests are very generic. "Hey man, go run over there and do that/grab this/kill him/turn on that" Every mission, be it story or side, feels the same. Very rarely do they change in some way, and when they do it's so much fun. But 80% of what you're doing is the same thing, over and over and over and over and over and over again. -The game can get very frustrating. I play on hard, so yes, it's HARD. But there are a lot of times where I throw my hands up and yell ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Some instances include:                   -Being spawned in a location filled with hard enemies that spawn killed me                  -Trying to kill gun users when I haven't even found a gun. (surprise surprsie, they kill me in 3 shots)                  -Certain challenges feel impossible, both in what you're supposed to use and where it places you                  -Driving the jeep in The Following is extremely frustrating, as it seems as though if you drive out at night and the fast zombies see you, you're screwed as there isn't a good way to knock them off.                  -Multiple times during missions I can't find what I'm looking for because I'm searching in a huge area for a cell phone the size of my fist. -In addition, the game isn't hard on higher levels, it's frustrating, which is a big difference. Hard would be more zombies added and fewer weapons and supplies, but as it stands, on higher difficulties zombies just have more health. Which means it takes FOREVER to kill a single zombie sometimes. In fact, I've had instances where they just don't die, even though I'm using extremely powerful weapons. The zombies also hit harder, which is fine if they wouldn't 3 shot you from the start. I remember playing on console with the difficulty being on normal, I would get really hurt if I ran into a group of zombies but it was at a point where I could escape, but at a heavy cost. This encouraged me to play smart because I would waste supplies. On hard...not so much. Zombies down you very fast, so even if you get hut twice, you're buring through your supplies to get yourself back. In fact, it's better to keep dying on Hard if you're trying to do something, as that way you're not wasting a bunch of supplies. That's not fun.-The game kind of looses its charm after awhile. Sure, what game doesn't at 40 hours, but a good game will keep you going with an awesome story, awesome gameplay, or both. Dying Light doesn't have this. Yeah, the story is decent, but it doesn't pull you in; I stopped caring after awhile and used story missions solely when I needed better loot and expereince. Yeah, the gameplay is fun, but when you have a series of frustrating events happen to you, you loose the desire to keep playing; why even attempt that challenge when you get two shotted and loose, for the 17th time?Overall, I do believe Dying Light is a solid game; it's incredibly fun and rewarding when you play well, but can be extremely frustrating when even the slightest thing goes wrong. I do believe that the postives overshadow the negative parts but only up to a certain point. That point could very well have been 40 hours to me; to you, it might hit at 10 hours or it could never be hit at all, it just depends on how you approach the game. Regardless, this game is a solid 8/10, and is something that I would recommend to everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: If you’re considering getting this on Sale, I HIGHLY suggest you do. This is one of the best games I’ve ever played.Imagine Dead Island, except:-Running is fluid, intuitive, and makes you really feel like you’re cruising, you’re not stumbling over things and zombies like a toddler-Hitting something with a weapon is strategic, solid, and feels like you’re really doing some damage, rather than feeling like a 90 year old man smacking an Elephant with a rolled-up newspaper.-There’s a ton to explore and virtually none of it is glitchy, there’s amazing freedom of movement; crafting goes from basic “OMG I may actually survive this!” to “Right, I’m going to rip your head off, electrocute you and set you alight at the same time, someone hold my drink.” The weapon variety isn’t amazing but what’s there works very well.-Voice acting is quality for the most part, Crane sounds perfect although some of the locals sound like they’re quite blatantly reading from a script. You. Know. The. Type. Right? Ha. Ha. Ha. Anyway. Crane – Back. To. Business. We. Need. You. To kill some. Zombies. Don’t become. One though! Or. We. May. Have. To. Kill. You. And. by “may”… I. mean. Will. Ha! Ha! Ha!In short, Dead Island felt weird to move around and fight in with an odd story and progression system. In Dying Light, you actually feel like you’re f***ed and fighting to stay alive, and you eventually become very good at it, there’s so much freedom and fluidity. What I would suggest is downloading Sweetfx to lighten some of the sickly green/rusty background colour, and enhance the colour saturation. Game looks so much nicer after that. And if you can get rid of Chromatic Abberation, DO IT, it’s the worst design decision I've ever come across. It’s like intentionally making a half-blind person glasses to see perfectly with, then making them completely out of focus and colouring each lens a different colour, just for “cinematic effect”.

_childDocuments_.review: I completed the entire Dying Light story via "other playable means" - I got this copy during the free weekend just to see how well it has aged. Not disappointing, but not exceptional either: 6.5/10.DL is your ye ol' zombie chompie game, with unremarkable hordes and horde kinds, shoot-em-up expectations, and a heavy focus on stamina-based mechanics and an unsurprising skill tree. However, the parkour - oh I could hug and kiss and spoon the parkour all night.First person parkour is the most exhilarating experience you can gain from being a dude in a game. Prototype? Bam, alien-bite superpowers make it go from nyoom to nyoooooooom. Uncharted? Bam, a single grappling hook is sufficient for the experience to go from a cover-based shooter to a rope-based shooter. Spoilers: this game  because it is a good game.With world models being used alongside first person cameras, DL goes from excited dogrunning to excited dogrunning with weapons. And flying! But not a lot. But still. Meh. I mean I ca-Dying Light is a well-crafted first person experience. Be THE generic dude to save a city by being an errand boy. Encounter a generic bald-headed antagonist that is crafted like the blend of Far Cry 3's Vaas and  Metal Gear Solid V's Skull Face. Work for a shadow organization as your character arc takes you from generic dude to generic dude with a god complex.  And zombies. What is this, 2014?Oh, THE PARKOUR MECHANICS FROM DOOM:ETER-

_childDocuments_.review: I first bought Dying Light on my PS4 through a fake, secondary account, because I saw a bit of it and decided that it probably was worth my money. PS4 games in my country are always expensive, hence the fake account, but I really wanted to play this game. I already knew the devs because of Dead Island, one of my favorite games back then. So, I bought the game, played, loved it since the beginning. And about a week later my fake account was terminated. I was angry, of course, but damn I wanted to keep playing what I thought was the best game I could've bought for my console. So I surrendered to Sony and bought the original game disk. Finished it, did every secondary mission, challenges, quarantine zones, got a set of legendary weapons including a 3k dmg legendary Katana.And later I heard about The Following DLC. I had built my own PC meanwhile, so I bought the game again on steam, and this time I went through the whole thing alongside a friend. And then I wondered why I hadn't done this back on the PS4. This game is the perfect zombie game so far, and the Techland guys are aware of this, still updating the game almost 3 years after initial release. Graphics are good, even for today's games, but they are quite recycled, although you can always expect this from RPGs like this one. Gameplay is awesome, you can go freerunning through Harran and behead thousands of zombies along the way without problems. The Story is a bit cliché, but it's enjoyable nonetheless, both main storyline and the Following. But what I find the most satisfying is grinding for weapons and mutilating any zombies that come across your path.So, all in all, this game is fun from playing the story alone to murdering the entire zombie population of Harran with your friends.Yes, I only did this review for the achievement. I don't care.

_childDocuments_.review: I like that Techland goes all-out with their games. A unique city in a strange part of the world, lots of interesting mechanics and gory animations, and things that shouldn't work, but sometimes do (vehicles, grappling hooks, first-person, etc.). PPersonally, the writing leaves a lot to be desired. Sometimes it's too in-depth, and other times needlessly repetitive. And the gameplay can be super glitchy and frustrating at times. But as you get more comfortable with the mechanics, and gain some skills, the world opens up in a very satisfying way. Plus, chopping through waves of zombies while still being afraid of the dark is an impressive balancing feat.

With Dying Light, I found often times having difficulty with having public players joining in my game, but when I had a full game, I found it quite entertaining, and we had more tendency to screw around, which was fun in itself.The game looked absolutely fantastic, and ran incredibly well on max settings. The gameplay is pretty fun and smooth, but something felt like it was missing. The parkour type free running made getting around very easy, but encourages skipping over a lot of the scenery and the action of the streets.My biggest complaint is with the multiplayer. You can "be the zombie" and basically invade other peoples games when their game shifts to night time, for a 1v4 mode. Fun enough as is, but much like in Left 4 Dead, people tend to quit shortly after I own them, otherwise people leave as soon as I invaded their game. If you don't want hunters invading, turn off the damn option.. jeez.3.5 out of 5

_childDocuments_.review: Dying Light is a thrilling experience that should not be missed.- Story - Story-wise, the game is a hit or miss. During my playthrough I ended up just skipping most of the cutscenes as well as dialogue. The game really shines throughout it's final missions as each mission/cutscene continuously gets more cinematic. Dying Light's story has something to offer to each player and it should not be slept on.- Gameplay -Dying Light is a fun, arcadic zombie game that has hours upon hours stored within it. As the game continues on your survivor will grow stronger, this unlocks cool abilities such as the drop kick, grapple and many more countless upgrades. The fighting is smoother than its predocessors ( Dead Island) and I found it more enjoyable this time around. I cannot tell you how many times my friends and I just messed around wacking off zombie heads and doing parkour. The combat has a very satisfying feeling that will keep me coming back even after the credits roll. One main selling point of Dying Light is its traversal system. At the start of the game you learn the common parkour system which I found slow and crappy, but little did I know it was only because I was a low level. As you progess, you get more fluid with the parkour system and add many moves to your running arsenal, many of which save a lot of time ( Grappling hook). While the parkour may be fun, I managed to have some scraps with it during my playthrough, many of which belong to the many climbings of attennas and tall buildings. Dying Light's gameplay starts off slow but it really begins to pick up once your character levels up. This is definitely a co-op game. Not mean't to be played alone but instead with a group of friends.- Bugs/Issues - Throughout my playthrough I did not run into any game breaking bugs, the only noticable mishaps happen with some of the game's AI and a few bugs with the buggy in The Following.- My Thoughts - Dying Light has made a stale genre fun again. It essentially takes bits and pieces of many famous games such as Mirror's Edge ( Parkour ) Far Cry/Dead Island ( Combat/Crafting) and it constantly feels like a new Left 4 Dead title, I have not had so much fun with a zombie game since Left 4 Dead. Dying Light has certainly earned a place among the list of best zombie games in my opinion.Dying Light gets a solid 9.5/10

The gameplay has a very nice progression to it, the world is fun to explore, and the parkour system makes maneuvering the landscape incredibly satisfying. The story leaves a lot to be desired, but it's a zombie game, so that comes as little surprise.The game plays primarily from a first-person perspective, and sets you on a path of blazing through the open world on foot, fitted with extremely satisfying parkour mechanics that honestly, more games need to copy. You start out with basic weaponry—metal pipes, wooden bats, frying pans—and progress through to the point of having crazy swords, guns, crossbows & more.As you earn XP, you're able to purchase perks that augment your gameplay. XP is earned for each aspect of gameplay, with more running & climbing giving you more XP to spend on perks related to traversal. _childDocuments_.review: Dying Light is an open world adventure horror game, developed by Techland and published by Warner Brothers, releasing in January 2015 for PC, PS4 and Xbox One. This game sort of came out of nowhere, it didn’t have very much hype behind it prior to release and it came as a welcome surprise to a usually quite month of the year for big game releases. The game play in Dying Light reminded me so closely of Dead Island. You play in first person view as you explore the world. Of course, the world has been overrun by zombies. One of the changes to the “Dead Island” gameplay style is the parkour system. We have seen parkour systems used in games such as Assassins Creed and Shadow of Mordor, but Dying Light’s version knocks them all out of the park. A third of the gameplay is based around the running and jumping across the landscape – you are able to hide from the zombies when you are jumping rooftop-to-rooftop so it is really in your interest to get to grasp with it as soon as possible. There are times when you will be thrown into the combat situations; this is where the Dead Island mechanics come in – melee weapons are going to be your primary source of damage and they work exactly the same as DI. Your weapons take durability damage each time you hit, but you can repair them on the fly with the required parts. Once you get your hands on a gun, the odds swing dramatically in your favour, but you do get the downside of the noise it creates, and it possibly attracting even more zombies to your location.  One of my favourite mechanics Dying Light introduced though would be the dynamic day and night cycle. During the day time, zombies will act in their usual manner, whilst they are still a danger, they can definitely be managed fairly easily. Once it is night time though; boy oh boy, you better have your running shoes on! The zombies transform into a much more dangerous form, they can sprint, and see a lot further away, as well as their heightened sense of hearing – meaning you will find it very hard to by-pass them.  The day night cycle lasts for about 70 minutes in total, about one hour in daylight, and 10 minutes at night. Graphically, I am very happy with the quality of graphics on show. I was nowhere near able to push out the game on 4k, even on the menu screen my frame rate plummeted, and I even struggled on 1440p, so I had to make do with just 1080p with all of the settings ramped up.  The lighting effects, explosions, and scenery all look absolutely stunning. Textures are all high resolution and the animations of everything in the game are faultless. Whilst there is a lot of animations that can be annoying after the first few times, such as when you open a chest, you have to wait 2-3 seconds whilst the animation plays out of you opening it; personally I would have liked this to be skippable but it is a really minor issue. Dying Light starts out in a very easy fashion, allowing you to get to grips with the game mechanics, and the tutorial at the start of the game introduces you to the game very well too. The parkour mechanic can take a little while to get used to as sometimes you will probably fall whilst climbing buildings because you aren’t used to the way it works and feels, but it just takes practice. The only time I had real issues with the combat difficulty would be the later stages in the game, when you are just getting hammered by hordes of zombies over and over again. Little tip; conserve your ammo!!!The vast open world you are playing in very rarely leaves you with nothing to do; there are tons of side missions, collectables and loot to find. There are over 100 different melee weapons, and they can be modified in different combinations (over 1000 of them!). The side missions do seem a little but samey after a while. I completed about 13 or so out of the 44 before I finished the main story and this was because they are very repetitive. A few other optional objectives consist of finding relief packages which is where you race the opposite faction to get a supply drop, saving survivors from the opposite faction’s men attacking them, and the same for zombies. You can also go out of your way to find collectable items such as trophy’s and notes around the world. Completing the main story and about a ¼ of the side missions has taken me just over ten hours. Right now I don’t have a dying urge to go back in and complete the rest of the missions, purely because of the repetitive factor, but I will be keeping Dying Light installed so that I can in the future as well as the anticipated DLC which will be releasing soon. The devs have reports that with all of the current content in the game, you should be able to push 50 hours. I struggle to believe that, I would say you can get about 20 hours out of Dying Light at the time of writing this. I didn’t have any technical issues. The game ran very well at 1080p at a steady 60 fps, the only time it dropped sub 60 was in extremely hectic scenes with hundreds of zombies and lots of explosions but that is to be expected. I played the game with keyboard and mouse, and should be strongly recommended you do not attempt to play with a controller.To sum up, Dying Light is a really nicely done zombie adventure game. Personally I feel it is a much more rounded off game compared to the Dead Island series, and adds plenty of depth to the genre rather than re-hashing content that’s already been done before. The main story and core gameplay mechanics make’s Dying Light one of the standout games to be released in 2015 and I would strongly recommend this game to any open world genre fans out there. 1) Stay away2) Not Recommended3) Only recommended when on sale4) Recommended6) This is a must playIf you found this review helpful, please consider giving it a thumbs up. _childDocuments_.review: Dying Light is a zombie game that focuses on atmosphere and player movement. If you have played Dead Island you already know the basic mechanics; craft melee weapons and bash zombies while collecting supplies. But Dying Light employs numerous changes that improve on this.Atmosphere is perhaps its best asset. The day-night cycle is a crucial component, as there are major changes to mood and gameplay as the sun sets behind the horizon. At night, the tension elevates as you experience reduced visibility and face zombies that are nimble, fast and deadly. You will be tempted to venture out at night for extra rewards. During the day, you battle hordes of shambling zombies that are fun to eviscerate with a broad selection of weaponry. The difference between night and day provides a genuine rollercoaster ride.Parkour movement makes navigating the world immensely enjoyable. You are able to run, jump and climb over buildings with ease. You just look at a ledge and hold the jump button to climb. As you come upon zombie hordes you analyse the area quickly. Do you attack or use the environment to avoid danger? Various slides and kicks make dealing with zombies, and human foes, quite interesting. Traps placed around the world can be triggered to slow pursuers or distract zombies, giving you an edge as you learn the world around you.The single player is surprisingly entertaining and lengthy, with side quests that are often better than those in the story. Characters are well-defined and memorable, with more effort given to justify the game world. You run between areas, clear safe zones, rescue people and collect items. Story missions might even feature shootouts in indoor levels. Progression comes via a skill tree that unlocks significant character upgrades. You will also learn to craft items like Molotovs and flares to make you more formidable against the various zombie types.Dying Light is also a cooperative game and playing with others is easy. The basic cooperative action works well, aside from rigid animations, and you can undertake just about every quest from the campaign. You can even open your game to a 'zombie invasion' where another player joins and takes the role of a dangerous night-hunter zombie that can instantly kill survivors with a pounce. Your goal is to destroy zombie nests before you lose a certain number of lives. Whether playing alone, or with a group of four, this versus mode is actually good despite its relative simplicity. It gets hectic when four players are battling tougher zombies and running all over the open map while being pursued by a night-hunter that can summon exploding zombies. Dying Light is a terrific zombie game that greatly improves the core mechanics from Dead Island. It emphasizes the world and how you move around in it. The changes between day and night are refreshing and memorable. There is a healthy amount of content that will provide dozens of hours of entertainment in solo or cooperative play. Dying Light mixes intriguing elements to craft a zombie experience that is entertaining, atmospheric, visceral, and frenzied.

_childDocuments_.review: I initially enjoyed this game during my first playthrough, as it was fairly neat both as a visual novel and a dating sim. Looking at this game again, however, I feel as though as a dating simulator, this game is very weak in the genre.In the game, you get to know and date a variety of different characters. To be fair, the art style and the animation is decent. Each character, excluding side-characters that don't serve much of a purpose other than to exist and sometimes be an obstacle for the player, have some facial expressions that fit fairly well with the dialogue. The way this dating simulator is set up, however, feels kinda off in my opinion.When you exclude Coby, you go on three dates with all the other characters you can date with. While I understand that this choice of time spent with these characters is because of the amount them, I imagine a real dating game would make you spend time with a given character for several days (maybe even weeks or months). This fact is why I think the choice of making this game also be a visual novel was a weak one.While visual novels allow for easy storytelling, throwing dating into the mix can make or break it depending on all the choices being made. In the case of this visual novel I feel as though some of the writing is very odd. The paths that come closest to me as actually being fairly decent are Seth's and Skye's. All the other paths, to me at least, feel very weird and forgettable.There's also some random minigames in two of the paths (Zenith's and Remy's paths) which both feel very awkward to control. Makes me wonder why there's no minigames in any of the other paths and I guess the quality of the two I just mentioned explains why. Throwing a minigame into a visual novel is no easy feat, which makes me also think that the addition of these minigames were mostly pointless (and no, they are not a fun diversion for after you beat the game).I've seen other visual novels try to weave dating in without having it be the main point and succeed far more than this. Some great examples that come to mind for me is the Purrfect Apawcalypse trilogy and Nekojishi. Both games have a slight dating aspect to them where the more you interact with the characters in the story the more you succeed, leading to a variety of endings and resulting in a far more memorable experience.I'd also like to mention the 18+ scenes (can be accessed by adding a text file with a specific name to the game's files). What I find funny when playing through the game like this is that it feels as though these scenes were where the most effort was put into the general writing. It is a shame that the devs did not really take the time to put more effort into the actual story because if they took the effort they had from the 18+ scenes and put it into the normal scenes, then this game would be so much better than what it currently is now.While I understand that dating was the main point of Amorous, I feel as though it isn't pulled off quite right. If it were a furry dating simulator I would imagine it would have more depth to it, but here it's just a collection of short visual novels that range from a few fairly memorable ones to some not-so-memorable ones.As far as recommendations, I have never played an actual dating game (aside from Blush Blush which feels more like a phone app than a legit dating game) so I instead highly recommend you check out the visual novels I mentioned earlier, Nekojishi and the Purrfect Apawcalypse trilogy.

_childDocuments_.review: ** I ended up playing this game again because I remember liking the game and thought that maybe I just tried playing it at the wrong time. After putting in more time with it I decided to recommend the game. Though I still agree with a lot of what my past self disliked, I did find NPC's to be less of a nuisance later in the game. There's a certain point when you can get stocked up on firearms and it just really turns the tide. I still found human enemies to be a little out of place. They're far too strong at first then far too easy later on. The zombies are fun all the time though and that's what counts I guess. Original review:There is a lot to like about this game. The zombie hordes, the melee head smashes, and the fear your first few night missions will fill you with. However, I also found a lot that I didn't like. Human enemies with overwhelming health pools are annoying to deal with until you find a firearm. You can use fire to make this process easier, but it just doesn't make sense to me that I can bash a human NPC in the head with a beefed up weapon nearly 30 times just to get the same old reply, "Your only making me angry!" Battling human NPCs was by far my least favorite part of this title.I also found myself being respawned right on top of enemies after failing a mission. This, alongside poor level design on some of the story missions had me banging my head against the wall. It's not a bad game, I just found parts of it to be very frustrating and unbalanced. This is my opinion, it may differ from yours.

_childDocuments_.review: I discovered this game by accident. I have more games that I have time to play them, but this... What a gem of a game. One of the things that stood out to me is how addictive and rewarding the gameplay is. This si how you make a game.Not much else to say. It will go in my list of favorite games of all times.Pros:Graphics: 10/10. Everythign is so alive and detailed. Lighting and oclusion is up there with the best-looking games in the past couple of years. The wind blows, gently caressing the trees and blowing debris. The rain and lighting will disorient you at nights. The sunlight almost makes you feel the warmth of it. Nothing feels stale or dead... except... well, the dead... because they are dead.Sounds: 8/10. Sound effects embrace you like the graphics, although the soundtrack is kind of dull.Controls: 9/10. Best I've felt in an FPS. It has a bit of a learning curve, but once you've mastered all your moves, you just glide through Harran or the Countryside. Melee usually doesn't work for FPS games, but for this game, it was meant to be. Fighting hordes of Zombies, jumping through buildings, sliding in narrow allyways, it all just flows so nicely.Replay Value: 10/10 160 hours on single player. 0 on multiplayer. Once playthrough on the main story and The Following. Need I say more?Content: 10/10. Developers are still adding stuff to keep this game alive. the expansion is an example of how you do it right. The Following by itself could be a game. Took me about 60 hours to complete.Cons:Story: A bit bland with forgettable characters.Enemy designs: There are about 5 or 6 different Zombies and a few special zombies. That's it.Performance: On a high-end PC. Maxed out. Even though for the most part I get around 120fps, in some areas, the game stutters a bit. Or even after an hour of playing, the game will slowly start to stutter. It is not bad and it can go unnoticed.

_childDocuments_.review: After a good 16 hours of gameplay I can say that I quite enjoyed the whole ride so therefore this review about Dying Light.While I'm not a huge fan of Zombie Games at all, I actually quite dislike them as they tend to be quite repetitive. I must say that I did enjoy Dying Light, with having the open world experience in a good combination of the story mode and the various side missions.That said let's get into more details regarding the game itself.The Story=========The story was decent, while very linear and pretty expected, it was still pretty lovely to go through. The ending however was quite disappointing however as it just felt a bit too open. I know this was done intentionally so you could still room the map to hack and slash your way through zombies and finish side missions but the story didn't felt right to stop there or at least not the way they did it.In general it was still pretty enjoyable, however I did enjoy doing the various side missions more than the actual story as they just felt more challenging and not too expected of what you required to do. All in all the story mode and side missions did gave you plenty to do that for me filled up a good 16 hours of gameplay!The Gameplay============While I still dislike zombie games I did play a wide variety of them (including various zombie mods) I must say that the overall gameplay of Dying Light was quite to my liking. On the counterpart of Dead Island which didn't spiked my interest at all, I tried both Dead Island 1 and Riptide but they just weren't to my liking. Perhaps I must give them another try and see how I experience it this time after now playing Dying Light, it's also perhaps good for the upcoming Dead Island 2!The only main thing that really bothered me was that the weapons you used would break only after like 50 hits, which isn't that realistic. Okay an old rusted pipe might break or so but a brand new katana I do think those can go with you a couple years without bending if used correctly. That together with the very limited choice of firearms, the only weapons types I found were a handgun, a rifle and a shotgun. The fact that there's a lack of a sniper rifle really bothered me for long range takedowns and the huge lack of silenced addons or weapons in general. While you can add additional stuff to melee weapons you can't to weapons nor upgrade them in anyway, so it would've been great if you would also be able to upgrade/customize the weapons of adding stuff like: silencers, scopes, extra magazines, less recoil, etc...That aside I must say that the overall gameplay of Dying Light is very solid and quite fun!The Quality===========I was actually quite surprised by the quality of the game and not that alone but the smoothness and optimisation of it as well.The textures and models were pretty lovely and together with the great detailed world you play in sure made a great zombie slashing experience.Various things did bother me like too many models using mirrored textures (like elevator doors, pipes, pillars, etc...).That if you have a bloody weapon and you into the water or it's heavily raining that the blood is still on it.The (night) skybox compression that tend to give off all  the green artifacts which really did bother me on various occasions.And the overall model repetition, but that's just nitpicking for an open world game after all.But in general I was still surprised from the quality of this game, really great quality textures and models and all greatly optimised!Overall=======In the end I quite liked Dying Light, while I'm still not a too huge fan of Zombie Games, this game sure gave my some interest to give the Dead Island series and some other Zombie games another try.In general a great game and for that I give it a solid 9/10!

_childDocuments_.review: So this is the first Review I have written here. I have nearly 200 hours into Dying Light and I am still trying to figure out why! Both of those games STINK on a whole new level UNLESS.... you are playing co-op. Yep, much like Borderlands, the Dead Island series kind of blows as a single player experience. The same can not be said for Dying Light. I will reitterate... I have NO idea why I have this many hours into this game. I think it might have to do with the following; 1. It's just fun. Yep, parkor and zombie killin is just plain fun.2. Techland has supported/promoted this game WELL! And NO, I have not spent ONE U.S. Dollar more than I wanted. (Of course I bought 'The Following').3. Weapons.... My god Mowing down dozens of Z's with an electric machete is just magical in my world. 4. Doing donuts in an open field with my OP car/dune buggy while running over TONS of Z's... This feeds my anti-social, escapist mentality. (Lets be honest... we all need some serious escapisim in the age of Trump and (fill in the blank) times..... Are there issues? Yep... but the game play more than makes up for it. Yep... GAMEPLAY.... I am a 99.99% graphics guy... I make a HUGE part of my living from game graphix. Don't care when it comes to this game. name: Crypt Custodian
detailed_description: Crypt Custodian is a charming metroidvania/zelda-like about cleaning up the afterlife. You play as Pluto - a mischievous cat who has just died, and landed in the afterlife's palace. After a brief and disastrous meeting with the Afterlife Guardian - Kendra - you are banished from the palace and sentenced to clean... FOREVER!! Explore the vast grounds that surround the palace, battle beasts with your trusty broom, and gain new abilities to expand your map. Solve puzzles, discover secrets, and… organize an ambush to break back into the palace! A Charming Cast Of Characters Meet and befriend all the other bad ghosts who live outside the palace. Learn how they died, and what caused them to face eternal banishment! And then head on over to the local haunt- The Sinner’s Inn- to chat with the ghosts you meet, and upgrade your gear. Tons of Upgrades Complete puzzles, battle epic bosses, and clean your way through ruined dungeons in order to collect new upgrades and abilities. Customize your play style by mix-and-matching your upgrades, and use the abilities you collect to expand your world. A Lively Interconnected World Traverse a vast landscape with secrets hiding at every corner. Form your own path and discover the afterlife’s many secrets at your own pace.

_childDocuments_.review: I recently (within this year) completed Islets, another game from Kyle Thompson. The week after I beat it, the trailer dropped for Crypt Custodian and I knew I needed it. Just like Islets, this game is adorable and engaging, with fun mechanics and it seems like a ton to do. I love the world and the characters and while I'm not very far into it yet, I feel like it's really important to support small developers doing really, really exceptional work. This game feels very polished and extremely fun. I've played exclusively on my Steam Deck and it's the perfect deck game. tl;dr if you like fun mechanics, cute stories, and metroidvanias, plus supporting the little guy, check this out.
_childDocuments_.name: Crypt Custodian

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first game I've played where I made extensive use of the "assist" options, and though I had mixed feelings about it at first, I'm glad I did. I really liked the atmosphere and exploration in Crypt Custodian, which to me are the best parts of a Metroidvania. On the other hand, I have a rather low frustration tolerance for pattern-memorization and bullet-hell-type dodging, so when I got to the first boss, I wasn't sure I was going to keep playing.But I still wanted to explore, so I switched to easy difficulty and gave myself extra life, and eventually beat the boss, even though it still took a few tries. After that I switched back to normal difficulty and life, and just turned off fall damage. I kept up that pattern for most of the bosses, though I did manage to beat a couple on "regular" settings.And then something odd happened. I tried Boss Rush mode on "Easy," and found that the first boss wasn't as difficult as I remembered. After several tries, I managed to beat it without taking damage. "Huh. I bet I could do that faster." And I did, until I was fast enough to get S+ ranking. So I went up to "Normal." And then "Hard." And pretty soon the boss that I had so much trouble with the first time around was completely trivial. Which I certainly would not have anticipated going in.I guess what I'm trying to say is, "Thank you to the developer for making a game accessible on my terms. In doing so, you also made me reconsider my own capabilities and what types of games I might enjoy."ANYway. If you're still reading this, thanks, and buy Crypt Custodian already. It's well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Crypt Custodian

_childDocuments_.review: Each game by this dev feels better than the last, while still retaining a lot of the same feel and vibes.Like Islets, this game is very smooth to play and explore.  There's paths branching out in every direction and it was pure dopamine uncovering every last room and collectable.  If you're struggling, there's a shop where you can pay to reveal a missing item or important location to visit.  It is very easy to 100% the game because of this.  I got stuck on one puzzle and one cryptic bit at the end though, which I had to look up, but otherwise I was able to figure everything out pretty easily.  The only QoL issue I ran into was that scrolling around on the map screen was too slow.The pet owner in me loved the cutesy pet-centric storytelling, it was wholesome and at times sad.  The plot had me wondering what was  going on too.I wasn't fond of the composers work on the previous games but he's finally won me over with this title, with plenty of chill tunes that stuck in my head.I'd recommend this to all fans of metroidvanias & Zelda-likes, it's one of the best games to come out this year for me.

_childDocuments_.review: A first look:At first, I was a bit afraid it might have been too hard, but I've been doing surprisingly well on normal. Yet the nagging feeling that I'll get stuck somewhere soon rose again. Then I discovered it has a lovely range of accessibility options that make it pretty much so anyone can tune it to their taste, making it as hard or as easy as you like. I was in heaven—no pun intended!This means I can enjoy this cute game to bits in my style and feel, aka just laid back and enjoying it to the fullest. I would have already thumbed it up just for that, but there is so much more to it.The fact that I can turn off photosensitivity is a massive plus for me, too; ever since my brain tumour surgery, I have been a bit sensitive to flashing, especially when I'm tired or having a bad day. Now, I don't have to interrupt my gameplay or flee for a while when it acts up, and I'm so thankful for that. It has to be said that the art style and music are amazing, too! The characters I've met so far are super charming. Kendra, for example! She gave me a few laughs, so calm and collected, while casually banning friends to the afterlife. Totally normal, no biggie! I think she secretly wants the whole palace to herself! And it's not only their personality but also their design and style that I like a lot. It just all feels so delightful, and I'm here for it. And Pebbles is so cute, too. It all excites me to meet everyone else (and their stories)!Of course, the hoarde... euh, I mean... The collector in me is very satisfied, too, since I already found a few of the collectables, and I'm thrilled to search for the others. I hope I can find and collect everything! I can't wait to see what other abilities I can acquire and collect. The puzzler in me is super happy, too; they're enjoyable. This whole game has been, so far, actually.And don't even get me started on the hack-and-slasher within me. I got a broom, and I can slap it around like there is no tomorrow, which kind of got me in trouble in the first place... But I think it's fun to have something else for a change, then yet another sword. Plus, it kind of really fits my janitor role, huh?But for now, I'm back to exploring since I have RL stuff to do soon and want to spend as much time as possible in the game until then since I won't be able to return for a while.

_childDocuments_.review: Crypt Custodian is the perfect cozy game while still leaving room for challenge. I love that I can fast travel from the start by opening my map from ANYWHERE and selecting a fast travel point and POOF I am there. I feel like my time is being respected.  I've defeated two Major bosses, saved a couple cats and made friends along the way. The humor is refreshing and the world is mysterious. I can't wait to discover what lies beyond what I've already uncovered!

_childDocuments_.review: The Thompson Brothers have outdone themselves with , their third outing. For me–and I love –this is the greatest Metroidvania game I’ve ever played. You can read through my detailed list below if you’re interested. All that I can express to you at the top here is that playing this game was the single greatest gaming experience I’ve ever had. Buy and play this game immediately if you like Metroidvanias!Here’s my breakdown advocating for  as the greatest game ever made:Game Controls/MechanicsEverything about the gameplay is incredible. Combat and platforming feels extremely fluid and responsive. Look, you can warp to a save point at any time in this game, but moving around and exploring the underworld felt so amazing that I skipped on using fast travel a good chunk of the time. It’s that good!AccessibilityBetween this title and , Kyle Thompson is killing it with accessibility features. The almost granular approach at which you can adjust the difficulty settings ensures that everyone will have an enjoyable experience. In a game that’s all about gatekeeping on multiple levels, Kyle has been so thoughtful when it concerns the player’s time and quality-of-life specs. Every game should have the fine-tuned accessibility features that Mr. Thompson provides in his welcoming Metroidvanias.Art Style/MusicFor me, hand-drawn video games are where it’s at. Sure,  and  are striking and beautiful, but their aesthetic is one of literal darkness. Trying to navigate through such dim/murky biomes gives me a headache sometimes. Kyle Thompson can create dark and gothic backdrops too, but his art style and animations are unmatched in the industry. The ultra bright color saturation that Kyle has basically trademarked in all of his games is simply gorgeous. All of the animations are crisp, sharp and beautifully rendered; truly a visual feast. And Eric Thompson’s musical scores are phenomenal. He manages impressive versatility with pieces that shift from whimsical, ambient, pleading, somber and spirited. The melodies are infectious, too. I found myself repeatedly humming certain biome scores after finishing some sessions. Both Kyle and Eric have left recognizable signatures in their artistry, and I am totally here for it! Check out Eric’s sky battle composition from  standing in for the gated battles in . And there’s nothing more pleasing to my dopamine hitbox than Kyle’s light-shattering spiral effect that blooms across the screen every time a character gets an upgrade. The Thompson Brothers are true masters!Metagaming GeniusWhat sets Kyle’s projects apart from every other game on the market is that he continuously subverts player expectations when it comes to interacting with modern gaming tropes. He clearly understands genre requirements, the role of NPCs, how UIs work, and all the rest of it. But all of Mr. Thompson’s games like to play tricks on us in the best way possible: by going against the formulaic nature of video games. He knows we don’t like grinding for currency, even though a certain NPC shopkeeper has set some nightmarish prices for items in his store. As the game progresses, though, you’re relieved to discover that grinding won’t be in your future play sessions because of a surprising narrative twist. This is just one example of Kyle’s metagaming genius. Mr. Thompson likes to bring us up close to the pitfalls of gaming that we’ve all come to expect in the Metroidvania genre, only to suddenly change the mechanics/narrative of the gameplay. Sure, the joke is always on us, but I love it!  is so refreshing and engaging because it knows how to manipulate our game sensibilities in the most delightful way possible. Quick shout-out to “Ghost Slaughter 3,”  the best metagaming boss fight that had me laughing for days. Pure genius!The StoryIf the controls are stellar and the level design is innovative, I think the last element that makes a great game is the story and  definitely delivers. Kyle Thompson’s absurdist comedy and sarcasm are spot on, and the character interactions/dialogue are highlights in all of his games. But this installment elevates the humor and unexpected plot developments, and the payoff is huge. Yes, the humor is tremendous here, but I was also moved by the other characters’ backstories (the photo section of this game is so beautiful and devastating, holy cow!). When the game was over and I had unlocked everything, the themes of the story really struck me as being subtle, powerful and very timely. Yes, the critics always write that Kyle’s games are charming, and they are. But this game has a level of subtext to it that allows for so many interpretations, and I find that remarkable. I think Mr. Thompson is going for something deeper with , be it messages about stereotypes and assumptions or exploring the importance of empathy. But that’s all surface level analysis. I won’t share my interpretations about the characters or the story’s conclusion, but I will say that the larger themes are dark, complicated, and political. None of this bad, by the way. In fact, it’s the opposite. Putting vitally important issues into a video game can be tricky. I understand that a game’s legacy doesn’t want to be known for being preachy or having an agenda. But the best video games out there have very strong messages, and they tackle uncomfortable issues–but they accomplish this through subtlety.  has a very strong moral center, and I believe that it has brilliantly coded messages buried deep within itself that are left for players to unearth. I will stress here that these are my thoughts and opinions; they are not the thoughts/opinions of the game developers. Anyway, I think it’s sophisticated storytelling that’s riveting, satisfying and poignant. You add fantastic humor back into the mix and you get, in my humble opinion, the greatest video game that’s ever been made.I’m so happy that I live in a world where this game actually exists, and that you can play it right now!

_childDocuments_.review: Crypt Custodian is such an awesome Metroidvania. One of the best I ever played. None of the achievements are missable, there are 3 very challenging achievements. I guess that completion takes around 14 hours.  14h+ 7/10 1 You don't need a guide No No No No Yes, in "boss rush" mode the time in which you defeat each boss matters No No Yes, but only for 1 achievement in "boss rush" mode NoYou're a cat and just died at the beginning of the game., You get sent to the afterlife where you first will be judged on your actions to determine if you go to the temple or are doomed to clean the afterlife forever. On your journey, you'll meet a lot of other ghosts and learn about their lives and how they have been doing down here. Crypt Custodian is such a great Metroidvania with a lot of quality-of-life features. It is one of THE BEST Metroidvanias I have ever played. The movement feels so good, the abilities you unlock are fun and the system to choose which power-ups you want to have active and the amount you can choose between are just awesome. I'm very impressed with Kyle Thompson's work. The game feels so responsive and the combat/movement just feels good. Furthermore, the game looks so good as well. I fell in love early on in the game already with the presentation and how the movement felt in the game, but my love for it only grew from that point on. You have a map on which you can mark with symbols things you saw but couldn't reach yet, but you even don't have to do that. There is a specific jukebox in the game that will sell you map markers and that way even if you didn't find them yourself it is very easy to clean up all the side objectives later on. Another amazing QoL feature is that you don't have to be at a warp spot to warp to somewhere else on the map. You can just open the map in your menu and warp to any warping spot. And it feels like there is always one close by. This helped during the game but also when cleaning up after beating the story. The achievements in Crypt Custodian can be separated in 2 groups and none of the achievements are missable: - 45 of them are for finishing the story and finding everything. As stated above, this is quite easy at the end of the game after finishing the story by buying map markers. That way you can easily see which items you haven't found and where to find them. There is one challenging puzzle on the NorthWest side of the map, but you might want to look around in your menus to maybe get a clue on how to solve it. - The other 3 achievements are for boss rush mode. You have to beat boss rush mode for every boss on S+ on every difficulty. This is a real challenge and tbh.. I wasn't able to get S+ ranking on easy on the first boss, let alone later bosses and higher difficulties. However, I know I'm not good at games and normally don't even try stuff like this. So I'm not a good indicator of how hard this really is. I give Crypt Custodian 4.5 out of 5 stars.

_childDocuments_.review: Crypt Custodian is such a great new game from Kyle Thompson!  About 10 hours to 100% main game, it has way more to explore than you'd expect.  Then another 5 hours or so to grind out S+ ranks on Boss Rush mode for all achievements.  Highly recommend!  And check out Islets and Sheepo as well if you haven't played those yet as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Crypt Custodian

_childDocuments_.review: Crypt Custodian has been a really great game experience, of the kind I have craved for for a while. I was seeking for a Metroidvania that I would enjoy playing with a history that would move me. Promise kept!Of course, the gameplay is not really inventive, but it does its job (very) well. The controls are pleasant, the bossfights represent a decent challenge, and the upgrades are satisfying. It is a well-done Metroidvania.The quality of life is also quite impressive for such an indie game. As a boss fight enjoyer, I am always disappointed when there's no boss rush to extend the duration of the game. Crypt Custodian provides a very nice one, simple to navigate, with a decent amount of challenge to get the maximal grades for each level of difficulty, You can skip much dialogs and cutscenes by pressing Y, and this is really appreciated when you try and retry the bosses. You can adjust the difficulty anytime (I recommend to set it to the maximum and, if this is too challenging, to adjust it until the game represents a fine challenge for you. I have played maximum difficulty all along, and it is not insurmountable, but I would get that players less familiar to this kind of game or who just want to enjoy some nice visual style while wandering prefer to avoid tryharding). Also, you can buy some markers for your map when you are out of leads to make progresses in the game (in-game backseat, so to say, but only if you want).But the main reason that kept me so late at night in front of this game is the visual style and the atmosphere. behind the cute design of Crypt Custodian lies a melancholic but also heartwarming tribute to our beloved pets. As simple as it was, I really was stirred everytime I discovered what the life of the animals I met was before they passed away. I also feel that there's an innuendo about the impact of human activities on animals, given the backstories of many characters. But maybe it is not the case. The music has this kind of Adventure Time Vibe as well: The world seems cartoonish and goofy at first glance but it really holds some depth if you take the time to explore the world around you. And maybe I'm the softhearted kind, but I had my tear to the final cutscene.Crypt Custodian does have some flaws. And the negative comments I've read covered them quite well. The regular mobs are not really a threat and have very similar moves, the level design might be considered too convoluted, which made it boring to some people who played. I also agree with one criticism about the use of the abilities, some of them are highly contextual and will be of no use in places that have not been made for them. To add to this, I would have enjoyed more music. They really have the kind of vibe I enjoy and there was simply not enough of it (e.g., one song per boss would have been so great). I also found weird the fact that some cutscenes/dialogues in the boss rush modes can be skipped, but not some others.  However, I really think these negative aspects should not dissuade anyone to give this game a try. There's much love and work put into it and it deserves to be appreciated. Much games that yet benefited from more resources do not even compare to that. Please, give Crypt Custodian a try!

_childDocuments_.review: This one requires an informational review, because the game comes with some potentially unexpected design decisions for the genre and presentation. So what follows won't be glowing, but hopefully helping you decide if this is for you. You start with exactly 4 hit points and can only ever upgrade to 5. Health is only replenished at save points and little fountains in between. And the majority of challenges are all about taking as few hits as possible. Be it the general game play, where you can only take 4 hits in a boss fight or between landmarks - or one of the many different bonus challenges like curses that lock your ability to heal until you've defeated a certain number of enemies (while adding additional hazards) - or chests that ask you to defeat a gauntlet without taking any hit whatsoever. The difficulty setting only affects enemy attacks (reaction times and patterns) as well as how tightly timed optional platforming challenges are. "Easy" is by no means actually easy. (conversely, "Hard" doesn't make the game much harder)Only the assist options will actually make the game easier. Here you get up to 200% attack damage, 3 extra hit points, no fall damage, and more leeway on timed challenges. (I forgot these options existed until now - but definitely recommend using them, if you are struggling on easy - hell, these might be the better settings to use in general, so you still get to experience more attack patterns) You always have fast travel to any visited save point available on the map. Health replenish points have infinite uses. You cannot walk off ledges. No hit challenge chests replenish the one hit point you can loose from them on a retry. You can speed up and skip death animations and cut scenes. Map markers for both items and quests can be bought (although item markers require that you have uncovered the respective room). Boss fights are always very close to a save point. There is an upgrade that can disable falling damage outside of boss fights. And outside of boss fights and combat challenges that lock you onto a platform until you have defeated a wave of enemies, you can easily ignore and sweep past all threats. (at least in easy mode - this is how I completed the game 100% in exactly 8 hours getting the majority of achievements except for the defeat 1000 enemies one) And there are probably more details like this. The amount of care taken to streamline everything is astounding. And from what I can tell, absolutely every feedback from the demo was taken into account without compromising on the intended design. Your goal in this game is to make 10 friends. And while the very first one may suggest the formula is one per area and defeating the areas boss will somehow make them your friend, the game actually shakes this up significantly beyond that. First of all, while the characters do have their main area, they will still appear all over the map. And making friends is not always tied to the boss fight. (those do give you required abilities though) Speaking of boss fights, I really like how uniquely the majority of the boss characters are tied into the narrative. I think there are only two that feel like they are just a random unique enemy you only fight once, without any relation to the friends you are making.Dashing around the map and the dash and jump attack feel really good.The game has a speed run mode. (auto skips all dialogue and adds a timer)It unlocks a boss rush mode the moment you defeat the first one.And it unlocks a randomizer mode on completing the game. (shuffles all item locations) The game unfortunately very quickly felt somewhat bland beyond the first area. While every area does have a new look, new enemies and new mechanics - it still all seemed mostly reskinned or very single purpose. It's been challenging to figure out why I got that impression, but I'll try to nail down things that contribute.Every room in this game is floating islands. I imagine this is very much needed for the kind of platforming challenge the game intends to deliver (you can easily swoop out and back onto solid ground to cut corners and avoid attacks), but never being boxed into physically closed rooms certainly added to every area feeling like a reskin of those floating islands.There were only 3 boss fights I remember as mechanically unique. (Spoiler for those:) All the others (many many more) were just bullet hell damage sponges to me (and I imagine the extra attack patterns on higher difficulties will further drive that home - I didn't have the patience for that).New area enemies are largely variations on their basic versions: melee, ranged (targeted or omnidirectional), flying and jumping. Apart from the area where all enemies share the unique mechanic of the boss, the challenge always felt the same. You never defeat enemies with something other than whacking them several times. (there are no weak points, pushing/reflecting/blocking interactions or required combat abilities)And all the abilities you get are mostly single purpose to cross larger gaps and gain access to new areas, which then often let you hit a switch to lower a gate or extend a bridge, rendering your ability unnecessary there in the future. This is good in service of smoothing out traversal, but it also speaks to the abilities not being very fun to use repeatedly. For most of them there are no clever ways to use them in combat or combine them with environment mechanics other than their intended ones.(there are upgrade perks and special attacks to find, purchase and equip besides the main abilities - but all of them only alter the mechanics in small ways such as changing your attack damage/speed or adding projectiles to your existing moves - I always opted for anything that made me faster)The only ability that can be used in more than one way as well as in combat requires you to hold the attack button to charge it up and later does not allow you to choose between an upgrade to it or the original (also very useful) behavior when used over ground. Because of these limitations I ended up not using it very much, even though it is the best among them. (aside from the dash, you get that one first and it feels so fundamental that it's easy to forget it was an upgrade)Alright, I think that covers most of it. It is a very well polished game. Everything works exactly as it should. It achieves what it sets out to do. So I can fully recommend it, if you like what you see on the store page and the details I described are either exactly your jam or won't stop you from having a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is super fun! The characters are sweet and funny, and it has so many accessibility options so you can play at your own pace if that's what you need. _childDocuments_.review: * The artstyle is really nice and some of the music is very engaging. I especially like the challenge room music.* Many upgrades that you can mix and match. These meaningfully change the gameplay as opposed to just applying a small bonus to some stat. * The atmosphere is nice and cosy* The combat is simple yet tedious with no environment interaction. There are some upgrades along the way, but in the end you still have to wail on even the basic enemies for too long. Since there is minimal reward for killing enemies you can just run past them, but often times a random attack will get you and remove one of your precious few lives. Special attacks exist, but there are mostly two that are strictly better than the others so there is little use for switching to different ones since you can only have one active at a time.* Enemy variety is weirdly minimal. There are lots of different looking enemies, but they all seem to be formulaic combinations of one attack trait plus a movement mode. There are jumping, flying and running enemies and they either shoot projectiles at you, do a short range area attack or an explosion of spikes around them. Sometimes more than one of those together. This makes the individual enemies pretty forgettable and boring to fight.* Tedious Leveldesign. The rooms feel like they have been assembled out of very basic tiles. Every biome has it's own tileset, but they mostly differ in look not in function. This makes every biome feel very samey apart from some biome specific but often underused puzzle elements. This gets worse because the individual biomes feel pretty big while not actually containing that many interesting things apart from some challenges and a boss. * Underused abilities. Some of the abilities that you collect have only very specific usecases and while they can be activated outside of those usecases they have no other utility or are too slow and weak to be useful.* Lacking reward structure for bosses. There are quite a few bosses but they often pop up suddenly without buildup. After defeating them sometimes you gain a new ability, sometimes a new friend and sometimes just nothing. The friends don't have mechanical impact so often times there is neither a form of emotional connection to the boss nor a reward for defeating it. They are just a roadblock. * Not a fan of the trend towards bullet hell style difficulty. Boss battles can be quite challenging but mostly because of the amount of projectiles on the screen. Similarly to the regular enemies bosses are mostly mix and match from a set of basic attack patterns. * Some of the music was very jarring to me due to the high metallic sounds used and short loops. Very uncomfortable to the point I had to turn it way down. This may well be a personal thing though. * Lots of challenge rooms. Either as a gate of progression through the map or for a reward. These I mostly dislike because the combat is not very interesting and they feel overused to me. The combat statues, challenge chests and curses were very repetitive to me. * projectiles often travel only slightly faster than walking speed and continue indefinitely which means you sometimes get hit after defeating an enemy or by an off screen enemy.
_childDocuments_.name: Crypt Custodian

_childDocuments_.review: Crypt Custodian is not the best Metroidvania you'll ever play. It's combat is very plain, and I found myself not very interested in the world or characters. I think the areas you explore have neat concepts that are explored well, but accompanied with upgrades and abilities that are too situational to see their full potential. However, I do think Crypt Custodian is better than the sum of its parts.While there are elements that are sometimes weak, the entirety of the game is still a good time. Crypt Custodian is a chill Metroidvania and excellently paced. Its not too difficult and yet you're always making progress and seeing new ideas. I blasted through most of the game all of the way to 100% completion and never found myself getting stuck or too lost. It was honestly refreshing to play a more simple game that's focused on you wandering around and having a good time. Would recommend to anyone looking for a laidback adventure that still provides enough challenge to be engaging.

_childDocuments_.review: 3 hours in (over 2 days) and am really loving it. It's a rather forgiving metroidvania which I appreciate - you still keep your items and unlocked paths upon dying. controls are nice and snappy. Music's nice and chill. Art's pretty. I like having a top down metroidvania. Quite a nice experience and contrast from the typical side scrollers. Ability upgrades are paced nicely and make the game more fun so far. Haven't found any secrets yet so am looking forward to those - would really love those.

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun game with a lovely hand drawn looking art style. It's nice to have a Metroidvania that isn't a side scroller for once, don;t get me wrong I love the genre in general but having it top-down like this is a bit of a breath of fresh air! I really love the soundtrack as well. My one complaint is the attacks feel like they could use a little more impact and the attack combo animations leaves a bit to be desired. It feels kind of like I'm just flinging a stick in the wind, but this isn't a deal breaker for the game in my opinion. Overall fun game!

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good metroidvania. The world feels almost too open--not entirely sure at any point what's the next location, I keep running around wherever seems interesting and there's often something new that isn't locked. The writing is cute and funny.Combat is not very fun, which is kind of a problem for a game where you're constantly murdering things. Mostly the enemies throw a bunch of bullet hell at you and you either dodge through it or jump over it while you're trying to melee (and mostly it's just bash-bash-bash-dodgebash). Everything is just a little loosey goosey with the sprite hitboxes unfortunately, plus there's no healing whatsoever except at campfires(!!). On the other hand, there's zero penalty for deaths and the ability to teleport to any campfire at any moment. The end result of both these negatives and positives mean that combat is kind of a chore that doesn't ever matter that much. If you're really bad at it, you may have to take 4-5 tries at a boss, but the retries are so quick you won't notice.The story is also kinda weird. Maybe I missed something obvious, but I did not see any explanation of why there's a bunch of random enemy mooks and bosses in the afterlife? I get that we're in the bad part of town, but there's at least a dozen ghosts that don't want to murder you on sight, so.. why do most of them? Or are the baddies manifestations of garbage in some way? I honestly don't know--the fact you're killing the ghost population seems to go entirely unremarked by your friends.All in all it's fine!
_childDocuments_.name: Crypt Custodian

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favourite Metroidvanias of the year — and I've played more than a few. The moment to moment combat is crunchy, the quality of life is exceptional, the map is vast yet easy to navigate, the characters are charming, and the text that accompanies the photographs you can find is often surprisingly dark.Top-down isn't usually the viewpoint you expect for a Metroidvania, and it highlights just how similar Metroidvanias truly are to Zelda-like games. I'd recommend Crypt Custodian to fans of either genre, as well as to fans of Bullet-Hell-Lite experiences.
_childDocuments_.name: Crypt Custodian

_childDocuments_.review: I've been looking forward to this game after playing Islets (which is also worth playing). Lovely artstyle and music with a lot to explore for a playthrough that's about 10-12 hours. It's pretty relaxed with three difficulty settings and assist options that can be freely changed, the ability to teleport around to found save points from the get-go, and being able to buy map markers for missed secrets. It's also got a good bit of goofy humor like with Islets.But you get to play as a cat, watch a scary movie, and spray paint art so that's already 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Crypt Custodian

_childDocuments_.review: My favorite indie game I've played this year :D This is my first metroidvania game, and I have to say I really enjoyed it! I usually prefer more laid back gaming, and this game is great at managing to be super engaging and low pressure at the same time. Save points are spaced out well, and short of being brought back to your last save location, dying does not set you back much.The controls feel smooth and intuitive, the puzzles are fun, the characters are charming, and the bosses are all unique and strike a great balance between challenging and fun. And from a solo dev? Incredible. I was able to 100% the main story in about 12 hours, but have not done much with the boss rush mode. Overall this game is a pretty fun experience for only $20 :)

_childDocuments_.review: I'll probably get some clown awards, but the question is, "Do you recommend this game?" and I do not.It's not a bad game by any means, in fact there is a lot of heart and the dev(s) are clearly talented.  The game just never really evolves beyond "press X as fast as possible while occasionally dodging".  The abilities you get are interesting though I think there was only one boss in the game that made you use your gained abilities.The story is fine, nothing to write home about, though I did have a laugh out loud moment when the boss tried to switcheroo me to trick me with which was the real boss.I was teetering on +/- for this game, but then to get the end game you have to solve a random 4th wall breaking puzzle all the sudden as well as do a tedious bug catch section which I won't be practicing enough to complete.  If this game wasn't overwhelmingly positive I might not leave a review at all, but it is so I won't be hurting the devs too much.  Grade: C

Amazing soundtrack with puzzles, combat and bosses, exploration and really creative mechanics on offer also (don't want to spoil).Another standout Metroidvania that might just be my GOTY. _childDocuments_.review: An indie metroidvania that isn't a side-scroller?! Tell me more, you say. Well, after defeating the first boss to get a traversal upgrade, I have stumbled on at least six different areas I can go through in a strikingly open game. And the cherry on top is an array of accessibility options you can use to tailor the experience for players like myself who may face added difficulty due to a handicap or age.
_childDocuments_.name: Crypt Custodian

_childDocuments_.review: Another excellent metroidvania style game from the dev here. Despite the camera perspective change up and a different style of platforming, it still is one of the best out there. Fast travel to save points (from anywhere), optional markers for missed collectibles, challenging curses, charming characters, satisfying smashing of stuff, frogs, I dunno what else you really want. Some of the fights definitely stray into bullet hell territory which isn't my favorite thing but I still managed to have fun (it's probably why Sheepo is my favorite of the 3, because no bullet hell, but still they're all amazing).In my opinion all 3 of these games so far should be quintessential examples of the metroidvania genre. They do so much right and don't forget what makes it fun like a lot of other games.If I had a criticism of this one, I would say I felt like the characters and dialogue in Islets was more fleshed out and enjoyable - it's not bad here, just feels like there is less of it.Edit: I wanted to edit to just emphasize how amazing the level design is. I did things way out of the seemingly "default" order but it wasn't through any cheesing or sequence breaks, it's just you often can go to one of several biomes and go about your business there. It can be fun going "back" several levels with the upgrades you get as you just fly through platforming and puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Crypt Custodian

_childDocuments_.review: A very fluid top-down metroidvania with a sharp focus on exploration and small combat arenas that reminded me of a mix of Zelda 1, Hyper Light Drifter and Death's Door (among many other potential references) The game's main strength is how freeform player progression can be, as many paths are available at any given time, and the game supports figuring out new pathing through a speedrun mode (and later allowing to shuffle some upgrade locations).Traversal is very fast and pleasant thanks to an array of motion skills that chain well into each other (as it was with the developer's previous title, Islets). Most rooms are simple to solve but the process remains engaging throughout, thanks to an enemy attack design that keeps you in motion at all times and some occasional conditional battles, such as "don't get it" or curses that you lift by meeting specific criteria for rewards.QOL is laser focused on keeping you in the flow at all times, with fast travel between all unlocked points always available, no penalties upon death and generally no loading screens (anything resembling a non-playable sequence can be skipped). The atmosphere is poetic and soft, a lighthearted children's tale with pangs of melancholy, and while the narrative is light, the aesthetic is striking with well differentiated vistas, beautiful colors and cool animations.Performance on Deck has been excellent throughout with no hitches of any kind, and achievements are mostly exploration based, apart from the three tied to the buss rush mode, which feel slightly overtuned for S+ ranks.The whole feels lean and elegant, "simple and effortless" even though game development is anything but, and that's the best testament to how good the game is. If you enjoy top-down traversal challenges and dash-avoid based combat, you'll find plenty to love here.
_childDocuments_.name: Crypt Custodian

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful, engaging, and unique metroidvania. This is the second game from Kyle Thompson that I've played, and both of these games (Crypt Custodian and Islets) have such a unique design and feel.- You'll get 10+ hours of enjoyable exploration and rewarding boss fights.- The plot is not repetitive and you'll encounter some really unexpected twists and turns.- The game map is actually much bigger than you might expect.In short: This is NOT another Hollow Knight clone, but a unique masterpiece that I fully enjoyed and highly recommend.🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟

_childDocuments_.review: Crypt Custodian is a charming top down metroidvania, sorta along the likes of Deaths Door. It's simple combat system gets augmented with dozens of upgrades and unique special attacks. The exploration was engaging and constantly pushed you to want to find one of this games many secrets. 8.5/10, was a very enjoyable experience
