_childDocuments_.review: It's Sunday after a week of staying home after a bad cold. Yesterday I was finally well again and went to the bar and compensated for a missed week. Something I'm paying for today. My friend sent me a suggestion to play this game and since I wasn't really in the mood for anything involving any kind of brain activity this seemed like a match. Breezing through the first few encounters and then my first death occurs - by the lack of fuel. A resource I really wasn't paying attention to. I think one of the pixly dwarf faces said something about it but I accidentally skipped through that dialogue. Oh well. Doesn't seem to be any penalty at all for dying anyway, so let's bore on.A couple more locations in and an alarming sound starts blaring. It stops, then comes back. I fly around, trying to see if there's some special enemy? A special block? Then I realize it's the song 'Hard Core' by Urban Thermo Dynamics that fooled me. My own fault for always turning off game music.Most temporary upgrades (the ones that only last for the current level) are quite underwhelming. At least until you unlock the third pilot. But even then the rate of fire upgrade is a sure bet. More often than not I have to choose between the least worst. Constantly wishing there was an upgrade that showed you where the closest fuel block was rather than the unending flood of upgrades that help you diminish foes. Foes that rarely pose any threat since you're hardly ever killed by them. It's still the fuel (which by the way acts as a timer for how long you can explore a location before finding the exit). But the fuel problem disappears a bit into the game. But talking of enemies, that crawling large goblin is the weirdest one I've seen in a while. I can't decide if that's a bad or a good thing. I pause a couple of times and look at it, scratching my head. It took 2 hours until I noticed my character had a surname. A while after that I decide to change character. Not because I want to but just because of deciding to write a review. And I regret not switching earlier. The description "homing missiles" made me think they were mainly targeting enemies. That is not the case. And when you unlock further dwarves there's never, ever, any reason to go back to the previous one. I should also add that there's no huge difference in play style between them at all. The game is really, really, repetitive and quite purposeless. This feeling is further enhanced by being too easy. The challenge curve goes from "no challenge at all" to "I can turn on auto-fire and play this blindfolded".Some other minor inconveniences:Accidentally entering a location - can't escape out of character selection you have to play the level (or enter the level and exit).You can't see which temporary upgrades you've already chosen when picking a new one.If you run out of fuel you can't refill by shooting a fuel block while falling. Enemies are nuisances. And only that. Not once did I feel an accomplishment of diminishing them. Not even the boss which only hit me once because I started looking at something else than the screen during the boring battle. I don't really understand the point of having such a large over world when there's not that many differences between the locations. Every text prompt, where the story is unfolded, interrupts your shooting so you have to repress the mouse button to continue shooting. Something that irks me more and more due to my Sunday state. But since there is no real reason ever to not empty your guns all over I think there should be a toggle button for us lazy individuals. And when I write this I realize I didn't check. ♥♥♥♥. There it is!

_childDocuments_.review: Very bare bones. Interesting for a while but could have really used some polish before release. There are some really basic QOL features that are missing, and the majority of the level up unlocks just bloat your arsenal with useless upgrades that in some cases (like the bot helpers) actually make the game harder to play instead of easier.For example you get a notification each time you kill a new enemy or destroy a new block, however there is no catalog showing what you have unlocked, which seems really basic and would provide an indication of how much you had left. Instead they just give you a bland progress bar that you actually need to access the Vault to even see. What should you be doing to progress the main quest? Who knows. The game certainly isn't telling you. Hell you spend the first hour even wondering if there IS a quest/story line.If you compare this to something similar, like Wall World, this just looks like it was made in a few days by a teenager with a Metal Gear fetish.

_childDocuments_.review: Bore Blasters is a gem that's full of gems.  The story is a bit humorous, and oddly seems to taper off once you hit 70% completion.  I played for a few more hours after that and perhaps something will happen once I hit 100%, but I'm now at the "play for 10-15 minute bursts" mode.  When I first played it sucked me in for 7 hours.  It's incredibly addictive and satisfying to play.You'll unlock a few dwarves that each have their own special ability, and then head down into levels to collect gems and complete the occasional quest or side quest.  Gems help you "level up" essentially during your excursion, which results in selecting temporary power-ups.  Any gems you earn during a level can be used on permanent upgrades that are for all 3 characters.The gameplay is pretty simple.  Fly your ship, shoot blocks, collect gems, kill enemies, reach the bottom and unlock new levels.  That's the game in a nutshell.  There's not a lot of strategy involved outside of choosing the right temporary upgrades as you play.  There are a few story-based levels that toss a boss fight or other cool moment your way, but there are very few of those.Graphically the game has fantastic pixel art with tons of shiny things and vibrant colors that reward you for a job well done.  It's incredibly satisfying.  There aren't a ton of enemies, and many look like they are just a reskin of others - but it's not something I consider as a problem.Music and sound are great - with the music being one of the best soundtracks I've heard so far this year.  It's rather exceptional.

There is an achievement for unlocking 100% of the game and a percentage bar in the game that you can fill to 100% but jokes on you because that doesn't mean you have actually finished the game.The dev recently updated the game to include a new biome but for those who unlocked all the levels and achieved that 100% your chances of seeing the new biome is nill.Could have had promise but doesn't feel like the dev really wants to listen to the player base for ideas or suggestions.

_childDocuments_.review: Key Lime PieINGREDIENTSFOR THE CRUST1½ cups finely crushed graham cracker crumbs, from about 12 whole graham crackers⅓ cup packed light brown sugar4 tablespoons unsalted butter, meltedFOR THE FILLINGTwo 14-oz cans sweetened condensed milk1 cup plain Greek yogurt (2% or whole milk)1 tablespoon grated lime zest¾ cup fresh lime juiceFOR THE TOPPING1 cup cold heavy cream2 tablespoons confectioners' sugar1 teaspoon grated lime zest8 to 10 thin lime slicesCOOK FOR THE CRUSTPreheat oven to 375 °F and set an oven rack in the middle position.In a medium bowl, combine the graham cracker crumbs, brown sugar, and melted butter; stir with a fork first, and then your hands until the mixture is well combined. Using your fingers and the bottom of a glass or dry measuring cup, press the crumbs firmly into the bottom and up the sides of a 9 x 1.5-inch (deep-dish) pie pan. The crust should be about ¼-inch thick. (Tip: do the sides first.)Bake for 10 minutes, until just slightly browned. Let the crust cool on a wire rack.FOR THE FILLINGLower the oven temperature to 350°F.In a large bowl, whisk together the sweetened condensed milk, yogurt, lime zest, and lime juice. Pour the thick mixture into the warm graham cracker crust. Bake for 15 minutes, until the filling is almost set; it should wobble a bit. Let cool at room temperature for 30 minutes, then place in the refrigerator to chill thoroughly, about 3 hours.FOR THE TOPPINGIn the bowl of an electric mixer, beat the heavy cream until soft peaks form. Add the confectioners’ sugar and beat until medium peaks form. Top the pie with the whipped cream. Decorate with the lime zest and lime slices. Store the pie in the refrigerator until ready to serve. Slice the pie into wedges, wiping your knife clean between slices, and serve cold.Make-Ahead Instructions: You can make the crust a day ahead of time, but the filling should be added on the day of serving, otherwise the crust will get soggy.

_childDocuments_.review: BORE BLASTERS is an excellent... horde driller?... mining shooter?... survivorslike that I've been looking forward to trying for some time. As a huge fan of Void Scrappers, I worried that BORE BLASTERS would feel a bit claustrophobic. It does not. It's a fresh and excellently crafted take on a genre I love full of great games, but also a ton of low effort clones. I played all 7 (around there) missions available in the demo tonight and promptly purchased the full game, only to be met immediately with so. much. more. variety! The demo is great and it sold me, but it does not speak to what the game really has to offer. I love the extent of the enemies so far, and the mining planet variations, including living minerals that slowly fill in your drilled voids and chase you. There are goblins, explosions, and best of all there is elf mockery!I love chatter between pilot and other characters, if you enjoyed the comms in Void Scrappers, this is much more fleshed out and there's a bunch of back and forth. The two gyrocopters I've flown so far have very different specials, and I'm kind of torn on which to use which is great because we all love balance and variety without taking a hit for it. Great graphics, sound effects, and soundtrack. Love the little workshop upgrade screen. I really appreciate all the little details this developer comes up with. Let's put it this way. 8BitSkull released "Fates of Ort" a "retro inspired fantasy RPG", and while I don't generally play fantasy RPGs it's on my wishlist and I'm eager to try it out.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a fun little miner game that's just different enough from the usual formula to stand out.It has some roguelite elements to it that sometimes provide some incredible builds: gems explode, explosions fire bullets, bullets bounce, bullets explode; alongside the modifier that generates more gems and the character whose special ability spawns gems. This can wipe an entire map, and feels so, so, so satisfying! I got this build in the treasure ship - it was incredible! Similarly, if you get the biome that spawns flies, then have enemies explode, explosions cause bullets, etc, you can wipe the entire biome.Unfortunately, it suffers from a common roguelite issues. The more options you unlock, that harder it is to make a good build because you don't get offered the right options. Mid-game was the most fun because of this, where I could get a great build every 5 dives or so. The late-game was more frustrating because I was unlocking things that weren't particularly useful or interesting, and the likelihood of getting amazing builds decreased.Perhaps allowing us to remove or reroll certain offers would partially mitigate the issue.All this being said, it was still very fun up to the middle game :) Recommended if you're into mining games :)

Lots of persistent upgrades to spend your gold on, plenty of biomes and enemy types, three character classes although I mostly used two, an actual story and bosses! This game offered up way more than I expected, and I will definitely perfect it, only about 36 levels left to beat 😁👍

_childDocuments_.review: The game is pretty fun but I'm on the edge about giving it a recommendation. If you enjoy the mining from games like Dome Keeper then this is like that but more exciting and the enemies are everywhere. You use the loot obtained from mining to upgrade your vehicle. I just lost all incentive to keep playing as soon as I finished upgrading the vehicle. If there were more things to spend the gold on then I would probably want to keep playing, but as it is there's no rewards for beating a level that matter anymore. No reason to try to stay alive longer and keep mining, just rush to the end because there's no reward for doing anything else now that the ship is upgraded, and this is with more than 20% of the game left ahead of me. The real reason this edges out a positive review over a negative one is that the game seems to get pretty regular updates, with a daily run and a few hotfixes added since I bought the game. HOPEFULLY they can figure out how to make the currency better than useless after fully upgrading the ship. Maybe wait until the game is on sale in the state that it's in now, I don't really think an average of 10 hours of gameplay for $10 is a great deal.

_childDocuments_.review: The meta progression feels shallow with everything giving small % upgrades. Every level revolves around finding fuel, which is a pain when bad luck strikes. Digging is incredibly slow, and neither meta progression nor random level upgrades made a significant difference. Most of the time, I was just waiting for the special digging ability cool-down to make any real progress. Playing the game in 30s increments wasn't very exciting.Also, enemies move through walls as if they aren't there. _childDocuments_.review: Bought this on a whim because it looked cool and mining games are fun from time to time. Well, it may entertain you for a few hours, but ultimately it turned into a bit disappointing grind fest. The tl;dr of it is that it has potential but doesn't live up to it, it feels empty and not paced well. (the devs are still updating this game, so keep in mind that later updates might improve on the issues i'll mention)The longer version if it interests you:All runs kinda look the same, there are a few different biomes for a bit of variation but most of the time you're just in a hurry to go down to reach the bottom before you run out of fuel. Not that you'd miss anything if you DID have the fuel to explore more sideways, though, because there's nothing to discover except more gem blocks and maybe a fuel block you missed.Beside the 3 different ships special ability (you start with 1 ship, the other 2 are unlocked through the story), all other play variation comes from choosing weapon upgrades in-run, most of which aren't terribly interesting or unique. Enemies randomly spawn in from off-screen and are generally more of a nuisance than a threat, unless you're outnumbered and/or haven't upgraded your ship well enough to venture into the 'further' maps yet (the further you are from the center map, the deeper the runs will be and the beefier the enemies).You'll have bought all upgrades WAY before finishing the story and then you'll have only 'completed' about half of the maps. If you want to 100% it (which i did) you just have to mindlessly delve into 40 more spots without any variation or other incentive than to get the steam achievement.

_childDocuments_.review: As with many of the people who have commented i feel like this game was good but not great. The story parts were alright but very limited, the abilities were not well balanced there is basically one set of abilities that is super powerful so i had no desire to use the rest of the abilities and since there is no option to re roll the abilities it was just either one of the things i needed or 3 abilities i didn't want. and there was way more play time then there was content in the game. once the upgrades for the ship are all bought there is nothing to do with the money making it to where you have no desire to mine any more just getting to the objective. there were two abilities that didn't unlock until the very end of the game which i found weird. overall if i had to rate the game i would give it a 3 out of 5 stars. all of that said it was super cheap when i bought it though and i did get 18.6 hours out of it by the time i got all the achievements. however the last 8 hours of that were not nearly as enjoyable as the first 10.

_childDocuments_.review: It's essentially Pacific Drive, if it wanted to be Deep Rock Galactic, if it wanted to be a Twin-Stick shooter.To be serious, it's actually really fun, and I've been promoting it wherever I can. For 20 minutes here or there; for this 'yet-another-run' feeling; all with a fantastic soundtrack... I love it.You know the rest; missions get more and more difficult, you unlock more and more awesome things that help you negate that rising difficulty, and then stuff explodes when you push a thumbstick in that direction.And what happens if you lose? Nothing, really, outside of not unlocking another item that can potentially drop on your next run before you've even seen the last one in action. Just run it again and see if you get that unlock next time so you can move on to the next level. Keeping the loot used to upgrade your ship makes it an amazing, relaxed grind, and I love it.Hidden Gem and my new favorite post-work game. 10/10 for $10

_childDocuments_.review: + Satisfying destruction & looting ( visuals & sfx )+ Procedurally generated levels ( a lot of different biomes )+ Responsive interface- Quickly gets too repetitive- No replayability - too few meaningful temporary upgrades & characeters only differ by their special ability- Missing some quality of life features like skipping dialoguesThere's a lot of content that's already there, but not used in its full potential. Some of the missing parts could be easily added to at least double the time that could be spent having fun in this game. Considering the fact it's just been released at the time of this review - If you're reading this in the future check if the devs fixed/updated the game & go from there on your decision :)Summing it up for now - would recommend if you'd want to play it for up to ~5 hours, but going for 100% at this point is neither rewarding or fun, so take this into consideration while deciding to buy.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid, quick, and short.  Took about 5-6 hours to beat and 13 hours to 100%.  Great for its price.As for critiques  -  You really only go through about 35-40% of the "levels" before you run out of story.  That said, there's plenty of room for the Devs to add more should this game be successful  -  Upgrades don't feel like they have a lot of impact as you progress  -  Even at max upgrades there's still multiple block types that take several seconds to blast through with the regular gun.  The game ends up being heavily dependent on your super move to progress.  -  The camera has a habit of zooming in way to far for some reason. _childDocuments_.review: Bore Blasters is yet another of these 'mining' games (kinda in the category with games like The Lab and Dungeons, Wall World, etc) that QUICKLY catch my attention and turn me into a raging addict within an hour. I have a SPECIAL love for the mining games in which the entire area will be just LITTERED with pick-ups (a big reason why I liked Vampire Survivors so much - those trillions of experience gems!), with the bing-bing-bing-bing-bing!! of picking up resources. It's so infinitely satisfying it's not even funny. Thanks to games like these, I will never need to try hardcore drugs, because I've found something that works for me and costs far less.You play as a group of dwarves who are going mining deep into the earth for gems. You get in your 'mining copter' and burrow through the earth, breaking through ground of varying levels of toughness, aiming for the gem blocks to blow them away and collect the hoard of gems. Along the way, you work your way through a story of the dwarves vs goblins, making your digs increasingly hazardous.One beautiful feature of THIS title is the biomes you encounter. A lot of games feature biomes to 'spipce up' their dig sites a little, but in this one, each dig site will feature multiple layers you'll have to dig through, each one of them presenting their own benefits and challenges. For example, each biome might have more or less soft or hard blocks, and each one will have unique hazards. Some hazards are temporary near-blindness, blocks which can 'creep' up to you and damage you, tons of hard blocks, and more.Of course, the gameplay loop is similar to the others: Go mine through a dig site, use the money you earned to buy upgrades. This allows you to dig a little faster/farther, which allows you to collect more money, which allows you to buy more upgrades. You'll then be able to dig faster... and so on, until you're digging your way down through sites that before would have been completely impossible. As you progress you'll encounter story missions.(Speaking of which, it needs to be pointed out how active the dev's are in their community. I have hit a snag- one of my missions did not spawn. I reached out on their forums and had an answer within hours. They had me send them my save file, and presumably before long I'll be able to complete that mission to 100% the game. Having dev's who are THAT active is a GREAT sign for this game.)There are multiple characters to choose from, each with their own unique 'special' ability, but I found myself only using one of them once they were available. I am not disappointed at all - just noting that one seems very powerful compared with the others. I would simply suggest powering up the other two a little more.I have seen some reviews complaining about hitting full upgrades well before completing all dig sites. This happened to me as well - I did wind up having all upgrades with quite a few dig sites left. I did NOT, however, personally find this disappointing. The mining/picking up zillions of gems gameplay is SO satisfying to me that I just continued to play onward, tackling site after site. It does change your strategy a little... but since the 'temporary upgrade' system is based on gem-collection, you're still incentivized to mine gems so you can get more 'temporary bolt-ons' to make it through each dig site. I did not personally find this to be a 'down-side' to the game.I have also seen a complaint or two about the temporary bolt-ons (upgrades you get during each run which are not a part of the permanent upgrades). Yes, there is no re-roll like in Vampire Survivors. Sometimes it can get slightly frustrating when you get bad luck and get EXACTLY what you DON'T want a million times in a row.... but at least you've got a choice of what to pick, so even though the RNG will play a role in your development at each dig site, you can at least still somewhat shape the course of that development. And, if you have a run of bad luck, you can always just.. go back for another dig :-) It's fun enough that this as not a problem for me.Overall, there's a lot to be said about this one. The preview video listed a description something like 'Brilliantly Frantic' or something like that, and that's an absolutely perfect description. There is just SO MUCH going on at any given time that sometimes it's hard to keep up. Constant gunfire, constant explosions, enemies coming at you in swarms, gems EVERYWHERE. The music is SO on point - for a player who often mutes music I left it running at all times - thumping, frantic music. The sound effects are like constant dopamine hits (bing-bing-bing-bing! of pick-ups), and combined with the beautiful dig world just creates an amazing atmosphere I couldn't get enough of. The story was 'just right' - not non-existent, but also not annoyingly long/tons of dialogue - it was that perfect 'just right' amount of story. The biomes are fun to blast through, the upgrades are fun to earn... Just overall, this was a FANTASTIC experience. I am CERTAIN I will be playing through this one again.The final question is always: is it worth full price? Oh yes. For ten bucks you really can't go wrong. This game has so much crap to do and so much going on, combined with that pulsing soundtrack, it's not even funny. I got it on sale for about $9 but can easily say I would have been happy to have got it for full price. I got captured and addicted so quick it was insane. I would recommend this game to just about literally anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun and relaxing game, with some interesting game mechanics combining Vampire Survivor type bullet-hell and random upgrades for that gambling addiction element with resource gathering.The main downside is that it lacks content, and will be very repetitive soon. You will make a lot of resources, but you will quickly run out of things to use it for. So you will sit on a giant fortune after completing about 30% of the levels, then they will be useless. There will be no more weapons unlocks, no more character unlocks (only three at this moment) and no more story elements. Just a lot of grinding to get through all the levels, without any real reward in the end.Seems a bit poorly balanced in this respect, too little unique content stretched over far too many levels. Hopefully this will improve over time when the game is developed further.

_childDocuments_.review: Bore Blasters: The Selected Works ReviewSteam Curator page: Bore Blasters comes from 8BitSkull, the studio behind Fates of Ort, a clever, very cool, and underrated RPG that’s really unlike anything else in its nominal genre. Bore Blasters, also clever and cool,  like other things, but that’s a good thing, because the things it’s like are in the neglected sub-sub-genre of digging games. You know, digging games? As distinct from mining/crafting-type games (your Minecrafts and Terrarias (Terrariae??), digging games are humbler in scope, informed by the arcade spirits, although they certainly come with their own clutch of un-arcadelike systems – usually in the form of upgrades to your drilling rig and the like.If you know the referents here – Super Motherload, Galactic Mining Corp, Mining Mechs – you know what kind of game this is fundamentally, and suffice it to say, if you like any of those games, you will enjoy Bore Blasters. It’s more action-focused than its peers, and feels fresh in that way. If you don’t know those games, or this sub-sub-genre, let Bore Blasters be your introduction, and let me be your introductor to Bore Blasters. Your chair...Here’s how Bore Blasters works. You’re in charge of a group of dwarf adventurers (including the rarely seen, but historically accurate, Bearded Lady Dwarf) who zip around an overworld map in an Age of Sail, but flying, ship that would do the Koopa kids proud. The overworld map is laid out in a grid, most of whose cells are locked to begin with; you open new cells by clearing unlocked levels adjacent to them. These levels are dig sites, and your job is to get all the way to the bottom of each one, in a mining vessel that uses a MACHINE GUN to dig. Each dig site is comprised of different biomes, with its own clutch of block types, hazards, and monsters.You pick a site, you pick a dwarf (each dwarf has a different special ability, which operates on a cooldown timer), and you start moving downwards in accordance with dwarf gun-mining culture. As you go down, every so often you’ll level up and get to choose from one of three random power-ups, plucked from a pool of powerups. If you get to the bottom, you’ll be able to open up an enormous floating treasure chest; this ‘clears’ the map and adds a new powerup to the powerup corral. But you’re also often assigned a, I guess ‘story quest,’ some other goal to work toward as you work your way down. This might mean locating a specific piece of dwarf- or goblintech, or blowing up a certain number of gun emplacements, or similar. I say ‘story quest’ because there’s dialogue tied to these, and some of them are linked to each other, but I believe they’re semi-randomly assigned.As is usually the case in digging games, you’re working under some restrictions. In Bore Blasters these are twofold: your steampunk guncraft can run out fuel, but it can also be destroyed if it takes too much damage. No harsh penalizing for death though, other than not being able to complete the level; you can just restart immediately, and you even get to keep all the gold you earned on your failed run.Oh yeah, GOLD: every block you bore-blast in Bore Blasters will net you some dosh. Even your unremarkable standard stone block is worth something, but obviously you want to be on the lookout for veins of gems & metals. These vary in value, with copper and tin being pretty low-value, and things like gold, diamond, and, uh, the purple one, netting you more.I say ‘copper,’ ‘tin,’ I say ‘gold’ and ‘diamond,’ but I’m not sure that’s what they actually are; and I say ‘netting you more,’ but I’m not sure of their relative values either. Numbers pop out of things as they’re destroyed but, given that you are mining with a literal machine gun, you’re seeing geysers of numbers constantly. If spraying integers qualified as gore, Bore Blasters would earn an M rating, EASY, there would be protests by anti-numerical-violence groups, parents would worry that their children, playing Bore Blasters, were being taught to devalue the life of values. All of which is to say that it’s hard to be sure which actions are the most profitable. One thing that Bore Blasters lacks, and that some of its digging peers have, is a lithopedia, a compendium of block and gem values you can consult to better know what to aim for.To be fair, it doesn’t actually matter that much; I don’t think Bore Blasters is meant to be a game you sit down and sedately plan optimal runs for - and I think this is its big strength when compared to other digging games. Stood against its peers, it’s much more frantic, unsedate, kinetic, more about the moment-to-moment glory of indiscriminately blowing up defenseless ore with improbable steampunk weaponry. You find a rhythm that works and play from the hip – certainly I haven’t had any issue making plenty of gold this way. In between levels your gold is spent on permanent upgrades to different elements of your ship: fuel reserves, gun damage, etc. Nothing surprising here, but all welcome, and while I did hit a mild early-mid-game difficulty spike, once I bought a few more key upgrade tiers, I felt on top of things once more.There is a story, and quests tied to each of the characters you can play as, but to me it’s all very ancillary to that core ‘dig-upgrade-dig’ loop, so I didn’t fuss myself overmuch about not knowing what was going on or what I had to do next; I just focused on clearing levels. However, there’s undoubtedly some issues with signposting; I think a little more direction wouldn’t be remiss, just some indicators as to what will advance the story along, or a quest log or similar to keep you on track, if you want to be kept on track. That may not work within the systems implemented here, but again, it’s a little hard to tell. Outside of the vibrancy of the play, much about Bore Blasters was vague to me.And that’s fine, it really is, for me, because the play is . Me, I’m simple, I want to blow things up and trick out my ship and blow more things up, while cool music urges me on (the music here is very good). I want to be able to transition frictionlessly between level, upgrade menu, and next level, in a brain-soothing loop that is engaging but not taxing, not demeaning but not too demanding, whilst I ponder life and its mysteries. By those lights, Bore Blasters succeeds unquestionably. There are caveats with regards to clarity, but I can live with them, and they may certainly be addressed by 8BitSkull, who are active and communicative in the Discussions page here on Steam. A recently-released Endgame Roadmap shows their plans for Daily Runs and postgame challenge content, and it all sounds excellent. All due praise to devs who continue to enrich their game in response to feedback.There aren’t enough digging games, but with Bore Blasters we can add another good one to the honor roll. Like some kind of homing steampunk pickaxe, Bore Blasters locks in on and strikes some very fundamental, very rich seams of core gamer dopamine, and if you get into it, it will probably instill in you a taste for these kinds of games for the rest of your ludic life. Welcome to the club.

_childDocuments_.review: I like the game. I feel like I got my money's worth ($1/hr). Overall I think it's a good time sink.Having said that, I got about ~75% of the way through when I hit the 11h mark. I got almost all of the upgrades except the last hull upgrade which costs ~5m gold. I stopped unlocking things a while back by that point, I just wanted to max out the upgrade tree. Unfortunately I'm at the ~15.5h and nothing else has changed except that I maxed out my upgrades with a bunch of money to spend on nothing.This is my main issue with the game. I feel like the game can be shortened with the amount of content it has. The issue only exists late-game but I do think it's a pretty big issue regardless. At least run modifiers would be nice, something to spend gold on and to spice up late runs. _childDocuments_.review: Bore Blasters ain't no bore. Yeah, I said it. LOL. But in all honestly this game is good stuff. Sometimes there's nothing wrong with a very simple concept executed well and that doesn't cost a lot of money and that's what is on offer here. Simple and addicting twin-stick shooter style roguelite mining action based on brief runs that you'll just keep doing one more of and before you know it, time has flown by. _childDocuments_.review: It's pretty damn fun. It's not a complex, long, and detailed game but it doesn't try to be. It's just damn fun to squeeze a short run or two between tasks.Flying around and dealing with the different enemy types is great. The visuals are neat and the upgrades you get mid-run feel like they really impact your gameplay.The only minor ting that might knock it from a perfect score is the very short looping music. Just a bit more variety in the score and this would be a 10/10. The music is good. I want a bit more.But that is really a minor nitpick. The game is well worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm hoping that the dev will release more contents in future and give the game a proper "finishing touch" (pun intended) or extend the game's story, because the story ended around 70% progression, so I assume there's 30% more to come. Otherwise, the actual game will only lasts for a day or two, then clearing the rest of stages is just like playing the demo.For those who haven't tried the demo, be warned that this game is designed to be fast-paced, and chances are, you will be rushing to clear a stage especially when you're given bad RNG.The game's replayability is very limited: after you completed a stage, you just move on to the next stage to progress the story. Also, most interesting challenges/dynamics are story driven, so once the story is finished, the fun part is gone and there's no point in repeating the same stage. There's no other modes like endless, speedrun or permadeath, which means zero replayability in my book.Finally,  with all the different copters / gears / upgrades + facing against the challenges thrown at you. Certain bolt-on upgrades have cool combo and some has hidden synergy Good potential once the devs extend the story with better ending; would be a great game if the devs manage to implement cool late-game mechanics in future.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little time filler.You fly a dwarven ship and have to battle your way to the bottom of each stage collecting gems and fighting goblins.You start relatively underpowered and it can be a struggle to finish a run, but luckily you don't lose any of the gems you collect when you fail a run. The gems are used to increase the various aspects of your ship like fuel, damage output, armor, etc.Gradually you'll have to accomplish objectives during the run, with the difficulty ramping up quickly but if you spent the time completing runs you'll eventually level the playing field.Runs are varying length, but get longer as you play, up to about 10-15 mins each.I played a lot of hours in the demo and your progress is ported across, so give the demo a try.
_childDocuments_.name: BORE BLASTERS

_childDocuments_.review: Bore Blasters is one of many great 2D digging games. I don't think it's got anything super new going for it, but everything it has, it does great. Nice art, an intense and surprisingly good soundtrack, and impactful, fun upgrades. The story is simple but keeps the missions fresh by introducing secondary objectives to each level, rather than solely trying to go deeper or make more money.I'm about 50% through, completion%-wise. By now I have almost all the upgrades maxed out, There's a couple hours of gameplay left, I imagine, so a solid 7 hours or so of game time is reasonable for what the game costs. Overall, solid. Rock and stone!
_childDocuments_.name: BORE BLASTERS

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a fan of previous 8BitSkull games, and Bore Blasters doesn't disappoint. It has everything I expect - an engaging core gameplay loop, upgrades and powerups, twitchy gameplay without feeling too punishing, and a pick-up and put-down type bite sized pacing that means I can play a little bit here and there when I need to kill a bit of time on my steamdeck or just feel eager to grab some more gemstones. You can forge your way ahead into the more treacherous levels if you want a more challenging time, or you can take your time upgrading to have a more sedate difficulty curve.So far I've unlocked the second character which has been a lot of fun and gotten partway through the story. It's been a blast (ha ha!) seeing my ship get more powerful and feeling that satisfying curve of getting into ever more crazy situations. I'm probably going to pace myself as it's not the kind of game you'd spend 12 hours in a row devouring - it's the kind of game you look back a year later and realise you have 50 hours in it somehow :).

name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers
detailed_description: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers - A Blackjack Roguelike Adventure Begin your adventure in a tavern that is home to a unique, corrupted version of blackjack you have never played before. You will need to pick up the rules and adapt to them as you progress through the tavern, challenging a colourful cast of blackjack-addicted townspeople. Discover the mystery of who runs this twisted casino as you progress through the tavern to take them down! Pick a suit: hearts for healing, spades to offer you some protection, diamonds for more currency for shop purchases, or clubs for extra damage. Remove cards from your deck as you progress. Pick up more aces and face cards, or fill your deck with tarot cards, business cards, birthday cards, hall passes and more! Make your way through the tavern challenging patrons, purchasing additional cards for your deck, resting up when your health gets low, opening boosters packs, participating in minigames and much more! Take on the run-based deckbuilding roguelike challenge, with endless possibilities for unique and interesting decks! Features Unique play styles based around card suits Ascend or descend through the tavern over and over by unlocking new starter decks when you complete runs for entirely new ways to play Discover incredible rule-breaking synergies in order to defeat the house edge. Over 300 unique cards! 60 characters to defeat Use unique chips to gain advantage and activate special cards Minigames and events to gain more chips or enhance your deck Unique grimy pixel art aesthetic All the degeneracy from a seedy casino but with no risk to your finances, mental health, or your loved ones

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE:  Since posting this review, the game has received a massive balance patch that undid a lot of the problems I'd had with it.  The review is kinda obsolete as a result, and I dont want to re-write the whole blasted thing.  Look, just go buy it.  This is excellent.---------------------Well this is a weird one.  This is good... and can at times be bloody brilliant... but there's some very odd factors here that can create a feel that some players just wont jive with.  While at the same time, RNG can be high.  Yet it isnt quite as high as it can seem at first.  Sort of.It took me awhile to figure out what I wanted to write about with this one, because it has an issue that I just couldnt quite put my finger on, but I think I've got it now:  This game is a slow burner.  A freaking CHAOTIC one, but still, a slow burn.  A long haul.  In other deckbuilders (most of them anyway) individual battles and such tend to be very short.  But not this one.  An individual fight can go on for quite awhile, many rounds, with each round potentially involving a lot of individual card plays & other things before you decide to stand (or bust).Now that's fine, but when you combine it with the nature of Blackjack itself, it creates a sort of sensation that you dont have all that much control.  At least, for a time.  See, the decision-space that you have available to you is entirely dependent on what cards are showing up, one by one.  This being Blackjack, you cant draw a card, look at it, and just not play it (except when you can).  So unlike almost all other games in this genre, you are, for the most part, not presented with a hand of cards where you make choices from every single round.  Rather, cards are drawn, they Do Things, and you decide to hit or stand.  The opportunity to make decisions (that arent just hit and stand) is, therefore, very erratic.  You have to grab cards between fights that CREATE those decisions in future fights.  And that, I think, is part of what can make this feel too RNG focused at times, because that just aint how this genre normally works.  And when you add that to the fact that runs can be darned long, well... yeah.There are actually a lot of types of decisions that you can have though, IF you pick cards that offer them.  For instance, some cards will offer you choices the moment they show up.  There's one card that's like, Geralt from the Witcher or something, and when he shows up, you get to burn one of the cards your opponent currently has played.  Sometimes this will whiff, sure, if it's the first draw of the round.  But other times, this choice can have a big impact.  Or maybe you draw something that's like, okay, this is going to copy a card in your discard temporarily, choose which one.   Other cards are more controlled.  "Exploit" effects are found on some cards, and this wont do anything at first.  Rather, it's an option that can be activated when the card is ALREADY played and sitting there.  Like, one of my favorites is just "AI Generated Card", which has a random value when played, but also has an exploit effect: activate it to create another AI card... which is again randomized (could be a negative value even) and dump it on your opponent.  What's that?  They already stood, with a full blackjack?  Well too bad, now they bust maybe because you just dumped a bizarro 9 onto their side.  The third type is "handy" cards.  You dont normally have a hand of cards in Blackjack of course, nothing that you're holding and waiting to play, until these show up.  These you can indeed hold, and just play whenever, which produces the tactical options it sounds like it does.  These are the main types of choices that can be available to you DURING each fight... there are of course other choices between fights, events and such.The issue with that of course is that if your deck just doesnt have many cards in those types, you wont be making many decisions during a fight, and the deck can feel like it's just on auto, just based on luck, even if you're winning. It also means that the early game... which can be long... DEFINITELY feels like not much is happening.  But also, there's the Advantage system.  To use an Exploit card, or play a held card, you must spend an advantage point, and getting those can be... strange.  Unless you're playing on just the starting difficulty, you'll choose a weird chip thing after the first fight, and this will determine how you will actually get advantage points during fights.  And these are... all over the place.  Certain chips can make it very easy to get points.  While others are very situational.  And a couple just seem utterly worthless.  This can have an ENORMOUS effect on the RNG factor of the run.  A bad chip means that even if you've got a lot of exploit or handy cards, they might simply not be able to do anything, and that's not a good feel.  The chip concept honestly feels a little busted, and I could see some players just restarting over and over until they get one that doesnt suck.The other big issue, at least so far, is the decks.  Different suits do different things when they are involved in scoring a blackjack.  Hearts will cause healing, and the others do... things that arent healing.  Seriously the deck that starts with the heart suit cards seems like the one that's actually, truly viable... the others always feel like I'm trying to fight King Kong with a butter knife, they're just so darned ineffective.  Since the game is so long and there's a high RNG factor, that means a lot of attrition, and healing is bloody rare... unless you are using heart cards, since any blackjack score is a chance to heal when you've got some of those involved.  I mean really the decks just feel ridiculously lopsided.  The not-hearts ones absolutely dont feel like they're worth anything.  Heck one of them, the "nothings" deck, doesnt do anything at all!  That's not very interesting.  This part of the game, the deck choices, seems like it needs a revamp, really.  And the non-heart suits need some sort of buff.  Just SOMETHING to make them not feel so terrible.  Or just, you know, balance the non-heart healing better.  Something, I dunno.Other than that stuff, the overall gameplay is pretty wild.  The cards can be all sorts of loopy, you never know what weird thing is going to happen next, and everything is erratic.  At one point I deleted my opponent's entire deck, just burned the whole thing away, and the remaining rounds consisted of her just saying "I'M OUT OF CARDS" over and over again.  And sometimes your own cards will sort of work against you, depending on the timing of them showing up and such (as expected, considering the nature of the game).There's a lot more I could say here, like talking about the events & shops and such, the different paths, that one stupid boss that wins by losing over and over, or other things.  But if you're interested in this one, I'd suggest having a look at some full runs on Youtube.  It's very hard to give a sense of what this one is like just from reviews.If it meshes with you, you'll probably love it, if it doesnt, you'll probably hate it, not much inbetween, I think.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of people are comparing this game to Balatro. Which I think is not only very unfair, but it's also very incorrect. The reason that Balatro is such a standout game in the roguelike scene, is that it's a wonderful subversion of the traditional roguelike formula. There are no complicated mechanics, everything simple and easy to learn. And you don't really need to rely on pulling good cards all the time. The game is so incredibly simple to pick up, and it's really fun when you can slowly get better at the game. There are no enemies or predicting the another entity's moves, It's just a very fun form of math you need to do.This game on the other hand, is pretty much just a normal roguelike. You have to figure out what the other person's going to do, you have to get certain amounts of damage in, you have to rely on the very slow deck building mechanics, and the game is much more difficult to get better at. Not to say that this game is bad, it's just not on the same level as Balatro.That being said, is this a good game? Yes, I think so. It has significanctly less charm and polish as Balatro, But in terms of gameplay, it's about as fun as any other deck building roguelike game. If you like to gamble and you like roguelikes, then you'll probably enjoy this game. But don't go in expecting Balatro.

_childDocuments_.review: Having played the game for a fair amount of time, and beaten it several times with different decks and approaches, I feel confident enough to leave my own review here to try and shine more light onto what kind of game this is, and what you should expect when playing it.A lot of the reviews compare the game to Balatro, which is more than reasonable (this game is literally in a bundle with it together with Luck Be A Landlord), and while I don't own Balatro, having only watched others play it, I can still say that the two games simply don't compare very well, just like how actual Poker varies greatly from Blackjack. They are very different card games, with very different objectives and very different strategies.Where in Poker/Balatro, you have the freedom to make decisions based on the hand you have, Blackjack/D&DA is a very luck based game where you NEED to balance probabilities and make gambles based on the deck you are playing. D&DA much more forgiving compared to Blackjack in the sense that it allows you to view exactly which cards you have not yet played, meaning that if you are currently sitting on a 15, and your draw pile consists of four face cards, a 10, a 7 and a 6, your chance to not bust is a 1 in 7 chance. You do not hit on a 1 in 7 chance. This is critical information you do not get in standard Blackjack, there are situations where you would absolutely want to hit on a 15 in standard Blackjack. But that is because the probabilities are different, the chances are different... the game is different.Not only can you view your own deck however, you can also check exactly which cards your opponent has to play, meaning that right from the start of an encounter, you can know exactly what you'll be facing, and create a rough battle plan before you even play your first card. The game gives you a metric ton of information you can, and should, use to plan out the encounter and how to react to any given play by your opponent. This is not a surefire way of winning every encounter you face, far from it. You will lose a lot, you'll get stuck in a battle of attrition, your luck may not be in your favor at either one of the bosses. But that isn't the game's fault, because that's Blackjack. If you don't enjoy the idea of the card game this game is based on, then this game simply is not for you, and that's okay. It's for that reason that I won't denounce the negative reviews for this game, because they serve to inform people who may equally dislike the fundamental mechanics of Blackjack.With that being said however, at the time of writing this review, the devs have released a public beta that aims to tackle a ton of balance points and concerns voiced by players, including healing 10 health up to 3 times after beating a stage boss where previously you could only heal with special and heart cards, the latter only triggering if you get Blackjack with said cards. They have also tweaked several decks to be much fairer to play against, giving the player more money at the start to more quickly build their deck, and many more tweaks to make the experience much more pleasant.These devs listen, at least at the time of writing this review, and the changes they are making actively make the game much more fun while still retaining the spirit of Blackjack.TLDR?If you don't like Blackjack, don't play this game. If you do, make sure you familiarize yourself with the information that is given to you, the player. It's best to double check before hitting and busting, rather than standing and surviving.

_childDocuments_.review: Describing D&D Gamblers as  is misleading. Let me explain why this game is worth your time, without ever mentioning Balatro again.D&D Gamblers is a highly underrated deck-building roguelike that deserves more attention. It hooks you with its absurd cards and humor while keeping you engaged through creative deck archetypes, a familiar but constantly shifting gameplay loop, and rewarding skill expression.As with most roguelikes, this game isn’t easy. Many of the foes you’ll encounter have decks built around specific mechanics or gimmicks you’ll need to adapt to. These mechanics become clearer as you gain more playtime and experience.In a way, this game reminds me of Hearthstone:- You can either play strategically, calculating and shifting odds in your favor to achieve the desired outcome,- Or you might find yourself drawn to an absurdly chaotic card, and let the RNGesus take the wheel... and still somehow win!There are no "bad cards" in D&D Gamblers, something I’ve come to realize after almost 30 hours of play. Every card has its use. Some are more versatile, while others trade potential value for safety. Figuring that out, while discovering new deck archetypes, feels like an enlightening process.D&D Gamblers isn’t without its flaws, of course:Overall, this game is amazing. It needs a few adjustments to its balance and more interesting starter decks, but beyond that? It’s a fantastic game for fans of deck-builders or roguelikes. And even if you're new to these genres, this game might not be the worst place to start!

_childDocuments_.review: I really WANT to like this game. It has great art style, music, gameplay, and replayability. But MAN is it hard to pick back up again once you've lost. It never feels like you lose because of something you did, it feels like you lost because you didn't know what was coming up.There's an opponent that only has 4 cards:  2 21s and 2 10s, and he shields when he hits 21, so if you didn't have cards that changed you opponent's hands and you only focused on your own deck, he'll tank everything you have.There's an opponent that copies your own deck, which if you built it around healing and slow pinging, causes both of you to be stuck in an infinite loop.There's an opponent who plays super low cards and locks yours down, so if you have a card that changes the opponent's cards to your own with a high value (to try to get them to bust), you're stuck in an infinite loop of infinite busts.There's an opponent who swaps his cards with yours constantly, and while that's cool, it negates any deck building strategy you'd want to go for, especially if you were going for a low-card build.It's hard to be excited to try again after you've lost on the 2nd to last level because you didn't know your opponent's strategy was "reflect all damage back" or something. It's still a very fun game if it vibes with you, but currently it just has too many balancing issues for me to recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers is a roguelike card game that often gets compared to Balatro, but such comparisons can be misleading. Unlike Balatro, which innovates on traditional roguelike mechanics with its accessible and math-focused gameplay, Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers stays true to the classic card game of Blackjack, adding a roguelike twist.In Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers, you navigate a series of encounters with deck-building mechanics rooted in Blackjack. The game allows you to view both your own and your opponent’s deck and discard piles, a feature not found in standard Blackjack. This added visibility helps you strategize, although the game remains heavily influenced by luck and probability.For fans of Blackjack, Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers offers a unique experience with its roguelike progression. You’ll need to manage the luck-based nature of the game while leveraging the strategic information available. The developers have been responsive to feedback, implementing balance improvements such as enhanced healing mechanics and fairer deck adjustments, making the game more enjoyable and balanced.The gameplay emphasizes managing probabilities and making gambles, which might appeal to those who enjoy the unpredictability of Blackjack. The roguelike elements and deck-building features add depth, but the game is fundamentally a gamble, reflecting Blackjack’s inherent randomness.If you enjoy Blackjack and are interested in a roguelike adaptation, Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers could be a fun and engaging choice. However, if Blackjack’s core mechanics aren’t appealing to you, the game may not be as enjoyable. The ongoing updates from the developers show a commitment to improving the experience, which bodes well for the game’s future.In summary, Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers offers a distinctive take on the roguelike genre with its Blackjack foundation. It’s worth exploring if you’re intrigued by a card game with a roguelike twist, but be prepared for a game that embraces both strategy and chance.

_childDocuments_.review: A decently fun game for fans of deckbuilder roguelikes. Compared to Balatro (or really any similar game) it skews a lot closer to playing like actual blackjack, which is pretty novel. Every enemy encounter has a unique gimmick deck, which is fun.However there are some balance issues and every-run-the-same issues. You can easily get your entire deck to contain no high numbers quite early in a run, and there's many cards that are essentially risk-free to add to the deck (either by having a printed value of 0-1 or by going directly to your hand). That's not a problem for the first few runs, but it might limit the game's longevity compared to others in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Balatro has set a high precedent for this sort of roguelike and it's simply not very elegant, well-balanced or enjoyable in its current state. It feels overstuffed with ideas, and would require substantial rework across several domains to be considered great. I feel sad to admit that this game would be better off in early access.A preface: I know it's not Balatro, it is quite different, but it is valuable to compare the two to convey the disparity of quality between the two roguelike deckbuilders. Some of the core tenets in Balatro's effectiveness are in its simplicity, and how cards are represented and laid out in the interface in a well-organised, eloquent way to best enable focused decision-making and strategizing. Behaviours of cards and abilities in this game are poorly articulated, and many abilities and behaviours in general are so hyper-specific or over-designed that it inhibits the ability to explore cool synergies and interplay between your cards. Representation of interface components and information feels poor as well. Two major examples: 1. I play a card that enables me to burn a card I have played - rather than selecting the cards from the location where they are played, a secondary, transparent interface overlay comes over the screen, representing the two cards that are already there. It breaks the immersion that I am playing and laying out cards in a virtual space, and reads and feels poorly put together.2. Secondly, there are times when you are required to make an in-UI decision, i.e. forced to select a card, but interface components prevent me from viewing my deck/discard piles via the regular means. Balatro either presents all the information I need to make an informed decision on-screen in an elegant way, or that information is a very easy to access. This game does not do this well.From a gameplay perspective, matches do not feel very enjoyable. The simple thrill of Blackjack is there, but battles where you chip away at one-another to deal damage, heal, shield and whatever else simply do not feel fun or enhance the blackjack experience - it almost feels novel. Progressing between events in a run doesn't feel very satisfying or rewarding, either. Art direction is charming but inconsistent. Some interface elements such as the board are designed wonderfully, but art direction is a mixed bag of quality and conflicting styles. The avatar creation, while only a small feature, is surprisingly restrictive, limited and feels feature-incomplete, with unusually limited options and a lack of color choices for each asset.There is an absence of proverbial 'juice'. Balatro finds ways to pack a punch through enriching audiovisual feedback of points accruing, flames simmering; this game has a lack of weight, hype or range in terms of its responsiveness. Playing a hand, whether its successful or unsuccessful, simply doesn't feel very different. I cannot recommend this game in its current state. I refunded this game because at a foundational level, it is a long way from being a good roguelike, and I do hope the developer refines this game a lot. Rework at a fundamental game design level is required to make this game into something that truly works. Beyond that, a big helping of tender love and care towards UX/UI/'game-feel' would be appreciated. I can appreciate the great effort and ideas that have gone into this - but for now, it's bust.

_childDocuments_.review: Balatro burned me out on being really fun at first but as soon as you actually focus on progression the unfairness is absurd. After a playing this for a while, it felt like it was going the same way, but it actually has one big thing that's different to Balatro: you can let yourself lose.In Balatro you just want to stack as many points as possible because every round matters. In D&DG, you want to play more strategically. One bust is worse than losing five rounds on 17, so you're essentially letting your opponents chip damage you until you can strike back, and finding card synergies to mitigate said chip damage. Short-term losses for long-term gain. I'm in the groove now and enjoying myself; there's still moments of awful RNG, but overall this feels much more consistent, and the higher difficulties aren't torturous misery.

_childDocuments_.review: Above is my initial review for version 1.0 of the game, I read other reviews which critiqued some of my issues and decided to give the game another chance, and then there was also an update addressing some of the issues I had initially.I would like to start by saying that I still stand by most of the criticisms I had of the game originally, but the more serious ones were actually addressed really well In the newest update.A lot of my problems with the RNG I think I explained relatively poorly. One of the problems I had with the RNG originally was that the player was given far too options rather than the fact RNG existed in the first place.For example at the start of the game you only had 2 chips to pick from which would be the only way you could build advantage for an entire run... and if you got 2 of the bad ones then its just a bust run from the off. The update changed it to 3 now, and allows you to re-roll them for a cost if they are all bad. Big improvement.My issues with the lack of healing I will admit were exaggerated but still existed within the game. It wasn't a massive problem since you just need to pick up heart cards for healing if you're not playing the hearts deck as you go through a run. Regardless, getting a small heal for free in both fortune teller encounters is a welcome change.Deck Building is also easier since you're given a lot more chips now at the start of the game which makes it easier to afford things such as the counterfeiter early on who can help you begin to shape your deck and the card removal shop later on for deck thinning and removing unwanted cards.The thing which I look for in a roguelike like this isn't absolute consistency, since if things are super predictable then they become boring. But at least a base line of  consistency because when things are too unpredictable then the amount of control you as a player have is extremely limited and you're at the mercy of the dice roll which can be frustrating. Its about getting the balance right. Before the game leaned too much on the unpredictable side. Now its in a much better spotThat being said, I actually enjoy the game quite a bit more now and will continue playing it, and happily recommend it to others. I applaud the devs for actually listening and ironing out a lot of the problems with their latest update.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Balatro but honestly I find Dungeons & Degens to be more rewarding. Blackjack is obviously a more binary type of game and you play against opponents rather than a score attack. But the strategies you can put together with the absolutely bizarre card library make this go way deeper than blackjack. Cards you'll find: The 11 of Nothings, the Spade of Threes, the Communist Party Membership Card, the infamous Four Mana Seven Seven from another game that will remain nameless, a card that duplicates four possible cards from Slay the Spire, and so many more.The special decks you unlock after going through the regular ones are especially fun and weird.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not upset the game isn't Balatro 2 but the game loop isn't great.The game is about dueling other blackjack players, you can slowly damage them with better hands but if they bust from a bad play you can do a lot of damage to them.  Two problems:1:  There is not a lot of variety between runs.  You will almost always fight the same exact decks with the only main difference being the route you take.  You will get a very similar pool of non-combat events per run.  Outside of cards you get, the deck you start with and the chip you get, runs are very very samey.2:  These decks are not fair to fight.  They are incredibly streamlined and full of gimmicks and hurdles to overcome.  This is fine in concept, in practice it means if you want to win you need to be resilient to tricks and also have tricks and this hurts deck construction. It means you need the limited amount of cards that can sabotage and big cards are too risky to run.  There is an NPC whose deck is all face cards.  You will have to beat a 20 every hand.  If you don't have tricks, this fight takes forever if you can beat it fair.  Any fight can take an absurd amount of time if your opponent keeps assembling blackjacks and healing or matching your hands.  I beat both routes once with the same low cost, negative card filled cycling deck that either doubles opponent cards to auto-bust numbers or discard their whole board when they stay.  No NPC has an answer to this deck since the cards that try to answer it, I can just get rid of them. Also when you fight the gamblers, they make an annoying chip scratching noise the entire time.  It made me mute the game.  I thought flicking was the limit of how annoying people can be playing cards.  Main thing I will wait for is deck variations of opponents or just different opponents.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played the demo a ton and hoped it would improve on the formula the demo promised. What it is in the end is a BlackJack based gambling game with lots of "illegal" cards that have funny references to popular card games and over the top effects. The core of the game is random - much like Black Jack - so it ends up a gambling game. With the additions of card effects you get even more randomness into the deck and it can be to your advantage or to your demise. Aside the "tactics" it inherits from BlackJack (i.e. where to stand) and your ability to look into the draw pile to estimate your chances... this is enitrely luck based. There is no progression, very limited choices and no meta-progression. It bareley falls into the rogue"like" category - but only in a sense that you learn which effects and minigames each choice will spark. There is no skill or economy involved which makes it vastly different from the obvious comparison to Balatro. With luck you can draw synergetic card (i.e. getting a 21 value card on hand so you can choose to play it on a 0 value card), but even then it is high risk - high reward.I've ended up pretty much slot machining the fifth run and didnt even care anymore because my choices mattered so little to the outcome of the fight. If that is your jam - go for it. For anyone looking for a card based rogue-like/lite - I can not recommend and requested a refund.Sadly the demo went offline as of today.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fundamentally flawed roguelike deckbuilder - a sort of inverse  where you waste your time on punitive events, rarely make interesting decisions during the card game portions, and are funneled towards the same strategies over and over again by the deck building. Some of that is the reliance on blackjack's inherent randomness, so if you like that gambling element, your experience might vary.I found the game's thin story equal parts insulting and boring. It emphasizes gambling as an addiction and a form of institutional violence (a reasonable position), but it mostly deploys that in a way that is infantilizing of the characters you meet or just a vague evil to provide context for an increasingly discordant cast of opponents.I know the devs have made some changes to improve things, but mostly I think you'd be better served playing other recent releases in the genre first.

_childDocuments_.review: DADG is more akin to a traditional deckbuilder like StS than balatro and so it's to be expected seeing balatro players have the wrong expectations about the game. In fact the only similarity it has with balatro is that the game has pretty much nothing to do with actual blackjack, just like how balatro is nothing like actual poker. This is more of an execution-based roguelite in the sense that you can't autopilot even after assembling your deck because of mechanics like exploit and most enemy decks having ways to mess up your gameplan or bust you. So far, this definitely feels like it has higher variance than other deckbuilders but that's just part of blackjack. Because of this, the gameplay is more moment-to-moment decision making (e.g. calculating odds of drawing a card, calculating odds of opponent busting etc) rather than a more macro form of decision making you see in rogue deckbuilders like balatro or StS where playing each individual turn/hand takes a backseat to the overall deckbuilding element, i.e. you can just autopilot once you get your deck going. However, at the moment it feels too hard and unrewarding to build a deck that isn't full of low value cards. Since low value/negative cards are basically equivalent to card draw, all of my wins so far have been with decks with low average value per card.  Which is annoying because there are many high-value or face cards with interesting themes but I have yet to make a 'blackjack in one' deck work so far because of how conservatively you have to play in the early game before it gets off the ground. Add in the fact that there aren't many deck manipulation opportunities in the tavern and floor 1 mostly plays out very similarly run to run.Overall a very different kind of game to balatro and probably requires some smoothing out and rebalancing, but still fun

The ambiguity between the unique card descriptions means the player has no control or way to devise a strategy. If you like slot machines, you will like this game.

_childDocuments_.review: A really delightful deckbuilder rougelike. Has a lot of charm. In an objective sense, it's not as well designed as something like Balatro. You are less incentivized to create a real build and are more-frequently rewarded for just taking lots of cards - but sometimes you just want to... well, take a lot of cards! The difficulty is sort of wonky - on release the game was tuned WAY too hard, and now I think it's in a pretty decent spot for beginner players. Though once you've gotten pretty familiar with it, I think it might be TOO easy now. It becomes a little too obvious which cards/events are almost always good and which are almost always terrible, which means you're thinking less about your actual deck and more just operating from general heuristics. Something to be ironed out as they go, I guess.All in all, a really fun, chaotic blackjack rougelike.

_childDocuments_.review: With the new balance update I feel this game is much more balanced than at launch. The times I lost didn't feel like RNG nearly as much as before, with it usually feeling like I just miss played my deck or didn't grab the right card synergy when I had the chance. It Feels like you have much more control over your build options with the inclusion of a re-roll for your chip at the start and the amount of chips I gained from encounters almost always allowed me to have options when it came time to buy cards. The inclusion of more healing options makes it feel like I could feasibly beat the game as other decks without relying so heavily on healing cards, albeit I still feel there could be more basic healing options for decks that aren't hearts so you don't have to rely on getting healing cards throughout your run. The constant looping and long hands have been mostly fixed from my experience. with the right cards I rarely had more than 10-15 hands in a encounter with the longest being probably around 20ish?  All-in-all I feel the game has improved on much of the RNG and difficulty issues that for more casual players might have turned them away and I hope to see some new content with cards and encounters added at some point to keep me coming back to this unique card roguelite.

_childDocuments_.review: Terribly weighted against you. Everyone you play against not only consistently draws better, but their decks are all far more specialized than your own. I've played plenty of these 'gambling roguelikes' (Balatro, Poker Quest, Bingle Bingle) and this one is the most explicitly anti-player of all of them, by far. You are shafted from the very moment you start playing - in my most recent game, the first dude, who you are intended to beat, nearly killed me because he hit 19+ on every hand but one, and any time I tried for more than a 14 I instantly busted.Is it realistic? Yes. But also? If I wanted realistic blackjack, I'd just go play blackjack. I wouldn't spend money on a game that hated me and wanted me to lose. This game, without a doubt, wants you to lose. Hell, there are so many enemies whose decks have like, 5 cards, and half those cards are just '21 of (Suit)', it's ridiculous. The Bouncer fight literally took me almost ten minutes just because we kept tying, or he got his Foil 21 of Spades to shield himself for 21 overhealth. It's ridiculous.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been giving this game a chance but it's trying to be something I'm not particularly interested in. Even though I don't think the Balatro comparisons are necessarily fair or apt, this game compared to Balatro is a completely different beast. Balatro is all about increasing the power of your deck with the shops influencing how your run unfolds. The challenges you overcome are mostly just about optimizing your score. In Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers deckfixing is infrequent, expensive, and not obviously synergistic in any way. The average deck card in this game is a lot more complicated than a Joker in Balatro which makes it difficult to plan for runs even if you know everything.The challenge structure of the game is also very different,where instead of hitting score thresholds, you're beating enemies who all have specialized decks that actually have a gameplan. You however start with nothing, and you also need to manage your extremely limited health. Victory is not meaningful long term, as poor performance early is lethal with little to no means to regain health or negate damage. Your run can end in as early as 5 rounds.This game is like trying to play Uno against somebody on a modern Yu-Gi-Oh deck, over and over and over. Enemies will almost never bust, and the player is frequently rewarded only meagre damage even for hitting blackjack, you know, the entire conceit of the game? So often you'll hit the low odds blackjack and deal 3% of an enemies health pool to them or 0%, because they have shields. Good luck doing that 30 times before the enemy kills you with a deck that is guaranteed to score between 17 and 21 exclusively every single round. It's all so "all or nothing". In Balatro one or even a few bad hands won't kill you most of the time. Here if you bust you are going to take on average a fifth of your health. You can and will lose runs to basic enemies.The part of the game that feels the worst is probably just that it's so random. It's Blackjack, and you can only ever hit. You can't discard, or control the amount of cards you play, the only control you ever have over what happens in this game is viewing your remaining deck. Balatro feels random at the start but time with the game teaches you how to guarantee victory every single run on low stakes. I don't even know where to begin with Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers because your chip is random, the ability to even change your deck comp at all is random and when you do the cards you get are random. There are too many conflicting gameplay ideas to be able to easily create a deck that makes sense for winning. If I played this game for 30 more hours I feel like I wouldn't learn anything.If I could leave a mixed review I would, because all the things I just complained about are things someone else might enjoy, but I can't. If you're looking to get into this game from Balatro, I do not recommend it, because the similarities start and end with the aesthetics.

_childDocuments_.review: Looking at all the negative reviews, they're full of crap. Some are skill issues, and some of them keep trying to compare to Balatro. _childDocuments_.review: Edit: After 12 hours my short review is this is a fantastic deck builder in need of balancing.  There are far too many battles where I am winning rounds but the opponent is stacking shield faster than I can deal damage, resulting in a near soft lock. Edit 2, well, the balance has happened and now the game feels far too easy lol.  I still recommend it, it's fun.Original review:On the venn diagram of Balatro, Slay The Spire, and Blackjack enjoyers, this one lands solidly in between them all.  Understanding at least a deckbuilding game is somewhat required as this game does not have much of a tutorial.This is a heavily Balatro inspired perspective, which matters here as the game is inspired by it as well as many other games, but is wonderfully defined, even if rough around the edges.You can increase/decrease card values to fit the ways you go about drawing a total value of 21, unlike Poker which has multiple ways to score. The suits matter differently in this game as there are no flushes etc in blackjack, so instead hearts heal, spades deal extra damage, clubs are shields, diamonds are econ.My first run I was confused, but after playing a few runs I had the hang of it to a pace of "dealing damage" that felt like Slay the Spire where I'm whipping cards out and smacking "end turn" ("stand" in Blackjack) to see the results of my play and move on to the next enemy or event.There's a lot to take in, but the difficulty is nicely balanced for learning the quirks and mechanics.Highly recommended.
