_childDocuments_.review: 8/22/24: Changed to recommended after playing the beta for a few days+new patch. Improvements across the board, especially balancing in the early parts; the game definitely still punishes mistakes or poor choices, but now I can explore and appreciate more of the games mechanics (which are far deeper than I first assumed). Was I previously just a bad player/didn't understand how to play the game? Possibly, although others definitely felt this way also. Other changes: 3 unique chip options instead of 2 (with ability to reroll!), starting run with more chips, opponent hits first now, opponent decks tuned/changed to be more reasonable early on, some UI improvements, QOL improvements, some tooltips explaining game mechanics. Although the game may still benefit from some type of tutorial, I don't think its really necessary (and probably doesn't fit with the "story" of the game) because the early game letting you experiment more freely.  Learning from mistakes is less frustrating; once you understand how strong certain cards can be, and how to manipulate your opponents cards to your benefit, the game really opens up. Only thing I would like to see is more chances to remove cards from deck early, but I can see how this could make things too easy. Highly recommend and it will likely only improve from here. 8/15/24: They have released a beta patch to address these issues and others, people seem to like it. It will go live soon, but can be accessed early if you go to library, properties, betas and then public betas. Eventually I'll be buying it again to see how it improved.Its blackjack so naturally its going to be more rng than poker. I only compare it to Balatro because its a deckbuilding game based on a card game; that's where the similarities end imo. I do not think that just because you like Balatro you will like this game. The objectives of the card games themselves are different; blackjack you can bust and lose very easily by going over 21, but with Balatro you just try to get as many points as you can to not lose. But in addition to this rng element, there is so little agency in what you can do deckbuilding wise that it feels like a struggle to affect the game in any sort of intentional way. Very few chances to remove cards, very restrictive and even forced choices that can ruin you entire deck and game plan, and most of the cards don't seem to really "go" with other cards. This is made worse by the fact that cards are drawn top-deck, so you might have a perfect card for a situation but guess what you didn't draw it so it doesn't matter (unless its a card that you can draw to your hand, which isn't always the case). Compared to Balatro, where jokers can apply to all your hands passively. Odds are heavily against you as your opponents all have tailor made decks that synergize perfectly together, while your own deck barely does anything you actually want it too. I get this is kind of the point (its even mentioned in the game as you enter one of the rooms) but it is not balanced to the point where it feels satisfying or enjoyable for me. Played the demo and was hoping the release would improve on the concept more but it didn't address glaring issues with the game play loop: not being able to build your deck in any intentional way (while your opponents deck is perfect btw!), combined with the heavy rng of blackjack just got old fast and I had to refund. The developers are aware of the balancing issues and intend to fix it, but the problems (in my opinion!) might take more than just a few balance tweaks, game needs actual gameplay changes made and not just balances. Hopefully it improves, I do like the concept.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game's biggest problem is pitting you against CPUs that are playing the same game as you, instead of against a system. Games like Slay the Spire, Monster Train, and Balatro all work because they are all against a system. The opponents you face in this game will have optimized decks tailor-made to execute a strategy while you desperately try to fight through it all with your pile only half working.Sometimes I would get out of the first act with an almost functional build, but then look at the fact that I have like 30, 40 or even 60HP left and just feel dread; dread that I am likely not salvaging this. That I will never get to enjoy the build that almost was, because you don't heal between acts.By the time I started gathering ideas of what decisions were right and wrong, and how picking almost every 0 value card no matter what is usually a good idea even if you dont think you'll need them, I was already tired of what the game had to show me.I think it can be improved into a state that is more enjoyable even in it's current system, but it's not quite there at the moment. I think at its core it will always suffer some flaws, but those can be easier to overlook if the balance wasn't also in a rocky place.

_childDocuments_.review: Even though this is getting a bundle with both Luck be a Landlord and Balatro, the two other popular "casino roguelikes", this game, unfortunately, is the weakest of the three. With this particular sub-genre, I think the hardest part is striking a balance between simplicity and how satisfying it is to play. Luck be a Lanlord is extremely simple with very little player input, but it makes it by being easy to pick up and play. Balatro is slightly more intricate, but again, easy to pick up and play and there's a satisfaction on putting Poker hands together. This game is NOT easy to pick up and play, despite just being Blackjack. Each card has the amount of text you could expect from a game like Hearthstone, but there's also other mechanics like Exploit, or some cards give you cards on your hands to play but not always. It throws you into it without a single tutorial, which would make sense if it was as simple as basic Blackjack is, but it isn't.This makes the first experience very clunky and unsatisfying as you try to understand all the mechanics of all the different cards and systems, but at the same time the gameplay will boil down to clicking "Hit" 80% of the time and trying to manipulate RNG to some degree. It's simply not fun, it's not as fast to pick up and play as Luck be a Landlord, and it's not as satisfying to play as Balatro. It's on a limbo where I'd say you should just play either of those two, as this one doesn't quite offer enough on either direction to be a fun time investment.PS: For people that say "this isn't Balatro, it's a regular roguelike!", I'm sorry but this game clearly wants the mass appeal of Balatro without being such, more complexity on top of a game with a low skill ceiling doesn't make it more engaging or interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is extremely random at the beginning and somewhat janky throughout and a lot of reviews are saying that the game is even too random. However, I disagree with those reviews: unless you deliberately pick up cards that increase the randomness, the game actually gets a lot more skill based the longer you play, since there are many cards, strategies and knowledge to be gained that allow you to handle the randomness and win consistently. For example, the opponents you face are mostly the same or at least you can always choose the same opponents each run and their decks affect your chances of winning just as much as your own. So it is useful to know what enemies are coming up and adjust your strategy accordingly.It feels great to pick up certain cards knowing that they'll guarantee the victory against a later opponents deck that bested you in the last run. And even tho the opponents aren't randomized, the game still never feels the same due to all the different cards and decks that you can build.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I recommend this game, I will say that it does suffer from some mechanical challenges that it has difficulty negotiating. For the most part, Blackjack may be a luck based game, however, there is some level of mathematical predictability that goes into it that allows you to know the general risk of any hand and the actions available to you. The problem with this game is that practically all of those instincts and awareness regarding probability go out the window because you manipulate the deck so heavily. This fundamentally means that you're largely trusting the build of your deck or randomness to dictate your success in any match, which leads to a pretty heavy skew of "randomness" dictating the majority of your situation.To compare this to Balatro, I would say that Balatro benefits from the nuances of poker, which gives the player a variety of approaches to achieve win conditions, whereas Blackjack is inherently limited to a much more basic and strict numerical practice that limits the player's ability to subvert or work with the game's rules. This just means that "broken" decks that are either good or bad just feel far more common in this game with less feeling of player agency regarding the outcome of a run. Granted, once you begin to know how the npc players operate, you do have the ability to anticipate some of their strategies and plan ahead with certain counter-strategies, however, I do find that to be a bit of a limitation to the game's replayability.All in all, I do enjoy the game and I do think there are really fun and interesting mechanical flourishes in the way it plays, I just think it struggles for some pretty foundational reasons that seem to be tied to blackjack more than any of the decisions the designers made to make the game more interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: Two things you should know off the bat - this game is addictive, and this game is HARD. Just like Balatro, the designers of this game have definitely considered a lot of different creative ways to play with the Blackjack mechanics. The game takes you through five stages - along one of two different paths - and each of the opponents and situations you meet offer compelling and juicy challenges. However, even once you start to get some winning deckbuilding strategies under your belt, it takes quite the combination of luck and skill to make it to the final stage. I can make the final stage regularly at this point, but I'm always slaughtered by its first guardian (hit point damage persists from one round to the next). I can't wait to actually succeed at a run.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the game on my first few runs, but as I continued, the cracks started to show. I think with a handful of tweaks it could end up being a really good game, but as is there are some flaws that still need to be ironed out.My main issue with the game is the lack of agency. I know, I know, it's a casino, it's black jack, it's supposed to be random. But Black Jack isn't designed to be a fun game, it's designed to make casinos money. Few alterations were made to give the player an edge.In other deck builders, there's a mix of both randomness and strategy. They always give a handful of options you can choose, mainly through giving options of which cards to play, although I don't necessarily think that's the right move for this game. Unfortunately, in Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers, you only have two options each round: take a risk or do nothing. Having other options is a privilege in D&DG. I've died to the first opponent multiple times, and the only way I could've prevented that was by predicting that my next card was going to be a 10 when I only had a score of 12. Near the end, when you have cards that enter your hand instead of being played immediately, cards that affect another card of your choice, or cards with abilities that let you affect their value, the game becomes genuinely really enjoyable. But until then you just have to pray that the RNG won't just screw you over and end a run before it's truly began.My suggestion would be to add one card to the hand at the start of a round if your hand is empty. Just one, the game doesn't need to be genericized by making the normal "hit" option obsolete. Risk assessment should still be a large part of the game. But I believe giving the player an option with little reliance on luck, even if it's not always useful, would greatly help the game. Alternatively, even just a guaranteed Foil card at the start of a run might do wonders.Unfortunately though, as the game is right now, there's a total lack of agency without any fancy cards, and I think that hurts it. The game could be great, I've even had a lot of fun with it when I get through the early game RNG-fest. But getting through said early game RNG-fest is just a slog.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't usually write reviews for games, but I really felt like I should do one this time.I've read through some of the negative reviews and imho the biggest error is to compare D&DG to Balatro, it's not the same at all, and it's not meant for the same audience either.Balatro is an easy game to get into, and to understand, and every run feels roughly the same with only a few mechanics to understand. You play for points and the goal of one round is always going to be the same. D&DG is complex and has a lot more depth, every opponent changes how you approach the encounter radically, and you have to make a lot of choices in how your deck is going to evolve, what card will help or hinder your strategy, etc.When I went through my first couple of games, it really felt difficult to make a proper deck, and to see how I could do something right. I mostly stuck to playing the deck of hearts, because it felt to me like I wasn't going anywhere without some form of healing.After about 10 runs, I finally  managed to complete a run and unlock the colorless deck. From there I decided to try to unlock the glitched deck, which requires to finish a run with colorless. It initially felt like an impossible task, but I just had to start building my decks, not just to synergise with the cards I was playing, but also to be more disruptive towards the enemy decks. Once you start understanding that, the game suddenly opens up.I'm now on a 4 consecutive runs win streak, each time with a new deck, and the fun is really starting to kick in after about 16 hours of figuring things out.D&DG is very different from Balatro because of how different one opponent is to another, whereas one balatro round is pretty much an exact copy of the previous one, especially at higher antes. Honestly, Balatro gets pretty boring after a while, because there's only so many strategies worth pursuing. Now of course, some runs are going to hit or miss, and you're always at the hands of RNJesus, that's what roguelite games do, and Balatro is no different by the way.I feel like I've only scratched the surface of D&DG and I'm looking forward to trying more decks, doing more runs and discovering more surprising strategies.So far my favourite deck to play is the Wizard. I got really lucky and got some sick synergies with the tower card, allowing me to beat most bosses in 2-3 rounds with an onslaught of scratch cards. So much fun !
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: Before you think this is just a Balatro clone, this game was in development before Balatro, so it's merely a coincidence. LocalThunk (dev for Balatro) has also given this game his seal of approval, which should speak volumes to the quality of this game. There are things in this game that were likely added after Balatro's release (for the better), but it is more than just a clone. It is way more like a regular roguelike with varying "paths" you can take and more opportunities for decision-making than Balatro. Only have done a few runs so far, but it's very addicting and I can tell there's a lot of depth to the mechanics. Definitely pick it up if you enjoy deckbuilding roguelikes.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: I've started and restarted this review quite a few times, because I'm having difficulty putting my finger on what I don't like about Dungeons and Degenerate Gamblers. It felt off from the first few moments I played, and that feeling only continued as I kept playing. There's a sense of clunkiness to the controls (I'm on Deck) that made a bad first impression, but the loose threads continued to unravel.I think the thing I think is actually bad is, sadly, the core gameplay loop. Man, it's just tedious. You're fighting through two layers of RNG (your own deck and your enemy's deck), and, especially with different shield and healing effects, it can be quite a few hands before either you or the enemy takes any meaningful damage. This can make fights, even with low-HP enemies, drag on for a while if you can't manage to get a good hit on them while they're bust, and it causes the pacing of the game grind to a halt. Unlike other deckbuilders, like Balatro or Slay the Spire, you're not really making decisions about what cards to play - in D&DG, you only hit or stand, and that's a much less interesting decision matrix than most other games in the genre. You're just hitting Button 1 or Button 2 without much thought, waiting for your RNG to align with the enemy's RNG so the battle will end and you can continue.I also don't think the deckbuilding aspects are very good. I distinctly remember the first time I came across Card Sharp, or Demon Form, in the respective aforementioned games; there was a distinct "OH, this is SWEET!" feeling to discovering cards, jokers, and relics in those games. I'm not really feeling any of that in D&DG; most of what I've seen so far in terms of buildcraft falls on a sprectum of "kinda useless right now" to "hmm, okay". There's no real wow factor to the decks, or the chips, or the cards. I tend to believe roguelikes live or die on the quality of their items/cards, as that's what provides both variety and excitement in a run. So far, D&DG has not impressed me on this front. I know I haven't played very long, but I kind of feel like I've experienced all I need to experience. I give props to D&DG for having an original idea in terms of the fundamental mechanical loop, but I just don't think that loop is very good. The moment-to-moment play is meh, the deckbuilding is meh, the AVFX are kind of meh too. I'm a huge fan of roguelikes/lites/whatevers, so I'm very predisposed to like this game, but D&DG just did not hit (blackjack pun) for me. It's a lot less impressive than its genre peers in pretty much every respect, and, considering you can play those games pretty much forever, a new game has to offer something really striking to warrant playing. I didn't get this spark playing D&DG, so it's back to the tried-and-true games for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: Great concept and you can tell that a lot of care went into this game. That said, from a mechanics and gameplay perspective, on release this still has a lot of balancing and reworking left to be worth your time + money.Check out this list below instead of this game:BalatroSlay The SpireCobalt CoreGriftlands (Underrated)WildfrostMonster TrainInscryptionDeckbuilders live and die by their synergies and giving the player meaningful decisions to make. This game does not have enough synergy to allow the player to consistently find decks that are fun. Specifically, there are not enough things to do with advantage which is one of the only non-rng mechanics the game provides. Moreover though there's just not enough cards that go together well and you don't have enough opportunity to find those cards.One example of this is that you can't see what choices you will have before you make them, i.e. Slay the Spire's map.Basically, this game is Blackjack, but more frustrating because you feel like you should be doing better and should be able to manipulate your deck to find fun builds, but you can't. It's not the player's fault. There just isn't enough opportunity to find the fun in this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a cool vibe. The problem is that the core gameplay mechanic (pvp blackjack) misses what makes blackjack fun. The adrenaline rush in standard blackjack comes from doubles  and risky hits. In this game there is no doubling, and the risk/reward is so skewed that risky hits (hits that might cause a bust) are basically never worth it. So essentially it plays out as an ultra-cautious version of blackjack.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly, you don't build a deck, you just toss cards into the wind and see what sticks. It's blackjack. There's no strategy involved, you're letting the deck play itself. The other cards you add don't really do much except either add or subtract to the underwhelming feeling of 'strategy' the game provides. To add, there's so much RNG that if you want to have a strategy you never actually get it:Want to do a hearts build? Want to build something with advantage? There's too much RNG in this game to warrant any sense of valid of strategy to the point to where if you're facing down opponents with actual decks, while you have a hodgepodge of cards that somehow 'work', and then you bust. If I wanted to slog through a 1.4hr session of literal brainrot copypasta for a straight hour because we're just trading cards back to back and not progressing anywhere, I would rather play against 3 stax players in a mtg commander match at my local tcg and hate my life that way. At least there I can just get out of that game, buy 5 packs of 'March of the Machine: Aftermath' boosters and get more return value and enjoyment over this game."Durr swap our hands" "Cool, I was about to win. That's a reset."
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: Chaotic, unfair, extraordinarily fun. A true old-school roguelike, not every run is winnable, not every fight is fair, but by playing carefully and well you can stack the odds (mostly) in your favor. The way so many zany mechanics interact over a simple premise is incredible. Do you have a good head for numbers, patience for rng, and like carefully reading mechanics and theorycrafting? This is the game for you.If you get mad easily, give this a pass. You have to laugh at the dumb stuff that happens sometimes. But that's the spirit of blackjack, right? Just like regular blackjack, sometimes your luck runs sour - and there's always another run!
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: D&DG is a VERY good game that takes blackjack and says "what if you could play your credit card against a goblin." The cards you use can either be used to attack if your cards are higher than the opponents, or defend if they're lower, to negate as much damage as you can.There's a lot of really fun cards that you can build a very synergized deck with, and a lot of cards that can really be added to any deck. People may look at this and think it's some Balatro-like but I assure you it's very different. (Also, this game released demos before Balatro even existed.)I love creating a deck, whittling it down to perfection and with the right set-up, beating the opponents in 1 or 2 fell swoops. Though I love it, it's by all means not perfect.It can, at times, through LOTS of BS at you. A deck that might've been cruising through enemies CAN and WILL be cut short by either the boss, or some random powerful enemy. At it's best, you can get through it scratched up and learn new things and predict the game before it predicts you. At it's worst, one of the final bosses of the game outright DENIES THE USE OF SOME CARDS. (And no, it's never explained to you that any enemy can do that, they simply are able to.) It's a bit disheartening to get all the way to the end and get bodied by something sort of out of your control.And the last thing? To even unlock a single other deck, you HAVE to complete the whole game. And to get another, you have to beat it again with an even HARDER starting deck. I'd love if unlocking new starter decks were based on beating chapters instead of beating the entire game, which may take around 30 minutes just to get to the final level. And there are 18 decks to unlock, which... doesn't sound fun.But besides those two relatively big things it's a very fun game to play. I'd love to see what new updates bring to the table, with new cards and maybe even routes to take-- hell, a multiplayer mode kind of like Super Auto Pets could be really fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: Funny and ridiculous, even if it means it's very random.All the card and most opponent appearances are based on some pop culture reference, usually funny enough, at least the first time. Finding combinations is very fun and the game usually gives you some chance of victory at least. You mostly work with what the game gives you rather than planning much upfront.This game has no patience for "balance" or "fairness," it's randomness on top of randomness. Maybe your winning card will be at the bottom of your deck. Maybe you'll get a foil library card and wreck the bosses. It's a fine line between funny and annoying and D&DG mostly lands on the good side. When you do get unlucky it doesn't feel too bad, runs are short enough.Each area has certain set events/encounters and you have to do most of them to get to the area boss and continue. There are only a few generic shop events and all the enemies are unique, with predetermined decks. Each enemy also adds their own sounds on top of the area soundtrack. It works out well to make each battle unique and to make it possible to win by going taking those events that can work out for you.The demo is close enough to the full thing. If you don't know if you'll like it, play that first.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish I could put it as mixed here. I'm very conflicted, since I beat the game for the first time, and there is a bunch of good and a bunch of bad.Graphics: Better than the demo, a lot of polish went into this area, everybody who put effort into this should be given a raise. Music: Starting song is good. I really do not like the music changing. Mainly since it sounds directly like from WolframTones, which is very low quality until the VIP section, and it made me want to mute the game. It's extremely mixed. The sound effects are good.Gameplay: Pretty mixed in general. The stuff in between card battles is really creative and fun. A lot of effort must have been put there. There are a lot of different cards. The actual card game itself is extremely luck based and unbalanced. Getting to 21 has a bunch of risk vs reward, so being in the middle of 12 and 18 is the best. Starting with the VIP section, doing that without lots of healing behind you is death, since they have decks made to always go close to 18-21. In the Hope area the first guy starts out always getting 21, forcing you to manipulate his max number count to win. If you do not have any cards for that, you lose. Even if you do, you need to draw it quickly or else you won't be able to counter. So the counterplay is much more limited, even before this. The advantage system is very mixed in general and feels like not a lot of thought was put into it. Mainly you have to get cards to use it for it, enemies cannot gain any advantage, and many things are infinite as long as you have advantage to spare, like the credit card blade where you can win instantly if you have any advantage to spam it, since there is no con for going negative chips. No cards that scale off the chips you have that I encountered. This leads all enemy decks to have one counterplay: screw over their win condition. When your whole win condition becomes based on how much you can screw over the opponent, it become much more limiting and everything in game feels directed to this one idea of screwing over the enemy deck and hand. And you can only do things when you get good draws, which impacts 90% of if you win turn one or turn 50 after lots of chip damage, and if you have no healing cards, you are screwed due to chip damage since enemies after the third section will mostly end at 18-21 unless you screw them over. So game design wise, it really doesn't feel good to play and is very one dimensional because of being forced into a single playstyle to get far. Compared to the Demo, when I played it, where it felt like there was a lot more than could be done, it's very disappointing. Card Designs/stand outs: Mostly putting this here since there are a lot of references to other games. Hell, I paid over 1k on Hearthstone when it was good, and 4 mana 7/7 is a great card. But visually the reference cards have more polish in the coloring to stand out, which makes the rest of the cards not stand out as much. I know that is the colors 4 mana 7/7 used in hearthstone, but it's much more colorful where it stands out too much compared to everything else being very much not impactful visually. It's a very small nitpick, but I wanted to bring it up.TL:DR: Music mixed. Graphics are good, but the gameplay got heavily changed since the demo to force every playstyle into one main one due to new mechanics introduced like advantage which are giving more power to the player than the enemy to compensate for enemy decks in the late game being heavily optimized with little counterplay. Get on a sale after many balance patches to fix the biggest fundamental problem or else there really isn't much that can be done for replaying the game and having fun with it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: i really really REALLY wanted to like this game. but as it stands, i'm not sure i'd recommend it. the idea is fun but in practice, it's not a very satisfying gameloop. for one, it doesn't feel like i can strategize my run at all. no matter what, it comes down to rng between my hand and my opponent's. the special cards are really interesting, but because of the rng, i never feel like i'm adequately able to take advantage of them. the style is fantastic, as is the writing, and i want to keep an eye on it to see how it develops

_childDocuments_.review: Previously gave this game a negative review, but after playing it for another evening I'm giving it the thumbs up.What turned me off originally is how steep the learning curve was compared to something like Balatro, but taking a step back and comparing it to something more like Slay the Spire did a lot to help enjoy the process of building up familiarity with cards and enemies.If you can get used to getting stomped by enemies/cards a few times, there's a lot of fun to be had here.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those rogues that doesn't give you quite enough control over how you play the game. Essentially, you always want to be building a deck aiming to get blackjacks, because many of the fringe cards that have random effects are only consistent when you have very many of them. You can almost never accumulate enough of these cards in time before dying. This sounds obvious because it's a game based around blackjack after all, but when so many cards have values lower or higher than 10/11, you don't really feel like picking any of them ever. Because picking one means you've got to go for ALL of them, and there's absolutely no guarantee that the ones offered to you will be beneficial with what you already have. Going with just a few of these cards almost always puts you in an awkward spot every other hand.Roguelikes, especially deckbuilders, tend to be popular for how you can take advantage of the systems available to you to weigh the odds of winning in your favor, using the strategy that you like. It feels like this game only allows one route, and every other option is pretty stupid to lean into. Especially considering your opponents are almost never playing normal cards themselves. Many of your effects actually tend to be beneficial to them. So why pick them at all?On the contrary, there are also too many cards that have absolutely no risk to add to your deck. These are mostly handy's and cards with 0 value. That's not even including the tarot cards, your reward for beating a floor. They pretty much immediately invalidate all the other options you have when you have to choose what to add to your deck, which is very often.In my opinion, you should be able to start the game picking what your max number before bust is. At least let it go up to 26 or something. There are many cards with values slightly over and far under 10/11, and even some that will bust you immediately if played. They are not beneficial enough to be worth picking, the benefits are minimal compared to the almost guaranteed ~20 damage you'll receive for taking the risk.The process of unlocking new decks to play with is also kind of annoying. You shouldn't have to win games just to be able to play the other options. You should be at least somewhat rewarded for doing good regardless of if you beat the entire game or not, that's kinda how most rogues have been for a long time for a reason.Gambling is fun when you can play in different ways, or there's a payoff. There's almost no payoff here, and you'd be actively throwing to not always go for blackjacks. You just play the game, the same way every time. Or not, if you want to consistently lose early.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: A great game! I've been following this game since the demo was first released, and it's a lot of fun. I've seen people compare this game to Balatro. These games are similar in that they both are based off of casino games and have deck building, but otherwise the they're very different. Balatro is more about building up scoring combos, while this game is more about building a consistent deck and disrupting your opponent's strategy as much as possible.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: About 8 hours into the game and I can't say I fully recommend this game. I think it is a cool concept, similiar-ish to Balatro, though Balatro feels more polished with several different deck styles and decisions to make as the game goes on. This game feels more like stuck in a loop. Before writing this review, in the last few games, I found myself just zoning out clicking hit/stand. If you end up with a few bad draws on the first and second encounters, you might as well end up restarting as you could lose 50-75% of your health which can essentially never be replenished unless you are playing the Hearts deck (the only deck which is worthwhile). The chips being only attainable at the start of the run and not switchable (at least I think they aren't) makes the game more rigid and less fluid as the deck builds over time. Would like to see a few improvements before a recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: I was excited to see a Blackjack game, similar style to Balatro. Reading other reviews and discussions, it's not kept as a good comparison, but I think these are the only 2 games like this out there right now.Building decks feels really odd, the cards have quite wacky and convoluted mechanics. Choosing cards between rounds doesn't feel like you are making yourself stronger. It's more like having an extra "ace-in-the-hole", but they don't really make you stronger, worse case scenario they just ruin your run.Some opponents are designed to screw you over unless you have a few specific cards that consistently make them bust. In poker even a bad hand is a hand (naturally), but here it's a choice between "Do you want to take 5 damage, or risk going for Blackjack and take 17 damage instead?" Then at one point you finally get a 21 and stand, but then your opponent pulls out a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ card that removes cards from your played hand, so suddenly you stood at like 7, and the opponent gets an instant 21 and gets massive shield so you have even more hands to catch up to. Watching opponents slowly gaining shields that you can't out-damage is quite demoralizing.Also sitting on a stalemate is really boring, doing 1-3 damage to each other and then healing/shielding between is really frustrating and starts to feel hopeless, especially when you know that multiple matches like these are on the horizon.The game is about blackjack, but the blackjacks seem to happen pretty rarely (for the player at least, the opponents are favored) and when you do get a blackjack, you barely get rewarded for it. Having the Hearts deck for healing when you get a blackjack is like the only good option out of the decksI would give a mixed review if it was possible, but I can't quite recommend the game due to the frustration it causes.I keep trying the game again multiple times but I just end up closing the game frustrated in the end.The satisfaction of Blackjack is missing for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: As it is at the moment I can't say I'm a fan of anything but the artstyle. It's such a pain to get a good run going and you end up taking way too much damage early on just to get cheesed by the AI with a perfect deck. I really wanted to be a fan as I was having a lot of fun with the demo and I love all its little references but its all for naught if you're not having fun while playing. Might continue on an update, but for now I think I'll go back to another roguelike that doesn't make me want to throw my mouse.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: So, on first glance this game is "Balatro but Blackjack", but I'm not sure that's a fair comparison. The biggest downside of this game is how random it feels over Balatro, there are less options for strategy in deckbuilding, and it seems hard to build a theme for a deck the way your opponents have, particularly in the later rounds. No battle really feels hard, but a few of them do feel unfair, even if easily beatable. I'm also not convinced of the "randomness" in some situations, though with an admittedly small number of games played, this could just be down to bad luck. There also seem to be a few things which are underutilised or underexplained in the game, such as the chips you get offered at the start of a run.Don't get me wrong, this game is fun, the card design is interesting, the audio is sometimes a little difficult to listen to with so much "ambience", but it works most of the time, and the gameplay loop is generally pretty fast and satisfying. I don't understand the complaints personally about card descriptions, but then I have a lot of experience in the genre, so maybe that's why. Anyway, I do quite like the game, I just feel like it needs a bit more work, and, ultimately, it's not quite as enjoyable as Balatro.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game, but after an hour I'm not impressed. Not sure what it is exactly, but the game is lacking something.The visuals are great! Love the presentation.The gameplay feels like it could be snappier. The card effects are hard to follow at a glance, which harms the playability of a game where you're supposed to lose and start up again.What I expected was a game I could keep playing back-to-back runs and lose track of time. This game feels like it should be able to do that, but that wasn't my experience. Really hope it gets some tweaks because I want to like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game - 8/10Really unfortunate to see balatro addicts review bombing this game because they went in with the wrong expectations. the way you approach the game should be much different from balatro - blackjack and poker are very different gamesAlso this game started development publicly before balatro and it isn't trying to be balatro.... just enjoy it for what it is and youll have a much better time.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: Man it's tough because I came into this game after a positive experience with the demo which has only soured with the amount of hours spent with the demo. I'm going to focus on what made this game a negative for me rather than writing up a full IGN review of what the game does well and what it does not do.The update felt like a hail Mary in order to make the game easier which doesn't address fundamental issues like super limited ability to craft and manipulate your deck or fish for specific synergies. Decks feel unimaginative, it feels so irrelevant that my deck heals or shields me on max score if there are only a very select few cards which synergise with them and half the time I'm playing to minimise damage from the AI which bust scarcely.The whole currency (chips) system feels unfinished, most my runs I never have to look at them unless I am trying to force a synergy/get a specific card. A lot of events do not feel adequate to the floor I am on. There is no point starting runs with so many options to remove cards from your deck when you yourself have no idea what the deck is going towards and only having options to bloat your deck with random cards later. Feels like something that should be at least slightly the other way around.The game likes to make references to other games so let me draw an example from slay the spire. STS constantly allows for your deck to take shape because shopkeepers can remove cards all the way throughout the game, you have another option which isn't adding or removing but upgrading your cards which again adds another dimension of priority within your deck building. Slay the Spire, just like balatro let the player take control and create a feeling of advantage in encounters through artifacts/Jokers. It feels so barebones being stuck with just one tag you get to choose at the start and have no reliant possibility of changing the tag itself or forcing a deck archetype in order to utilise the chip. The fun from the aforementioned games come from being able to utilise synergies and combinations as best as you can in a given situation. D&DG has striped that ability from the player and is my suspicion of why the game feels more like a chore than it's competitors.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute banger of a game. Card themes, an absolute tonne of content in terms of effects. _childDocuments_.review: Good visual, music and feel. It's blackjack, with lots of references, broken cards and broken people. Once the strategy clicks, it's extremely addictive, as you can tell from my hours played at the time of review.This is where the review could end, but I want to address the two elephants in the room:While the concept of "fake casino game" is similar, the execution is completely different. We are not even in the same category here.The formula of the game is really much closer to your classic deckbuilder formula. Construct a deck around a strategy, play encounters against with a particular theme (they heal a lot, they steal your cards, they make easy blackjacks, etc...). Health loss is also permanent between encounters. We are much closer in terms of feel and difficulty to a game like Slay the Spire. If you buy this game thinking it will be like Balatro, you will definitely be disappointed.Rather, the difficulty of this game relies on encounter knowledge, mechanics and some deckbuilding sense. This comes with playing the game for a few runs and getting a feel for the kinds of builds you can make, and knowing what comes ahead. You know... like in every roguelike in existence. In this sense, the game will feel very unfair at the beginning (and it is, in some ways) as the enemies can and will do some extremely dirty things against you if you just let them. This can range from taking more damage than you should to you literally being unable to play the game and forced in a continuous losing state. Bad deckbuilding can also more commonly result in much longer fights, akin to a battle of attrition. These gotchas are definitely frustrating as you start playing, which explain the negative reviews. While that is a thing, I am here to tell you that these elements definitely lessen as you play more. As you get better at the game, you find more and more ways to have game-breaking decks and strategies to take care of every encounter coming your way. This also happens to be the strongest element of this game for me. The payoff of making a good deck is extremely satisfying. The game's paths and encounters are also almost entirely the same between every run, so you can more or less plan ahead what your ideal build looks like, and what you are exactly looking for. There is a surprising amount of depth in this game, you'll find more and more interesting and wild synergies as you play along. You are definitely rewarded for your experience and knowledge, and that is all you could possibly ask from a game like this.So, yes. This game is awesome, and if you are a deckbuilder or roguelike fan, and that this review resonated with what you are looking for in those, you definitely should grab it. On top of that, the developer is active on discord, and already has updates planned for the future. Here's to many more hours of gameplay!

_childDocuments_.review: Tough one to enjoy. It's really less about making blackjack and more about not busting. The difficulty, where it exists, is in grinding it out against opponents who play decks that functionally only go to 20, 21, or bust. Yes, there's the occasional bit of "ah ha" when you see a way to break that pattern for your opponent. But you actually have very little agency in the game beyond deciding when not to push your luck. Building a deck with a strategy feels impossible. Chips feel very useless; the pricing makes your choices very easy, and your opponents can go negative with absolutely no consequences to them, making me wonder why they're there.It has potential, but something about the gameplay loop needs work.

_childDocuments_.review: Really disappointed because the demo was a great premise for a game, but unfortunately, they pretty much didn't add anything when they made the full release. Yeah they cleaned it up, added more floors (which are extremely similar to the existing floors), added starter decks (which are as lame as possible, literally just different suits), and added extra difficulty modes (which don't actually explain what they do? Like the first one is just "advantage is harder to get". How do I get it now??), but they didn't add many new cards (seriously not sure if I've seen a new card, they might not have added any) or mechanics (besides advantage/exploit which is really just like bare minimum making the game function).Ultimately the problem does not lie in the failure to expand the game between demo and release. It lies in the fact that the core gameplay loop is just not there. You're just not building a deck the same way other games in the genre let you do. The cards don't really synergize, they pretty much all just make your deck better is some small way. There's a little bit of synergy in regards to the fact that you want to make 21, so your cards should combine to get there, but that's not really how that works considering you have extremely limited options to control card draw order, so two cards don't really synergize, unless each of those cards synergize with themselves too (e.g. a 13 of spades doesn't exactly synergize with an 8 of hearts because you can only put one 13 in your deck without ruining it). Its fine for roguelikes to have unconditional bonuses/perks/etc., they don't all have to depend on situation or synergy, but those boons almost always exists outside of the deck (e.g. relics in slay the spire, or jokers in Balatro), so they don't warp your deck into a meaningless direction. For example there's a card that's got this interesting ability about dealing damage when you hit at 17+, but its really clunky to add to a deck because its a 4-score card. Nothing about the ability really makes it have to be 4-score, but its a card so it should have a score I guess. Most other cards like this are just 0-score cards, making them effectively not cards, but this slows down the game A TON. Imagine if you had to draw all your relics in slay the spire, but each of them let you draw an additional card. That's just a bunch of fishing for no reason.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, and after 12 hours of playtime, I feel like I’ve given it a fair shot. Unfortunately, it didn’t quite click with me for several reasons. While I can appreciate the attempt to add a theme through the different opponents, locations, and events, it often feels forced. Personally, I would have preferred a more streamlined experience focused purely on match after match.There are definitely some clever card mechanics, but many of them seem included just for the sake of variety. Some card descriptions are also quite confusing, making it harder to strategize effectively. Overall, the game gives off a sense that you could almost watch someone else play and still get the same experience. There's minimal planning involved, and it often feels like taking risks isn't rewarding. Luck plays such a significant role that matches can feel inconsistent — one minute you're winning in three turns, and the next you're stuck in a 30-minute battle against a similar opponent only to lose.The control you have over the matches feels very limited, and the choices you make between matches don’t feel meaningful. I’m not opposed to RNG or luck being factors in a game, but when you invest 45 minutes into a run and lose due to one overpowered card that locks your opponent at 21 points every round, it’s hard to enjoy the experience. Unfortunately, this has left me feeling frustrated and disinterested in continuing to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, that I think might be marred from it's very high difficulty from the get-go. While both Slay the Spire, Balatro, and other roguelikes have difficulty modes (e.g. acensions, stakes), DDG doesn't. So the higher, or deeper you go into the rooms, you get faced with exponentially tougher decks that rely solely on you knowing their strategies and pre-planning your deck before you encounter them. This means that manipulating your foe's deck is always extremely high value, and seems to reduce the value of cards that simply make your own blackjack easier to obtain (I don't have that many hours yet, and I might be wrong here). That being said, I do think this is a fantastic game with a lot of thought and love being put into it's development, and considering it just released yesterday (from time of review), I think there's so much room for patches to be developed. An absolute buy for anyone that loves to spend time thinking and calculating the gamba.---After winning my first run:This game is cracked. This game is so good.

_childDocuments_.review: I went in expecting to love this game, and I was really disappointed. By the nature of the main mechanic (blackjack), combat goes very slowly. Ties are frequent, meaning even simple battles early are a game of chance on who busts first. Card mechanics in the game feel ignorable or have effects that are detrimental to a wide variety of builds (burning cards on play, forcing stands, shredding cards for little benefit, etc). I think the archetypes are built pretty narrowly, with little overlap. Card removal is difficult to come by, meaning creating consistency is tough. Tarot cards, while an interesting concept in the spirit of boss relics in Slay the Spire, often feature abilities that force your deck into a certain archetype. I played around 200 hands before refunding, and I often had to take tarot cards that made my deck worse, causing me to lose on the next floor. They are not skippable (I may be wrong, but I could not figure it out) and do not get re-randomized after each boss, meaning you must take one of the ones you skipped the first time, muddling again the focus of your deck.I think the core idea of the game is interesting, and I think that the card designs and theming are great. After playing the demo for a few hours, I guess I expected the full release to be more polished. Hopefully, I will come back to this game in a year and revise my review, but for now I can not recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Failing to understand how these negative reviews are complaining about a blackjack game being "luck-based".  Like, no ♥♥♥♥. Even more confusing is how they actually believe you can't impose your will on the game to force a win. The counterfeiter in the tavern allows you to build a predictable base deck to add on to with the cards you receive in the shop or at the end of each encounter. Removing cards through various means creates a more unified and, thus, stronger deck. The advantage chip you choose dictates which type of cards you want to pick up on the way. On the surface this game seems like pure rng but once you put some time into learning the cards and encounters the game becomes remarkably simple. I really think this game does a good job of allowing the player to stack the odds in their favor, while still maintaining the random "feel" of blackjack. You win some, you lose some.

_childDocuments_.review: Perhaps I'd feel differently if I hadn't played this alongside Balatro, but I really just cannot recommend this game. The rules of the cards are difficult to keep in your head, partially because they're needlessly complex. Similarly, the cards, especially the special cards (probably because they are all trying to reference something), don't do a good job of telegraphing what they do for your deck. Sure the game is about stacking your deck right like any good deckbuilder, but it leans a little more into luck and withholds the knobs you usually get to use to fiddle with chances. Because it's more luck based than skill based, games can feel very swingy (plus the rule where you have no defense if you bust encourages oversafe behavior and seems overly punitive if you take a chance). Blackjack's just not that compelling of a game, and the video game does little if anything to salvage it.In terms of setting, it's a hodgepodge pastiche. Not particularly interesting or original, but pleasant enough if you recognize the references.

_childDocuments_.review: D&DG is a pretty interesting game but it’s one that I think would only appeal to a very specific type of person. The most obvious game to compare it to is Balatro because Balatro came out half a year ago, was really popular, and is also based around a casino game (poker). So, I imagine a lot of people that liked Balatro will look at this and be interested. The problem is that D&DG is almost nothing like Balatro. Balatro is a fast and simple game that’s pretty carefully balanced. None of the cards do anything too crazy, at the end of the day you’re usually just getting more points. No matter what, you’re always playing something that resembles poker, even if it’s a lobotomized version of poker where you just need a pair to win.D&DG has a blackjack theme, sure, but if you’re playing the game correctly you aren’t going to be playing blackjack past the first few enemy encounters. There also isn’t even a semblance of balance in the game, with the focus in most cases being on flavor instead. The best cards are those that have a low value and disrupt the enemy in some way, for a few reasons. First, if your deck is all low-value cards you can play a bunch of cards in a round without worrying about busting. Second, if you stand before your opponent does (because your deck has a lot of high-value cards) they can play a disruptive card and force you to bust or lower your score. Third and most importantly, late game enemies can almost always hit a 20 or 21, so if you just try to play basic strategy against them without disruption you can easily end up in an endless war of attrition where busting once knocks out a fifth of your health. In most cases your goal should be to force the enemy to bust since that drops their defense to 0. Cards like Geraldo, Yellow Card, Break Limits, and 4 Mana 7/7 are absurdly strong, then, because they either remove important cards from your opponent’s deck, force them to bust, or clog their deck with trash. On the flipside, basically every card with a random element to it or a value higher than around 5 or 6 isn’t worth taking because boosting your own score should always be ancillary to trying to disrupt your opponent. What this means, in technical terms, is that like 80% of the cards in the game suck.I imagine a lot of people would look at the number of bad cards in the game and go “Wow, there sure are a lot of bad cards in this game, they really need to balance them!” Again, however, the focus of the game clearly is on flavor more than balance. A 21 of diamonds is a funny card and there isn’t really a way to make it less useless without ruining the joke. All the cards that are king, queen, and jack puns don’t work if they aren’t kings, queens, or jacks. The design philosophy in many cases seems like the devs said “Wouldn’t it be funny if…” and then added a card without really caring if it was balanced or not. As a result, there are a lot of amusing references to other card games or just types of cards in general (like a “Get well soon” card or a credit card) and they don’t feel forced because they fit with the game’s theme.So, I suppose you need a certain type of mindset to enjoy this game. You shouldn’t expect things to be balanced and you shouldn’t expect to play blackjack. There is a lot of RNG at certain points depending on the starting deck you pick (the Birthday "deck" can literally lose to the first enemy encounter without you being able to do anything), but in a way I feel like this is more of an experiential game in the vein of something like Inscryption. Sure, all of my wins have come from abusing the same pool of 5 or 6 cards and I’ll probably get bored of that soon, but I appreciate the game for what it tries to do. Maybe you won’t, maybe you’ll hate it and refund it. So, I’m basically trying to prevent that from happening by writing this review. If this game doesn’t sound appealing to you don’t buy it, because you might hate it so much you’ll send a bomb threat to the devs and get sent to prison, then in prison you might get sodomized by a big black bull named Tyrone, or maybe a guy covered in Nazi tattoos named Ralph. You’d basically be ruining your life all over a video game. So think carefully, okay?

_childDocuments_.review: In it's current state, there's still a lot to be desired. By 'desire' those things seem to be very basic things that should have gone into the game from the very beginning. Some of those things are:- ability to properly manage the deck- ability to heal outside of random healing events- more opportunities to explore the game mechanics before losing a run quicklyA lot of the game is based on RNG to the point where it doesn't seem like a game of strategy but a game of chance.The gameplay formula is similar to the childhood card game most know as 'WAR' where you and an opponent each shuffle a deck of cards and blindly pulling the top card with the highest value card winning.You can't base any strategy around the RNG or 'trap' the opponent into anything as your only 'strategy' in the game is being made only after the initial cards are dealt in which you have to attempt to plot a tactic around that falls apart instantly as the next card is dealt.A lot of times it feels like your opponent has complete control of the rules for the encounter and you don't with the opponent presenting weird and obscure 'debuffs' that aren't explained and with the complete randomness of the cards being given to you you'll be praying on the 'Heart of the Cards' like a vintage Yu-Gi-Oh duel hoping the ONE card that can counter the madness shows up in a manner that you can actually use.For example:There's a card that creates an instant blackjack but it can ONLY be used if there is already a Jack present in your hand.That card is literally useless unless RNG favors you a Jack before that card is drawn randomly off the deck. So 9/10 times, this card's effect is never used.Another Example:A card that swaps your hand with the opponent's hand. Sounds nice, right? That could be helpful if the opponent has a winning hand, right? NOPE! Because RNG can play that card and its effect is INSTANTLY activated the moment it's drawn without giving you ANY choice in the matter so you'd end up swapping YOUR good winning hand with the opponent's losing hand which results in whatever diabolical strategy you attempted to create to be used against you which in a lot of cases the damage you've been building against your opponent gets used against you.Some cards are absolutely confusing you get. There's a card called Memory Card that memorizes a card to be played later. But... the game doesn't explain how to recall the memorized card. Another example of confusing thing is that some cards are automatically 'locked' when you play them (meaning they don't get discarded and remain in play until they are unlocked or discarded) but here's the silly thing: you need a card to be drawn to unlock them or you have to wait for the opponent to destroy it. So lets say you have a card's value at 14 and it's locked. 14 is a low number to STAY on so you decide to HIT and 9 TIMES OUT OF 10 you will always bust on the very next card. So RNG has handicapped you the entire round and your perk turns into your punishment.ALSO, if you're using a controller then most of the time you're trying to figure out at which angle do you need to move the left analog stick to select an certain option and a lot of times I just found myself reaching for the mouse because the game just doesn't understand what it is you are attempting to select with a controller.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Balatro! But with Blackjack instead of Poker!That sounds like an interesting idea at first glance, but the gameplay is painfully on rails. Unlike most other deck-builders, you have zero control over what gets played. And as the game goes on, you have the opportunity to get a card here and there, making small changes to an otherwise static deck. Meanwhile, after the first "bar," your opponents have increasingly custom-tuned gimmick decks with very specific win conditions... that they will definitely meet, unless you stop them. Except that your deck is probably not built to stop them.I'll check back after this has some updates, but a "Blackjack Slay the Spire" this is not. Save your money - there are better gambling-themed games out there.

_childDocuments_.review: I got quite excited when I saw this game. Will be a game to check out again in six months to if balance and bugs get polished out. As of now, I can't recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: At first I kind of thought this game is... not good. However, after few attempts I have realized that there is something here. There are various strategies that you begin to see.For example:- build your deck to "stall" long enough to see your opponent bust/stand,- get cards that discard/burn your opponent's cards,- fill your opponent's deck so they bust more easily.Cards can be exploited (clicked) for unique effects. Some go to your hand where you can exploit them later anytime. Cards can be exploited both from the hand and the table. Exploitation uses "advantage", the way you gain advantage differs each run based on the chip you get at the start (you can pick 1 of 3 random chips each run).Many cards have on play and/or on discard effects. Some trigger when drawn.You can view your opponent's deck anytime.Though there is still a lot of RNG here. Getting a blackjack is up to your luck, but it's not really necessary, as long as you get a tie or higher number, it's fine. Each suit of cards has an unique effect for blackjack though, for example: the heart deck heals you for the blackjack amount when you get, well, a blackjack.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Here's an edit I'm happy to make. They fixed the game! No, seriously, the update they did to balancing makes this so much more enjoyable to play (and really highlights how odd some of the initial balancing was) but its an absolute slam dunk and I can happily say this is worth your time with NO caveat. Rest of review remains unchanged.So I initially threw this a positive review with a promise to update, and here's the update. This is good, really good, actually. But it does definitely have some problems. You should buy this game and support it, because its already very fun, and with some balancing changes it'll easily be a classic. Lets start with the good before the bad. The aesthetic overall is fantastic, its grimy and gross and as you move through the zones the board you're playing on and the music you listen to reflects the area you're playing in very well. Also, references galore. There are so many subtle (and not so subtle) references to other popular media. It never feels like too much, but there was a lot of little "oh no way" moments I had. To touch on the music again briefly, I love it. There's a little trill or change in the music for some of the opponents you run up against (I love the tune swap when you face the bard) and its the kind of thing that you could leave on forever and not be bothered by. Its a bop, and thats a good thing. Now the bad.I think if I had to pin down the main issue, it really feels like the game ramps up the people you're playing against much quicker than you can ramp yourself up to a "build". Blackjack is a game of playing the odds and chance moreso than poker, but by the end of the *first* floor (of five) you are already encountering people with like 5 cards in their deck and a specific playstyle you have to beat. That's fine, but by that point for you, you still most likely have almost all of the cards you started with plus a few more you picked up after wins. The opportunities to trim or focus your deck are few and far between and really expensive. I actually don't have a problem with the opponents, they are all clever fights and demand that you actually counter their mechanics, but I do think that the player's ability to fight those mechanics can be really difficult to manifest. The 4 starting decks all don't feel fantastic to use because they only activate powers if you deal damage at Blackjack (meaning if you hit 20 and win the head to head, no deck powers. Has to be 21 and cant be a tie of 21). There's also way too few options or opportunities to heal, and what is there costs too much. I'm not saying make the game easier, but at least give the player the tools to forge their way to victory. At the moment it really does feel like random chance on the players part if they end up winning or not, which is part of blackjack, sure, but if I get a 21 and stand and then the AI steals my ace... well thats not chance anymore is it?I love what is here, genuinely, but the balancing isn't quite right as of right now. I would recommend you wishlist this at the very least and keep an eye out for a big balancing update. This is good as is, but it could very well be great with some tweaks.

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah its more fun than balatro.i mean it feels silly to compare it to that but ever since balatro came out there's been this frenzy of poker roguelikes so yeah. and this is a pretty good one. to be honest a lot deeper and more complex than balatro, and more atmospheric.a big plus is that it never really feels like you are guaranteed to lose. there's almost always a chance you draw just the right cards or your opponent busts and you come out on top, not matter how low your life is. _childDocuments_.review: This game shows promise, but several design flaws hold it back from being enjoyable in its current state.Firstly, the lack of randomization severely limits replayability. Enemy and boss encounters are static, with the same enemies appearing in the same locations every playthrough. This directly contradicts the core principle of roguelikes. For instance, encountering  downstairs every single run eliminates any sense of surprise or need to adapt.Secondly, resource management feels restrictive and hinders build diversity. While many builds seem viable in theory, the scarcity of resources renders them unattainable. Successful roguelikes often allow players to manipulate game mechanics for near-infinite resources, enabling "god runs" and rewarding creative strategies. This game's limited resources and underwhelming opponents prevents such experimentation and powerful builds from happening.This game has the potential to be enjoyable, but until these issues are addressed, I cannot recommend it in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: There's little to no strategy in the deck-building. There is little variance in-between the decks as their main effects only happen if you manage to get a blackjack. The "wacky cards" are almost always aren't helpful as they don't synergy at all with whatever build you expect to run.Want to run a build about using advantage? NOPE! Here's cards that literally cripple your deck if you use your advantage points.  It feels like later during your runs, you don't actually know how to win with your deck as the strategy of winning changes drastically due to whatever effects your enemies throw at you. You try to little down your deck and try to get a blackjack with 2 cards? WRONG! The opponent just decided to steal your only winning card. Oh and don't even think about thinning the deck by removing cards, because most of the runs you'd be facing, you never get that opportunity.I do not recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll give it a recommend because I want to support Indie creators, however I doubt I will replay this a lot unless substantial updates come. First of all if you want to buy this because you like Balatro: this game has nothing to do with Balatro. The joy in Balatro comes from "seeing the number go up" and getting progressively more insane combo's to see the number go up. Whereas this game is more about defeating bosses. At least I think so because I honestly don't really know. In my opinion it lacks depth in both the deckbuilding aspect, and in the "writing" of the bosses. The bosses and opponents should have had more themed decks and some more flair in how they engage with you, if that's what the developer was aiming for. The cards and decks are not interesting enough to really get into them and several aspects are either missing or I'm too dumb to have noticed them. Card rarities would have been nice, so you have an indication as to whether "this is something you might want to try and build around". Also, runs are too short I feel to really build a deck. It's more: take stuff that you think kind of works and try to cut out the 6 and 5 from your deck. By the time you feel your deck is halfway decent you're at the final boss. When you start the game you have absolutely no clue what your opponent is doing, there's no "slow mode" that shows you exactly what is happening. You can obviously take the time to read every card in their deck, but even then: there's some keywords and mechanics that are explained, but often not really adequately, so you still don't really know what's going to happen/what's happening. I'm pretty disappointed because I really wanted to like this game, but like I stated at the start: unless a lot is added I won't be. I've beaten the game twice and I'm already not interested to boot it up anymore. On the other hand it's cheap and the developer clearly has love for their game and video games in general, so if you want to support someone who deserves it definitely buy, you'll get a few hours of fun out of it at least. Very last point of criticism: this is very personal, but I'm kind of sick of the whole "let's make our games look like it's 1974"-vibe. I'm not a graphics-dude AT ALL, but being able to read the text on the screen without hurting your brain is nice, and what's the point to the avatar you can mess around with on the top left corner, if it's just adding some random pixels that are supposed to represent a hat or a haircut? You could have spent that time writing some funny dialogue for a boss or, I don't know, developing another card. I'm sorry if this is very negative, I really had high hopes for this and imo it just failed to deliver.

_childDocuments_.review: While I admit I expected a more Balatro-like experience, I have to say that even trying to hamper my expectations and thinking "not every gambling deck-builder is a roguelike", I still feel intensely disappointed. In short, I feel like this game lacks in everything it promises and that I expected from it: the roguelike aspects are hampered by the lack of meaningful unlocks, the deckbuilding is lackluster at best and downright useless at worst due to the absence of any outside influences on the deck, and the core mechanics turn blackjack from a quick little gambling game into a luck-based not-really-strategic slog against opponents that are at a fundamental advantage against you, both due to the strength of their decks, but also due to them having access to gimmicks the game pretty much doesn't allow you to have.I just think the game fails at almost everything it tries. Clearly monumental love and effort has been put into designing the pretty fun minigames, into designing the characters and the excellent soundtrack, the cards and NPCs... but it all falls short due to fundamental failures it has mechanically. There isn't much to strive for or play with, besides just clicking hit, and not only praying that you don't bust but also that your opponent doesn't play some card that triggers a condition that instantly kills your family dog. It just is not satisfying.In long:I do not have a problem with the luck-reliance or randomness aspect of blackjack, but I feel two things really made me just not want to play this game: the fact that this game doesn't feel as satisfying due to how it treats blackjack, and the lackluster "deckbuilding".On the satisfaction of playing blackjack, I feel like this game failed to deliver (perhaps only to me) by really heavily amplifying it's extremes. Unless your opponent busts, the damage you deal (unless they score very minimally) is going to be lackluster, but if they do, it might win the match instantly. Also, none of the suit bonuses activate unless you actually hit blackjack. I feel like it feels unrewarding to play unless you get a 21 (and then only situationally) or your opponent busts: I've had rounds drag on and on and on for what felt like ages because I kept outscoring my opponent (or the opponent kept outscoring me) by 1 or 2, and we kept gaining shields or regaining health from the occasional 21s that popped up, only enhancing the torture, to the point where I just up and closed the run to start a new one. However, even this is only a relatively minor gripe, and my issues with the game reach far deeper.The deckbuilding isn't satisfying. You just get one card to add to your standard deck after every encounter beaten, with the occasional shops mixed in, as well as minigame events (which are usually glorified shops anyways, not that there's anything wrong with that). It doesn't feel like anything you play changes anything at all, though, since (at least with the standard decks I've tried) you just don't get the ability to alter your playstyle. There's no meaningful upgrades to the cards, there's no meaningful changes to how a deck is played depending on external factors like Balatro's jokers or Slay The Spire's relics, in fact there's not even an equivalent for them. It genuinely feels super dull, like a contest of hitting or standing depending on the number, and also praying, while seeing your AI opponent play a genuinely interesting gimmick deck.The closest comparison I can make, knowing most people come here from Balatro's sphere of influence (myself included) is... imagine if, after beating a blind, instead of a shop you add one playing card to your deck, and nothing else. That is genuinely what it felt like playing, and I hate it.Don't get me wrong, the interplay between cards is there for sure, as evidenced with one enemy on one of the last floors I was quite impressed by, who had the gimmick of constantly playing a card that ties whatever you have, and a different card that deals damage to you when you've tied; or the Wizard that plays 1s and adds more and more 1s to his deck until he just gets a guaranteed 21 so you have to rush through him before you just bleed out. However, these are all just NPC decks, and you only get to unlock them (and mind you, you get pre-built versions of them, instead of them being some kind of build you can go for) after beating the game many times over. It feels impossible to get that one King that turns to an instant blackjack if you have no other faces, because the cards that sound like they could have interplay with it (like a different King that burns all other face cards) don't play together, they actively ♥♥♥♥ gimmicks over. It really feels like you're at a disadvantage both mechanically and fun-wise, since you have to probably be dipped in the river Styx to actually get a gimmick deck working. The part I mentioned about this not being a good Roguelike in my eyes is the unlocks. Every other Roguelike I've played or seen being played and have been captivated by is always the quirky achievements that let you play the game in new ways. For an expected example, it's a new deck or joker in Balatro, new cards and characters in Slay The Spire, new items and characters in Isaac, new characters and pathways in Tiny Rogues, etc etc. They keep you playing, keep you engaged, and once you got them, you're there to try a new playstyle and get a new outcome with them, only to have the cycle repeat. This variety is, in my opinion, is what gives Roguelikes their amazing replayability. Here, your reward for the incredibly luck-based and honestly grueling challenge of beating the game for the first time is... a deck filled with card that do nothing. That's honestly baffling to me: the reward for actually completing the full challenge set before you is a downgrade from everything you've had before. And I feel like that mentality follows through to the rest of the game too, because besides lackluster new decks (like just 2 starter decks mashed together, or two other starter decks mashed together, or random cards...), there's... no unlocks. No new special cards or gimmicks to orient your deck around, no alternatives to anything. This isn't just because most of those things are unlocked by default, but also because there is simply nothing meaningful to begin with. In other Roguelikes, getting an item can shift, curve or instantly flip the direction of your build. Here, this is not the case.I mean absolutely no offense to the solo dev of this project, who as I stated must have put tremendous love and effort into this. But I also think the issues with the game run incredibly deep. Take everything I said with a grain of salt, but I simply do not enjoy this game, and I would not recommend it.
