_childDocuments_.review: The game has serious potential, but it is balanced so poorly that it makes me question the design ideas behind it.As the easiest example, you boot up the game, you begin your first run. You are matched against the bartender. Cool, this is a tutorial enemy! He's only got 5 health. he pulls a 10. You hit, you get a 6. He hits, and pulls an ace. Ouch, bartender blackjack is rough. You can now hit without much worry about busting, you do, you get a 9 and you're at 15. If you stand, you take 6 damage. If you hit, you might bust and take 21 damage because the bartender's blackjack will not be blocked by your 15.The next hand rolls around, your bartender got 19. then he gets 20. then he gets 17, stands, and you hit him with a 21. he's now at 1 health, but you are at best in the 80s. This was the tutorial enemy.This is a game where it is extremely easy to get bad RNG and die before ever meeting the first boss.Why do i say that this makes me question the design rather than just saying "game hard, git gud?"Because there's no player interaction with this extreme RNG slugfest. I've had HP in the 63/100 range coming out of the tutorial bartender fight, on the lowest run difficulty. I could not choose cards, I could not build my deck, I could only have played strictly to mitigate damage and not hit above 13, but that would only have saved me a bit of health.One of the game's first major updates was an adjustment of the difficulty. This definitely means that the devs are listening. Unfortunately, the change that is needed is more of an overhaul than a balance adjustment. Compare to a solid analogue like slay the spire, where even on a high difficulty you have real choices about the path that you take from screen 1, advantages built into your choice of class, and the game opens with the option to change your build in serious and meaningful ways (unless you've just lost, when it offers you a strong catchup mechanic!)Or take the comparison with Balatro, where the first few rounds are easily and smoothly winnable with a single hand, often without a discard. The game allows you to see a shop, get jokers, and start working towards a build in an early ante before the difficulty ramps.A balance adjustment will not provide the kind of change to give the player any kind of meaningful engagement with the very early game, and this sets the tone for the entire run. The game is currently in a very playable state, and has a lot of potential. It's just not good enough to be worth sinking in the time, not in its current state.

_childDocuments_.review: Criminally underrated game. As a "rogue-like deckbuilder" it is interesting and unique with extensive content and character to make it a worthwhile experience regardless of your experience with the genre. There's an impressive amount of depth in the decision-making during every part of the game, with chance being a surprisingly minor factor for the most part (aside from a few pain points, like certain overpowered cards). To compare this game to Balatro (which was conceived after this one) would be doing it a disservice, though unfortunately it is a relevant comparison: D&DG unlike Balatro is a highly dynamic game, with buildcrafting and gameplay being engaging and demanding. The cards themselves encourage more active participation in the games systems, and are consistent in their adherence to a style of theming and direction that provides for a strong identity in the game. Beyond that, the enemy, world, music, and art design are quite strong and make for a game that's enjoyable even just for navigation of its setting. That said, the content in this game is designed to played in a more arcade-y style than similar games that encourage completionism and long-term time investments. You can try to play this game to 100% collections, but it isn't built for it. If that sounds fine to you, then I highly recommend D&DG.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of people see a deckbuilding game based on an actual card game that uses goofy variations on cards right now and think "oh, that's like Balatro"... In fact in writing that I am perpetuating the issue so let's just get this out of the way first: if you're looking for Balatro and that crazy thrill of card combos leading to insane high scores as the dopamine floods your brain... This is not that! It's its own thing and I'd say it's all the better for it.So what this is is blackjack, draw cards, try and get a score 21 and not over, but instead of money being your driving goal, instead you are always playing blackjack against someone and are trying to build decks to be stronger, more adaptive, reactive, and to completely mess with your opponent's play. Like blackjack luck is a huge factor and (thanks to being able to see what's left of your own deck at any time) so is educated gambling through card counting. And that luck factor is something you cannot escape; you can do a lot to reduce it and recent updates have helped massively in giving you power over your own deck but that aspect of gambling is built into the design itself, it's a game about taking risks, the thrill of a great plan and deck paying off, and the pain of losing everything to that 1 card you didn't want to see. If you prefer chance to be a less prominent factor in your game then this game is not for you.But say you're still reading this and think that you don't mind that thrill of chance at all, then what you got here is a great game that has a surprising amount of personality for as simple as it looks. your opponents are just 2 text lines, a portrait, a deck, and a value that they'll hold on, but through that the game gives them a surprising amount of character. When an opponent holds and how their deck interacts with that can lead to some interesting strategy but also just gives these people personalities that are fun to see. Stuff like how the wizard's deck starts as nothing but grows and grown, how a knight prioritises defense, or even just the comedy of a dog that has a deck consisting mostly of 2s, while also standing on a 2, it's silly, it's funny, and it's incredibly charming; especially with these characters all adding their own little sounds to the backing soundtrack that makes them even more distinct in their own little ways. These are seemingly little things but they're appreciated, they didn't have to be there but the game is so much better and more charming for it and is something that does a great job of separating it from the dry exercise of "just blackjack but roguelike" that this could've become.So yeah, it's a great little game that has been paired with many a long-form video recently and has been wonderful to have, I really recommend it (unless you happen to be my friend who was a blackjack dealer for many years and, because of the rigid way casino dealers are made to play blackjack, finds this game weirdly infuriating for breaking literal years of forced habit xD)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game concept let down by the core design not taking enough risks, which feels like a crazy thing to say for a Blackjack game where you can play a Charizard card. The basic decks are boring, highly limited by doing nothing whatsoever unless you pull a 21, offer no alternative win conditions (Balatro manages this because it has a bunch of other hands which score points and can win you matches in different ways) than "Score 20/21/22 and hope your enemy only ever busts" and offering little to no synergy with the Advantage chips and the more creative cards you can purchase and receive as rewards. And of course, as always with non-Slay the Spire deckbuilders, there's too few nodes that let you remove cards, leaving you stuck with a bloated deck of cards with awful values that make it harder for you to reach 20/21/22 (depending on if you modify your hand value cap). Moreover, if you ever do manage to remove a single card from your deck, good luck winning with that card's "pair" (6 and 5, 8 and 3, etc.) gone when you want to reach 21.Overall, I really like the concept, and I even really like a lot of the execution. I would really love to love this game because it is right on the cusp of actually being a rewarding partner to Balatro's earlier success. However, as it stands now, I do not plan to play the game any further until the core decks, advantage chips, and gameplay loop receive serious top to bottom reworks and cannot recommend it to anybody expecting anything more than about thirty minutes of going "Haha, that card doesn't belong in Blackjack! Funny!"

_childDocuments_.review: I remember liking an earlier demo version, but I can't say I enjoy this game right now. Roguelikes are one of my favourite genres and I like a healthy dose of RNG. Unfortunately, this game largely lacks meaningful player agency.You are at the mercy of the order in which you draw the cards, which would be fine if you had any reasonable tools to mitigate bad luck. Special cards with effects can manipulate your cards, your opponent's cards, the cards you draw, etc. But then you have to actually draw those cards, and often times you need to combo multiple cards to trigger any sort of  impactful effect. This furthers the reliance on RNG giving you the cards you want to perform the special card effects that separate this game from normal blackjack.The game also has a mechanic called Advantage that allows you to spend it after generating it via a few means to "exploit"  cards, triggering their effect, as well as to play cards from hand. However cards only go into hand if they have the "handy" keyword or through the effect of another card. Playing cards from hand feels like it is supposed to get you out of a tough spot by playing your "ace in the hole" so to speak. However, since it requires generating advantage to do so, you can easily end up in a situation where you need the ace in the hole but don't have the advantage to use it. What this game truly suffers from is the culmination of all these different RNG mechanics that could potentially be fine if not for the fact that there are so many of them that you need to rely on. Needing to have the "handy" keyword to put something in hand to use at a later time. Then needing advantage to play it from hand. The individual card effect not being that powerful so it needs to be played with another card that you have to draw. Needing to actually be offered those cards in a shop or from rewards to begin with. It was all just extremely unsatisfying to me when the few times I was offered cards that I felt like could work in my deck, that the draw order or other cards in play didn't allow me to make use of them.The cherry on top is that you might have to slog through combat if the game didn't see fit to give you effective cards or just not in the right order. Damage is dealt through the difference between you and the opponent's scores, with going over 21 (in most cases) making your score zero. You can have round after round of chipping away at each other. Sweet! You got 21. But your opponent got 19, so that's 2 points of their 50+ health gone.It feels like the problems with this game are inherent to the limitations of blackjack, as the attempts to change the formula outside of the zany cards fail to make your actions feel meaningful and therefore, worthwhile.

_childDocuments_.review: This concept feels like it has alot of potential, but unfortunately it does not seem like the potential was used wellThe core mechanics are very simple (I mean its literally blackjack) and the extra mechanics (mainly cards with special effects) and each suit having a different effect on playing a perfect 21 are a nice addition; While still keeping the mechanics simple and easy to grasp. The effects of the games cards are however not interacting well with each other, alot of the cards I thought would be fun, seemed hard to fit into a deck. And it feels like the deckbuilding is so much more RNG based in the first half (?) than it should be. Only with luck in events and pulling cards did it feel like I could actually starting building up my deck somewhat.However thats not the main problem, the main problem is the enemy design: They might just be basically perfectly immune to whatever deck you are building or have some crazy synergy immediately beating you into the ground. I assume after playing the game alot it would be possible to figure out how to build your deck, to make sure that cant happen - but thats not a way of progression I could recommend. You should have a fair chance from the getgo. Additionally they seem to always have the same deck, which would probably make this game feel boring and repetitive quite fast. (Especially if you have to replay the beginning cz a enemy youve never seen before just has a perfect counter to you) Also bonus (Might be how I played, instead of a issue with the game itself):The fights (atleast with the way I built one of my decks) can drag on. The fight against "Celubutante" was her pulling a 20 every single round. My deck at that point was good enough to get 20 or 21 every round...but so I needed to use my 1/3 chance for the 21 to win the fight slowly but painfully (As it was literally not possible for me to lose) - The fight has a mechanic which makes her easily beatable...but I wasnt able to use that with the deckTl;DR: Good concept, lotsa potential - but needs polishing before I can recommend it; Once its polished I think it will be a very good game

Game is fun but want to be a Balatro-like, but here it's 99.9999999% pure random (and the odds are so stupidly in your opponent favor that's just ridiculous).9/10 times when you have a card that do something like burning an opponent card and so on, it'll be the first card drawn so it will have no effect. _childDocuments_.review: I feel like Balatro will be seen as a blessing and a curse in the coming years.  Just like we see every year with the plentiful seasons of offspring of “Soulslike” games birthed from Dark Souls and Bloodborne, and the many roguelike card-builders spawned from titles like Slay the Spire, we will eventually see the increased traffic of “Deck of Card games with many twists in them to make them something completely different” games to hit the market.  Some will be good.  Some will be bad.Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers takes a lot of what makes Balatro such a tantalizing piece of gaming and combines the storytelling of Dungeons & Dragons with the money-sucking casino game, Blackjack.  You walk into a seedy tavern with a deck of cards and your wits and your task of discovering who runs the seedy and shady casino is masked by a litany of patrons to combat against and several floors to traverse.  What starts as a small deck of numbers and face cards soon evolves into a cavalcade of boosts and rule changers as you dip and dive through the house-of-mirrors' worth of encounters.  But if you bust your HP: you’re out.  And back to the bartender with you.Your starting deck means a lot to how you start your run, as each suit provides a different buff when you hit a blackjack: hearts heal, diamonds cash out, clubs shield, and spades hit harder.  Whether you want to play a more defensive and reactive build or a more forward, hard hitting style, the options are there for you.  You start with 100HP and a couple chips in your pocket, used primarily for acquiring new cards, playing minigames, or spending on certain abilities.  After a friendly spar with the Bartender, you’re shown after each victory you’re awarded a choice of one of four cards, the fourth requiring you to pay chips to see.  This is the start of where you can acquire one of the over 300 cards to unlock throughout the game.The range of cause and effect on these cards is an immense undertaking where if you think of something whimsical and ridiculous to do with a blackjack hand, there’s a good chance the card exists in its portfolio.  Most cards will be activated on different set situations, aptly colored in red and politely given a definition at each notice, but almost always needed a commonly used D&D term: Advantage.  Advantage is a finite resource that allows you to do a multitude of things to gain the edge against your opponent, such as playing cards from your ability-made hand or activating secondary buffs and debuffs on your cards.  Advantage is gathered through one of three random passive buffs of your choosing provided at the start of your run, and it would be wise to work your deck into making as much Advantage as possible because you’re going to need it.When engaged in combat, your goal is to hit 21 for a blackjack or get as close as you can as it is the same for your opponent.  You will Hit to add more cards and Stand to end your turn, with you and your opponent taking turns adding cards to your hand until both have stood or busted by going over 21.  Whoever has the highest number at the end of the hand will take the difference between the two hands and deliver that amount in damage: rinse and repeat until you have a winner.  Hitting a blackjack will not only provide the most amount of damage, but will activate the suits on the cards used in your hand allowing for any of the four buffs to proc, giving you life, shields, cash, or damage.  If you’ve ever played blackjack before, you know that it’s like that one Fort Manor song but instead it’s 80% luck, 10% skill, 10% concentrated power of will.  D&DG does little to this formula because you will live and die, a lot, on your ability to hit 21.  It’s how you heal, how you crush opponents, how you mitigate damage, and how you cash out for better things.There are several stages on each floor for you to build your deck out with battles, but there are optional events that can happen in place of a good ol’ fashioned throwdown.  Pay some chips to take a nap and restore some HP, play roulette to change the number value of cards in your deck, rob a sleeping man, pay taxes, channel your inner Shawshank Redemption, the list goes on.  Each game has the ability to provide you with extra cards or set you up for success for your next fight, but some can also financially ruin you or dwindle your HP or burn cards in your deck, the only way to know is to go into the event and coin flip some trial and error: a recurring theme within this casino.While your HP is higher than almost any opponent you face, your HP does not regain after a fight, so you will have to pick the right events or work your deck to gain more HP while you fight or use cards that provide shields to mitigate damage as it happens.  But get ready to be peppered with some tailor-made shenanigans when you see what the CPU can accomplish most of the time, because your opponent’s hit 21 a lot.  There’s no shame in losing a hand, so smart play is rewarded with small losses instead of big chunks if you bust.  You will have to play steady and not be reckless or the game will punish you for it.The issue with each of the 60 characters, all come with specific decks they’ll use to put you in the dirt but the later game foes have truly evil setups that are flat not fun to fight.  Each enemy will have a glaring weakness within their deck for you to find, which can be a fun test to see how you can handle the deck in front of you, but certain decks require certain cards to exploit that weakness, and if you don’t have that card there’s a very very low percentage chance you’re going to win.To go full circle, Balatro avoids the problem of “randomized instant death” by giving you two opportunities, the Small and Big Blind rounds, to cycle the shop and give yourself a fighting chance to overcome the obstacle in front of you.  D&DG does provide two choices per floor, minus boss encounters, but no way to see what is ahead so if both the choices are two enemies you don’t have the cards to fight against: you lose and there’s no going back.  Nothing is more debilitating for a game than to provide the enjoyment of the fruits of your labor only to lose to something you can’t control.And this feeling will follow you throughout your playthroughs.  There are plenty of times where I misplayed a hand and put myself in a scenario to lose, or I didn’t clock my Advantage correctly and didn’t take the shot when I should have, but it’s mirrored by your opponent tossing out 21s like they’re fun coupons or you run into a foe who’s deck is so blatantly powerful it’s clear you’re headed for a restart because you didn’t grab that one card 3 floors and 15 fights ago.  D&DG revels in the fact that you will go on losing streaks so you can unlock more of what is to offer but where games like Dark Souls or Lies of P counterbalance these losses with taking what you’ve learned and using it for the next fight, you’ll leave most losses just hoping the next time they don’t get the House Luck as much as they did this time.Which is a real shame, because the labor of love to provide a near infinite amount of deck combinations, the instilled humor of the characters and situations the D&D style setting travels you through, and the pure card-comboing shenanigans that you can pump out within a run is fascinating and can be really fun when it clicks.  But there is, and I shouldn’t really be surprised in this, a frustrating amount of luck involved with having a good time, and no game’s final outcome should have you winning but feeling like a loser.Aw, dang it.

_childDocuments_.review: Many reviewers are focusing on the state of the gameplay but I only want to highlight one thing: This game has no Borderless Fullscreen option. This wouldn't be a massive issue if it weren't for the fact that the game crashes when entering fullscreen. Not for everyone, but for me, and for many other players who started/replied to threads about this issue. I bought this game on launch and haven't been able to play it once. I tried everything. Updated drivers, edited the user settings file, restarted my PC, launched the game at the native resolution of my display, tried it on a TV and a monitor. I made a thread in the forum, waited, bumped it, waited. Nothing so far. I haven't had this issue with other, far more system-intensive games. I'd recommend avoiding this game for a while and maybe checking back in a couple of months, especially given the other reviews re: player agency and decision-making within the game's systems; and the news that the devs are going to try and address these problems. Proceed at your own peril until then.August 19th Edit: The beta update didn't fix this, but if you have this fullscreen issue, try this, it worked for me (with an AMD graphics card):Open your AMD Adrenaline software, navigate to the Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers entry in the Games section, go to Graphics, Radeon Super Resolution, change from Enabled to Enabled (Borderless Fullscreen) and the game should launch. Hope this helps someone. Now that I can actually play the game I'll update my review with thoughts later.

_childDocuments_.review: Honesty I really want to like this game. I've been through the gauntlet a bunch of times now and its very apparent that there is one successful way to play this game. It however is not a git gud game, due to the heavy reliability on RNG mechanics for YOUR random deck. The opponents decks are all catered to synergize together and work incredibly well against you. You will have an incredible run only to be met by a hard counter to what you were able to throw together throughout play. Losing does not feel like a step forward for next time it feels incredibly cheap and will eventually show you the only way to build a deck to win the whole game. If this is a deck building game with multiple choices on how to play, then why is there really only one way to succeed. This game has a great potential to be really good and I have had fun playing it but overall I will be waiting for some game play changes or balances. I cannot recommend the game in its current state. I think if the developers added options to the game to create a balanced game then I will happily continue to play. (such as removing healing factor for enemies)

_childDocuments_.review: It looked really good at first blush and the first few runs I was riding the high of the excitement of discovery. I started to see interesting and fun cards that I was looking forward to collecting and forming into some sort of strategy.Unfortunately it's ultimately just too chaotic for strategy most of the time. It's mostly a 'fair' sort of chaos in that sometimes it works with you, and sometimes against you-- but when it helps you, wins often feel 'unearned' and when it hinders you it feels punishing. But also part of that chaos is whether or not you even get the opportunity to build a plan depending on event and card choice. Some small QoL considerations could also help-- since you're allowed to view what is in your draw pile at any time (just not the order) it could be helpful to have some sort of ratio display that tells you without having to count how many cards left in the deck can bust you for when you feel you have to push your luck (but really this feels nearly always a poor decision since it is often the difference between taking a couple of points of damage versus taking 10-20+).If you're fine with your luck being served with a side of luck, this game may still appeal to you. But for me, I think I'm done with this until some balance and gameplay revisions happen.

If you were hoping for a game where your decisions matter, look elsewhere.

This game revolves around, a lot of RNG and the balancing is also not that very good, the game is fun but it can be frustrating sometimes because of the RNG, for example your opponent gets a blackjack 3 times in a row, while you get a 20 or just barely a blackjack yourself. You also need to have good cards or else, your run is dead, same as the advantages. 1 opponent copy's your deck, while the other switches their cards with yours, while you cant do anything about it, so you lose.... the game is not bad, but it just needs a couple more updates, for the balancing, cards, etc. I personally would wait until 2.0 drops, then the game will be ready. With balatro for a example, you may have bad cards but the jokers will save you, also other way around, sure you might have some bad runs, but you almost always have a chance of winning, but with Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers, you don't really have a chance, also when you are low and don't have a chance of healing whats so ever, your most likely dead. _childDocuments_.review: I loved the game system... BUT: Not the Luck sistems... and absence of RNG...There are few events in each level, and they are not very varied. If you are lucky, some are good, but others break the game.For example, the SUN card. There is an enemy that as soon as you draw 4 cards, he has a 21 card that he draws every turn. And it is not the only card that the enemies have synergy with... for the worse.Not to mention that if you do not have a heart deck, healing yourself is quite difficult, and some tokens that give you "Advantage" points are also useless. There is no progression whatsoever, and repeating scenarios only serves to hit a wall.Anyway. I like the game, but it is VERY GREEN, still... it needs to improve a lot, and balance many things. At this point, for now it is only unfair and insufferable, and does not reward you with anything for advancing in it.The problem is that it's not an early access game, it's a full game. And it seems that it still needs a complete overhaul of the systems.

_childDocuments_.review: Once again, steam REALLY needs to change their review system from just "Yes/no".Like Balatro, Like Slay the Spire, or really any non-action roguelike, loss is just a bad RNG seed away, even with optimal play.However, unlike Slay the Spire which can take ages and the issue comes from what enemies you encounter along the way, DnDG is more like Balatro, where the player may or may not find what they need. There's a lot of useless/filler cards here, or cards that only work in specific settings or with specific deck types. There's no way to guide yourself into a build, instead you have to hope you happen UPON the build starting off early, then move forward from there.Resetting on the first floor is not uncommon, and losing dozens of times despite playing optimally because the game simply doesn't start you off with a lot that could really be used to make a build. Compared to what your enemies start with, your deck is INCREDIBLY limited until you get a few stages in. For example, try playing with an "Honest" deck and go to the sewers. Unless luck is on your side in a BIG way, the first encounter will likely eat 50+ HP, even with a healing/shields deck.It mostly comes down to "Do you mind winning being up to luck in a card game."If you're used to real blackjack, you'll understand that even the best card counters can't force the order to be perfect for their needs every time. That's the nature of cards.But to some people, it's going to be amazingly frustrating as you throw yourself at a wall over and over until something sticks or you unlock something you can build off of to make a consistent gameplan.That's just how the cookie crumbles, but if you're used to roguelikes being reliant on skill, you'll be a bit let down.I enjoy a bit of luck sometimes, so it works for me. I wouldn't say it's the kind of game you sit down with the intent to beat, but rather you sit down to screw around and end up at the final boss by accident. It's a happy little accident, but it's not ever something you shoot for.

There's not really any passives and you just hope that if you pull an illegal card, it's good for that specific hand. As a result, the illegal cards themselves feel non-material since you can't cater a deck around them. I eventually felt that I didn't need to add any cards, and I would just hit until I'm either past the dealer's hard hit, or felt I could get a blackjack. The only strategy I implemented was reduce the value of my cards and remove cards until it was more probable the next card i had wouldn't have me go over.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played over 180 hours of Balatro and about 6 or 7 hours of this so far. While it's certainly playable, it's very far from equal to Balatro. I was kind of hoping for something that would scratch the same itch but in a slightly different format; unfortunately the format is too different, and Blackjack just seems too random and unpredictable compared to Poker (which is exacerbated by the fact that you're effectively 'playing against' other characters, and their cards also trigger special - and unpredictable - effects). In particular, standing before your opponent and then being literally unable to do anything to respond when they play a few more cards that mess with your played cards or your score limit (e.g. turning your blackjack into a bust) is pretty frustrating; a general rule of game design is that being stuck in a situation where you are just watching someone else play the game and can do nothing to influence it doesn't make for a great experience, particularly if what they do makes the difference between you winning and losing and it feels largely random, etc.Not only that but the progression is more like Slay the Spire with different 'random events' coming up rather than having a shop, and you're not really able to 'keep digging' to find what you need in many of these random events (as opposed to the way that you can reroll in the Balatro shop in hopes of getting better options). It also really needs some QOL features added: e.g. when I'm faced with adding cards to my deck, it would be handy if there was an obvious indicator of which cards are not yet in my collection. It's certainly a playable game, and entertaining for a few hours, but I'm not sure whether I'll end up much longer, and I'm certainly finding it more frustrating than some of the other games I've played recently.

_childDocuments_.review: After having played the game for ten hours and only recently winning a run I have to say that there are two issues I have with the game: First, it doesn't really feel like a blackjack game. Sure, you typically have to hit 21 without going over, but the core issue is that barring some special cards, there is little agency to do with your opponent. Second, I feel the blackjack mechanic should probably be extended a little as it seems a bit limiting especially if you become 'set' to 20 max and lose your blackjack possibility. However, that aside, the game IS fun, but I would recommend all players learn about ALL the mechanics before heading into a game. A BIG MECHANIC that isn't thoroughly explained is that the randomness is CONSISTENT randomness. This makes the "Save and Quit" option a KEY MECHANIC to winning a round. Effectively, Save and Quit RESTARTS the round against a player allowing you to make different decisions against a consistent AI. Another key mechanic is learning which events heal you and which encounters damage you. Health is a resource, but the main issue I have is that HEALING is very limited unless you traipse around encounters like the Cultist or Marketing. This can make forced encounters like the Cardian Angel feel like an instant loss because you don't have enough health to handle its gimmick. The final mechanic is deck reliability. As said previously, the randomness is CONSISTENT randomness, not just for AI decisions, but your own deck and draw order. Unlike Slay the Spire or Balatro, smaller decks have a CONSIDERABLY higher potential than bloated decks. Additionally, I would highly recommend getting rid of your standard number cards from 2-9 as soon as possible allowing you better consistency for draws and wins. This game effectively forces card counting and manipulation and leaving it to luck rarely works. For beginners I would recommend the Basement route first only because the Cardian Angel and the Deity of Hope can feel debilitating to lose a run against. However, this only means that if you go for the 'Heaven' route, you should build your deck around these encounters focusing on deck flexibility and health gain.One final issue I have is the encounters, they will get very repetitive as there really isn't much variety yet and the event encounters are currently locked per floor. However, if you can look past that, the game is pretty fun and requires much more thinking and time efficiency than other card games. I would not recommend this game to casual players or even blackjack players, but if you are looking for a challenging card game, give it shot.

_childDocuments_.review: Pro: It's a creative game, with a lot of satisfying strategies to discover and use.  Addicting and interesting.  I love it.Con: Roguelikes add an element of chance onto a different core game type. Like platforming or dungeon crawling.  This game adds an element of chance onto... a game of chance. Chance X2. Chance squared.  Don't get me wrong, strategy is your friend here, you can sometimes just cheese your way to victory, and random chance can fall in your favor.  But sometimes you just won't get the pulls you need for your deck to survive a run.  Sometimes your enemy with a gimmick deck based around cards that have random values on play or exploit will just get 40 blackjacks in a single game, and 10 of those will be retroactive blackjacks after they've already busted. It doesn't happen a lot, and the more you play the more resourceful you learn to get with your pulls, but if you can't handle the occasional "Rocks Fall, Everyone Dies," then you probably won't like this game.Tip:  Hope is easier than Despair.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 gameAfter playing this game for 25 hours I have learned quite a lot, from which cards are aggressive, defensive, passive or sabotage-esque, to how to properly manage and maintain your deck, checking on what is in draw and discard, and even which cards are more valuable to your play style.This game has a learning curve, and in the beginning you will likely fail even though you think you have a good deck, but taking the time to get used to cards and decks helps you realize that though this game is about "gambling", it also requires a lot of planning and playing.Overall I find this game to be not only fun, but a good challenge for balancing your play style with different decks and cards.

_childDocuments_.review: Luck is an sob at the very start of runs. But it lessens by stacking the deck appropriately and understanding the fights and events. It's a deck builder, after all. Past the basics, there are some very broken synergies that trivialize fights. And that's where the fun and replay value are, imo.Other than that, more cards would be nice. Blackjacks and not busting are really valuable, and the card set seems to have a few BJ math/number schemes that shouldn't be intermixed very often. So, winning means limiting your card picks to those math/number regimes. It isn't a deal breaker, tho, and it's still a fun game for card players.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic addition to the Roguelike Deckbuilder genre! I love blackjack, and this gives me all the thrills without any of the chills of not being able to pay rent (though it is hard to stop playing and go to my job).Important to Know: There are TONS of cards to add to your deck, and it will take a while to understand what they do and what your opponents do. There is definite potential to build synergistic, powerful decks that will see you sail through the game, feeling like a gambling god, but with diverse enough enemies that you can still get hoisted by your own strategy if you're not careful (cries in Pit Boss hitting me for 1,000+ damage). That said, it will take time to settle in to what works and what doesn't.Two critiques:One, there are a fair number of different decks you go against, but once you've seen them all you've seen them all. After 16 hours I don't really expect any surprises from the run anymore, it's all about exploring new ways to solve old puzzles and experiencing the thrill of pushing your luck (or not if you build a good deck). I would love to see more enemies in future updates.Two, I think the standard decks you start with are easily the most difficult to win with. Conversely, I think you would really have to try to lose with the Wizard or Giant Rat's Deck. 2 Notecards is absolutely busted. Either deck gets their hands on a Break the Limit card and you'll basically beat everyone but the Pit Boss without breaking a sweat. I hope the developer continues to work on and add to the game. They have a great sense of theme and parody and I look forward to whatever jokes and easter eggs they're cooking up ahead.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who adores card-based roguelikes, this is certainly a worthy entry into the genre.I've seen reviews that this game is akin to a combative (1v1) Balatro. However there is a clear distinction which has me much prefer D&DG, which is the complex decision making - as instead of going for a high score, you are factoring how a decision will increase your likelihood of beating your opponent. Perhaps you need card removal for your opponent's deck, perhaps you need sustain cards to stay alive, perhaps you need a more consistent 20/21/22. These decisions feel very fun and reward the player for knowing about the games mechanics and enemies.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: I've been having entirely too much fun with this game lately. Admittedly I haven't been listening to people talking about "the meta" or the great decks they've found because it feels like that would ruin it. You see, I've done my first clears on all but four of the starting decks and I get to thinking that having all the strategies in play in advance would ruin it. There have been some starts where I say...excuse me? Why would this even be a possible starting point? This is cruel. Then soon after I find how there's potential that I'd never imagined and it's absurd.That's the thing that makes this game so great. The best thing in a roguelike (using the term loosely) is when you get to the end, you look at your build and the progression, and you say...what just happened? Let me go back and figure out what just happened since this is incomprehensible. At the point I'm at, where I've been doing base difficulty runs on all of the decks, most of the successful runs are successful due to entirely different reasons. They're runs that go deep into despair, into total chaos, and then into a conclusion that only makes sense after you step back and think about it for awhile. I'll think that I've seen all the weird ways a run can go and then I get surprised again. How many games give you that feeling repeatedly?Other than that, it looks charming. It sounds charming. But that's not what we're here for. We're here for the satisfying chaos and oh you get that.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm glad I don't gamble, because I gamble hard in these games and lose everything. Greed keeps me from winning. :)It hits the same dopamine receptors that Balatro did for me. Instead of poker hands, you play blackjack, but the rules of blackjack are flavored with additional mechanics which gives DnD Gamblers its own unique spin. It's easy to learn but difficult to master. You can play strategically than depend just on luck/greed; each round you face off against an opponent. By beating your opponent's hand, you deal damage at the difference of your win or in the alternate case you take damage. Going bust will set you or your opponent's score to zero, and you or your opponent's hand will deal the full force of damage so long as the score has not gone bust. In typical rogue-like fashion, you pick your cards and try and build a strategy around your deck. The opponents get harder with their own gimmicks, and when you lose you pick a deck and start again. Games are pretty quick and you lose track of time.Absolutely love playing this handheld on the Steam Deck as well. This is a great game to just have handheld.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun game and unique take on the deck building genre. At its most basic level it is blackjack, but not in any casino way. Its not a game of hot streaks, you really have to play against the AI as much as you have to build your deck around probability. Patch 1.1 really makes the game viable for many many hours of play time and I expect the Dev to issue more balance patches. Special card design isn't as complicated as some other reviews make it out to be- you're gonna need to play a few runs before things start clicking (duh).For everyones sake, please stop judging this game against Balatro as the benchmark. It is a fundamentally different gameplay loop, look, and feel.

_childDocuments_.review: Brass tacks. For 15 bucks, I feel like it is worth it and I enjoy it. If you want to play blackjack but "weird" this is what you want.Minor nit picks. I feel like this game desperately needs a relic/joker system. The poker chips that dictate how you get advantage is cool, but really feel like you don't see nearly as much variety in decks due to not having some sort of static buff/penalty that your are building around.I really don't think the "beat the bouncer" before you get your chip or first card reward adds anything to the game and can just lead to some really annoying starts where the you keep getting stuck at 17/busting and the bouncer ties or hits 20 over and over without you really having any sort of control or impact. Just feels weird to force every run to start with "play the game in its least interesting form before you get to do anything fun" it isn't hard, but just a weird speed bump right at the start of the game.I have definitely not unlocked or seen everything the game has to offer yet, but I would like to see the design space explored more. Relics would do a lot to help with that. "When you hit, you pick one of the top two cards to play, but you must hit twice each game." or "a random card in your deck becomes foil each game, your aces lose variable." Things like that.

That's the charm of this game though and all the negative reviews are not seeing that. You have to adjust on the fly depending on what cards you get.However, there is a lot of strategy involved (much more than people think). You can see what cards you and your opponent still have to play, so you might need to risk busting or tanking damage in order to get a better hand the next round.Overall, give this game a chance. It'll be frustrating at first when you are learning what cards do/what cards work well together, what events will reward/hurt you, what enemies are tougher than others (with their specific decks), etc. You won't be good at the game right away, and probably won't be good until many hours of trial & error, but once you get it, you'll be hooked!

_childDocuments_.review: Those saying this isn't Balatro are correct.  This also isn't Blackjack, so stop comparing it to such as that's what's making you lose so much.  Play the game you're given, not the quirky tweak to a game you think you've been given.In Blackjack, you're generally going to statistically want to go for 17 to stay.  This is because of a general assumption that busts happen.  In this game, that's actually not true at *all*.  You practically don't want to bust nearly at all.  Your gauge for a situation will depend on your deck, but you're probably going to want to stay at 13-15, even if your opponent is already staying at 21.  The damage differential is large if you bust, and if they bust, you can generally knock off almost half their health (or even all of it) many times with 13-15 and your hand will go up to 20-21 (22?) naturally anyway.  Taking 2-3 hands worth of 5-7 hits and killing in a few rounds vs busting and taking 3-4 20+ hits are a major difference to just one round, and since it sticks with you, you'll lose quick.Your health is persistent, and that matters, so that's why every bust is basically a massive run mistake.  Your deck building is the largest influence and it definitely lets you do all types of things once you stop losing so quick, just don't use Blackjack statistics on this and you'll get through this quite easily.

Sure, the balancing is a little off and could be tweaked a bit (though really, isn't blackjack just a game of chance anyway?), but the sense of achievement when you manage to claw yourself back after taking a bunch of damage is great. _childDocuments_.review: Ever wished you could play blackjack with Charizard and Black Lotus in your deck?The easy comparison for this game is Balatro but they're mostly very different games aside from being playing-card-based roguelikes. There's less of an exponential element to this game, but the process of constructing a deck that will always (eventually) blackjack, or lock your opponent at 22+ so they can never score, or heal you to full hp every round, is just... so much fun. My only real criticism is of the game's high variance. As you play, you'll get a sense of what works and what doesn't, but ultimately there's only so much you can do if you're scoring 14s and your opponent is scoring 20s round after round, especially in the early encounters when you haven't had much time to modify your deck. This problem is exaggerated when playing anything other than one of the hearts decks since you won't have any innate healing until later in the run. I hope to be able to modify this part of the review after future balance changes.Ultimately though, the resets that sort of variance incurs come relatively early, and the runs that do work out are so satisfying that I still highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys intricate deckbuilding.

_childDocuments_.review: It's literally Blackjack, The Rogue-like. If you think there isn't going to be a fair deal of luck involved, I don't know what to tell you except don't go to Vegas. In all seriousness though, from my roughly 15 runs so far, I believe I can say the luck required that people seem to be upset about is mainly concentrated around the first 5 or so minutes of your runs. As you play the game, the more encounters you win, the more special cards you get that go into your deck, as well as being able to modify the cards you have in your deck already. The best way to put it is you're pretty much just playing regular blackjack for few minutes, and then the real deck building begins. I do think the deck-building isn't as intuitive as one might first assume, but if you're persistent you'll quickly start finding some combos and playstyles you'll enjoy. Sometimes you do get unlucky, yes, but I think many people who think there is too much luck involved, you have to remember you have a 100 health buffer that you can mitigate the damage you take with by willingly standing on a, let's say, 15 and take 6 damage, rather than just risking every single time and busting, causing you to lose in 5 hands. I would say, if you enjoy card games like blackjack or poker with a twist, you'll enjoy this, but if you're looking for something more nuanced, go play Inscryption. There is a lot of linear thinking that doesn't involve too much planning in the moment, more so having a plan for the whole run to make you more powerful by using certain card combos. Great game to play while watching Youtube or something.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Fun game concept that needs more time to cook to not feel so frustrating when the RNG makes feel unbalanced. I think it's a 6/10 game in it's current state where I don't really have the urge to continue playing after beating a run like with similar gambling rogue-likes especially as the new game+ system is just "What if your cards and effects were worse" which just isn't appealing after how unbalanced the base game already felt.Just completed my first run after about 5.5 hrs which felt like gave me a good grasp of the game to leave a complete review.It's tough to say whether or not I recommend this game because I did enjoy it, but I also echo a lot of the sentiment I've read that the game does feel brutally rng dependent in every aspect that it can sometimes take away from in. I did find however that the most enjoyable way to play for me was adding tons of effect cards that gave me playable copies or interactive mechanics which made the game feel less RNG based and more strategic. If you aren't very good at deckbuilding type games I could see this game being extremely frustrating as it is extremely unforgiving and a bad card choice could lose you the game easily. That being said I definitely think this game could be fun with a lot of quality of life changes, for example I definitely don't know how to approach this game without a hearts deck as healing really is too scarce which really makes the hearts deck feel mandatory to even have a chance of survival. It's a pretty weird move to not have some kind of post battle healing mechanic to spend the chips on. Also would be cool to have some kind of reroll mechanic for card rewards as there are so many cards that don't synergize that you might need to fish for cards that work unless you get a really good run.Overall I think this is one of those games to wishlist and check back in a few months to see if they've improved it at all, otherwise I don't think I would bother unless you are really into the card game and blackjack appeal.

_childDocuments_.review: D&DG is a lot of fun but with a massive caveat: the RNG in this game is brutal and will actively stand in your way of having a good time. Getting a run off the ground can be either incredibly easy or incredibly difficult and the amount of times you're given actual agency in your deck dwindles the further you get into the run. Additionally, options for healing are very sparse and decks that aren't leaning into hearts for healing need to find a way to sustain quickly or they'll get chipped away before making it to the end. Even the moment to moment of the battles is incredibly RNG-driven. In a comparable game like Balatro, you can draw badly but you feel like you have some agency because you're playing from a hand of drawn cards. In D&DG, particularly at the start of a run, what you draw is what you get. A single card is drawn and played regardless of whether or not it makes sense in context. Is it a one-shot card that only affects other cards drawn at the top of the run? That's a shame. It won't be doing anything for the rest of this fight. Is it a card that provides healing when you're already at full health? Not a choice I would have made...To add to this, late game enemies have highly optimized decks, where your ability to optimize your deck is mediocre at best. The game already seems to give the opponent blackjack often enough but when you get to the later enemies, their decks are also constructed to frequently give blackjack. It's very frustrating.At the end of the dare, my not recommendation for this game is a near thing. It's a lot of fun when you get a run going. Then you abruptly lose because all your cards come out in the wrong order and you can't do anything to stop it.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Currently there is a beta version of D&DG that addresses some of those complaints below! For example unwinnable fights such as the pit boss have been significantly changed - his decks is now 5x 25's, 1x emperor (deals damage on bust), so you no longer watch as the pit boss endlessly shields and pummels with you endless damage, furthermore if you remove the emperor then that fight is completely neutered. You get a little bit of healing during tarot reading as well! No card balance changes as far as I can tell. Also you start with 250 chips instead of 50, which is huge - means you can go for an early counterfeiter much easier and change more cards to suit you, or to buy cards from early shops easier.Unfortunately as much as I want to like D&DG, the balancing is atrocious and absolutely frustrating. There is very little deck manipulation or actual decision making in your plays, thus the game just feels like an absolute rngfest. In Slay the Spire the first fight can be sometimes rough due to a bad draw, but this usually means you just lose a few hp more. In this game you can end up getting chipped over and over and over again with no way to heal back unless you're playing the hearts deck. High cards are trash and will brick your deck due to increased chances of busting, if you include cards higher than 10 then you will bust super often, which means you'll tank 20 damage. Again, there are very few ways of healing. One of the events in the first area is a heal, you can either heal 3, 10 or 15 hp. 15 hp I believe for 85 chips, it's ridiculous. Every fight WILL cost you hp but the amount of hp you pay can vary wildly. The best cards for scoring are the round up cards (halves, pis, dark flower, beanstalk jack) because they will very often and safely bring you to blackjacks. The next category would be disruption cards, ones that allow you to swap cards with the opponent or outright destroy them. Boy, if you don't get any disruption cards then don't even think about going the underground route, the Pit Lord boss will destroy you - his gimmick is locking two tarot cards that grant shields and deal damage based on how high you bust, and this happens twice each round - on bust and on stand. And Pit Lord has cards that have a value of 25, so if he draws 13 and then hits the 25... have fun. You need to kill the arcana somehow, but this can be very often impossible because the game just didn't give you the appropriate cards. That fight is unwinnable without either super high damage of clubs and ending it in 3 blackjacks back to back, or super high and consistent healing, or disruption. Also if you get disruption cards that burn on discard then you can end up drawing it as the first card of the round, resulting in the card not doing anything and just disappearing.I managed to beat both final bosses somehow, but I don't feel like I got any better at the game, it was just pure luck. In Slay the Spire once I beat the heart once I was able to much more consistently reach act 3 final boss. In Balatro as I played and studied more I could make much more optimal plays and the game gave you enough leeway to let your skill shine, randomness is always a factor, but understanding how to mitigate risk helps a lot.In this game if you play overly safe by standing on 13-17 a lot you will just get chipped a ton, but you really have no other choice, if you bust early on and get hit for 17-21 or even more if the opponent has a blackjack with clubs, then you might as well restart if not playing hearts.The advantage system feels really bad and getting a useless chip can render a lot of powerful cards useless. Exploiting your cards (and also the opponent's!) is very important to making more consistent plays, but if you don't have any advantage then you can't... well, take advantage of it. tl;dr Balancing is all over the place, low consistency, no sense of agency, pray to get a good chip, pray you get high value cards, just pray in general because decision making in the early game is non-existent.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't recommend this game for a couple reasons, but one of them is extremely important to consider before buying.The game is well made, without a doubt. And if you're a huge fan of 21/Blackjack, this will be a very enjoyable game, however some of the cards, in my opinion, are completely unbalanced and some their mechanics aren't abundantly clear, essentially causing you to throw a round as you waste the card trying to figure out how to actually use it. That isn't even the horrible part, though- at least, the lack of explanations aren't. The part that's difficult to understate is that this is far more faithful to 21 than it might let on. Yes, there's silly cards and combat mechanics, but it is entirely RNG based, through and through. There isn't any more skill involved in this game than a real game of 21, and while that may seem obvious, I don't believe it's immediately clear how detrimental this is to a video game with real progression.Entire runs can be rendered impossible due to some enemies and special cards they use and rely on, and there doesn't seem to be an abundant source of healing outside of using the deck of hearts- or just getting lucky with events. If you really want to cheat the system, as it stands, the game has an unintended feature where closing the game immediately and opening it back up allows you to restart any encounter completely free of negative consequence. Unfortunately, I feel like this is almost required to progress deeper into the game without a mountain of luck or knowing how to count cards (which can become even more difficult with some of the special cards played)... And even then, all it does is give you a few more chances, because some encounters *truly* are impossible to pass. Each encounter starts with a predetermined deck, meaning resetting it doesn't change what cards you get in what order. This means that, once again, the numbers can be stacked against you, and you're left hoping for a better draw as the enemy whittles away your HP and racks up shields in the later floors.Now, there are a few caveats. Firstly, this is... Basically advertised. It's Blackjack; of course this is going to happen. Secondly, there's the chance it truly can be more of a skill issue than I believe. But, as far as I'm concerned from giving it an honest shot, I just can't say I recommend this for the stated reasons, unless you find those reasons thrilling for a roguelike.I wouldn't refund the game if I could; it's legitimately very well made and I did get some enjoyment out of it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're like me and were obsessed with Balatro but got kind of tired of it and were subsequently dismayed that it'll take until 2025 to get a new update, this is a great way to fill the gap. It scratches a very similar itch to Balatro with its deck management and randomness, but it also has its own unique feel, almost being more like an RPG that requires a lot more strategy and, well, gambling than Balatro. It's a very fully featured and fun interpretation of a usually pretty mindless game (blackjack) that takes that game's simple mechanics and creates a ton of interesting and unique interactions and strategies from them, which is very interesting since I myself am a game designer and actually work as a blackjack dealer every now and then. It is, of course, not without its issues. Blackjack itself is inherently a very random game, and the epitome of a gambling game, so it naturally has its euphorically clutch highs and its hairpullingly frustrating lows, which can create a very inconsistent play-feel at times. Some of the enemies in the game can be incredibly difficult if they set up their win condition, which can either lead to long-drawn out games where you whittle their health down one hit at a time, or just flat out unwinnable scenarios if you don't randomly get the right cards beforehand. I like that the game is difficult, it really makes it feel like a battle, but some are just too overtuned imo. But overall, DnDG is an excellent deckbuilder roguelike that has some great ideas and just needs a little tuning to be about on par with Balatro.(also please make it easier to restart runs k thx)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough recommendation, but overall I do recommend it. The developer has put out a post saying they will work on balancing and as other reviews have mentioned this could use a tune up. I am reminded of the launch of Wildfrost (most of my hours on Switch) where reviews were really punishing for what was a very fun game because of the punishing difficulty which they turned around later on.The other tricky thing is that because almost every card is a reference (which I find to be quite fun), it's not immediately clear what each card does, some of the abilities aren't that memorable so you need to keep looking at the individual card as a reminder, and there's very little "theming" like Balatro had with its planets, tarots, seals, etc. which means it's harder to know what you're looking for in a particular build.I have some minor UX qualms as well (you have to unhover and rehover over cards to see their abilities, you have to click out of dialogue boxes of your opponents before doing anything, etc.) but nothing that's enough to sour the overall experience.What it boils down to for me is that the game is fun and I'm enjoying it despite the things that I'd like to be addressed. If that's not enough for you now then consider this as a recommendation to try it later down the line when things have been tweaked.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR: Game hard, learn, lose zoomer brain, game fun.Coming from Balatro the game felt slow and in a way painful. Balatro being a game where you can get ridiculous points and mind boggling synergies isn't really comparable to this game. Dungeons and Degenerates is more about cumulative damage and minimising damage to yourself, balancing on trying to handicap your opponent, trying to prevent them from getting too much shield or damage built up, while trying to maximise the same yourself while trying to win at blackjack at the same time. Building your deck is quite RNG as you get only 4 card choices after each battle and you are in a way forced to experiment. Personally I really enjoy experimenting, finding new ways to stay afloat. Sometimes the game might feel like you're just scraping by, but it kinda compliments the story and the atmosphere of the game.The game really doesn't let you run around defeating opponents and sometimes you might lose half of your precious health to the first opponent because the draws just weren't in favour, but during each run you gain knowledge and learn to pick your opponents based on their deck and your own build. Some opponents seem to have "OP" builds, but to beat them you might just need (not required but is easier to beat) a specific card type. The Bouncer for example has just 2 10's and 1 21. If you can get his 21 out of the play it makes things worse as he then is unable to bust, but if you burn 1 of his 10 and the 21 he only is able to play 10 and that is easy to beat. You can also lock his 10 and hopefully burn his other 10 so he is forced to bust every round. Without modifying his deck you only pray to either get only 20 or 21 all the time to slowly damage him or pray for him to bust all the time. Otherwise he can be quite deadly at first.The game sure has some RNG but the beauty of the game for me is learning what risks, paths, opponents and cards to take making myself better and every run takes me further closer to finish. Currently my favourite play style is to accumulate advantage and have alot of "in hand cards" to have flexibility so the RNG with the card draws is minimal. In hand aces or negative cards can sometimes save you from a certain death.A bit of a ramble review but I truly enjoy the game and if you're a patient person and enjoy card games or rogue likes this is the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is interesting but is fighting an uphill battle. The game will inevitably be compared to Balatro both in game-play and value, and will lose that comparison every time. This game is interesting, but tends to lean towards a more traditional card based rogue-like in that RNG plays a huge factor in whether you have a chance to win or not. Even more so in this title since it's blackjack and you can bust. The game just isn't balanced well at all. There are certain opponents who's decks will always take a huge hit from you because they have pre-determined decks and you just got whatever the RNG gods gave you that run. There are 4 starting decks and only one of them is even viable since they only proc on a 21 and only when your opponent doesn't ALSO get a 21 (which again because of the hand crafted decks will happen FAR more frequently than you can ever hope for). There are certain cards / chips that are just always obviously better as well making deck building kinda boring at times since there aren't a ton of viable options. The game is alright and will scratch that itch when you're getting kinda bored of Balatro, or would rather play blackjack than poker. Game is closer to $10 in value though and I'd get it on a sale unless you're really into this genre niche. Recommending the game because it can be fun, but prepare for some bouts of frustration as well.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: After savescumming a bit, I've had such a great time with the Wizard Deck that I have to change the review to positive. Really wish more of the starting decks were like it. It gives access to more strategy and weird combos much sooner and much more reliably than the other decks.Also, the 1.1 balancing patch was a first step in the right direction.Still not a perfect game, but the concept is really great, I'm sure with a few more patches it can become a great game.------ORIGINAL REVIEW: ------Meh.Really great concept, has a ton of fun potential, lots of really cool cards, but the brutal difficulty is ruining it for me.Here are the most egregious issues for me:- All starting decks are really weak, with most cards being junk. This is expected from the genre, but in this game there is not a lot of accessible permanent card removal. My suggestion would be to at least add buyable card removals in the shops.- You will get lots of inevitable damage in this game, not having any reliable form of healing is brutal. You risk getting ~20 damage (out of 100 hp) every time you draw the "wrong" card. Should at the very least fully heal when changing area, but a choice for some healing in events would be really useful.- The only *decent* starting deck is Hearts, due to the point above. It is the only deck that offer some form of healing from the get-go. The others are very very very weak, with the nothing starting deck being absolutely dumb.- The chips you get at the beginning of a run will dictate which cards you should get. Some chips are terrible and require heavy investments to make them work, some are so easy to fulfill that you'll not have any way to spend them. Being offered a single choice between two for a whole run can really make or break the run (had to restart a few times because the choices weren't cool).- The advantage mechanic is really cool, but criminally underutilized.I really wish for a balance patch update, so that I can update my vote.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of goods and bads but I'm recommending it cause I have fun playing it.As with most small teams they might change it so here's hoping cause it's decent.Basically it's Blackjack Balatro with a lot of choices and things to think about.I applaud the game for actually thinking outside the box with playing.You have a lot to consider. In regular blackjack you'd try to beat or at least match the dealer,Here, that's not the case. The total value of your cards is used against the opponent's, and if you bust, you got 0. So your opponent attacks your HP fully.So it's more of a risk vs reward. Also if you hit the max value (21 by default), depending on your card suit will have a bonus effect.THEN as you go, you add in more and more card effects with funny cards and making adjustments to have a unique playstyle.Card counting is good here! But luckily you can check the decks at almost any time.There is a mana system called Advantage you get that helps run card effects.Pros:+Great concept+It is similar to Balatro, but it is not a total copycat, but with an entirely different spin on it. They even have a Jimbo card from Balatro that quips at you as you play :D+No toilet humor! :D+Good bit of inside jokes of other games. (Memes to nowadays people)+Character creator is a nice touch, a little limited, but it's just for fun. Devs: Steam Icon or just a image in a folder might be a nice option to add+Deck variety is crazy. Bust yourself and do damage type, exploit heavy decks, send trash to your opponent, lock your opponent from doing ANYTHING.Mehs~The game gets a bit out of hand lategame... I've done rounds where I just hit twice or three times, and the computer does this insane combo I can't keep up with :D. It's so much to check and consider that by the end I was having a hard time keeping up. You CAN check your opponent's deck and your own at almost any time, keep in mind.~Are the inverted Tarot cards called something different?Cons-Unlocking decks is boring. The 5th starting deck, "The NOTHING deck", that you get from your first time beating the game, is extremely bleh as it's more of a challenge yourself deck rather than a fun deck to play as it has no suit for all the cards, and since there's no downside to having a card suit, it's by default it's harder than the others. There's 18 decks to unlock but I'm still stuck on this dumb thing... Personal opinion: Make this either the LAST deck you unlock or put it in a challenge menu or something. I hope that not all of the decks are unlocked by just "beat it with the previous"-Starting enemy that gives you your first card and warmup thing is equally as powerful as you are! (except his HP) No really, he has the same 12 cards +1 other card. With bad luck, or if you make too many mistakes, you can wind up losing most of your HP quickly on him.-Some cards need more info.-I'll add to this as I remember more

_childDocuments_.review: I have played countless roguelites copying the framework of Slay the Spire but having one gimmick to try to set itself apart from the others. Games where you don't get any gratification from figuring out broken combos, because you already know what they are when you see them since they are just a copy of a system you've played many times before. The roguelite deckbuilder (and similar) have been in desperate need of some inspiration and developers with a vision of their own rather than "let's make a poor copy of a masterpiece game, but put a different color lipstick on it".Luckily, we're finally seeing some innovation, with Balatro and now with Dungeons & Degenrate Gamblers.While both games might seem similar on the surface, they are very different. Both great in their own right, but go about their gameplay from different angles. Balatro challenges you to a game of optimization with putting pieces together to create a precise point scoring deck.Then we have this game, which throws most other conventions out the window. The game basically puts you in the position of a mad scientist who can control a ton of what's going on in the duels. It rewards out of the box thinking and wild experiments, and it can become very, very complex if you want to. Reading other reviews that talk about frustrating stalemate situations etc sounds like what I too experienced before I started understanding that I had to approach this game differently than other games of the genre. I've only scratched the surface, but my impression is that there's a ton more to explore with the tools the game gives you.For those that want something that feels familiar to the classics of the roguelite deckbuilders, this might not be the game for you. But for those like me that are tired of all the copycating with next to no innovation or iteration and want something different that can't be solved with the same approach as the 1000 games before it, then this is well worth picking up.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing on Steamdeck, runs great with great battery life.Won my first run with the hearts deck that heals you, and I am now continually losing with the suitless deck. Without some form of healing, it is impossible, so unless you pull some hearts or other healing, your run is toast. This is because, no matter how good you are, you can't prevent taking damage and slowly having your health chipped away.Another complaint is the first battle against the bartender. Just two standard decks against each other. He only has 5 health. Sometimes he busts and you immediately win. Sometimes you just get unlucky and take several turns of damage. Any time I take damage on this first battle, I feel obligated to restart my run. Getting hit on this is 90% luck. In addition, you're presented with your advantage chip after this battle, so again I find myself tempted to restart the run if I'm not given the chip I want.Playing a few more hours, I decided to just flip the switch in the settings to unlock all decks (which I'm very grateful to have). It has made me see that there is just too much RNG. The glitch deck, for instance. Can I hit on an 11? Will I draw a King, Queen, Jack, or a glitch card that's a 12 of hearts. Suddenly, there is next to no strategy when your next card could be anything between -11 and 21. And there isn't really any way to work around this. I would really like more ability to remove cards from my deck as well. There are very few events that let you reduce your deck size, which means you can't effectively build a focused deck like how many of your opponents have. I want a deck of 3s and 7s and the queen the does damage when I play those. Or a deck of nothing but cards that round, etc.That said, I am enjoying it. Many of the decks are great, and I'll just not play the decks I don't find fun. I just really would like to have a little more control over my deck.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good bit of fun. The memes and references to other tabletop and video games is awesome, and it's definitely got replayability potential. A lot of people are saying they don't see the strategy in it, but ultimately it's 1/4 deck blackjack (as opposed to casinos where they play 6 or 8 deck blackjack, you're only playing with a quarter of a deck), and so the strategy isn't in knowing what card will come next, but in hedging your odds based on what cards are left in your deck. Tracking the cards as they move is a fun challenge, and remembering how they work. There is definitely skill here beyond just hitting HIT or STAY.
