_childDocuments_.review: Like Balatro, this game is a rouge-lite deck building game revolving around a familiar card game. Blackjack. The one where your max score can be 21 and you Hit and Stand along the way.After playing this for an evening, I feel that's where the Balatro resemblance ends. This game moves along much faster, you can have a hand of cards that look wild in minutes. You can have cards such as negative numbers, cards that you hold (like holding a shape in Tetris) that you can play once you're in a bad spot (like busted), there's too many to mention and there's some wild ones. All this wildness happens pretty early on and can seem somewhat overwhelming. Especially when your opponent plays a fancy card and you didn't get a chance to check what the card's attributes were. You kinda just learn on the fly and to be honest it only took my a few runs to make sure I was checking all fancy card skills etc. but yeah I'm still learning. I think there's something like 300 odd card types to discover. Oh there are decks too. The first 4 unlocked decks are simply the 4 standard card suits (hearts, clubs, spade and diamonds). Each deck has its own perk. A perk is triggered by hitting 21. Hearts will heal you, clubs will deal extra damage, spades will give you shields and diamonds, well I forgot what they do, maybe more chips? Chips are your currency used for buying cards and buffs etc.The game's progression plays out similar to something like Slay the Spire. You start at The Tavern where you play about 5 opponents during your time there. Beating the area boss will give you a choice between 2 new areas to visit. In between opponents you will run into shops, inns, tarot readings and mini games such Roulette, coin flip, stocks (here you will by some stocks and watch a line graph peak and dip where you have to click at a point to sell!).When you face off against an opponent, hands played will determine both your attack power, but also your defense. For example, you play a 21, but your opponent plays 20, you hit them for 1hp (early opponents have total HP of approx 5-10, but that quickly ramps up). You yourself start with 100hp. If you or your opponent bust (cards add up to over 21) though, then you will be defenseless, meaning your opponent can hit you for 20hp.On my first attempt, I made it to about the 5th area. It was a chilled run and a great opportunity to learn the game somewhat. Since then I've had about 3 runs both ending at area 2. Mainly for being greedy and not standing at the likes of 15 or 16 to give me some defense.I came away from this game (when I decided it was bed time) feeling it was well worthy of my time and I'm looking forward to chilling on it tonight.Not a Balatro clone, but a worthy and very enjoyable game of crazy black jack, but played through a dungeon where you'll meet drunks, bards, gamblers, skaters, wizards and more.Love it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dungeons & Degenerate Gamblers

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy blackjack, this game was MADE for you. It all really feels like you suddenly bought the last 15 expansion packs for blackjack that you never knew existed and are playing it all for the first time.It adds so many new cards that add a whole host of new complications to your comfort in knowing the odds when you choose to hit or stand. There are negative number cards, there's a hand that can be activated by certain card effects and can allow you to play cards at the cost of an action point, there are straight 21 numbered cards which always is annoying because you either draw it first or bust, there are fraction cards (like 0.5 of hearts or the pi of hearts). The suits of the cards have certain effects too, that trigger when you get your max 21. Oh, you can also steal opponents cards, force them to draw, change the blackjack number to 20 or 22, and so much more. You have health and deal damage based on the difference in card numbers between you and your opponent. When they tie, no damage is dealt. If one busts, it's akin to having a 0 score, and thus you take the full damage of the other's card number. This adds a REALLY interesting mechanic and strategy to blackjack as a whole, as staying at a lower number than your opponent would actually reduce the damage you take, if hitting would otherwise result in you busting. Sometimes you don't even need to go for blackjack, so long as your opponent busted (and you didn't) you'll do damage that round; as opposed to doing zero damage if you pushed for the blackjack but busted.The ONLY gripe I have with this game is ONE PARTICULAR loop an AI got me in and forced me to slowly lose, with no chance of winning. In the game, you can lock a card on your opponents side to be there on the next draw, with a particular key card. I did not have the opportunity to grab one of these in my run, and what happened was an AI slowly locked my cards one round at a time until I was locked at 34. I couldn't draw anymore cards, I could only stand on bust, and wait for my health to slowly drain to zero, forcing me to lose all my progress. I was hoping I could draw a steal card to steal my opponent's key card, or even just swap over one of the 10's that was locked, but since I couldn't draw since I was locked on bust, there was literally nothing to do but hit Stand. Kind of infuriating, but I still love this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is a good game that had some genuine effort and imagination put into its creation, but it's certainly less fine-tuned than its obvious inspiration, Balatro. It requires/earns less respect than its precursor: it's easy to get into unwinnable positions, some of the card effects and rules are unclear, you have less control over the cards that end up in your deck, etc. Balatro also required a bit of luck, but you were presented with all the tools to create your own luck. That's not really the case here. On one hand, that makes it less satisfying, but also less intense. If something goes wrong there was nothing you could really do about it.I still haven't managed a single full clear in 4 hours of play (the "campaign" is rather long), but I think it's interesting and I'll keep at it.

_childDocuments_.review: Dungeons and Degenerate Gamblers is among the recent spate of roguelikes that realized that gambling is fun, cheating at gambling is even more fun, and never having money at stake is the most fun. It's snappy, speedy, using the simple format of Blackjack to its advantage and keeping things mostly simple. The cards snap quickly into position and turns take seconds to pass. ...which is about the only real weakness in the midgame. Turns zip by sometimes with strange card interactions, often leaving the player bewildered and confused - why did I suddenly lose my blackjack, hve half my cards fly over to the other side, and take thirty damage? A play log would be an excellent helpful addition to the game, but it's a minor complaint. Otherwise, a lot of Balatro's sauce is here. It's a solid game for the price it's at, and with just a bit of work, could stand among the greats.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game but it's unfair and can learn from other rogue likes when it comes to decision-making.  Without a map to route between encounters and events it's a coin flip.  Due to the rules of the game you can simply lose a run two fights in, I've had runs start against opponents on Black Jack streaks.  I've also beat bosses with shear dumb luck.  Winning the game is simply impossible without luck and memorization and mitigation against the various abilities of the bosses / levels (very much Slay the Spire with this) but sadly this also means that if you have a fun deck it's probably not going to win.  It also means certain cards are just straight up better than others so I hope you're feeling lucky.  With that all said, it hits all the spots when it comes to rogue like deck builders but I hope they improve run consistency and let difficulty be in ascensions but right now base difficulty will filter out the majority of players.

_childDocuments_.review: Really on the fence of whether or not to recommend this game. On one hand, it somewhat scratches that Balatro itch, but on the other hand, it tries a bit too hard to the point of it being more confusing than anything.The premise is fantastic, and they have cards taken directly from other trading card games (Gwent, Pokemon, Yu-Gi-Oh, Magic) if you're a fan of nostalgic references, but the problem is that the game quickly becomes too complicated for its own good. Even from the first round, different suits have different effects, then you bring on cards that affect the draws, the count, the board, and even the whole game. By the third level, I was so confused about what my cards did, what my opponent's cards did, what was even going on, that with every hand as there were more non-playing deck cards on the table than actual cards, and even at my game over I had no idea what the hell had hit me because it all comes at you rapid fire - watch the gameplay video trailer above to see what I mean. This sounds like it's a learning curve problem, but I want to insist that by the time you get additional cards in your deck and get more difficult opponents, it no longer feels like you're playing Blackjack but some very weird fever dream version of it.Still, I see myself opening this back up and trying this again for a while, so I suppose it's worth giving it a positive review. The game is just over-engineered for its own good and it's going to take a long time to figure out what you're actually doing.

name: Ace Attorney Investigations Collection
detailed_description: Experience both Ace Attorney Investigations games in one gorgeous collection! Step into the shoes of Miles Edgeworth, that prosecutor of prosecutors from the Ace Attorney mainline games! Leave the courtroom behind as you walk with Edgeworth around the crime scene, gathering evidence and clues and talking with persons of interest. _childDocuments_.review: I'm so thankful that the Ace Attorney Investigations Collection is here because a lot of people probably haven't played the fan translation of Investigations 2 and now they have an easy way to experience this game.I love the new music arrangements.  I wasn't sure if I'd like the new chibi art style since I've appreciated Capcom's sprite work ever since I played Final Fight in the arcades. Fortunately, the new style is very expressive and clean so I warmed up to it quickly, and I can always switch to the old style if I want. I played Investigations 1 a long time ago on the DS, and though I enjoyed controlling Miles Edgeworth, the game felt a bit underdone compared to the Phoenix Wright trilogy.  While I liked being able to move around the environment to investigate, I missed the courtroom drama and the gimmicks such as Wright's Magatama and Ema's forensic minigames.  The villains were also overall on the weak side, especially the one in the third case.  However, I did like several of the new characters such as Shi-Long Lang and Detective Badd.  Investigations 1 might be one of the less memorable games in the Ace Attorney franchise, but it does a good job of presenting an overarching narrative.While I enjoyed replaying Investigations 1, the real treasure is still Investigations 2, which is my favorite game outside of the original trilogy.  Edgeworth gets his own gimmick known as Mind Chess, which is one of the better ones in the series, and there are also more forensic moments.  I also ended up liking his assistant Kay Faraday a lot more after playing this game.  Franziska von Karma fans should also be happy since she gets a lot of great moments with her whip. Verity Gavelle and Eustace Winner are excellent new characters that I had no trouble getting attached to.As for case quality, even the weakest case (2 in my opinion) is still pretty great, and I've browsed enough tier lists to know that this isn't a controversial take.  Case 4 is easily in my top 3 of the entire series and the tutorial case is one of the best in its class.  Investigations 2 doesn't suffer from a weak third case, either, because it has an amazing setting, good mysteries and interesting characters.  Controlling Edgeworth's father was fun, too, because he looks like Gregory Peck who played Atticus Finch in To Kill a Mockingbird. The final case deserves a great deal of praise also, since it does a fantastic job of tying all of the other cases together into a satisfying conclusion.  I played the fan translation of Investigations 2, so I knew all of the game's twists and turns, but it was still a wonderful experience to replay it.  The localization team did a great job and I liked most of the name changes. Fans of these games will probably be happy with this version and new players will be in for a real treat if they enjoyed the original trilogy.  I highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is coming early because as usual, I've already played these games on the DS. It's surprisingly convenient to go through and check the overall quality, because nothing is restricted by progress in this collection; you're welcome to start from wherever you want, even accessing the individual chapters of each case from a new game. Each collection they release seems to do a little better about letting people who have already played the games skip around, and I'm happy to see it continue.When AAI first released on the DS, I really wasn't a fan of the change to third person. It seemed like it was done in response to the large amount of pc point-and-click games that were being ported to the DS at the time, and it felt like a downgrade in most ways. The character sprites were low res and not very animated, the backgrounds only looked worse from the new zoomed out perspective, and frankly, having Edgeworth walk around on screen just wasn't a very fun change. All it really did was make you waste milliseconds of your life watching a little pink man walk across the screen each time you wanted to do something, instead of just clicking something and examining it. That last point still applies, but they've done their due diligence to make it feel worth it; remade graphics look great, and the character sprites in particular are both pleasant to look at and charmingly well animated. Gone are the days of having to squint and shuffle over to the 7 pixel wide gun on the floor, making it easier than ever to inspect every suspicious looking nook and cranny. It feels like a much better fit all around, and I found myself not minding the point-and-walk gameplay nearly as much this time.In terms of the story, the first AAI is a little rough. There's no such thing as a truly bad Ace Attorney game, but it's a low point that's often compared to Dual Destines. In order of hottest take to coldest: Kay is a great character and great assistant, but her Little Thief gimmick (which essentially replicates crime scenes in a room-wide, neon green, high-tech virtual reality projection, and despite just being a simulation is sometimes kind of treated as a more factual source of reasoning than it should -- which I guess was arguably just ahead of its time these days, right ChatGPT?) just feels like another weird and arbitrary time waster, using up more time to explain it than it would have ever taken if it were just presented as Edgeworth imagining the scene. Edgeworth himself suffers the same problems Apollo and Phoenix do in Dual Destinies in terms of characterization, and he gets treated as the butt of the joke often enough that it doesn't always feel like it lives up to letting you play as the cool, sophisticated foil to Phoenix you see in the other games in favor of just another flavor of funnyman. And while the first four cases never really dip lower than the other lesser AA games, at most being occasionally uninteresting, the last case is such a devastatingly low plunge that most people have completely erased it from their mind until a meme triggers their ptsd, and stick to arguing safer discussions like Turnabout Big Top vs Recipe for Turnabout instead. Somehow, the same people that made that game went on to make AAI2, which bafflingly had never been officially localized until now. Everything that AAI1 did badly, AAI2 does better, and then some; it's funnier, it's smarter, it's all around better written, and it's hard to put down from pretty much the very start. More than just giving the character his due reverence, this game seems to much better understand the difference between "a game where you play as Edgeworth" and "an Edgeworth game". This collection could have only included AAI2 and I would still say it's worth $40, but Capcom was nice enough that they threw in the first one for free since they were already remaking most of the assets for 2. The general consensus is that it's at least very close to Trials & Tribulations in terms of quality, sometimes noted as slightly worse and sometimes lauded as being even better (in this debate, I am a fencesitter who considers them equal) and after giving up on seeing it officially localized years ago I'm incredibly happy to see everyone finally getting to play it in a more conveniently accessible form. Anyone who's played the previous collections probably doesn't need to be told to buy more Ace Attorney, but any fan of the series owes it to themselves to play this one. As Edgeworth would say, it's sublime. As Kay would say, peak is back on the menu.

_childDocuments_.review: Ace Attorney Investigations Collection? Miles Edgeworth’s Time to Shine! (ฅ'ω'ฅ)The Ace Attorney Investigations Collection brings together both entries in the spinoff series featuring Miles Edgeworth, known for his sharp logic and no-nonsense attitude in the courtroom. In this collection, the courtroom drama is replaced with crime scene investigations as you gather clues, interrogate witnesses, and use deduction to solve complex cases. Both games have received an HD facelift, along with quality-of-life improvements, making them more accessible than ever to both series veterans and newcomers. This is also the first time that the sequel, Prosecutor's Gambit, has been officially localized for the Western audience, which alone is a huge draw for fans.The Ace Attorney Investigations Collection shifts away from the traditional court battles of the main series, focusing instead on crime scene investigation. Playing as Miles Edgeworth offers a unique perspective; instead of defending clients, you're out to prove guilt and uncover the truth using Edgeworth’s sharp deductive skills. The gameplay consists of gathering evidence, cross-examining witnesses, and piecing together events to solve each mystery. A key mechanic is the "Logic Chess" system, where Edgeworth mentally debates with suspects, adding a fresh strategic layer to interrogation.Visually, the game has been enhanced for modern platforms, with both a new chibi art style and the option to switch to classic pixel art for a retro feel. The HD upgrade shines, especially in character animations, bringing more life to Edgeworth and the colorful cast of quirky side characters. The environments are also crisp and detailed, enhancing the crime-solving experience. Audio-wise, the remastered soundtrack adds extra drama to pivotal moments, though some may feel the new orchestral arrangements are a bit too over-the-top.A major strength of the collection is the inclusion of Prosecutor’s Gambit, which was previously unavailable outside of Japan. This game improves on many of the first title’s shortcomings, featuring tighter storytelling, more engaging puzzles, and a better balance of humor and seriousness. The storylines maintain the franchise's signature absurdity, while the writing in Prosecutor’s Gambit is particularly sharp, elevating it to near the heights of the main series' best titles like Trials and Tribulations.The Ace Attorney Investigations Collection is a fantastic package for fans of the series and those who love mystery-solving games. It successfully brings Miles Edgeworth’s sleuthing to modern platforms with beautiful HD visuals, smart quality-of-life upgrades, and the long-awaited localization of Prosecutor's Gambit. While the first game has its rough patches, the sequel more than makes up for it with better pacing, writing, and puzzles. Whether you're a longtime fan or new to the Ace Attorney universe, this collection is a must-play for those who enjoy a good mystery.If you’re a fan of the Ace Attorney series or enjoy mystery-solving games, this collection should be on your radar. _childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic collection that offers us both Ace Attorney Investigations games, spin-offs featuring our dearest Miles Edgeworth as a protagonist. It's the first time Investigations 2 gets an official Western release and that alone makes this package a must buy. Investigations 1 is also great in my opinion. Capcom went the extra mile and remastered both games well, with crisp visuals and incredible chibi HD sprites in lieu of the pixel art ones featured on DS (still available if so inclined). An amazing package for sure. Detailed individual reviews below: I originally played this on the Nintendo DS and replaying it after what felt like a billion years was awesome. My boy Miles Edgeworth's first game as a protagonist shakes up the Ace Attorney formula far more than any other mainline game did. The funny thing is that the changes aren't that major when you really dig into them, but they shift your perception of the game a lot.Basically, you don't really go to court anymore. Investigations is all... well, investigations. You explore locations by physically moving Edgeworth around (the original sprites were very cool and the new HD chibi sprites are incredible, super fun and expressive, great job on the remastering front), exploring every nook and cranny and finally confronting witnesses to basically solve cases before they even get to court. It's not like you don't have the distinction between investigation and "trial" anymore, you still do, but the new format makes the game feel far brisker than the mainline games, even though the playtime is about the same. The new mechanic is Logic, by which you can link different information and come up with new conclusions, shedding new light on the cases.The plot deals with Edgeworth finding himself entangled in various cases related to an international smuggling ring. People always b1tch about Investigations, saying that the story isn't great because it's not "personal"... I say who cares. It's less melodrama and more "murder mystery" than your typical Ace Attorney game, which I welcomed then and welcome now. The Yatagarasu subplot is great and that's where the main emotional weight of the game is at, so I was satisfied. Sure, the cases are not what I'd consider the most brilliant overall, but they're good across the board and, like I said, they work wonders as mysteries to solve, rather than story chapters to get through. I also liked the infamous final case, though I can certainly agree that confronting the culprit takes a lifetime and a half and gets a bit silly with how drawn out it is. But I'd say that this is the only relatively big criticism I have for the game.I like Investigations a lot, and Miles as a protagonist is the bomb . Plus, I like many of the new characters, with Kay Faraday being a favourite of mine and agent Lang as a very enjoyable rival. I'd rate it about the same as  Apollo Justice and Dual Destinies overall, it doesn't have the highs and emotional beatdowns of those games but it also doesn't have their bullsh1t gimmicks and stupid logic. It's a different flavour of Ace Attorney, but I dig it. I never played the fan translation of Investigations 2, so it was a totally new experience for me. This is always considered one of the best games in the whole franchise, usually to the detriment of Investigations 1, and I have to say that I agree (on I2's quality, not on I1's alleged mediocrity, that's a bunch of bullsh1t). I2 plays off of I1's international smuggling ring plot and evolves into something much greater, keeping the world building heavy angle of the first game while offering five elaborately interlocking cases and telling a much more personal story all at the same time.The formula is the same as I1's, while featuring one new gimmick, Mind Chess. It's a sort of a mixup on the usual witness testimonies, as our boy Miles the eloquence master plays mindgames on whoever he is confronting, trying to make them spill the beans. It's a neat concept, it's not executed with finesse and involves a good deal of trial and error, but it isn't outlandish in the slightest and I have no strong positive or negative feelings on the mechanic. The rest of the gameplay is pretty much unchanged, bringing the focus squarely on the scrupulous exploration of crime scenes and on logical deductions.The writing and characters are where the game really shines. I2 features two memorable new rivals: Verity Gavèlle, a fearsome, intelligent judge (and hottest Ace Attorney character by far I will NOT accept any other opinion on the matter) hell-bent of following the "Godess of Justice"'s will, and Eustace Winner, a rookie prosecutor with a massive ego and no skills whatsoever (but very influential connections) to back it up. Verity is elegant and a fierce opponent, to the point of being frustrating. She feels like a wall for the player to overcome. Eustace is no threat whatsoever, but his character arc is one of the highest points of the game, though obviously I won't spoil why. The other notable new entry is Eddie Fender, a defense attorney who used to be the apprentice of the late Gregory Edgeworth, Miles's father. He is an oddball and an endlessly endearing one at that. There are also memorable villains and one very special case that allows us to play as one very special character of the series. Again, no spoilers from me there. Characters from the original trilogy return, sometimes masterfully so, with reappearances of characters I would never have seen coming again. The core cast of I1, with Edgey, Kay and Gummy in the spotlight, performs admirably here and I have never seen a better Miles or a better Gumshoe than in this game.The story is incredibly ambitious as well, with every single one of the five cases intricately connected to each other, a series first if I recall correctly. The mysteries are well crafted and the intensity never lets up, with every case from the third onwards feeling like "final case material". There are countless twists and memorable climaxes, and the most surprising thing is that the game never trips itself up with the dense and complex narrative involving multiple incidents over a span of eighteen years. It really is Ace Attorney at its finest, with zero ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gimmicks, little padding, no major annoyances and characters being absolutely beautiful.It's been a phenomenal ride and Investigations 2 is for sure one of my favourite Ace Attorney games, I'd say in a three-way ex-aequo with Trials and Tribulations and The Great Ace Attorney 2: Resolve. I really hope that Capcom and the Ace Attorney team can be inspired by these two amazing spin-off duologies when they eventually deliver Ace Attorney 7 to the world. Investigations 2 will be a high bar to surpass for sure. I'm so glad Western players can finally enjoy it officially.

_childDocuments_.review: SEBASTIAN DECEASED!Now that I have your attention, I'd like to discuss a few things about the game that perhaps might pique your interest toward the collection if you're wondering about picking it up.Best thing about this is the fact that this marks the first time that the second game, Prosecutor's Gambit, was released outside of Japan since 2011 and given a proper localization. Before today, a fan patch was made for both the mobile and DS versions which was positively received by most fans. I won't go deep into the games themselves since I don't think I'd be much capable of articulating my thoughts here, but rather I'd like to bring up my own thoughts to the collection.The most notable change made here is the new chibi art style. I wasn't too particularly fond of it at first but ever since I played the demo and I got to see how more characters translated into them, I started to appreciate the amount of effort it took to make everyone expressive as hell. With the original pixel art style, the faces of characters aren't really meant to have much detail. Whether you're liking the new art style or want to return to the original look, you can thankfully change between them! I would much prefer to play with the new one for the sake of having a new experience. Older style is still good, though some might notice that the sprites' outlines have similar problems to the mobile versions? I wasn't too observant on them but I liked both art styles.The gallery is a new addition! As with the recent previous collections, it allows you to browse through the OST, concept art pieces, and in-game achievements! Comparing this one to Apollo Justice: Ace Attorney Trilogy's addition, the gallery here unfortunately doesn't allow you to mess around with the animations with a green screen but you can still look at the sprites' animations and change their art style. I'm also a little bit disappointed that the concept art gallery doesn't have commentary pieces like The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles has, but again, minor criticism.The arranged soundtrack is a bit of a mixed bag. If you've pre-ordered the game, you'll notice that you can toggle between arrangements of selected tracks in the game and their original pieces. The new ones are much heavier on being dramatic, so some might call it overproduced. I still like the new OST, but whether its fitting to the games is debatable. Again, I would also have this on for a new experience.Anyway, those were some quick thoughts that I wanted to get out of the way. Overall, still a great collection and the last that was necessary for this series. As an Ace Attorney fan, I would definitely recommend this even if you've already played these titles. If you haven't yet, you're in for a ride. Both titles are great.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a collection of two spinoff games for the Ace Attorney series that were originally released on the DS. Both titles have been remastered with gorgeous HD graphics!The original Investigations is a relatively simple title. It was the first game headed by Takeshi Yamazaki, who would go on to be the main writer for several later games in the series. I will admit a certain fondness for this game, since it was the first in the series I played. Certainly not the strongest entry though.The second game however is widely regarded as one of the best entries in the entire AA series, and this is its first time getting an official English release. The game has great mysteries, great characters, the works! The new translation was also very good and full of the distinctive humor the series is known for (although there were occasional typos that could stand to get fixed).Easily the best way to play both games now. I really can't emphasize enough how good the second game is in particular, truly an entry any AA fan should play.

_childDocuments_.review: Above all else, this collection is worth it just to finally play AAI2, a criminally overlooked title that legitimately has a case for  the best game in the series. That it comes with a pretty solid prequel is just a bonus.The first AAI is decent, if on the lower end of the series in terms of quality. It feels a little too derivative of the PW trilogy. The music sounds a little too close, Kay is a little too much like Maya (although still likeable) and it doesn't really kick into  high gear late-game like the others do. Still, it's novel playing as a prosecutor even if not a ton has changed about the gameplay flow, and the cases focus much more on the overall structure of the law in the series which is a unique twist on things. It's also fun having Edgeworth's skill simply being smarter than everyone else in the room rather than relying on anything supernatural.AAI2, however, is incredible. Getting to be on both sides of the hero/villain fence has given Edgeworth more character development than anyone else in the series, and all of it pays off in AAI2. The best AA games interweave all of the cases together, and here that's done by utilizing Edgeworth's past, often only touched on in prior entries. The game juxtaposes his present insecurity regarding the role of the prosecutor in AA's oddball legal system with his father's time as a defense attorney, and it's an incredibly interesting conflict. Calling back heavily to his portrayal in earlier titles, by the end of the game Edgeworth becomes the most fully-realized character in the series, with the only comp being Phoenix himself (and PW doesn't really come close imo.)AAI2 also has the best Pursuit theme in the series don't @ me

_childDocuments_.review: I'm still playing through the first of two games but as someone who has played all of the mainline Ace attorney games this is turning out to be one of my favorites. I think at times the investigative phases of the mainline games would drag on and be a little sluggish to get through, but were saved by the high action and twists in the courtroom. Ace Attorney Investigations finds an interesting middle ground, making the investigative phases more interactive with courtroom elements from the mainline games at the cost of having more condensed cases overall. If I had to put it in a different way, the lows and highs of Phoenix Wright games are more extreme, while Ace Attorney Investigations appears to have a more consistently good and sometimes great experience. Will update as my opinion changes as I play through the cases ahead, but I do wholeheartedly recommend this game so far!

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely worth buying for any big fans of the mainline Ace Attorney games, especially if you have recently finished a playthrough of the original trilogy. I had never beaten the first Investigations fully before this collection came out, and the second entry was new to me as well. Having played them both to completion now, I'll say a few things about each game (no spoilers).Investigations 1 is not a great Ace Attorney game. In fact, I'd say it's easily one of my least favorite games in the series, though I haven't played Dual Destinies, Spirit of Justice or the Professor Layton crossover. It has its charming moments for sure, and I like the various cameos from characters introduced in the original trilogy.However, there is almost ZERO emotional core in this game; the underlying story beneath all of the cases is just not that memorable or interesting when all is said and done, and the way the game plays out just doesn't allow for many dramatic moments that feel on par with the first four games in the franchise. I do think Investigations 1 had a lot of potential, especially with the setup for the final case, but this is squandered by some pretty horrendous pacing and questionable writing decisions. If you've beaten the game, I'm mainly referring to .My main criticism of this game is that there was seemingly VERY little QA testing done with the new localization, because there are a ton of pretty obvious typos/errors in dialogue, and that difference in translation quality is jarring coming from the first game where there were basically no errors (at least that I noticed). This obviously isn't a massive issue, but it was enough to make me at least a little disappointed that more care didn't go into the new release. There are threads in the game's Steam forums pointing out many of these typos that I'd like to think Capcom would notice and use to patch all the errors they left in, but I'm not holding my breath unfortunately.I also think the game's "Mind Chess" gimmick is pretty uninteresting. I like that they tried something new for the second spinoff, but it really doesn't add anything or serve to make investigations more fun.All that aside, overall, Investigations 2 is great. For years, the consensus I've seen is that this is one of the best games in the franchise alongside T&T and TGAA2, and I think that's a pretty accurate assessment. However, I do think it is a little overrated and I'd personally rank both of those other games higher. That said, I2 is still a high point for Ace Attorney and the fact that I feel it's overrated is probably in large part because I had unrealistic expectations from hearing people praise it endlessly for the better part of a decade.

_childDocuments_.review: I think many people will enjoy this collection, but I didn't really enjoy this one too much.This spin-off of Ace Attorney series took the boring part of the games (investigations), and made it worse. Then removed the good part of the games (courtroom sequences), and replaced them with much inferior arguments. I never enjoyed the investigation sections that much, but I let them be, knowing they lead to fun and exciting courtroom battles. Also, the investigations often were quite linear, but they had twist and turns and reveals for the upcoming trial. Investigations in AAI are almost always locked to a single room, and they are just limited to click on everything and talk to everyone. There is not much story development that takes place during those sections. Sometimes my investigations would end up with me looking at "This has nothing to do with investigation" object, because that was the last checkmark to click.Also, the creators had this big gimmick of "you can walk". But I don't think it brought anything of value to the games. Now "walking Edgeworth" is just glorified cursor, that is less precise than the cursor in the previous games. It seems like there wasn't much budget for those sprites to, as most NPCs have only 1 pose and 0 frames of animation. Even the final boss of the last game only has 2 poses, each static with no animation. There are no chase sequences, no moving objects like in Ghost Trick to make this perspective actually matter for solving mysteries. It looks cool, but it's pretty much useless.AAI comes with a mechanic called logic, where you gather "things to think about", and then connect 2 of them to move the investigation along. I like the idea of this system, but it has two huge problems. First of all - it's all to easy. You are connecting things so obvious it's not even worth connecting. You might have "Miles is breathing" and "Breathing people are alive", and you'll connect them to discover "Miles is alive". Furthermore, the interface and investigations are build in a way where you can't have more than 6 items in this menu at once. So even if connections were too obvious, at worst case you'll have 1 in 5 chance to get it right. Sometimes this logic system is used for "hype" moments, where Miles will suddenly remember some minor things from the past and be able to "connect the pieces" to turn his thinking around, but each time this happened I have figured out those things hours before the "hype" moment. That's another issue I had, especially with the first game, where the cases were just much too obvious and easy.AAI2 brings another mechanic into the game - Mind Chess. Here you select options with time limit, and try to get the information out of the person you're talking with. It's my second most disliked mechanic in the series, with only Perceive being worse. First of all, time limit for choosing answers doesn't make sense in AA series. Furthermore, I never "got it". I always felt like I was brute forcing the answers until I got it right. Edgeworth would say something "watch his reactions, don't push when he is agitated", and I wouldn't push because I would think the person is agitated... and that was wrong at some point. This wouldn't be so bad if each mistake didn't put you at the root of the discussion. So to get back where you were you have to go trough every dialogue on the way, which can sometimes be 4 or 5 options to chose and A LOT of talking between each option(which you'll fast forward, but it's stupid anyway). Very often you'll chose an option, and then after 2-3 GOOD answers you'll hear Edgey say "nope, I dunno what to say", and you'll have to go to other path, get a clue, and then go again trough the same 2-3 answers. It's all so badly done, I didn't find it exciting, but boring.Now, between each investigation your "opponent" will come, and you'll discuss with them your findings. The problem is, those discussions are bad. Everyone talks and acts as if they were in court... but they aren't. I couldn't find those dialogues convincing at all. And because the investigation gives you all the clues for very small part of the case, and you're then asked about the same things you just found out, it all feels like pop quiz "did you learn last lesson". Furthermore, despite being chief prosecutor at the time, Edgey constantly "can't investigate" for some random reason, and hours upon hours are wasted on Edgey convincing the other party to allow him investigate. It got old quickly.Second game has some subplot about taking away Edgeworth's badge for... not being excellent? I don't know, because no actual accusations were ever put against Edgeworth. It felt to me like another "Dark age of the law", where cool sounding words were glued together to sound important, but there was no rhyme or reason behind theme.The second game improves upon the first one, but also becomes more bloated. The cases are very, very, very long. Twice as long as they should be with the amount of actual mystery they have. Both games also try to connect every case in the game into one big internationak scandal. This sounds good in theory, but the scandals are underwhelming. And because the games try to connect everything too much and build around the big mystery it falls flat. That said there are good things in this game. Fay is one of the best assistants in the series (too bad she is missing in many cases). Last 3 cases in the second game are good. They were a reason why I considered thumbs up despite all the issues I've listed. But in the end I don't think they saved this collection.As a package this is also very good. It has everything you might need - chapter select, gallery, achievements with built-in guide where to get them, autoplay mode, sprite viewer, music player. The menus are done very well.Also the walking sprites were drawn from scratch for this version (you can still use pixel art ones if you want). The new sprites are great, and I believe they have more frames of animation. That doesn't help that much, since most characters can't even move.There are also tons of cameos of well known characters from the original trilogy. AAI2 has a lot of references to AA2. It brings a bit of smile to the player, but you can't save a title with just referencing other good things. Honestly, I've played the big top case from second game, often seen as the worst case in the series, and I had more fun with any of the cases in this collection. I've played it as a break from AAI2, so that showed to me... how this style of game doesn't mesh with me too much.I think you might still enjoy it if you love investigation sections in original games. Also, if you really, really love Edgeworth and Gumshoe. I don't think those games are bad, they are just not something I can recommend to others with good conscience.

_childDocuments_.review: I have a strange relationship with the Ace Attorney series. On one hand, I do admire the original game and the rest of the two titles in the original trilogy have lots of wonderful moments as well. On the other – I’m not a fan of the ration between adventuring and visual novel storytelling they ever had, very heavily leaning into walls of text and sacrificing gameplay logic over plot twists. That’s the main reason why I stopped playing a couple of hours into The Great Ace Attorney Chronicles as it bored me to tears and I’ve never bothered with the second trilogy either. Which is why I wasn’t sure if I should give Ace Attorney Investigations Collection a go. But after playing the demo and discovering to my relief that this game, as the name implies, is far more into investigative adventuring than the other titles, I gave it a go. And I’m glad I did, as Ace Attorney Investigations: Miles Edgeworth is easily the most enjoyable entry in the series I’ve played. And it will probably be the last one I ever finish.If you’re unfamiliar with Ace Attorney series, they are titles that combine light adventuring elements and visual novel-style storytelling to bring a rather unique experience of a court room drama. All the rest of the titles in the series are focused almost exclusively on said drama itself, with occasional investigative bits that are entirely linear and extremely primitive. So most of the time is spent on cross-examining someone’s testimonies in court and presenting correct evidence to highlight contradictions in them. Which, as I’ve mentioned already, involves way too much expository talking for my personal liking, as the games feel far more like barely interactive storybooks than adventure games. The original trilogy is still quite fun, especially the first game, but for all the fun twists and funny moments, the further the games went, the more they decided to sacrifice fun adventure elements in favor of guessing correct inputs to move plot forward, even if it’s not always logical. And the plot itself went from over the top and silly, to completely absurd and obnoxiously overcomplicated.Ace Attorney Investigations breaks away from this approach. Instead of ditching the investigative part, the games (or, well, the first one at least) focuses a lot more on them, providing relatively simple, but genuinely engaging investigative gameplay where you examine the crime scenes, question the witnesses and suspects and connect clues. If you’ve played any of the titles that focus on the similar things, be it Sherlock Holmes titles, Detective Grimoire series or something like L.A. Noire, you know what to expect in general. It’s just somewhat simplified, without (at least usually) holding your hand and still providing the excitement from discovering hidden connections that may change your understanding of the case. Cross-examining testimonies is still present as well, but this time outside of the court setting and is used to bring out new information out of someone who intentionally or accidentally lied, or putting a criminal in a spot where they might reveal who they are to the surrounding crowd of witnesses, making the job of the police easier.And given that the only game in the collection that I’ve completed is the first one (I’ll talk about the second when we get there),  I have to say that Ace Attorney Investigations: Miles Edgeworth is worth the purchase of the collection alone. It’s not without its flaws, for example the final case lasts way too long and becomes increasingly more absurd and convoluted as it goes. But even that one has strong moments and in general the flow of the game and its story is perfectly delivered. It makes sense, nothing feels too absurd to ruin the gameplay process, cases are interesting (even if they are way too reliant on murder) and vast majority of the logic checks are indeed logical and not of the “guess what the developer was thinking” kind. It’s better enjoyed if you do play the original trilogy of games first as some of the references and returning characters work much better with that knowledge. But it’s not like the original trilogy wasn’t worth playing on its own anyway, so you might as well do it. This isn’t Ghost Trick: Phantom Detective – that adventure game is beyond fantastic, while this one is just very very good. But it’s worth experiencing if you like investigation focused titles or like the Ace Attorney series.Then I started playing Ace Attorney Investigations 2: Prosecutor’s Gambit and gave up in the middle of the second case. Apart from adding a horrendous new mechanic of “mind chess”, which might be the worst “dialogue battle”-type mini-game I’ve ever experienced in my life, this title just starts with the clown makeup half-applied, and rapidly continues to become a farce by the end of the first case. It’s incredibly stupid, throws several logic-defying “logic checks” at you from the get go, makes several characters that worked so well in the previous game unbearable and then somehow keeps getting even worse as it goes. It also seems to have almost entirely decided to ditch the focus of the investigation in favor of the mind-chess and testimonies, as while investigating still happens, it takes far less time then the talking bits. So after I realized that the game is actively irritating me and doesn’t plan on stopping, I quit it and doubt that I will ever return to finish it.That said, as I’ve already mentioned, this collection could be not a collection but just Ace Attorney Investigations: Miles Edgeworth and I would’ve still said that it’s worth buying. Maybe not for the full price… but I honestly can’t say that it’s not worth that price, even if you would just play one of two games. It’s a shame that the series are, in general, not really my thing. And reactions from other people to the second game that I couldn’t stomach were quite positive from the fans of the franchise… So I guess, if you’re like me, just like a good adventure game and Ace Attorney never clicked with you before – the first game in the collection might be exactly what you’re looking for. Thankfully, you can try the demo to see for yourself if you want to get it. But I’m glad that I did.

A new script for the second game with all-new character names will take some time to get used to for veteran players like myself who played the fan translation prior to this official localisation. _childDocuments_.review: Miles Edgeworth here.  Yes, the Miles Edgeworth.  I trust this review finds you well, and in good spirits.  As you may know, I am not one for frivolous displays of enthusiasm, but even I must admit a certain degree of...excitement regarding the release of the  on Steam.  This is not merely a port, my esteemed colleagues; it is a meticulously crafted compilation of two exceptional titles that were previously confined to the Nintendo DS.  Now, with enhanced visuals and a host of refined features, these gems are poised to shine brighter than ever before.While I hold a certain respect for Phoenix Wright and his...unorthodox methods, I believe it is high time that the spotlight shifted to a more refined practitioner of the law.  That is to say, myself.  This collection allows you to step into my impeccably polished shoes and experience the thrill of justice from the prosecutor's perspective.  Prepare to delve into two captivating adventures where I trade the courtroom for the crime scene, utilizing my keen intellect and unwavering logic to unravel the truth. introduces a novel gameplay dynamic to the series.  Forget the tedious back-and-forth of courtroom cross-examinations.  Here, you will immerse yourself in the very heart of the investigation, meticulously examining crime scenes, gathering crucial evidence, and confronting suspects with the full force of your deductive prowess.  The "logic" system is a particularly ingenious addition, allowing you to connect seemingly disparate clues and construct irrefutable chains of reasoning.  The satisfaction of cornering a suspect with an expertly executed "Logic Chess" combo is truly unparalleled.This collection is a veritable treasure trove for any discerning investigator.  It includes both  and its exceptional sequel, .  Each game boasts a unique and compelling storyline, populated by unforgettable characters (ahem, Kay Faraday, you are a credit to the detective's profession), intricate mysteries, and shocking twists that will challenge even the most astute observer.  And for the first time,  allowing international fans to finally experience this previously elusive gem.Capcom has not simply ported these games to Steam; they have meticulously refined them.  The visuals are crisp and vibrant, with high-resolution graphics that bring the characters and environments to life with unprecedented clarity.  And the soundtrack?  Ah, the soundtrack.  Those iconic melodies have been remastered to perfection, immersing you in the world of investigation with a renewed sense of depth and atmosphere.This collection is replete with quality-of-life improvements that streamline the gameplay experience.  Features like chapter select, autoplay, and story mode allow you to tailor your investigative approach to your preferences.  Whether you wish to savor every line of dialogue or focus solely on the thrill of the investigation, these features provide a welcome degree of flexibility.I must confess, I am...rather fond of this collection.  It is a testament to the enduring appeal of logic, deduction, and the pursuit of truth.  But even if you are not a seasoned veteran of the courtroom, I assure you, this is an excellent entry point into the world of .  The  is a masterclass in game design, storytelling, and sheer entertainment.  It offers everything a discerning player could desire:  intriguing mysteries, compelling characters, witty dialogue, and gameplay that will keep you engaged until the very end.  So, my esteemed colleagues, what are you waiting for?  Sharpen your minds, don your finest attire, and prepare to experience the thrill of justice alongside Miles Edgeworth.Hey there, chum!  Mr. Edgeworth might be all about that "logic and deduction" stuff, but let's be real, this collection is just plain fun!  The mysteries are super cool, the characters are quirky and hilarious, and the whole thing is just bursting with personality.  Plus, you get to hang out with yours truly, Kay Faraday, the Yatagarasu!  So what are you waiting for?  Let's go catch some crooks!Aw yeah, pal!  This collection is the real deal!  It's got everything a detective could ask for:  crime scenes, evidence, and even a little bit of romance (if you know what I mean, pal).  Mr. Edgeworth might be a bit stiff sometimes, but he's got a good heart, and he always gets the job done.  So don't miss out on this awesome collection, pal!  It's worth every penny!

_childDocuments_.review: The ace attorney collection series returns. This time bringing with us a spin off series focused on Miles Edgeworth, in these games you step into the investigation shoes and try to solve crimes. All of this sounds very new and shiny but these games at their core are still ace attorney games, instead of arguing with people in the court room you are doing it outside of the court room and more time gets spent into investigating scenarios. So how do these games compare to the mainline games and is it worth your time?In general they have the quality you would expect from these games, they sound great, have incredible character design, and they present interesting puzzles to constantly think about. These are also REALLY long cases so even though its only 2 games you still have a ton of content to explore. One really fun addition they added are new sprites, you can play with  the original pixelated style or new HD drawn characters, its something they didn't need to do but it adds so much more character to these games. I personally preferred and loved the HD style. They also did an excellent job with the arranged tracks that you could get for pre-ordering the game. The only drop in quality I noticed was in investigations 2, this is the first time the game has gotten a proper localization, but its also the first time I took issue with some of the translation work in this series. There are spellings mistakes from time to time and some sentences didn't feel finished. I also noticed there is a weird bug where my controller would input 2 times when I only clicked 1 time, I would have to restart the game daily to make it go away (playing on Playstation 5 controller). Its nothing game breaking and the rest of the localization is great but those mistakes are worth noting.Besides these aspects, the most important thing in an ace attorney game is the story. Good or bad writing makes or breaks these games, and the writer of the original trilogy is not involved in these games. This originally made me worried the writing would be bare bones like in some of the later ace attorney games, but I am happy to say that these games manage to tell compelling stories.I felt like these games did an excellent job showcasing off a different side of the world of ace attorney. You are investigating a lot more and as a result you also end up meeting with people that are mostly irrelevant to some of these cases, its fun to see some characters again from previous cases/games and I feel like the new perspective makes for more immersive investigations. You can really explore how a crime scene is put together and that also makes you think about about how something could have been done.That being said I will say that Investigations 2 is miles (Hehe) better then investigations 1. To me it felt like investigations 1 was formulaic. Every case felt like the same song and dance, a lot of the twists were VERY predictable, the discussion you need to have feel nonsensical and most frustrating of all are that I often felt like there were filler sections to make the game seem longer. I would often have already been 3 steps ahead of what the game wanted me to do, as a result a lot of the evidence I had to select didn't feel logical at all to me. I still could enjoy 1 from time to time, but I was also bored for most of the game, sadly this game feels like a requirement before you get to dive into investigations 2. A lot of the open plot points get continued in 2 and you won't understand a lot of character motivation by skipping 1.Investigations 2 is a master piece and in my opinion is able to compete with some of the best in the series like ace attorney 3 or the great ace attorney collection. I love so many of the characters like Eustace Winner or Eddie Fender. I love how wild some of these cases are and how they allow us to explore the main cast in such an interesting way. I love how it explores what justice really is and what the roles of the defense and the prosecution entail. I love how it explores time in a way the series has never done before. Only the first case in this game bored me, the rest of these cases are long but I never lost interest in them. I constantly felt like I needed to know what would happen next and if my theories were correct or not. It manages to hide just enough information to keep you guessing but also allows you to figure out the puzzle on your own. Its not perfect, there are moments where I feel like im playing investigations 1 again or that the plot is so absurd that I feel its extremely unrealistic even for ace attorney. But in the end you get left with a collection of cases that feel like nothing the ace attorney series has done before, it feels fresh, engaging and as a result its become one of my favorite games in the series.I think its clear that I loved the 2nd game and just for that I will recommend this collection. I would usually not recommend the first game but its enjoyable enough and I think the 2nd game feels like a much better game because it builds off of so much that the first game set up. If you somehow are considering this for your first Ace attorney game then I would first recommend you at least play Ace Attorney 1, so much of this game is exploring who Miles Edgeworth is, the introduction of who he is in these games starts in that game. If you are planning to play the entire series then I would recommend playing this between the first and second trilogy, but honestly this feels separate enough that you can play it whenever you want. If you want more ace attorney or want a mystery visual novel then this is an excellent purchase. Overall this is an easy recommend from me.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, I would like to mention that I wrote this review after completing only two cases in the first game in the collection. However, I played these two games when they originally came out on the DS which was... many years ago. Still, I have fond memories of these games. Many years have passed since then, and I forgot some plot elements, so it is nice to experience them again. It feels like new.Chronologically, they (most of the time) take place between the first three games (featured in Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney Trilogy) and the second trilogy of games (Apollo Justice: Ace Attorney Trilogy). While overall this collection can be experienced without playing the other games, there are some nods to the characters of the first trilogy. Some even return as side or background characters. Naturally, the protagonist's - Miles Edgeworth's - story is continued as well. So I would recommend playing this after completing the first trilogy if you want to understand everything in order. It makes the experience so much better.Since I played all Ace Attorney games back in the day on the DS (even the Layton crossover), I can say that these Edgeworth games are one of my favorites in the series. Of course, I have a little character bias, because I consider Edgeworth's character and his character development the best in the whole series. Not only that though, I like the shift in the gameplay as well. Here, you can actually walk around the scene of the crime and investigate things as well as talk to witnesses. For me, that made the games more immersive. Of course, you could do that in the other games as well, but in a more "visual novel-y" style.It is also a nice port, the graphics are glorious in 4k. The added extras in the menu are also neat.Overall, thank you Capcom for porting these (and the other AA games) to the PC. Now, we need more games featuring Edgeworth as the main character :-)

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Investigations 1, but felt like it was missing a certain je ne sais quoi that makes the original Ace Attorney trilogy—and the second trilogy, to a lesser extent—feel like Ace Attorney games.There are both upsides and downsides to the aspects that make Investigations different from the mainline Ace Attorney games. The new protagonist of Miles Edgeworth feels more competent and in-control than Phoenix Wright, but has less possibility space for comedic inner thoughts and interactions with other characters; his secretive Steel Samurai fanboying and some of his reactions to other characters' ridiculous antics were funny, but despite seeming more serious than Phoenix, the latter was less prevalent. In fact, overall, humor seems much less of a focus for Investigations compared to the mainline games, and, for me, it was sorely missed.The side characters were hit-and-miss, too. Lablanc from the second case was a major highlight: I loved his broken English and haughty, impatient attitude and how Edgeworth reacted to his persistence. It was also fun to see Calisto Yew's uncontrollable outbursts of laughter at Miles's sesquipedalian manner of speaker. On the other hand, many of the returning characters were some of my least favorite and some of the most Flanderized of the series's recurring cast. Also, the cast of the third case was somewhat weak.I liked how the new way of interacting with the crime scenes worked. The top-down perspective made it much easier to conceptualize how the crimes were committed and made the locations feel more real—and it was simply fun to run around an actual environment rather than clicking onto a location and fading into a still 2D image. However, the rebuttal sections were not of the highest quality in the Ace Attorney games I've played. I found myself running into more situations where I accidentally got ahead of the script because I was supposed to present something to establish a fact that I thought was already accepted knowledge in Investigations than in any other Ace Attorney game, other than Justice for All, perhaps.The overarching story was interesting, too. Many of the big reveals caught me by surprise, but were exciting because they immediately made sense in hindsight. The final case is definitely the highlight of this game, as it tends to be in most Ace Attorney games (although I have a sweet spot for the second case, too). The final section of it, the confrontation with the true culprit, was perhaps a bit overlong, though, and despite the fandom's seeming love (with perhaps a dose of ironic enjoyment) for the culprit, I found them to be merely alright. Additionally, as I mentioned before, the third case was somewhat uninteresting with a boring crime, motive, cast, and culprit, and the first case was slightly lackluster, even for an introductory case.Overall, Investigations 1 is missing a certain indescribable quality that makes the Ace Attorney series special. If I had to point to what that is, I'd say, maybe the comedy? but the strength of the cast of side characters throughout all of the cases is also an option. I ultimately enjoyed Investigations 1, but it was admittedly quite dull compared to other entries in the Ace Attorney series.Miles Edgeworth: 7/10Investigations 2 is my new favorite Ace Attorney game.The only complaints I have about it—that it has somewhat of a slow start (at least comparing the intensity of the final two cases to the first three) and that the comedy is still less prevalent than in the mainline games (although not to the same extent as Investigations 1)—are minor and negligible.Despite (barely) having a somewhat slow start, the first three cases of Investigations 2 are all top-notch. None of the cases in this game are noticeably worse than the others, unlike the second and third cases from Dual Destinies, the fourth case from Spirit of Justice, or the third case from Investigations 1. And for their respective case positions within the game (first, second, third), each of them has a strong argument for being a "best in slot" pick.The most notable quality of these cases—and Investigations 2 as a whole—is that it feels like there is not a single wasted moment within them. Within every 30 minutes of playtime, there is some new revelation that turns the current case on its head. (I don't care as much as others about the criticism of Apollo Justice's cases as being logically unsound, but I could appreciate how airtight the logic of the crimes in Investigations 2 seemed.) The pacing of this story is impeccable. The last two cases especially had me on the edge of my seat the whole time, anxiously anticipating the next turn the investigation would take.Investigation 2's thematic elements were also much more refined compared to the first game. Investigations 1 liked to constantly mention how Edgeworth's philosophy on his role as a lawyer had shifted from striving for perfection to uncovering the truth, even if it means losing, but its approach towards doing so mostly relied on telling rather than showing. Investigations 2 is similar in how it focuses on this change in Edgeworth's philosophy, but does so in a much more natural way. The story puts Edgeworth into a number of situations that actually test his morals and require him to put very important things on the line in order to show that he is now more committed to truth rather than winning.There's also a smaller motif of the relationship between parents (primarily fathers) and children in Investigations 2. The story has a fairly nuanced take on the lessons that can be taken by children from observing their parents' lives. It takes neither extreme position—that a parents' lessons should be entirely embraced or entirely rejected—but rather suggests that children should critically analyze each aspect of their parents and choose which parts to keep and which parts to discard.Overall, Investigations 2 is better than the first in every way. Its mysteries are better, its pacing is quick but not overwhelming and nary a moment is wasted, and its themes are handled much more elegantly. Investigations 2 knew what story it wanted to tell and what messages it wanted to deliver, and executed both (almost) flawlessly.Prosecutor's Gambit: 10/10While Investigations 1 is lackluster compared to other Ace Attorney games, Investigations 2 is well worth the price of admission. It executes on its vision incredibly well, making it my new favorite Ace Attorney game and worth playing through the just-okay Investigations 1 in order to experience it.Miles Edgeworth: 7/10Prosecutor's Gambit: 10/10Whole Collection: 9/10

AAI2 will always be my favorite in the entire series without a doubt.I am extremely elated that this collection as a whole is very high quality. _childDocuments_.review: While AAI 1 certainly has some issues regarding pacing, it was always my favourite Ace Attorney game back in the day. Naturally, re-playing it 15 years later was a joy with beautiful HD graphics.Since AAI 2 never was released outside of Japan and I didn't play the fan translation, this was a complete new experience for me. And, oh boy, was it a ride. In my opinion, AAI 2 is the best Ace Attorney game as I already was a fan of the first game, and it tops AAI 1 in almost every aspect. The game had no filler cases, and closed the story without any plot holes. It took me about 40 hours to complete it, and every single one of them was enjoyable.If you like the Ace Attorney franchise, be sure to pick up this collection. It's completely worth the price tag of 40 EUR.
_childDocuments_.name: Ace Attorney Investigations Collection

_childDocuments_.review: The Investigations Collection is a fantastic HD port of one solid game and one amazing game that together tells one of the best stories in the entire Ace Attorney series of games. The HD sprite artwork is fantastic, and sets a far better aesthetic standard for the series going forward than the ugly, made-for-handheld 3D models used in Dual Destines and Spirit of Justice. The collections run perfectly on both PC and Steamdeck and I've had no trouble with running them at my monitors native refresh rate and resolution (165hz/1440p). As for the games themselves, it's a bit more subjective but the takeaway I'd want to give is this; while the first Investigations game is only *good*, AAI2: Prosecutor's Gambit is a high point for the series not seen since the original trilogy and manages to tell a story that one could argue tops even the original game and Trials and Tribulations. If you are an Ace Attorney fan, it is truly unmissable. I'd say you could get through both games here in around 40 hours (I took my time). Really hope they continue down this path and expand on the Investigations format and the series as a whole.

_childDocuments_.review: Spending 62 hours to finish both AAI and AAI2, it is a really nice experience. Before playing AAI series, I have played all the other games of Ace Attorney series, and I am absolutely the fan of Ace Attorney. Because I love the rest of games of the series, once AAI can be pre-ordered, I purchased it with no hesitation.For the game content, the new versions of chibi sprite are really really nice and delicate, which can definitely show the efforts of developer team. Meanwhile, the story and characters are also awesome, and Edgeworth is a better protagonist than Apollo and Athena from my point of view. I also like Shi-Long Lang very much, whose kindness towards his followers attracts me a lot. In general, I like AAI series more than Apollo trilogy and Great Ace Attorney series. The story of AAI2 is more interesting than AAI, but AAI is also a great game with lots of turnabouts. I highly recommend people who have finished and like Ace Attorney Phoenix Trilogy to play this investigation series, where you can find a lot of familiar faces, too.
_childDocuments_.name: Ace Attorney Investigations Collection

_childDocuments_.review: To sum the rest of this review up, these two games are absolutely excellent titles in the Ace Attorney series and a must-play for anyone who enjoyed the other games. Both games mix up the Ace Attorney formula a bit by not actually occurring inside the courtroom (for the most part), but in turn spice up the investigation portion by giving you the ability to actually walk around the crime scene and make deductions yourself. These games are more fast paced than other mainline entries, and I don't ever recall being particularly stuck on any investigation section unlike what happens in a few cases of other Ace Attorney games. I definitely missed the courtroom sections from other games, but you still retain the gameplay of those for the most part, since you will often listen to testimony and issue rebuttals (essentially just cross-examination). Overall, the gameplay is both familiar enough to be fun for any Ace Attorney fan, but different feeling enough to stand out from the rest.As for story, both games have excellent cases and characters, and I would rate many cases among the best in the entire series. I definitely must say that, in my opinion at least, the second game of the collection is by far stronger in terms of both overall story and character development. I won't spoil anything specific, but the second game spends a lot of time fleshing out Edgeworth as a character as he moves through the events of the game. I'm glad that Capcom released this collection, because before this the second game was never officially translated into English, which is a crying shame. I concede that I never played the fan translation, which I have heard is excellent, but I am nonetheless glad we finally have an official release of the game outside of Japan. This collection is absolutely worth playing for Ace Attorney fans both for more Ace Attorney kino in general, but also the great character development we see in classic characters like Edgeworth and Gumshoe. If nothing else in this review convinces you, please play these games so you can witness Gumshoe's finest hours.
