_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good game.You control huge mechs and fight alien robots and mechs to protect what remains of Earth. Battles are very short, few minutes long generally (some of those you overlevel can be completed in just 10 seconds). There are a lot of customization options and a lot of things to collect/craft/upgrade. There are several types of battles, like challenges, farming, repeated story, extra fights, bosses, conquest (set of battles with extra bonuses after each one resulting in a huge boss fight), pvp. Several weapon types - 5 melee, 4 ranged with their own special abilities. Several types of huge attacks.At the end new difficulty unlocks for some boss battles which requires a ton of investments to progress in. So it will be a while before you complete everything the game has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: There is a lot of game here.  Like, ridiculous amount/  Core Gameplay is similiar to small scale Musou game, fairly simple, though there is a Weakness system that rewards you for matching elements and attack types.  Lots of stuff to collect and unlock. Ridiculous number of missions.  Decent enemy and weapon variation, with the meat being the wide variety of special attacks.The most interesting thing is probably the story.  Much deeper than you'd expect, and ridiculously long.  The most interesting aspect is that the game leans into Tropes as a kind of shorthand, keeping the plot moving without getting bogged down in repetitive scenes.  It still manages to do character development at the same time.  I'm not sure its style of storytelling will work for everyone, but for me, its a big plus to the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game plays a lot like Gundam Breaker 3.  If you don't know that game, its a bit of Dynasty Warriors and armored core.  Fast paced, almost arcade like combat engine with Armored Core tier customisation and a genuinely good story straight out of a super robot anime series.  But the main draw, like in Gundam Breaker, is grinding for top tier parts and weapons for your mechs, then limit breaking, levelling, and customising them.  The game has plenty of optional missions to help you grind levels, parts, weapons, and pilot points.  But those optional missions are always the same.  Beat some grunts, beat some more grunts, another grunt rush or two, then boss battle.  Maybe two.  Or just a straight boss rush.  Leveling up is done via a system much like FFX's sphere grid, and also by swapping out higher level parts and leveling up your pilot abilities.  The game knows its audience, and the audience knows what they like.  So one look at the trailer and a few reviews should tell you if this game is for you.  The game really does do what they marketing says it does, and does it with spirit and style.

_childDocuments_.review: Story:In short, it's the typical humans versus aliens with a focus on providing the good and bad of each side. The main story follows the typical trope of a classic Super Robot story with characters that fit each trope. Yamato for example is the hot blooded character that jumps straight into action. If you're into anime (which I'm not), then you might find some interest in the story. However, if you like big giant mechs, you can likely forget everything and focus on the gameplay. From what I understand, the game follows the anime's two seasons with some extra content in the end. Unfortunately, since I find many anime tropes to be annoying, it was hard to enjoy the characters. Due to the bias, I don't think it would be fair to critique the characters.You do have the option to skip the story, so if you just want to grind through the game without the need to go through the story, you can.Gameplay:This game is a glorified looter RPG with mechs. You figure out a build that works with your mech, and you roll with it. Like burn damage? Make a build that procs burn damage and adds more damage when an enemy suffers from the ailment. The game has enough options to make building your mechs better. The gameplay can feel fast paced and the weapon variety is enough to make each weapon feel different. You can equip up to 6 weapons at a time (3 melee, 3 ranged) Dual Blades are quick and combo easily while Greatswords are slow. Like in Monster Hunter, mech parts you gain from battle may not essentially be optimal for a certain build, so you might find your mech more on the ugly side. Luckily, you can have "layered" armor through customizing your mech and select parts that you have in your inventory to make sure your mech looks great. You can also add decals. You can even repaint the part to ensure you're looking fancy. However, you're unable to do it with the licensed mechs. (Getter Robo, Mazinger, Voltes, Combattler).The game poops out a LOT of equipment during each mission. So if this is overwhelming for you, make sure you set filters that will automatically filter out equipment. During my game play, I have it set so that it filters out item quality up to epic and for items that are a level below my current rank. (The problem is that by setting it by your current rank, you will need to continuously update it since it filters by actual rank and not by a specific level range).There's a lot of customizing and upgrading in this game, which can be overwhelming. Luckily, if you're playing the game for story, builds won't matter much, because it's an easy game. The real gameplay is in the game's side missions and challenges. There's even "raid" style battles and PVP options which adds to the variety.Unfortunately, outside of the mech piloting, the game feels very flat. You essentially fast travel to each location, go through the story, and eventually go into a story battle. Quests given by NPCs feel pointless outside of ones that give you more customization options. You'll normally unlock a room that you couldn't access before which gives you another place to pick up items from the ground. GraphicsIt's serviceable. Some textures look dated (Due to the original release coming out for older consoles), but it's not bad. It has a charm to it. The 2D characters look nice and sharp, but the environment itself will look bland, especially in battle. Due to this, the game should essentially run on older computers and will run well on the steam deck.Originally, the game was a freemium game. It kind of shows itself as one when you play. Battles can feel short and there's things such as login bonuses, passes, and a lot of features you find in a freemium game. the usable items in the game are things that boost your exp/item drop rates, revive you. Again, very common freemium items but this time, without the need to pay. Sound:The music is quite forgettable. From what I remember with Level-5, whenever they develop a game for a bigger company, the scores for the game are a lot better due to budget. So it wouldn't be fair to compare this game's music with the original Ni No Kuni for example. There's a song that is meant to invoke emotion out of you, but it didn't really do much for me during the scene.Weapons may sound like an 80s mecha anime, which is a good touch. Steam Deck:Assuming once the steam deck status shows up, the game might pass as "playable" since there's some options to rename mechs that will require the steam keyboard. However, it's pretty much a plug and play game without any requirement to alter anything with your deck. With missions lasting a few minutes, it's a great option. However, battery will drain fast, so you might want to play with battery settings to get the most game time. Otherwise, I wouldn't be surprised if this game was verified.OverallI really enjoy the game and the amount of endgame content tickles my fancy for looter RPGs. There's a good amount of dopamine if that's what you're into. Unfortunately, the story and map traversal are weak parts of the game and with missions being short, the actual story may feel like a drag. If however, you can get through that, there's a lot of gameplay to be had once you go through all the side content. Just like Diablo, I'm here for the loot and see how I can use the build to mop the floor with the end game content. Due to this, you can easily lose many hours of your life grinding for gear which helps justify the price point with hours of gameplay.TLDR: Play for the game play, not for the story.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: This game is far more fun than it had any right to be and I am all here for it! Delightfully fun hack n slash reminiscent of the gundam breaker series. Absolutely the most fun I have had in a long while and it will tide me over till gundam breaker 4 comes out! Simple systems but a deeper build system that helps fit to your play style. Not super serious, complete with super anime feeling in the cutscenes in the VN parts of the game. Story isn't super deep or crazy but it is entertaining. However if you are just there for mecha, it won't even matter. 100% best value for a mecha game. Replay value as well with the grind for better gear for your playstyle. Tried co-op, seems to work fine via steam x steam matches. Have not tried PvP yet. If you stream it, do be aware it will trigger a music content warning......Other than that, have fun and smash those aliens!As a big mecha fan in general....9/10 Adjust accordingly if you are not XD

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting for this game to be localized since it came out on the Switch in 2021, now that it has the wait has been worth it. It contains all the content that has released so far except for Grendizer which got skipped over for some reason, maybe licensing issues.This is not comparable to Armored Core, this is very much more of a hack and slash game with plenty of Super Robo fanservice. I've only completed up to the end of the initial base game and started what can be considered 'season 2' and it definitely has all the tropes of a Super Robot anime combined in it. We got (both literally and figuratively) Getter, Mazinger, and a dash of Gurren Lagann flavors mixed in here.Please don't let Level 5 contain this much kino in Japan only again.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredibly tokusatsu with the mech designs, the campy plotlines and increasingly ridiculous special attacks. It really should be emphasized that the combat is very smooth and just feels good. There is also a good amount of customization available and ties into the games 'looter' feel that lets you make your units pretty distinct between the gear/Illegal Modifications/pilot skills/motherboard tuning/special attack selection/research/etc. Even better in how (in singleplayer) you bring in a squad of 3 so you can have the different specialized builds that you can freely swap between during a missionMy biggest criticism is that the game is definitely on the easy side although this mostly depends on how much of the non-main missions you do. Thankfully this can be offset a bit by being able to select higher difficulties for main missions if you are overleveled. Unfortunately the game's combat isn't especially deep either (compared to JRPG's like Xenoblade etc.) despite the customization options (the weapons don't feel all that different from each other). But that is fine, it is easier to overlook that when (to re-emphasize) the actual gameplay feels very good and enjoyable.Is it worth $50? I am not sure. I think it is something that if you watch the trailer and think "This game actually looks pretty fun" and enjoy a sort of campy romp and playing around with the dozens of different ridiculous special moves, then you will enjoy it. But outside of that I think generally it is something I would more suggest as being a really great $20-$30 game when it goes on sale as an mecha-action JRPG.

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of charm and heavy on the anime story telling. Combat is mid and repetitive. It's kinda like SD Gundam mixed with Gundam Breaker. Lots of content and characters, good music, well animated....If anime and mechs is your thing then you'll enjoy this, if you're looking for super mecha combat action...head over to AC6.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun spiritual successor to danball senki with very responsive controls and attack cancels on almost everything so far. There is a TON of customization to the point where it is frankly overwhelming. These customization ranges from parts to damage modifiers to how your mech's moveset/attack will function. The actual action is a mission based third person action game where it ranges to waves of enemy to a big alien.This game frontloads you the story first but the amount of story pales in comparison to the amount of missions and fights you do since they will give you so much missions to go through as side content. The story isnt bad since it is about an angry xenophobic guy named Japan and some love-hate obsession with xenos. The town is well designed and had a ton of effort put into it along with every piece of dialogue from npcs being voiced. If you dont care about the story just hit skip. Only real issue I have is the scummy day 1 dlc practice but luckily 90% of it are cosmetics and outclassed after a few missions.  The other 10% is the premium pass which isnt needed since it basically speeds up farming parts in a game about farming.Otherwise this port runs smooth and crossplay in coop/pvp has been fine. Get it if you like robots.
_childDocuments_.name: MEGATON MUSASHI W: WIRED

_childDocuments_.review: The intro theme song threw me off and I thought this was gonna be a bad game, however I guess the trend is Bad theme song, amazing game.My literal only complaint with this flawless game is that the terrible theme song is in english, but the rest of the game is voiced in Japanese. Fortunately the voice cast, animations, story and dialogue are quality.It goes from feeling like I’m watching a morning cartoon, to an enjoyable visual novel like relaxing adventure game, to a fast past action game where you customize your mech, score loot and take on arena like missions.This game is fully packed with content and its all quality. I was not expecting to like this game, but it surpassed all expectations.Side note, not a single performance problem or hitch to spoil my experience. Completely immersive from the start. 4k maxed out. I’m so happy to have finally purchased a game that works from the start.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Sit up and pay attention, all you SRW fans!  This is one you're probably going to want to check out.  It's like playing through a Super Robot anime, but one where you get to customize your own mech with various parts.  That includes, but isn't limited to, the mechs from licensed IPs like Getter Robo, Combattler V, Voltes V, and Mazinger.  Combat is a basic action-RPG affair, not super convoluted, but with a fair few options in terms of weapons and plenty of supermoves.  Basically, if Armored Core is a gritty Real Robot game, MMW is its less brutal little Super Robot brother.  Don't waste your money on the microtransactions, just get the base game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is mostly placeholder review after only few hours to boost game visibility. Cause it's that good.Still, initial impressions are great, first part of the game is never released in west Megaton Musashi for PS4/Switch, which I played a bit. Game should follow whole anime plot and afterwards, meaning there is a lot of to do and it's mostly singleplayer.Coop and vs are more of a side activities to do after or during beating main game. There is probably more to it, but it's impossible to figure out within few hours.All DLCs are cosmetic or boost your resource gathering, I doubt it'll be noticeable until mid or late game, game has system like daily logins and such, which is leftover from 2nd game which gone F2P for a bit.Seriously this game is very solid, if you like your giant robots - there is nothing like it on the market of that quality. Closest gameplay comparison would be Gundam Breaker 3 (the good one), if you didn't play Level 5 LBX games before.So please give this game a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: -Quite a bit of cut scenes as expected of these types of games (pro tip: use Auto), and lot of ground already covered for me after watching and enjoying the show when it came out. -Full list of DLC that doesn't matter (except for Jibanyan navigator he should be free, wtf L5. Also Ota-Cross from LBX, or any LBX rep for that matter). -However Game-play and customisation is top notch, the art keeps up with the anime, and if what I hear about the second half is true it just gets even better. The true conclusion to the show.From what I played so far, this is the best modern Super Robot game.Having Mazinger Z in it doesn't hurt either.

_childDocuments_.review: Im not a big mech fan to be honest (only watched Gundam and thats a stretch). I have a couple mech games on my account but only becuase the only mech game I truly got into was Gundam Breaker 3 on PS4/PS5 so I been looking for something like that. I played MechWarrior 5 and Armored Core 5 for a couple hours each (AC5 only 5hrs as of today and I bought it on release due to the hype), After trying out those games I realized Im specifically a fan of robot games but only the types with Gundam like robots. This game scratches that GB3 itch. While mech customization isnt as in depth as GB3 it definitely is pretty good. Story also looks to be interesting too. I definitely recommend it, Its worth the $50.

_childDocuments_.review: At first I did not use a Controller so my first mistake. Yes it does INGAME Have a Message that says HEAVILY ENCOURAGE USE OF A CONTROLLER. But my old setup required my to charge batteries so i tried with just mouse and keyboard...don't do that. Aside from this its abit story heavy as many of these games are. IT's not bad, just wanted to get into the game more, but the anime movie feeling is there and I did not expect the kinda visual novel kinda of wandering around the town and such being part of the game. Its good and I am only about 5 hours in. For Comparison I loved Gundam Breaker 3 and this is similar in some ways and different in others. The Controls here are good, best on controllers. There is a lot of customization and Layers to upgrade ur Robots/Rogues they are so named here. I will have to update this review as I get farther into it, trying out the controller helped a lot. Overall I had No real expectations or Knowledge of this franchise or anime going in and ID say its worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: An Anime game that feels like you are actually watching an Anime while doing the battle sequences yourself.Rarely does a game actually accomplish that feeling, This game does it with flying colours though!So this Mecha game just popped up when I was browsing the Store, Seemingly coming out of nowhere.Being completely unfamiliar with the IP I looked at some gameplay and such.It looked interesting.So what is the game like playing it myself?Perhaps you might be familiar with PSO2? Well the gameplay in it's core feels something like that.It also seems to share some artistic similairities, Damage Numbers, Loot Boxes, Sick OST.Something else really cool is the Cutscenes and attention to quality overall.Cutscenes as I was already hinting at earlier are fully animated+CG and it really makes you feel like you are watching an Anime.Performance is hard to miss for a game like this, Or rather I would be scared if it was.But the amount of polish for this port is nearly unheard of for a game like this.Perhaps even less buggy then AOT2 and from my experience that is one of the best Anime styled games on Steam.Really if you are at all interested in Mecha/Anime then this game is something you should probably at least give a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: MEGATON MUSASHI W: WIRED

_childDocuments_.review: Played it earlier on PS5, so playtime in steam is not accurate to total time.Story is anime as it gets, gameplay is solid, the loop itself can be a bit repetitive but if you're a loot goblin you'll appreciate the short mission types.It is mind numbingly easy early on, but once you start unlocking colossal battles you'll be using those healing tanks. Until you get to that point though, you'll have to slog through a few hours of single player content before co-op is viable. Still, it's a solid hack and slash mecha game, great for killing a few minutes or slaughtering a few hours.

name: Radiant Silvergun
detailed_description: ＜Story＞ July 14, 2520 AD. The light emitted by a 'stone-like object' excavated from the strata of B.C. enveloped the earth, destroying the human race. Only the four crew members of the space cruiser TETRA and one robonoid barely escaped into satellite orbit. ...... One year later. The TETRA is forced to re-enter the atmosphere because the ship's supplies have finally been depleted. The battle for the survival of the TETRA begins. ＜A highly strategic shooting game＞ The battlefield is a stage with various terrains, including intricate crevices and moving containers, where enemies attack from all directions, up, down, left, and right. Twenty-three bosses await in six highly strategic stages. There are also secret bonuses that occur when enemies are defeated in a specific order, as well as hidden score items. The key to obtaining a score is to cover all of these items, build your own original attack pattern, and accurately destroy the targeted enemies. Use weapons that level up in accordance with your score to update your high score! ＜Game Features＞ Score system specialized for the origin of shooting games. Weapons that level up as you defeat enemies. 5 difficulty levels for beginners to enjoy. Story mode with a strong message. Beautiful 3D graphics. Sound that colors the game world by Hitoshi Sakimoto, who is highly acclaimed both in Japan and overseas. Game mode with the rules of 'Ikaruga,' the second installment of Project RS. CLASSIC / MODERN mode that can be enjoyed with different viewing angles for SegaSaturn version and XboxLiveArcade version. Compatible with keyboard operation. Online ranking to compete with rivals from around the world. ＜New Function＞ Compatible with all Xbox / Nintendo Switch / PlayStation controllers CLASSIC / MODERN mode that can be enjoyed with the aspect ratio of the Sega Saturn version and Xbox Live Arcade version Compatible with keyboard operation. One keyboard can be used by two people, and can also be used in conjunction with a controller. ＜Notes on controllers＞ When playing with a SWITCH controller, be sure to set 'Nintendo Button Layout' to 'OFF'. ＜Notes on play environment＞ If you are using a PC with the minimum system requirements, you may experience processing delays while playing. We recommend playing on a PC that meets the recommended system requirements, including a graphics board.

Enemies attack from all directions. There are 23 bosses in total. Aim for a high score by making full use of score bonuses and level-up weapons!

_childDocuments_.review: Radiant Silvergun, restored by Treasure, is now available. The shoot ‘em up gameplay that made this a legend remains unchanged, but a hidden "Ikaruga-style" shooting mode gives everyone something new. Previously only available in Japan, Radiant Silvergun on Xbox LIVE Arcade also provides leaderboards, co-op play locally or over Xbox LIVE, downloadable replays, and improved visuals making it the version to own.

name: Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven
detailed_description: Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven Demo In the demo, you can enjoy the beginning of the story, up until Emperor Leon and his teammates challenge Kzinssie, one of the Seven Heroes. Save data from this demo can be carried over to the full game. About the Game Save Your Empire. Defend Your Legacy. Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven is a full remake of the groundbreaking non-linear RPG Romancing SaGa 2, which originally launched in Japan in 1993. Embark on an adventure featuring both new and classic SaGa franchise features, complete with Japanese and English voiceovers, original and rearranged compositions, and much more! This is an ideal entry point for new players and provides an amped-up experience for longtime fans. STORY The Seven Heroes were once hailed as saviors, but the ancients feared their power and banished them to another dimension. It was foretold that they would return to save the world once more... Thousands of years have passed, and the heroes have become legend. Furious that humankind has forgotten their many sacrifices, they have now returned as villains bent on revenge. As legions of monsters swarm the world, take on the role of Ruler of the Empire of Varennes. Defend your legacy across successive generations, expand your realm and defeat the vengeful Seven Heroes one by one! KEY FEATURES Characters & Imperial Succession Join forces with characters from over 30 different classes featuring a wide variety of professions and races, each with their own favored weapons, unique abilities, and effective tactics. Choose the next Emperor from this wide pool of candidates, each eligible to inherit the throne and become the next protagonist. The knowledge and abilities of previous rulers are passed down to the next through the mystical art of inheritance magic, forging a lasting bond between you and your chosen characters. Free-Form Scenario The game presents a unique story structure that offers a vast array of narrative experiences in response to your choices and which objectives you tackle first—from how you expand the Empire to what order you challenge the Seven Heroes. Your actions and decisions will dramatically alter the course of the Emperor's journey. Combat The strategic turn-based battle system of the original has been further enhanced to a timeline system. Enjoy all the classic SaGa mechanics like 'Glimmers,' where you learn new abilities whilst in the heat of battle, and 'Formations,' which provide unique benefits to the retinue based on composition. Furthermore, the remake welcomes the new 'United Attack' feature to perform combination attacks with your retinue members to turn the tide of battle! Graphics The 2D pixel sprites of the original game are now modeled in full 3D while retaining their charming, familiar appearances based on the beautiful concept illustrations by Tomomi Kobayashi. All towns and dungeons are now also fully rendered with reworked terrains and layouts. Difficulty Settings Select from one of three difficulty levels to match your preferred playstyle, from Casual, Normal, to Hard (Classic). Casual offers a story-focused experience with less emphasis on battle, while Normal is recommended for veteran RPG players looking for a balanced game. Hard (Classic) is perfect for players looking for the brutal but satisfying challenge of the original 1993 version. Music & Voices Kenji Ito, the composer for the original Romancing SaGa 2, returns with a vengeance to present a beautiful soundtrack full of new arrangements! The music can be toggled between the original and new versions from the Options screen. Furthermore, all event scenes in Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven now feature full Japanese and English voice acting!

Enjoy all the classic SaGa mechanics like 'Glimmers,' where you learn new abilities whilst in the heat of battle, and 'Formations,' which provide unique benefits to the retinue based on composition. Furthermore, the remake welcomes the new 'United Attack' feature to perform combination attacks with your retinue members to turn the tide of battle! Graphics The 2D pixel sprites of the original game are now modeled in full 3D while retaining their charming, familiar appearances based on the beautiful concept illustrations by Tomomi Kobayashi. All towns and dungeons are now also fully rendered with reworked terrains and layouts. Difficulty Settings Select from one of three difficulty levels to match your preferred playstyle, from Casual, Normal, to Hard (Classic). Casual offers a story-focused experience with less emphasis on battle, while Normal is recommended for veteran RPG players looking for a balanced game. Hard (Classic) is perfect for players looking for the brutal but satisfying challenge of the original 1993 version. Music & Voices Kenji Ito, the composer for the original Romancing SaGa 2, returns with a vengeance to present a beautiful soundtrack full of new arrangements! The music can be toggled between the original and new versions from the Options screen. Furthermore, all event scenes in Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven now feature full Japanese and English voice acting!
short_description: In this non-linear RPG, rule and expand the Empire of Varennes across multiple generations. Discover a vast array of story experiences as you fight the Seven Heroes in an epic battle that plays out over thousands of years.

_childDocuments_.review: The SaGa series was never your Mommy and Daddy of JRPGs. Where they tell you what to do, what and how to use your weapons/armors. No. You're born, that's it.. good luck! Now get a job and start working from scratch, quite literally. The "free scenario" system was one of the few charming aspects that truly gave players the freedom to shape the story on how WE wanted. Multiple narrative routes, lots of missable sidequests, time events, and recruiting party members. It was always encourage to do 3 full playthroughs but you can be sure that the experience will hardly be the same thing as the last playthrough. Far before what games like Octopath started to achieve (JRPG not telling what to do and where to go, want to explore on your own? Things like that..) except far more grander and convoluted. If anything, the series tends to be the school bully who loves to pick on you when you press New Game. Back in the day this game was (and still is) hailed as the hardest JRPG series out there. Even past entries had this thing called the "LP (Life Point) system". If you go down in battle, you lose a point towards your LP,  but if the enemy decide to continue beating on your incapacitated party member (or if you use a skill that eats away at your LP) it can dwindle down to 0. Once that happen, your party member stays dead, forever (at least for that playthrough).What made this series stand out was the "SaGa battle system." Basically, no levels up or learning magic as you grind. You buy magic, and use it more than once to make it stronger. Simple, yet takes time, especially when you unlock far more complex systems like fusion magic. There's also the signature game mechanic known in the series as "glimmer system". Whenever faced with a powerful foe, there's a small chance a party member can learn a new move. This will be pivotal at winning a decisive battle, that not only heightens the thrill of taking risks facing power foes but gives a massive sense of satisfaction when you actually learned something new/powerful. It's like something straight out of a shounen anime. Not only that, SaGA 2 had a really unique feature called the "inheritance" magic system, whenever your emperor dies (through plot or conventional means), the next generation emperor will acquire the skills/knowledge the last emperor had. This didn't just applied the the story focused emperor either, the starter characters all have their own branching routes too. Aside from Gerard and Leon and the final emperor, all the other emperors are chosen from members of job classes you’ve unlocked. They also cycle through different characters with each generation (or character death). So while the trailers gave the impression all of the characters are story-related characters, the vast majority of them aren’t. Some of those job classes are different beast races too so you can make a mermaid or reptile emperor. The freedom is there for you to choose and shape.Granted, like many other SaGa games, this game didn't stand the test of time and did a lot of things that put off many people from trying. Such as, party recruitment and item/gear management. You lose a fight, then pick a successor, then go all around the castle (and sometimes far out of the castle) recruiting your team, then you go BACK to the castle and pull all the equipment out of storage, gear up your group, set up their skills, go to the magic lab and re-teach them all their spells, one at a time...then, you go out, fight the boss, win this time...aaaand it forces a time skip, causing you to have to do the entire process all over again. It was torturous even amongst people like me who loved these games.  Which is why I'm glad that the team behind the Trials of Mana remake picked up SaGa 2 and streamlined the most annoying aspects of it. Some might argue, it's a bit TOO accessible to newcomers. Things like having a glimmer icon reminder next to a weapon/spell that's about to discover a new skill, adding a way-point to everything on the map, even quest markers. To their credit I think it's tasteful and not egregious, but part of the fun of the original was discovering things on your own (it had a CRPG feel to it). Luckily, this can all be disable. However, despite the devs taking liberty to streamline the game, they removed the feature to save anywhere. Now you can only save at save points. Which is a odd change but nothing deal breaker worthy. In all honesty though, I love the changes, the revamped QoL, the detailed 3D models transitioned well from its 2D counterpart, well polished fluidity to everything, optimized performance, Kenji Ito masterful music composition in all its glory (with the option to switch between remake or original audio).The SaGa (and Mana) series were always the two that could never catch a break, especially SaGa. It does a lot of things that are unique, but the devs (mostly Kawazu) always had this knack of going "How bout we take everything from a graphical to gameplay standpoint, and make it weird. Yeah, let's do that." On top of having less direct storytelling and guidance than your typical JRPG. Stats increase based on actions in battle instead of normal levels gained through experience. Enemies also grow in strength with your party, discouraging mindless grinding but promoting more thoughtful strategy (sometimes). It was really a black box as to what you’ll get from a new game try comparing SaGa Frontier (PS1), Unlimited SaGa (PS2), and SaGa Scarlet Grace (newer consoles). They are all radically different in terms of animation, exploration, world maps, etc. Truly the "anti-mainstream" series. The dev team really out did themselves with this remake however, I can without a doubt say for certain.. this is the best starting point for new comers, mechanics are explained well and have some transparency. Newcomers are in for what is essentially "one of" the best Saga titles, as for returning players, prepare for the storm.... Termites!

_childDocuments_.review: Romancing Saga 2: Revenge of The Seven is the remake of a classic that brings back Saga 2 now modernize for new audiences. The game offers a lot of depth thanks to its inheritance system, which allows Emperors from different eras to pass down their skills to the new generations, with the goal of defeating the Seven Heroes, a powerful group that threatens the Empire. The game starts with Emperor Leon, who is teaching his son Gerard how to protect the Empire and become stronger when the Hero Kzinssie decides to set his eyes on taking the Empire under his control.That premise is what makes Revenge of The Seven so unique as a JRPG, if the Emperor falls in battle, they will be lost and a new Emperor will be chosen, but passing down their skills allows them to dodge the most dangerous attacks of the heroes and become stronger. From being instantly killed, to mind-controlled or overwhelmed by sheer force, you must cultivate your Empire and defeat the Seven!Revenge of The Seven might not be graphically impressive, but the art direction along with the voice acting in English and the lore makes the world truly come alive on the screen. Every location matters, and the game gives you the freedom to tackle the Heroes in any order as well as choose what territories to acquire first. Because of that freedom in the choice of how you play the game, it makes every playthrough special as your decisions shape the world in a branching storyline. The story is pretty good, as you can discover the reasons why the Seven Heroes are so bent on destroying the Empire, and the side quests are sort of mandatory in a way, as doing them will reward you with new classes, areas, and open up your choices for new Emperors to come, both in terms of their race and their class. It is a challenging game as well, so if you want an immersive JRPG that offers some serious obstacles, you might be interested.In addition to being one of a kind and obscure, Revenge of The Seven is incredibly in-depth. Gone are the usual levels system that games of this genre use, instead the game comes with LP or Life Points. Each character has a fixed number of LP, and when it goes down to 0 they are permanently killed in battle and lost, meaning that your party members can only get knocked out so many times before they perish in battle. It adds a layer of strategy in the long term and it makes it so party members only need to be healed rather than resurrected in combat, which allows for more options at the cost of the risk of losing people.There is also Glimmering, which is how characters learn new skills. In combat, a character might have a lightbulb in their skills, when this happens there is a chance that using said skill will make them learn a new one, which they will use immediately. Glimmering as a system is interesting because sometimes, sacrificing the optimal move for the chance of learning new skills is worth it. Magic meanwhile is a random chance after battle, provided that the character has the magic tree leveled enough. The more a weapon is wielded and used or a magic tree is cast, the better characters get at using them. The main goal is to defeat The Seven Heroes, and the order in which you tackle them is important as it mixes up things. Knowing which evasions to equip, what formations to use, and which classes to bring can be the difference between a certain victory or assured doom. The game has a steep learning curve, and some combats such as the Hero Noel can be particularly high in spike difficulty, but with the inheritance system and some patience, one can eventually surpass obstacles. Each of the Heroes is a show on the screen, some mock you, others intimidate you and they always pack a punch both in their presence and their super-powerful skills. Learning the lore of the game is important, both for the story experience but also in a practical manner. As you develop the Empire, you can make new buildings such as smithies or even universities. In the latter, you will get tested on the lore of the game, and if you pass you will get handsomely rewarded each time. In addition to that, some quests won't be tracked by mini-map, requiring the player to pay attention to know where to go, which enriches the world exploration. Some decisions, such as deciding to let a volcano erupt or stopping it can change areas of the game and the consequences of it.The attention to detail doesn't end there, as some Leylines affect the potency of spells and skills in battle based on their usage, but outside combat, there is an integrated world that offers plenty of goods. Making a garden gives revenue to the Empire while annexing territory gives plenty of other bonuses. Each location has its particular vibe to it and makes exploring it enjoyable as you find treasure chests and new secrets.Revenge of The Seven shines in all of its aspects, and the only weakness the game suffers from is that with so much depth, it can be overwhelming at times if you don't get into it. It doesn't help that despite having a Casual difficulty, combats are so challenging in the latter half that missing a certain spell or tactic will make victory almost impossible. Nonetheless, it is a game that focuses on experimentation and being able to become stronger each time, so with some patience even the hardest battle becomes bearable.  At 50$ bucks this is a wonderful game to get, with an amazing soundtrack, story, voice acting, and gameplay. The replayability is up to the player, as playthroughs can be quite different based on choices and the order the heroes are tackled. That being said, some players can be done after one run due to the game being 20-50 hours long based on choices to do or skip, along with the difficulty setting.Revenge of The Seven is a remake that one asked for and an interesting proposal by Square Enix, but it shines in all of its areas, resulting in an enjoyable game that feels so different from anything else in the market. If you enjoy challenges, immersive stories, and a deep combat system, I recommend giving this game a try, for you be surprised at how good it is. 9/10 AMAZING:) If you enjoy and find the review helpful, please follow my curator!

_childDocuments_.review: So I recommend this game with the caveat that it is VERY apparent that it is a remake of a very old game. By that I mean, the story is relatively barebones, there's an ass ton of combat (probably around 80% of the game), and the characters are all (mostly) without personality and just randomly generated. Don't expect a gripping narrative or endless variety, this is a very straightforward game and if you don't like turn based combat stay away. BUT. It is incredibly unique and has a very clear appeal. There's a great sense of forward progression, every combat sees skills leveling, opening potential new skills. Difficulty is well balanced, with death having long term consequences and enemies always being dangerous even if you can burn them down quick. Quests lead seamlessly into each other, connecting areas in ways you hadn't even considered (following a random thief sidequest leading to you getting to skip a huge chunk of a fortress as they give you a secret path, as an example). There's also long term progression as each leveled skill can carry over into the next generation, you can build new facilities in your town, etc. It is also SIGNIFICANTLY more user friendly than any other Saga game I've tried. I'm sure some people will be upset at how much info it gives the player but as someone who struggled with previous titles it's awesome to not feel lost all the time. Again, stay far away unless you're fine with a game that is almost entirely combat. But if you enjoy turn based stuff? Definitely worth a play.

_childDocuments_.review: The original Romancing SaGa 2 was nothing short of a technical marvel when it was released on the Super Famicom in 1993. But as is true with the majority of Square’s long-running SaGa franchise, its intricacies were often difficult to follow, especially for newcomers to the series. The full-on remake in , however, completely removes those blinders, making it by far one of the most approachable entries in the series to date.  While it may lack the depth of entries like Emerald Beyond and Scarlet Grace, there’s still plenty of strategy involved in felling enemies efficiently, and especially bosses. Status ailments matter on both sides, and can easily turn the tide of battle. The inclusion of the Overdrive mechanic and its powerful capabilities give more reason to diversify character builds and damage profiles so that you can exploit as many enemy weaknesses as possible. The staple glimmering (or learning) new techniques mid-combat remains an enjoyable endeavor, and its accompanying chart and icons help you better understand how to unlock even more techniques. The LP (life point) system, also a recurring mechanic, helps make every moment meaningful since one too many deaths can permanently kill party members (or the emperor). Party formations from the original return to incentivize certain character loadouts with various strengths and weaknesses to consider (though some of the perks don’t feel as potent as you might expect). “Nonlinear” is the name of the exploration game. Many locations have branching paths to other destinations, which are supplemented by meaningful choice and consequence that will most certainly shape the world around you. No two runs are likely to be the same and it’s not possible to see everything in one run, encouraging you to start another to see different outcomes.  follows an emperor and his descendants, passing down the experience and knowledge gained with each new successor to the throne. Expand your kingdom, making new foes and allies while increasing the capability and coffers of your empire.  The graphics are faithful to the original release despite being in full 3D this time around. Kenji Ito never disappoints when it comes to the soundtrack, and the ability to go between the original and remake compositions is a nice touch. While generally disliking English voice acting in most JRPGs, the performance here overall is not bad. Speaking of performance, the game runs silky smooth in almost every situation even on the Steam Deck.  An immense amount of QoL has turned this into one of the most convoluted titles into one of the most - arguably THE most - approachable entries in the series to date. Except for maybe the original SaGa III on the Game Boy…but that’s hard to count considering it’s not really even a “true” SaGa game from a mechanical standpoint.  This is VERY minor and certainly exclusive to Steam Deck, but you occasionally have to close out and reboot the game in order to fix a sporadic choppy sound issue. But this only happens if you’re coming out of suspension, and it does not seem to happen too often.You’ve always wanted to try a SaGa game - or tried one and were put off by its vagueness and complexities - and want an amazing introduction into what makes this series unique and compelling without really sacrificing what makes a SaGa game, well, SaGa (looking at YOU, SaGa III on Gameboy). Or perhaps you’re just looking for a challenging turn-based JRPG that goes against the conventional grain for the most part? That’s here, too!For me,  allowed me to finally complete one of the few remaining SaGa entries I had not beaten, and did so completely without guides or references. Overall, series fans and newcomers alike have an abundance of things to enjoy in this latest entry into one of Square’s longest-running franchises.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a remake of an old game, but the formula feels insanely fresh and modern. Light on story but heavy on combat, variety, and freedom of choice, a solid JRPG for turn-based nuts who have turned to roguelikes in recent years. Contrary to the in-game advice, I recommend choosing Classic difficulty if you're a JRPG vet, as Normal is too easy to allow you to fully engage with the game's systems. There's plenty of QoL and guidance to make this a far less daunting task than the original, but you still feel like your journey is fully in your hands. This game is for a certain kind of person, but it will make that kind of person VERY happy.

_childDocuments_.review: If you'd told me going into 2024 that we'd get two major SaGa games released and that arguably the better one was a surprise remake of a 30 year old SNES title, I'd have been skeptical. But we got it and it's fantastic.Romancing SaGa 2 got its first release/translation in the West in 2016 or so, and it was perfectly serviceable, but it had a lot of issues that were inherent to the original game's design; it was very unfriendly to play in many regards and I never actually finished it despite being a SaGa fan. Revenge of the Seven takes the base game, gives it a really nice 3D glow-up and presentation (including a way larger - and notable - VA cast than I'd have expected) and some extremely nice QoL while still being, at its core, a SaGa game. The main gimmick it has is that the fight against the formerly-heroic Seven Heroes is something that's going to be a generational effort across multiple centuries (or in my case, over a millennia), so as you progress through the game the controllable Emperor is going to either age out or die in battle and pass their skills and knowledge down to a new Emperor. Every so often you'll shift forward a frankly comical number of years, pick a new Emperor from the increasingly large number of unlocked classes, set up a party for the new generation, and resume adventuring. While the world (due to this being originally an early SNES title) is weirdly static in many aspects, there's a decent number of outcomes for a variety of quests, both positive and negative, tied to your actions or inaction - you really can't sit around and ignore that impending volcanic eruption and expect that it's going to wait for your next generation to deal with, as one example.Combat is going to be a bulk of the playtime of RS2, and honestly it's really good in the way that almost all SaGa games excel at turn based JRPG combat. You've got a variety of weapon categories and spell schools to balance, with some spell disciplines being mutually exclusive, and some weapon techs being elementally aligned, which means that there's a lot of nuance to party building, covering all your bases, and trying to hit as many enemy weaknesses as you can. Some of the most welcome QoL comes in battle, with the game automatically tracking and displaying known weaknesses and resistances for you, as well as an indication that a particular skill might be ready to glimmer and teach you a new combat tech. The combat's a real winner - battles look good, they progress extremely quickly, and they reward good prepwork and party building while constantly giving you a feeling of getting stronger and more capable.There's other nice quality of life features in this remake too that make the experience smoother while not making it feel boring or trivial.  The big winner is the ability to adjust your party roster from taverns (including a new tavern in your castle), which solves the biggest and most annoying part of setting up a new generation - no more running over half the world through dangerous combat zones trying to recruit that Amazon.  There's also fast travel added (limited as appropriate but largely available), full quest markers for tracking what you can go do, bonus upgrades to know how many unopened chests are in an area, and even sensibly placed save and BP restores before boss fights.  SaGa games historically have been difficult to get into as much due to lack of consideration of the player experience as due to the generally opaque mechanics, and RotS smooths out a lot of the more unnecessary rough edges.RotS has some degree of postgame content to look at and fully supports New Game Plus runs with some restrictions, which means that if you want to keep going when you've completed and perhaps see how you can resolve quests and events differently or experiment with different Emperor classes and formations, it's going to be easy to do so.  Even if not, however, Revenge of the Seven is just a really good JRPG and there's now a definitive answer for folks who ask the common question of "I'm curious about the SaGa games, which one should I start with?".

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely stunning. I'm completely new to this series. Never heard nor anyone in my country had ever mentioned to me about the existence of this franchise. This is the first game from it that I've ever played and I'm blown away by its sheer amount of entertainment it has given me through 200+ hours journey. I discovered this game by completely accident, as I scroll through new upcoming release and saw this one on the list.I'm sure I would have loved this game in its original form if I'd known about it. I've played a lot of game with niche or something that wouldn't stand the test of time. Suikoden did come to mind while playing this, some similar aspect like a lot of missable characters, choice that matter, customization skill, formation and some so I did have this tolerance to go through something so daring such as this.This game is so addictive. The amount of free style you can have with your team build, the main single plot but with several non linear routes that you can take, so many consequence of action and choice you've made, the difficulty of battle that put understanding of game to use. It's really full of dynamic as every play-through feels different and unique to its own. I completed the first playthrough in Classic and second one on Romancing. Every minute of it is awe inspired.The game carries out the story and world progression in form of "Generation". In which the world move on as each people carry the legacy of those come before and to complete the grand mission that was bestowed to them against the struggling world tormented by the Seven Heroes. It starts with Leon's Generation and then every new emperor after him is appointed by your own choice and every story after it is narrated by your own chosen path.In battle feature the turn based game. Every unit take action based on their speed. In their turn they can choose to attack using Tech or Magic or use defend or item. Simple enough. The dynamic comes from that every character's tech and magic can be customized to see fit your preference or battle. It's basically what make game feel fresh and fun all the time.There's no character level in this game but a level of Tech or Magic determine how proficiency the character is with respective skill. Which become more powerful each time they use in battle. For example using short sword in battle will earn them experience in that particular weapon in which each time it levels up they will deal more damage with shortsword. The same is applied to magic.It doesn't stop there. The best part is, In battle, there's chance they will spark a completely new move on the fly. This is called "Glimmer". A mechanic in which a character will learn a new Tech or Magic while fighting in battle. The chance will increase when they're fighting the stronger opponent. Also there's small chance they will learn the "evasion" tech which sometime spark when they're attacked by certain move cause them to effortlessly dodge that move every single time it's used on them. Glimmer is my personal favorite mechanic because it looks cool everytime it happens, especially when they're fighting boss. It's also very unique coming from all RPG out there. it's basically a trademark.There're several characters in this game where they're all assigned in their own respective "Class". These classes and each individual from the roster of respective class will have their own base basic attributes and class ability. For example a Vagabond will naturally have high SPD but each individual from this class may be faster than other or they have more STR than other. Giving the sense that each generation have their own unique niche to it. The fun part was to discover who or which class is your favorite, then try to make it work in your teamcomp in any generation.There's permanent death but no permanent deadend. Every character carry one stat called "LP". It's basically their life force. Which deplete each time they're KOed in battle, when it reaches 0, they're considered killed and gone forever. And new generation will take their place. Technically, there's no game over in this game. If your party get wiped out. The game doesn't end and the screen will bring you to appoint a new MC or new Emperor, in which they will continue to struggling in their place. Dead is not an ending and may open up new opportunity for something better. This too is different from other RPG as dying is considered a progression itself.Each enemy will have weakness to certain weapon or magic element. Attacking these enemy by exploiting their weakness will deal more damage and fill up "Overdrive" gauge. Overdrive is a union attack perform by several allies at once which allow player to burst the enemy to their death. This existing mechanic will further emphasize the important of team diversity which you must allow to exploit these weakness as many time as possible to turn the tide of battle. In additional to weakness is status aliment which matter a lot on battle against several enemies, especially on high difficulty where one or two hit could KO your unit, by inflicting stun or sleep on enemy will definitely increase the chance of surviving for your team. Vice versa, an enemy can also inflict these on your team and may end the battle quickly so you will put into considerate that power isn't only thing that matter.There's one more important mechanic in this game called "time skip". Basically after every major story quest the game may trigger the timeskip in which the story moves on to the next generation. Through plot point the new emperor will be chosen, inheriting all those abilities and memories that come before as they continue to carry the legacy. Every new Tech and Magic learnt in the last generation will be registered in the training hall, allowing the new generation unit to directly learn from it. The new generation may use these tech with ease, and they may glimmer an even more amazing new Tech and Magic than the last. This is general flow of the game and how they choose to emphasize how the people of this world grow stronger to combat an even greater threat.There's no side quest in this game. Except, every quest is a "story" itself. Which will allow you to experience the world in your own pace. There's no fixed order except in prologue Leon's generation where it's scripted, you're free to explore the entire world and discover all matter of region and cities at your own discreet. You can literally start any quest in anywhere as your own choice truly emphasize a true non linear RPG experience. In different order come different consequence each time, this is called "Free-Form Scenario" in which the world always move on with or without your presence. If the story say the situation is immediate, it really is, nobody know what would happen if you leave to do something else or get killed in battle, appoint new emperor and only to find out the story has moved on for the different outcome, there's more but this review shall not spoil its charming any further. Discover all of these blind is a fun itself.It's honestly beautiful anime style-ish game. It's well optimized throughout with stunning effect. I can see that they've recreated something based on original and make it even more hype for those people. For someone new like me, I understand why people praise the game being faithful to the original.You can choose between original soundtrack or the remake one. I've listened to both and I'm amazed by how faithful the remake remix can get despite original already sounds so amazing, but the remake managed to make it sounds even better.If you really like the degree of freedom on customize your team ability, picking whoever you want to journey on the non linear world full of dynamic and choice you can make. This is your game. It's the best of its niche and will offer exactly what you're looking for.

_childDocuments_.review: Play the demo. The demo is long, and generous. It's representative of the full game experience. If you enjoy the demo you'll probably enjoy the game. If the demo doesn't sell you, skip the game.Light mechanics/story spoilers will be in this review, though only for things that'll appear in the demo.tl;dr - It's okay, borderline good, but not great. There's fun to be had here though I've found it's quite repetitive and the core mechanics make it hard to get invested in the story or my party.The game starts off completely linear, but after a short prologue it opens up to being a bit more freeform. The player's able to pick their party from any of the available classes, and tackle the available quests in any order. This gives the loose impression of an open/non-linear game, but in practice all the quests are so detached from each other that it's more like having a bucket of small linear side stories to pursue. Choices somewhat matter in quests, in that they can change which character/classes unlock, how the player's income changes, and generally what rewards/follow up quests happen.After doing enough questing (or if you die/party wipe) you have to pick a new main character. This has a few quirks to it, but notably all your highest skill levels are added to w/e the class would otherwise have. This has.. issues, as it makes it really difficult to tell after a few generations what people were meant to be good at. It also has a really annoying UX issue whereby your current techs/spells will be auto equipped to the new Emperor, and these frequently are not the ones that character will want to be using.'Fixing' the setups only takes 5-10 minutes per party, but (with abdications) it's frequent and annoying enough to make the game drag. I wanted to like this feature but I was tired of it within a few generations.Characters/classes are pretty dull. I keep lumping these together because the system in RS2 is weird. There's a fixed set of classes, and a fixed set of characters within each class. Each generation it'll rotate through the pool of available characters for that class, and the player has no control over this. There's not a huge amount of difference in these characters though, they're just some small stat differences, a cosmetic change to their appearance, and a different name. The skills, spells, and levels of these characters transfer between generations, so if generation 1 knight gets to level 10 swords it'll be (at least) level 10 in generation 2, etc etc. I can see what they tried to do here, but in practice I found it a bit annoying. This partially comes down to the annoying UI issues, partially down to having way too many classes that don't differentiate themselves much, and partially because there's an obvious 'correct' way to build characters and obvious incorrect ways. Just slap the preferred weapon on the character, a healing spell or two if they're physical, and all the dang spells if they're not.The generation skipping ultimately adds nothing to the game for me bar annoyances, and it makes the writing weak. 150 years will pass and the whole world is the same, but 1/2 quests will progress as if a singular day has passed.As a remaster, this is simultaneously extremely impressive and a bit of a letdown. It obviously looks nothing like the original 2D game anymore, and the 3D movement/battles really enhance the experience. The combat feels pretty great with slick animations and a rapid pace. However there's been poorly thought out changes, such as dedicated equipment slots. The player's able to combine multiple pieces of armour into a single suit that uses all slots. This made sense in the original - where it still only used 1 slot, but in the remake these items are strictly and objectively inferior to their single-slot counterparts.Overall, RS2 isn't bad but it shows its age - they've been mostly authentic to the original, albeit with a few small changes here and there. The ideas here were great for a 30 year old game, but they're fairly routine now. There's untapped potential here and I wish they did more with it. It's unique enough to be worth a play, but hard to care about finishing.

Fully visualized progression system (Master Level and Enemy Level) makes it relatively easier to understand. Probably the easiest we have ever seen in Romancing Saga Series. While Casual and Normal are aim for newcomers, Classic is the one close to the SFC original aiming for old Saga fans. Expert and Romacing is for hardcore Saga Fan and the difficulty is what we have seen in hardcore mods for the SFC Roms and will be unlocked after beating the hidden boss after completing the game. (And I am trying to beat Expert at this moment)New game+ also avalible and well balanced so far, it is quite challenging even keeping most of the charater progress. And most of the changes they have made on the original progression system (e.g. Glimmer spell instead of simply learning it at Avalon, Changes on synthesized spells etc.) are probably because of this new game+ mode. On the other hand, they also doing a great job for  filling most of the missing pieces in the story of original SFC version by the supplementary cut scenes.In conclusion, Revenge of The Seven is recommended for both newcomers and fans of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: This is more of a first impression, but I’ll edit this with a full review when I’ve cleared the main story.So far Revenge of the Seven is a very fun JRPG that deviates from the norm in terms of gameplay systems and non-linear story progression. It’s like a refinement/iteration of what Square tried to do with FFII before mainline Final Fantasy went it’s way to become what it is today narratively and gameplay wise throughout the years. If it wasn't already apparent this is a full on remake of a Super Famicom title from 1993.The difficulty for this is quite high if you play on classic mode and the consequences for falling in battle means a party member is one step closer to permadeath since everyone has a set LP (life points) which represents how many times a character can fall in battle before they’re done-zo. Leveling up is non-traditional as stats are determined by gear but ability and weapon strength are determined by the usage and their own separate experience bars so to speak. So the more you use certain weapons or magic the stronger a character becomes with those. Glimmers are a cool mechanic specific to SaGa where characters can learn new abilities mid-battle and they can proc at random (higher chance during boss battles) when a lightbulb icon appears next to one of the normal attack skills. And the first cast of a newly glimmered ability is free. These new abilities can at times change the tide of battle especially during a boss fight. This game also uses one resource pool for magic/skills under the moniker “BP”. Boss fights in particular can be rough because you need to consider party comp and their weaponry/abilities, formation, strategy, and builds. You will party wipe if you're unprepared.The story so far is semi-stereotypical for a JRPG you have 7 heroes who saved the world in the past but return as demons seeking revenge against humanity and you have to stop them. However where it gets interesting is the lineage system since no one set party or character will fight all 7 heroes and be there at the end of the story even if you survive. Because the passage of time will eventually occur after a certain amount of quests are done and a new party leader/Emperor and members must be chosen with abilities passed down through the inheritance system. So don’t get too attached to anyone as eventually their time in the story will end. As future generations of heroes will work towards defeating the next in line of the 7 heroes until they are eventually all no more.Overall just a lot of cool stuff that feels way ahead of its time. But in this remake compared to the Super Famicom original the systems are a lot less obtuse and much more approachable. So much work aside from the graphical overhaul was done in QoL to make this more palatable to digest as an experience in 2024. Also you can choose your difficulty from casual, normal, and classic/hard. Great for newcomers who may just want to enjoy the plot without feeling stressed during gameplay.The 3D anime art style pops and feels like it represents the original pixel art well. Not the most visually mindblowing game, but the art direction makes up for it. It's the same visual fidelity (equivalent) of DQXI minus Toriyama's art style (RIP). The OST is nice and is enjoyable to listen to, you have an option of using the remake’s version or the original. The newly added voice acting from my limited experience is solid too. I could be hearing things but it sounds like some of the cast also did voices for games like Octopath Traveler. And lastly you can really just personalize your experience to be your own in all senses of the word.Just a refreshing game that differentiates itself well with how many turned based games are releasing these days. I like how Square priced this as it’s in that AA range at $49.99 USD MSRP. It definitely feels like a AA game too, but in the upper echelon of that spectrum in terms of the Dev team making the most of the limited budget given to them to create this. If you’re a JRPG fan you need to give this a try. This is the most newcomer friendly entry point into arguably Square’s most obscure, but insanely beloved franchise (Especially in Japan, but there’s a smaller hardcore fan base in the west). And depending on how financially successful this is relative to the development budget might dictate what the long term future holds for the SaGa series. Runs buttery smooth for the most part with very minor and infrequent framerate drops (Native Res 800p). I have it locked to 60fps with it basically maxed out settings wise, I lowered shadows to high. If it does happen it mainly occurs for like 1-2 seconds immediately after transitions loading into a new zone or sometimes during unite attack animations. You can probably get roughly 4-ish hours of total game time (from 100% battery) if you have the OLED model. Maybe stretching that a bit more if you're willing to lock it down to 30fps and are fine with TDP and GPU clock setting tinkering.

_childDocuments_.review: I type this with a decent amount of hours into the game, three runs, full knowledge of the original and a full set of achievements, this is not mindless contrarianism, it's the honest opinion of an old fan who gave this remake a serious chance but was ultimately let down.Long story short, a remake should be something that surpasses the original game, or at the very least fix most of the issues while leaving the core elements untouched, this remake not only does neither but it does a 180° and makes the game worse outside of some minor QOL improvements.Since the list of grievances is far too long and this isn't really the point of a review I'm gonna keep this orderly and give you a quick rundown of the major issuesNot only did the game not receive any sort of mechanical update, the people at XEEN arbitrarily changed longstanding mechanics of the series in favor of turning this game into Octopath Traveler with some vestigial SaGa mechanics that have also been greatly tampered with.RS2 was a great, but fairly unbalanced game with lots of mechanics that should have been fixed if not replaced by more modern and better versions, we all know that completely invisible armor values weren't a good idea, the people at XEEN disagreed, however.Instead of making armor values visible they're now gone entirely and regressed to rudimentary physical&magical defense values, sparking weapon techs now requires a minimum proficiency level, and so does inheriting techs in the dojo which adds a lot of unnecessary grinding, speaking of which they nerfed all the core functions such as debuff or counter accuracy only to tie them to switchable class passives which, guess what, also require you to fight a grand total of 60 FIGHT PER CLASS (Different genders have different passives so in most cases 120 fights!) only for your counters to work, and this is also locked behind the main story progression for some reason, not to mention it makes classes less unique as well since even the four elementals lost their identity entirely (and in the Nereid's case, her tail) now that everyone can gain their elemental gimmicks, even Coppelia no longer has her customary mecha immunities as an inherent part of her identity.I could go on and on but expect all of the major mechanical flaws of the original to be here as well, more often than not in a worse and somehow more obtuse form, but the thing that irks me the most is how entire mechanical layers have been removed altogether, the Class personality system, which gave each class unique reactions and options to quests is gone, and only some vestigial elements survive in the form of the Comroon Strait and Miles route of the Landship quest being the only quests that still have the original class unique interactions, even the exploits like grinding the Guardian in Eirunep got worse as now that BR does not change enemies you can beeline for Lake Wyringa and grind Albions immediately at zero risk or investment.The bosses have been turned into mindless damage races, with the final boss being the most insulting one as it's completely different and now designed on a timer where nothing matters but simply using Rapid Stream and frontloading as much damage as possible before it nukes you, how they managed to make something worse and more rudimentary than a 30 years old SNES game is beyond me.The "difficulty" setting are abysmal as the only thing they do is bloat enemy HP and attack even further to the point it's impossible (and worthless) to play on Romancing as you unlock it as it forces you to grind through Expert first, and the lack of NG+ options in terms of carryovers makes it clear this was intentional since the only "strategy" there is to this game is charging your OD gauge, using Berserk and/or Shadow Servant and nuking anything in three turns even on Romancing.The design philosophy of a game that tried its best to distance itself from generic, lazy JRPG conventions is also gone, now every single place in the world is sprinkled with generic treasure chests and shiny MMO drops that make zero narrative sense, a lot of dialogue makes no mechanical sense either now as the emperors and your annals claim that you eradicated goblins out of their hideout but if you go there 1000 years later they're still full of goblins because XEEN wanted generic JRPG grinding spots, now I'm supposed to do my smiths' work and go around the world gathering materials for them, making them look like incompetent idiots who can't do their job, and why in the world would an Emperor waste time on dozens of nonsensical JRPG quizzes in the university they funded? The original quiz made sense narratively and was a fun moment, having dozens of those is pointless bloating for the sake of having generic JRPG minigames.Even the series longstanding tradition of free saving is gone now, and this game regresses to save points for no logical reason, with some egregious Dark Souls 3 moments with two save points next to each other.Most zones look okay and clearly some efforts have been put in keeping the game in line with the original for the most part, some zones like the Melu desert have been overall adapted to modern standards in a satisfying manner, but in many parts there's now Xenogears tier platforming that does nothing but annoy you due to the exceedingly slippery and floaty movement and the needlessly large environments.The campaign content is, for the most part, largely unchanged, outside of some aforementioned annoying limitation, the Ninja and Diviner classes have been integrated in the main game now that the Maze of Memory does not exist anymore, and the story moments have been adapted in a good way, the ending is still as good as the original, but the new stuff about the Seven heroes is handled terribly and characters that needed more content, like Sagzaar, received absolutely nothing.Kenji Ito being the only returning member of the original staff has delivered a fantastic OST, but outside of two new tracks for the Dread Queen fight, the OST leaves something to be desired as again, the game needed more content on that too, especially since normal bosses still reuse Kujinshi's battle theme for no good reason, Minstrel Song and the DS remakes got this right, this game did not.The japanese VAs delivered a very good performance, despite this game's awful localization which unfortunately happened due to the series' localizer being on leave, the cast is really good and they clearly had fun and put a lot of effort in their performance, not to mention many of them like Sugita and Nakamura are fans of the series so you know they gave the characters the respect they deserved.As a fan, I do not know who this game was made for, the unicorn of the "wider audience" the producer mentioned surely made this game more popular than the previous releases, largely because it's not really a SaGa game anymore and because the executives decided this deserved more budget and advertisement than the others, so what we're left with is a Guilty Gear Strive situation where the original fanbase gets a fat middle finger in favour of pandering to people who never cared and probably will not care outside of this game.Is it worth it to utterly bastardize and dumb down a beloved game series for money? Only time will tell, I can only hope Kawazu and the actual team will know better and that we never see something like this again, I know for sure I won't buy another "remake" of this kind.

_childDocuments_.review: Game has possibly the most obnoxious and awfully implemented level scaling system I've ever seen.I've always hated level scaling, even when done RIGHT it's bad and unnecessary and punishes the player for growth.Here it's not done right... You'll go from an enemy being manageable one second to getting absolutely one-shot by that same exact enemy type in literally the next encounter and you'll say? "What gives!?"Well... "What gives!?" is that a magic number in the game's systems incremented because, unbeknownst to you, you got "too strong"... Fought "too many battles" and now the Goblins that were tough but manageable have become giga Goblins that treat your attacks like a mosquito bite and one shot your mage despite trying to keep them in the backline (where the game tells you they're "protected" ... Yeah... No.)Speaking of being "One Shot" this game f***ing LOVES one shotting you. The bosses will one shot you, the Goblins will one shot you, almost everything will one shot you."Well... I just need to gain some levels!" You'll think to yourself. "I'm getting one shot because I need better equipment and higher HP!"So... You go about trying to raise your HP and get money for your Equipment upgrade, only for the game to say "Gee, nice prep work, it'd be a shame if level scaling showed up and ruined it all."Then level scaling will show up and ruin it all and next thing you know you're back at the bottom of the totem pole getting one shot by Goblins again.Maybe that wouldn't matter if the game didn't give you an LP system where every time a character goes down they lose LP (which is IMPOSSIBLE to recover) and upon losing all LP they just die.No... F*** this game, F*** level scaling in all its grotesque and miserable forms and F*** the developers who use it.Stop. Let ME decide how hard the game will be by deciding how much time I want to spend grinding levels. Don't go "Oh look, he's trying to grind levels to get more HP!? Because he's tired of getting ONE SHOT! You know what he must want!? For every single enemy in the game to just magically get stronger for no reason thus rendering his attempts to correct the One Shot problem totally null and void."I want games that have level scaling to advertise such in big, bold, beautiful letters so that I can know to absolutely not purchase them.
