_childDocuments_.review: Visions of Mana? A Nostalgic Journey with Modern Flaws! (ฅ'ω'ฅ)"A charming return to the classic Mana series with a vibrant world and engaging combat, though marred by a few design missteps."Visions of Mana is the latest action-RPG entry in the beloved Mana series, taking players on an adventure with Val and his childhood friend Hinna as they journey towards the sacred Mana Tree. This game brings a mix of nostalgia and innovation, offering a semi-open world full of elemental spirits, strategic combat, and a narrative that delves into themes of fate and sacrifice. Fans of the series will find familiar callbacks, while newcomers can enjoy a standalone story that’s accessible yet emotionally impactful.Visions of Mana excels in creating a world that feels alive with the spirit of the classic JRPGs. The semi-open world is vast and vibrant, filled with lush environments that invite exploration. However, while the world is visually stunning, the exploration itself can feel somewhat repetitive. The game’s decision to embrace a more open-world design, reminiscent of Ubisoft’s "checklist" style, might disappoint those who prefer the focused progression of previous titles like Trials of Mana. The abundance of collectibles and fast travel points sometimes detracts from the sense of discovery, making exploration feel more like a chore than an adventure.Combat is where Visions of Mana truly shines. The game offers a dynamic battle system that allows players to harness the power of the Elementals through different classes and characters. Each character brings a unique playstyle, and experimenting with various combinations adds depth to the gameplay. The battles are swift and strategic, offering a satisfying mix of action and tactics that keep encounters engaging throughout the game. However, some players might find the difficulty lacking, even on harder settings, which can reduce the challenge for seasoned RPG fans.The narrative in Visions of Mana strikes a balance between simplicity and emotional depth. While the story follows a somewhat predictable path, with familiar themes of destiny and sacrifice, it’s the characters that bring the narrative to life. Val and his companions are well-developed, with their personalities and backstories gradually revealed through the journey. Yet, some may feel that the character development is rushed, particularly when it comes to resolving personal struggles. This can leave certain arcs feeling undercooked, especially when compared to the more nuanced character interactions seen in previous Mana titles.Visions of Mana is a game that walks the fine line between paying homage to its predecessors and trying to innovate within the action-RPG genre. While it succeeds in delivering a vibrant world and engaging combat, its open-world design choices and uneven pacing may not appeal to everyone. Nonetheless, for fans of the Mana series and those looking for a JRPG with a blend of nostalgia and modern gameplay, Visions of Mana offers a memorable, if imperfect, adventure.If you enjoyed Visions of Mana, consider exploring other action JRPGs like the Ys series or Ni No Kuni II, which share similar gameplay elements and aesthetic appeal. And if you’re a fan of classic JRPGs, be sure to follow our  for more reviews and updates on the latest in the genre!ヽ(´• ω •`)ノ

_childDocuments_.review: So. Another year, a new Mana game, I see. First of all, before I give this review, this is gonna be an honest as a fan of the series since 2000. This by any means a bad game. It's rough on the edges, but no means a bad game. What I love about this game, is the battle system and music. The music can go heavy metal to charming that everyone loved the series. I mean, heck, I would rather play this game over Dawn Of Mana and  Sword Of Mana any day. The less we talk about those  games, the better. I loved Val and Hinna's relationship. Even though I've seen it many JRPG do that, it wasn't shoehorned or forced. Just right. VM however, feels.... cheap. The graphics are amazing and all, but for some odd reasons, feels like I'm not playing a big budget game. For an example; the game can have tons of stuttering midway when I'm walking or during battles. That even the game's FPS gone and reached peak 1FPS for about 10 seconds. Some of the boss fights I didn't see cause the game kept freezing on me. I have a 3060 RTX and 16GB of ram. Surely this game can handle it. The side quests, God. If you love games that tells you "Bring me this, kill that monsters that." Then this game is for you! I don't mind doing that, but at least give me EXP. Oh? You didn't know? The game has this weird way of not giving you too many EXP unless you're fighting a boss. So if you want to level up, better find some good monsters with the red orbs, and use an item to get 15 or 20% EXP. And you might get 10K EXP. Which by the way, that's not much when you're level around 60 to 70. The game seems to love 30FPS during cutscenes. Which I despise. You *can* make the run at 60 if you press F11. Which is...odd. Final thoughts:Pros: Good Mana game. Probably one of the best in the last 15 years. Pros: Fun characters and pretty diverse.Pros: Great music can make you hype, or calm you down. (Kinda wish Yoko did it, though.) Pros: Class systems are back, can be OP. :P Pros: A good edition to the series. Cons: Feels cheap and rushed. Cons: Lack of EXP. Cons: Can overstay it's welcome time to time. (I hate when JRPG do that. >:( )Cons: Side quests = Blah! Overall, I liked the game, but far from everyone's hype around it. Which hurts my childhood fandom. I would give this game a 6/10.. Not good or bad. Just....it's okay. Wait for a sale around 29.99 or 19.99. Trust me, you'll thank me later.

_childDocuments_.review: Visions of Mana is a faithful entry into the Mana series. The game features beautiful art direction that has almost a painted or watercolor feeling. Perhaps a small nitpick would be about the texture quality on some environmental objects and weapons, but this game was never meant to be a graphical showcase in that regard. Despite that, it has had a number of vistas and set pieces that are simply majestic. Seeing the Mana Tree in the intro alone was like seeing the Secret of Mana Cover Art come to life in Real-time 3D. Truly amazing. The music is quite good as well, providing fans of the classic OSTs with some revised tracks, some songs that have similar motifs to old-school tracks, and plenty of new music that feels right at home within the series. Some new tracks don't really carry the feeling that I've grown accustom to in the series, but they are good in their own right.The gameplay has been quite fun. As you acquire new elemental powers, the system really starts to shine. It also boasts a fairly deep system to control your secondary character. Besides allowing you to switch to characters on the fly, you can also assign specific AI modifiers to finely tune how the party acts (similarly to something like Final Fantasy XII).The Story is serviceable enough. Not being too in depth, but providing enough twists and emotional moments to remain engaging throughout. This is a wonderful entry into a beloved franchise, that I think it will appeal to younger and older audiences alike.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a budget jrpg, so don't expect something as grand as Final Fantasy XVI or as polished as Metaphor ReFantazio.But, for what it is, it is still a gorgeous game (seriosuly, it looks like a watercolour painting) with an alright combat system (which does benefict greatly from the class and elemetal systems) and a entretaining albeit superficial story.It is basically a PS2/PS3 action JRPG taken to our era with (sort of) Modern graphics and a few QoL elements.If you liked games like Kingdom Hearts 2, Ni No Kuni, or Nier (the original), you will probably like Visions of Mana.If you're not fully convinced, wait for it to go on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly I beat the game....             Honestly, this is the WORST Mana game by FAR. The plot was concerning, like they tried to take a page from the Tales series but done poorly, They want you to care for one of the main characters family/village but failed HARD. The whole village was insufferable and I didn't care if they all lived or died with how they acted. A lot of NPC's are copy/pasted throughout the game, which would be fine if they were background characters with no name, but some of those models are named here and there. Two of the are even voiced, but their models are still just used over and over again.           The "storytelling" was interesting in a bad way. An enemy would do something like summon a monster, the Main would defeat said monster, the summoner would run away by going THROUGH the main characters group and they'd be like"oh no, they got away. How are we going to stop them?" like WHAT!!? This also happened MULTIPLE TIMES.           Traversing towns is a slog. For whatever reason as soon as you enter a town/village or a city you can no longer double jump or dash/ air dash. Which means you can't just get around as easy as you'd like, which is only annoying because there's literally NO explanation as to why, you just CAN'T, even though you could in the prologue.           Tho overworld voice acting and little quips get annoying real quick. GRIZZLY is the most mind numbing thing to hear in the world while you're just trying to explore the overworld and listen the the music (which honestly might be the ONLY good thing in this game). Grizzly Syrup are giant egg looking things in the world that you collect to trade for items. Only problem? there are WAY TOO MANY. By the time I beat the game I traded and got everything I could get for them and still had hundreds left over, and no they're NOT infinite. They could've been items in the chests as those items are just as useless.               Really the only PRO is the music, when it's not ruined be nonsense chatter...

Maps are big compared to other ARPGs I've played, and full of detail and stuff to find. The design of the classes are also really cool, unlocking them got me hooked. _childDocuments_.review: Usually i'm not a big fan of pro / con list reviews, but Visions of Mana invites this structure very well.Pro:-This game is a visual treat. While not technically impressive, it makes up for it in spades artistically. It captures the Mana series' style to a T. Everything is crooked, crowded, colorful and whimsical. The art direction overall is phenomenal. -The gameplay itself is really fun. Exploration feels great and rewarding. The combat system is great. Not overly complex but with enough depth and customizability to cater the experience towards your playstyle. It also rarely if ever overstays its welcome. Encounters rarely take longer than a minute, rewarding more EXP for shorter clear times. On top of that, encounter can usually be avoided entirely simply by not engaging with them at all. They never feel as if they bog down the experience.Con:-The soundtrack, usually one of the highlights of this series, is incredibly forgetable this time. While no piece is bad, quite the opposite in fact, few of them manage to stick out. Most of them are very quiet, almost ambient background music instead of the series staple heroic, driving tunes. Not the end of the world, but disappointing nontheless.-Sidequest design can be a bit monotonous. There are countless "Go to X and kill 6 Y" quests that don't really add anything to the experience and simply pad out gametime.-Partner AI that lacks any kind of survival instincts. While mostly servicable and thanks to functions to babysit them a little, later regions and bosses show their blatant weakness. Their AI simply isn't good enough to deal with platforming challenges or skill based boss atacks that require more than walking to get out of the way.-Its story is, by a wide margin, Visions of Mana's biggest blunder. It's quite possible the worst written story in its genre. Each and every character, not only the playable ones, operate on room temperature IQ because that's the only way this story even exists. A moral conundrum so hopelessly contrived that the supposed villains turn out to be entirely right in their assumptions and motivations, while everyone else sticks to the script without ever showing agency or a unique thought.Visions of Mana's gameplay and presentation are genuinely so good that they can keep you engaged even if the story needs to be endured rather than enjoyed. If you're only here for the story, this isn't the game for you.If you want a fantastic gameplay experience and can ignore a bad tale? Treat yourself! Ultimately, Visions of Mana is hard not to recommend. The overall package is solid, the gameplay experience is fantastic. But i wish is three writers were awake during their work hours.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best RPG's of 2024.Game-play = 9/10A surprisingly deep and rewarding combat system with up to 40 playable classes (not including non-vesseled).Plenty of ways to customise your group to your own play-style and a addictive monster deleting cycle, adding monster abilities to your own characters skill-set with the use of core-stones. Story = 8.5/10Personally enjoyed the twists and turns in the story, with much of the English voice acting being a lot better than i expected. Replayability = 8/10Plenty of post credits game storyline too! Including an additional difficulty level and New Game Plus beyond that!Music = 10/10I mean, it's a Square Enix game. The music is fantastic.Summary : Probably the best RPG of 2024. It scratches the nostalgic itches you have been looking for if you loved the older games in the series, yet rewards new players alike with challenge, fantastic visuals and a deep experience in customising how battle plays out depending on how far you delve into it, yet not hurting you if you elect to not dabble too much.An engaging series of open world activities with actual rewards that are useful and fun to collect, plenty of side quests and memorable locations, dungeons and boss fights.Feels like we are back in the 90's and it feels good :)Amazing Game. _childDocuments_.review: Pros:-Gorgeous colorful and lively graphic that tells you "this is a Mana game"-Good atmospheric music-Exploration-focused gameplay with relevant rewards-Fun class change on-the-fly system-Combat is similar to Trials of Mana, but faster-Good story with proper character growthCons:-Cutscenes feel stiff-Music is good and mood-fitting, but are not as eargasm like ones in Secret or Trials of Mana-Terrible teleport system that goes through various loading screens.-Terrible side-quest system that requires you backtrack every time a major event happens and some event require to load out and load in the map.-Combat difficulty is not very well-balanced toward the end-New Game+ feels lacking due to level carry-over, making a majority of the game feel irrelevant difficulty wise even at the hardest difficulty-Price tag is hefty.Verdict: 4.5/5Comment: A love-letter to Mana fans and a good modern entry to the series along with Trials of Mana. Whether you are long-time fans of the series or just someone who is attracted by the game's colorful breath-taking art direction, the game would be able to provide dozens of hours of immersion into the world of Mana.What comes with Ouka Studio is a shame, but you should not let that deters you from this wonderful game. After all, Square-Enix has no power regarding the sunset of Ouka Studio which is under NetEase. Still, considering patching still happens (v1.03 is updated one day before this review), I believe the game is not abandoned or anything, so Visions of Mana deserves a chance, whether at full prices or discounts.

_childDocuments_.review: Ever want a game that has a soundtrack that warps you back to the early days of the 90's Squaresoft games? Visions of Mana is your game. Game is an action RPG, in the same vein of games like the Ys series, with a crap load of stuff to do. Gunning through the story will probably last you about 35'ish hours, but good lord is there a lot of side quests, and things to explore and collect. In total there's, I believe, about 120 side quests, most of which are fetch quests/kill this monster style quests, but some quests have an expanded story line all their own, so it's not like they're completely generic quests. Then there's post game content, which I'm honestly not going to bother with since I just spent 60 hours doing basically every quest in the game, a ton of side content, and I have games coming up that I want to move on to, I feel at 60 hours I got my money's worth all the way, a definite banger with a sound track that had me getting nostalgic, missing the 90's Final Fantasy VI/Chrono Trigger/Secret of Mana days.Break down:Graphics 9/10:I love the art style. In fact I love games that look like this; especially on an OLED screen. Though, in this case it's not exactly perfect, some of the texture work is low res, mostly on environmental objects, but it's easy to spot, and can be distracting at times. The level of detail these devs put into the art work is astounding. Sound 10/10:Outside of the questionable English voice overs, the sound was perfect. As I stated above, this game took me back to a time I miss, my teenage years. The sound effects were on-point as well, everything sounded full and meaty.Gameplay 8/10:The game was fun, no mistaking that--but it gets to a point to where "enough is enough." I didn't want to bother with the post game content because 60 hours is a lot of time, and I got to a point to where there really was no point is completing every side quest, and most of the post game content is all just for the challenge, and completionists out there who need to get every achievement. There's no multiple endings, no secret ending, nothing, just harder than usual content that you can just out level, look up a quick build guide, and decimate. Then there's also a jump in difficulty, near the end I went from fighting monsters in the 40's level range, and within a few hours of progressing the story they all of a sudden were in the 60's, luckily with all the side content I did I was able to be the right level, but for those looking to blaze through the game, you might want to grind a little bit of side content first. AFAIK there was nothing missable, so you don't have to do like I did checking each and every area after every quest completion, or story advancement. Character building in this game is fairly basic, nothing super in-depth. Controls 6/10:Controls are simple, and fluid, while exploring. Why I deducted four points? The camera and targeting in fights--c'mon now, it's 2024, can't we get a camera that centers? Can we get a targeting system that isn't ultra sensitive as to switch body parts by tapping the stick you'd normally use to pan the camera? Then there's also interacting with people/objects--you have to come to a full stop first before you can interact, otherwise you'll jump right over, and I can't describe how frustrating it was if the object/person was near a ledge and I'd jump right over and down the ledge and have to run back. Technical 7/10:System specs: 5800X3D/4080S/32GB RAM 1TB NVME/2TB NVME. Game for the most part ran smoothly, outside of some frame drops here and there when cutting from a cut scene to live, but it stayed capped I'd say 95% of the time outside of cutscenes. Unfortunately though, there's a 30 FPS cap on cut scenes that requires you to hit F11 twice if you want to uncap the frame rate so it doesn't look like a stuttery mess. Then there's no native ultrawide 21:9/32:9 support without modifying the executable file with a third party program. Even with modifying the executable file, it doesn't fix it for cut scenes, so those are still set to 16:9, and the UI elements are stuck in the same spot they'd be on a 16:9 monitor. There's also a load screen for what seems like every screen transition outside of teleporting to another part of the area, got annoying after the hundredth time of seeing the same loading screen. Overall: 8/10. Game was enjoyable while it lasted; definitely worth it's price tag and then some, I just felt at points doing side content that it became long in the tooth. For some that might be what they're looking for, for me though, once I completed about 115 side quests, got about 90% of all the collectables in the game, enough was enough, it overstayed it's welcome, while I didn't mind because the game was very enjoyable, I have other games I'd like to get to, and the post game content was basically more of the same--with no real reason for me to bother with it since it literally is just gameplay focused only.

The Bad:- The writing is atrocious, the ending is outright insulting. It is puzzling how a studio can have the talent to make such a gorgeous looking game. And yet have a laughable story and characters. All the classic bad anime troupes are here but dialed to 11. - The main character is the ultimate jobber. _childDocuments_.review: --- Edit after 20 hours of gameplay ---Word of advice, this game has an interesting class progression system that really starts making sense after you play a significant part of the story (close to the end of chapter 4). Before that point, you may feel like there's not much build variety and you're stuck with a bunch of resources you don't know what to do with. Furthermore, a lot of the more interesting/challenging side content also relies on unlocking more classes.Before you go and do like me and play 10 hours of side content only to feel like there's not much sense in doing it, stop! Push the story to at least the end of chapter 4 and the game will open up a lot and the class system will make much more sense, that's when it clicked for me.At the time of writing, I see only about 3.5% of players have unlocked an achievement that indicates they reached this point where the game opens up and you can travel by sea, this means a lot of the playerbase has not seen the true potential of this game.--- Previous review content ---Sometimes a game is not just about the game but also the circumstances in which you find yourself when you approach that game. I've been eyeing this game ever since I saw it was coming out, but when they released the demo I was starting to go through a rough situation that affected my family and made me wish for better times when I could just care about being a kid and not think about every little detail critically all the time. The demo totally made me feel like that kid who didn't know he had things to worry about, and I needed that. I'm approaching this game trying to be like that kid again, putting aside that part of me that has been conditioned to think like a game designer/critic by YouTubers and other people's opinions, and just immersing myself in the experience like a kid would, much like my own kid does things in games that seem pointless, like jumping in place or dropping the character in a pool next to a waterfall just because I can do it.I want to experience something without all the baggage the world put on me and I came to think I had to carry, so that's what I'm doing in Visions of Mana. I'm exploring a beautiful world with my pretty characters, taking it all in, talking with NPCs, feeling like I'm part of that world, doing every little side mission and detour.It's a nice break from all these games about being competitive or getting good, no worrying about perfect parries, dodges or combos, or minmaxing and whatnot, just a fun experience that you can enjoy for the journey rather than the imaginary gamer brownie points.Reading this review, I see that I still focus too much on what I should not think or do, and so I hope to keep healing and through games like this focus on what I can do.I recommend this game to anyone who likes JRPGs but would like a bit more action-oriented combat, beautiful environments and characters, and wants to just have fun without looking super deep into every little mechanical aspect. It's a polished experience with some rough edges that do not at all take away from the enjoyment.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to have to give this game a Not Recommended, because there are a lot of things it does well. The graphics are vibrant, and a very nice callback to the colorful SNES titles. The localization was handled with care, using the enemy, item, and elemental names from the US release of Secret of Mana, for maximum nostalgia. If you remember something from the classics, it's probably here in some form.The story has an interesting premise, and although it doesn't necessarily live up to it, I enjoyed speculating on things in the early hours. There are some really good character moments, including one that made me extremely emotional, although others are telegraphed heavily and fall flat. The character designs are fun, and every single character has a unique class based on each element, making for tons of different outfits and abilities. But is the gameplay fun? For a while, it's enjoyable. But the battle system never really clicked for me- the computer controlled characters are mindless- that could be the case in Secret of Mana, but should not still be an issue in 2024. The combat is so fast and chaotic, especially when there are many enemies on screen, that I didn't find it fun to try and strategize like I would in the older titles. The story starts promising, but started to fall apart for me as I made it past the halfway mark and they really missed the mark with the main villain. The delivery of the story can also be an issue. The game loves to drop you into cutscenes, and then have you walk for five seconds only to start another one. It's jarring and they tend to be really long winded when they don't need to be. Sometimes you can press a button to advance the cutscene dialogue and sometimes you can't, can never really tell what it's going to be. The towns feel a little half baked, with generic NPC's, a very large number of boring sidequests, and they're full of buildings that you can't enter. I was having a great time for a while, but once the novely of running around in a new Mana world wore off, I started to sour on the game a little. It also repeated what I considered a game design fault from Trials of Mana almost verbatim, but hard to touch on that without giving away plot details. May still be worth a purchase if you're a long time fan of the series. I had a blast just seeing Salamando, Undine, Rabbites, Mushbooms and all the rest in lovely 3D. But sadly, the game is not destined to be remembered as a classic, and this may be the Mana series swan song.

_childDocuments_.review: Fans of the Mana series are almost guaranteed to love this. Classic Mana story with some good twists; essentially a story of three similar men in similar situations whose circumstances lead them down different paths. Love and duty are central themes to the plot.Mechanically, a more kinetic and vertical combat system similar to Trials of Mana. Most of the game is spent fighting large groups of small enemies or huge bosses. Characters have clearly defined roles, but the class system lets you customize your experience to a sufficient degree. Over time you gain access to so many mechanics the game gets a little easy even on the Hard setting (which I played through the game on exclusively), but the final post game superboss definitely puts up enough of a fight to leave completionists satisfied at the end.The English localization is competent and sufficiently inventive, and the actors' performances good to a degree where I never considered setting the voices to Japanese.The only real frustration was how most of the sidequests were menial MMO fair. I recommend skipping the ones where the reward is just lucre.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of SoM and ToM, Visions left me bored by the end of a 25 hour playthrough. I really wish there was something else other than Yes/No options for recommendations, but at it's current price there's no way I can recommend it.The Mana series never got the love that Square's other titles have, so I was stoked to see we had another Mana game releasing. The game started off kinda strong but everything in the game feels undercooked and there's not a single ounce of imagination save for the visuals.The visuals are the only thing that really stood out to me, you get to explore vast areas of vibrant colors that really pop and make the world feel alive. However, those areas tend to be way too big for no reason other than to scour around and pick up useless crap. There's nothing interesting to find in any of the fields and while they're "open," the game is so linear is basically doesn't matter. Going off the beaten path only wastes your time and hardly ever are you rewarded with something worth the exploration.The audio is okay, you got some tracks from Kikuta that shine above the rest but the soundtrack here doesn't hold a candle to SoM or ToM, I guarantee you won't remember any of the music or nod your head to it like I find myself doing when I play SoM/ToM.The game falls apart in two departments:The Story: The story is the most basic JRPG fair, save the world from a one dimensional bad guy as a group of one dimensional good guys. Nearly all of the plot points and story beats of the game are lifted from other Mana titles so if you've played other games you've already seen the show. If the characters were interesting and fun then it wouldn't be to bad, but you won't get attached to any of them. They're also all lifted from other Mana titles: the spry swordsman, a lonely rogue, a plucky sprite, a sassy mage and a posh one. It's every basic anime trope shoved into one single game.The Gameplay: Here's where the game falls apart fast, the combat feels like the ToM remake, but slower. It's your typical action RPG a la Kingdom Hearts, but instead you have a shallow combo system for your basic few attacks, special moves that you can't combo into or combo out of and magic that takes a long time to cast. It's also quite mindless and you won't need to be strategic in any way. The game is pretty easy for the first 80%, not even bosses will pose a threat so you'll just steamroll your way to the back half where bosses won't really challenge you as much as become sponges that take too long to take down. The combat aside, what else is there? The "exploration" is just as shallow as the combat and the only other thing to do is one of the over 100 meaningless fetch quests that net you nothing of value. I don't know about the later games, but SoM and ToM didn't have any side quests really and they were all the better for them. None of the characters that give you side quests are important or memorable anyway so "helping" them isn't rewarding at all.At the end of the day you have an incredibly linear experience with a dull combat system and a weak story with forgettable characters. If you want some pretty crap to stare at for 20 or so hours, you could do better than this and I would certainly wait for this to be on sale (I'm talking like, sub $20 here) if you really want to play it.Oh also, I played the whole thing on Steam Deck and it has some noticeable hitches, the only way to get a smooth experience is if you turn on the FSR to "Performance" but even then it'll still hitch and it looks awful. There's also a single, ambiguous graphic setting to change without any way to tune it. The game either looks bad and runs decent, or you're getting an good looking game that can't maintain a solid 30 (forget anything higher).

_childDocuments_.review: Visions of Mana is visually arresting. There are moments when meandering through its lushes landscapes that stun the senses into total titillation (that alliteration is for you, Palamena). The music is also lovely. The gameplay, story, characters, and overall design are very straightforward, trope-filled, JRPG affair. Collect the 1-dimensional heroes, traverse the world gaining power and prestige, then face off against a big-bad to save the world from destruction. You know the drill. But not rocking the boat here is not a bad thing. Playing this game is like eating comfort food, especially for those older gamers of the SNES/PS1 era. Visions of Mana will entertain and delight, especially if its design constraints are accepted.

_childDocuments_.review: tldr: Buy on a sale, it's pretty good but nothing too special and hella expensive.I love party based action RPGs, I love class systems, and I've always loved the Mana series so this game did really hit it out of the park expectation-wise. The story opted less for series of interconnected events loosely strung together by a flat cast and leaned more towards a "Tales of" or late-90s "Final Fantasy" era RPG storyline. The characters have a bit more depth here than that of earlier games, but it's still quite shallow if you were to hold it to more modern gaming standards. That being said, I found the earnest way it committed to its themes at least impressive, it never tried to be more than it was. If you find the story boring, I'd at least say the cast is worth investing time in. They're not the most complex, but they all have cute personalities and their chemistry is really fun to watch. Downsides to the story mostly lie in the pacing. A lot of things happen earlier on and they happen at a relatively natural pace. I feel Eoren needed more development with the cast and Hinna needed more time to bond with everyone, but either way things hit where they needed to. Otherwise, once the main villain joins the plot start to really fall off the deep end and it becomes inter-connected exposition dumps and Daedolus constantly whining about his dead girlfriend.Gameplay-wise I loved it, I just wish there was more. The classes especially had some bafflingly weird decisions. When compared to Trials, they play it really safe in the options these classes give you, at least in terms of party flexibility. They also didn't expand on the movesets enough to give them much of an in-game difference. Also seriously the choice to spread out the weapons as they did was so annoying because Palamena with boots is far less fun (imo) to Palamena with a Flail but sometimes you need fire damage, y'know?Other small notes:Palamena was great, I loved her big obtrusive tailBut seriously her Light class design is the most disgusting thing I've ever seenIt's sooooo prettyBut the cutscenes are really awkward sometimesNPC designs had a lot of detail shockinglyLyza was massively misused, as was Eoren, the villain suckedBig magic was soooo fun to play around withEndgame bosses sucked so muchSummons were a cool idea but their execution was such garbage

_childDocuments_.review: A Rough Start for Vision of Mana: A Hopeful Glimpse Beyond the FlawsI'll admit, giving this game a thumbs down was a tough decision, but the cons just outweighed the pros. Despite the game's potential, its flaws are hard to ignore. I'm planning to explore more and holding out hope that a wave of patches will sweep in to fix these issues.First, let's talk about the good stuff. Combat and exploration feel solid, and the story has its hooks, even if it doesn’t stray far from the usual JRPG/Anime clichés. The dialogue can be a bit on the juvenile side, and our hero seems blissfully unaware of the chaos unfolding around them, just drifting along without a care in the world. But hey, who needs self-awareness when you've got oversized swords and magical powers, right?Now, for the not-so-good. This game isn’t a AAA title, but it’s being marketed—and priced—like one. The textures sometimes look like they were pulled straight from 2015, and some of the effects are questionable. Also don't get me started on the overall geometry—it’s quite light on details, luckily the amazing art direction and the over architecture shine through any flaws the game might have and makes it quite nice to look at, especially the big city after chapter 1.The real kicker for me is the PS4 compatibility. We’re years into the PS5 era, and yet here we are, stuck with 30FPS cutscenes, minimal graphic customisation, and PC features that are basically nonexistent. No ultra-wide support, no Steam Deck resolution—it's as if they forgot PC gamers exist. Square Enix, in classic fashion, seems more interested in raking in sales than delivering a polished product.And seriously, in 2024, 30FPS cutscenes? Not cool. Having to hex edit the game just to get proper resolution support and pressing F11 twice every time to get cutscenes to run at 120FPS is beyond frustrating. That’s not something any gamer should have to deal with.I'm willing to change my review if Square Enix steps up and patches this release, but until then, it’s hard to recommend Vision of Mana in its current state.Vision of Mana is a game that delivers an enjoyable and engaging experience, especially if you're a fan of classic JRPGs. The combat, while a bit on the easy side, is undeniably fun and addictive. The wide range of character class customization options adds depth and keeps the gameplay feeling fresh. This is where the game truly shines.The artistic direction is another highlight. Despite the technical shortcomings, the character and environment art is quite appealing, with a dreamy, nostalgic vibe that captures the essence of what makes JRPGs special. However, the game is held back by some glaring issues. The textures on background objects are kind of ugly sometimes, and the lack of terrain geometry gives the game a dated feel, reminiscent of the PS4 era. This clash between beautiful art, amazing background and poor technical execution can be jarring.As for the story, it’s generally enjoyable but leans heavily into the "anime" side of things. Characters often behave like children, with the main cast being overly single-minded in their goals, lacking the complex, introspective thinking that would make them feel more like real people rather than just video game characters.In general, I’m favorable toward the game, but its technical flaws are hard to overlook. Players often find themselves tinkering with files and mods just to make the game more appealing. Coupled with its $60 USD price tag, it’s hard to recommend a day-one purchase unless you’re a hardcore Mana fan. If not, it might be wise to wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: The Secret of Mana series has been a part of my life since I was very young. I remember the leveling system in the first and many of the subsequent series very fondly. You use a weapon or mana type to level said weapon or mana type up, levels for these weapons are seperated from your character level, and gated behind collecting new weapons, or unlocking new mana types. Every new level a character gains with a weapon or mana type unlocks a new charge or casting level, which lends itself to some of the fight dynamics, where you choose between finding opportunities to charge your attacks for bigger, more punchy attacks, or dodging attack patterns, and getting in smaller more convenient hits as the situation calls for it.In Visions of Mana, your abilities are gated behind finding new mana types, but their levels aren't. instead, you may occasionally find an item hidden in the world that allows a single character to unlock the next tier of abilities, and cannot unlock the final tier until you complete the base game once. Levelling those mana - paths? lines? lines. - up requires you to invest points that you get by levelling your character normally, and finding elemental nodes, which are scattered around the world. And levelling each of these elemental lines up doesn't necessarily unlock better things for that elemental concept. To use the very first unlocked element as an example, the main protag focuses on elemental weapon enchantments in that line, called saber magic (it's just enchantment, there are no fancy moves), but most of the saber magics are unlocked in other elemental lines, and some of the better abilities that buff saber magic, - which until you beat the base game once, are locked to the use of that element - are scattered randomly in the other elemental lines. I'm trying really hard not to call them skill trees, there is no tree, no trail, it's just a line. There are 8 of them, one for each element, they all fit on the same screen, and the only skills that aren't magic are unlocked in the very first two nodes of each line.Levelling mechanics aside, there are two stories in the Secret of Mana series. The one that tells the tale of the Hero of Mana, and their companions, chosen by the world to vanquish the evil forces that lurk in the shadows, eating away at the worlds very foundation, and the one of the Alms, chosen normally by their people through some means, as sacrifices, on a journey offer their souls to the world, to replenish it's supply of mana - but wait, how can just a small handful of people power the whole world? they can't!, what a twist. and now your party needs to become the worlds heroes, and root out the evils that don't lurk in the shadows, and are right there, but no one before you wanted to deal with them, because that is just the way of things...In case it wasn't obvious, Visions of Mana employs the story of the alms. I don't hate this version of the story, and in this case, there's a good nod to the hero's story, but it's just so... boring. The BBEG who is the BBEG and remains the BBEG (I say this because there are plot twists in other games, where they were actually not the BBEG, and there's a Bigger, Badder big bad evil guy, or guys, they're trying to thwart. Not the case here.), and their motivation is petty at best. Good villains think they're doing the right thing. Unless tehy are kefka levels of evil. This one is neither. The story is very on the rails, you can see all the plot points coming from half the story away, and the only plus is that most of your party, save the main protag, are not annoyingly, irredeemably stupid, and at least they're not as bad as the big bad stupid villain, and all the other characters know it. That's what we're going to use for this kind of villain from now on. They're just too stupid to be called evil. BBSV. Big Bad Stupid Villain. AKA, don't play that game for it's story, unless it's a comedy adventure. it's just not compelling.Replayability is non-existent. I am tired of the endless fetch quests that have you scrambling around the world, either defeating some minor group of enemies, or retrieving an item, or both, for little to no reward. In previous alms titles, New Game + allowed you to play the game from the perspectives of the other characters, and in at least a couple of the titles, it all tied together with an end-game that you could only access after puzzling together story bits from all the campaigns. so while you often ran through the same areas with the same or similar enemies, it felt fresh because of the new perspective, and all the nuanced little interactions, and playtime wasn't padded with side-quests. - which I have done all of, and am disappointed to find that my last achievement isn't to complete all the side-quests, it's a hidden achievement which requires I replay the entire game, to defeat a final boss on a higher difficulty. - This game doesn't do any of that. All of the characters eventually tag along, there are no alternate paths you can take, there's nothing that would be unique or exciting in the new game +, you can, and probably will, do it all in a single play-through.The game also holds your hand from start to finish. Save for some of the bosses attack patterns, everything is explained to you with intrusive pop-ups fully covering the mechanics, almost none of the mechanics for each area are ever recycled, and they almost all involve you pressing a single button at your leisure, or something that is entirely outside of your control, and you don't really need to worry about.I love this series, but if you haven't played some of the earlier titles, don't buy this game, buy one of the earlier titles. This game is for a long week, when your sick, and don't have the motivation to do literally anything else, or the brain power to really think about what you're doing. Equip big sword, big sword smash, follow stars.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the most beautiful game I have ever played. They really outdid themselves on the design, colors, ambiance and all graphical things. Not from a technical standpoint but an artistic one. Entering the Sanctuary of Mana and seeing the Mana tree in the distance for the first time is a truly magical moment.It's also a Mana game, so it has pros and cons. If you're a fan, it's a must have. If you're not a fan but you like action RPG games and don't worry too much about the story, it's a must have as well.Not that the story is bad, just that it's not its strong point like other Mana games (with the exception of some Legend of Mana quest paths). The story starts by being very thought provoking, it puts the player in the uneasy situation that they must sacrifice their friends so that the world can avoid being destroyed, as has been done every four years for a very long time. The evil actions of one character end up being the key to find a third path that does not involve sacrifice and opens up a new era. It is a pretty neat plot, but it doesn't have the best execution.

_childDocuments_.review: Realized it's probably past due for me to leave a review after binging it for 20 hours. Game might honestly be my GOTY if the momentum keeps up.-All the open world zones look absolutely stunningly beautiful and are incredibly fun to explore and get all the chests/elementite-The Nemesis enemies are all fun to fight and make exploring little corners feel a lot more worth it, giving regular enemies expanded mini boss movesets is a fantastic idea-Both types of aeries are very fun, with lesser aeries being ways to test how good your current party comp is (or just class strike to win) and greater aeries being very fun gimmick fights testing how good you are with the elemental vessels-The dungeons tend to be short and sweet with very fun boss fights at the end (earth being my personal favorite so far), and the environments for them are incredibly varied and fun-The story feels comfy and familiar so far, like I've heard it a thousand times before (in a good way). While there will probably be twists ahead, (only halfway through chapter 4 right now) I'm very happy with how the story has felt so far, including every party member's strange speech.All in all, this game has been fantastic so far. Also, all the advertising kept talking about how it's a 30 hour rpg, yet I'm 22 hours in and have yet to get the last party member lol.

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly I just want to clarify that I refunded this product after 90 minutes so I am not going to comment on the story of the game as I feel I really haven't scratched this. As someone that LOVED Trials of Mana, I came into this game with an open mind and optimism for what this game has to offer. However after 90 minutes of playing this, I soon realised this wasn't a game I was willing to dive into for the many hours that I had previously done with Trials of Mana. First point I want to make clear, this is not a terrible game. I've seen a lot of comments and reviews bashing this game but actually its OK, in the end there was just too many concerns for me to ignore and I decided to refund this and come back to it later.ProsThis games looks beautiful, and there is no denying they have made some amazing areas and the characters look great too (albeit generic at times). The music is wonderful, similar to Trials of Mana the game produces some great soundtracks and the sound effects compliment the game quite nicely. The combat was actually fun too, which I think is important if you are going to be spending the next 30 plus hours using it, I don't think its perfect but its straightforward and easy to learn. ConsMy first concern was the actual performance of the game, I had already seen that people had to install mods for this game to run with less stutters and glitches etc. That is never a good sign for a new release. Secondly, the character model themselves seem to never agree with the terrain. Sometimes you'll just catch a foot or leg glitching out on a bit of rock or a change of angle. This may sound minor but when you see a foot do a 180 spin just because its stood a small rock, that stuff will start to bug you. Once again, this was never present in Trials of Mana. When using Val at the start in idle mode, the basic outfit you start with even clips into itself. Another small issue but if thats the starting outfit, you would expect some collision there. Another issue was the immersion. I love the areas and the music and the first time I saw a field of crops I wanted to run through it so bad....what I didn't realise is that the crops have no collision on them, so you just walk straight throw them, and same with the bushes. They went to the extent to allow for water collision and snow but they couldn't do it for grass, fields of crops or bushes. It is these little things that started to stack up and take me out the immersion. On the prologue when you use double jump for the first time my character landed and went INTO the platform. Only my head was showing, and then later on after a cut-scene the game just simply froze. I could move the camera but nothing else. Not a deal breaker but just letting you know it happened. The defining moment for me was the combat. I mentioned above that the combat is good, and it is HOWEVER there is an option in the settings which I like to use which turns off battle animations. When the player uses a CS, it stops the 4-5 second video playing of them carrying out the strike. I turned this off (just a preference) thinking this would just shorten down some of the combat as I knew I would personally get bored of seeing the CS over and over again. To my great surprise when you turn this option off, rather than the player carry out a simple move mechanic to provide the CS, they just flashbang the screen with a white overlay and once your retinas have regained sight, the enemy is on the floor dead. WHY WOULD I WANT TO WATCH A 2 SECOND FLASHBANG EVERYTIME I CARRIED OUT A CS!! After hitting all of these issues, and they really just are small changes (which I really hope change in the future) you can see why I eventually decided to refund this and come back to this down the line. Because for 50 pounds, its just not clean enough. Too many little things which are not sorted, and a few choices which they made (like the white screen flash) which I just personally don't like. In Trials of Mana I felt immersed and I didn't mind if the story was silly or the voice acting was over the top, it was fun. This game looks like it could be like that but at the moment I am just not buying into it. I hope to be wrong in 6 months time.

_childDocuments_.review: Early review which I'll change over time as needed.Visions of Mana is a game that, to me, *fully understood the assignment.* While it doesn't take any massive leaps, it's an incredibly comfortable and visually stunning game. It feels like they took what they learned about the Trials of Mana remaster and just pushed it forward to make a really sharp game. I already find myself really hooked into the feelings of these characters, who despite how you feel about the voice acting (I like it, but people are complaining about it) I feel are pretty neatly written.There are a few cons, though. I thought Square learned some of their lessons on this, but the graphics options are just not enough for a modern-day full price PC release. Framerate locks, jitter, and *very* sparse customization abound. This is not enough to kill the enjoyment of the game for me, but hopefully they definitely put some patches through down the line.If you already like Mana or the Super Famicom RPG heyday, get this and I really think you won't be disappointed. And if you're not sure how you feel yet, I feel like the demo will give you a decent idea right away.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a good JRPG for those who want a classic feel and it's overall a good game, there are some flaws I'll get into but here's my thoughts:The GoodThe world is lush and vibrant, and exploring it is a joy, there is some seriously impressive scenary and attention to detail to emphasize the elements of the world. I might have a lot in the "Meh" category below, but this aspect of the game is seriously so good it gets a recommendation for that aloneGameplay is simple "target elemental weakness" stuff but it feels impactful and fun, it's classic gameplay mostly for betterMana fanservice - if you liked old games, you're going to love seeing your favorite characters and familiar locales realized in the highest definition we've seen so far for these games.The Meh (minor vague spoilers)The story is pretty average, and I was hoping for something a little more from the final boss to be honest. I thought it started strong and got weak in the later half, and it really falls flat with the ending for what was some solid pieces of lore the game built out. It turned out unexpected, but not in a good way I guess.The characters have cool moves and amazing designs, but I couldn't say I care for many of their personalities.The animation rigging could have used some work, there were some emotional scenes that felt like the graphics were incredible but with facial expressions from the PS2 era.Voice acting is mixed in English but Japanese was good throughout, I'd just switch to that and don't look back.I do wish we could get co-op back in this series.Overall it's an easy recommendation at full price if you have played a Mana game before, and if you're just into JRPGs in general maybe wait for a sale for this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Allow me to preface this by acknowledging the closure of the studio.  I don't really follow the industry so I don't know who was in charge of what, and what's important to me is that the overall aesthetic has gotten rarer in the genre, so I think it's worth highlighting this title.  I played this game right after finishing the Trials of Mana remake, so I'll be making comparisons between the two.  Also be aware that I played with JP audio, so as expected, I don't have any complaints about the acting.tl;dr: Worth playing if you like JRPGs, even if it's not quite worthy of being a flagship title imo.Gameplay:Pros: There are a lot of system improvements over Trials of Mana.  You're able to swap out classes whenever your'e not in combat.  Map traversal is more fun due to double jumps, air dashes, and interactive terrain.  You acquire a mount fairly early in the story, and it only feels necessary to use when you don't want to fight monsters in the area.  There are a good amount of abilities, some of them as slottable items, other unlocked per character via skill points.Cons: The combat itself doesn't feel greatly improved over Trials of Mana.  If anything, playing a melee character feels more frustrating, because you don't have staged combos, and you can rarely get more than 2 or 3 hits on a monster before it either gets knocked away or jumps.  Only the ninja character even comes close to mitigating this, and that's because he has attacks that warp him directly to a nearby target.My recommended way to play is either choose the mage, or abuse the supers (or "class strikes" as the game calls them).  It seems there is a way to pick and choose skills but it is unlocked very late into a playthrough, and you can only max out a character in the post-game content.Story:The story is quite predictable if you've got any genre awareness, but the handling of the script and broad strokes of the plot are quite competent.  There are a handful of scenes, however, that fumble some plot points, create plot holes, or else feel disjointed.  I heard that there were series veterans on the dev team, but they were in charge of monster/environment designs and music.  I am therefore assuming the writers are inexperienced, because it shows.  To the writers' credit, I did not skip any of the cutscenes, and I have definitely skipped a good bit in Trials.Visuals:Pros: This is the strongest and most noticeable upgrade over Trials of Mana, which had charming characters, but often suffered due to the lack of animation budget.  In Visions of Mana, characters have much smoother animations across the board.  There are still a few animations that stick out as stiff, but it's all quite forgivable compared to Trials.  It's also very nice to see this kind of illustration art style rendered with more modern techniques.  The lighting engine makes all the characters look beautiful, with shaders that do a great job of translating the 2D art into the game.  The maps are all very pretty, with good water and foliage effects.Cons: The facial textures on the main protagonist are oddly low-resolution.  I am unsure if this is due to a loading issue of some sort, but every other character has a much higher-resolution face.  The modeling of many of the NPCs is also jarringly different from the main characters.  Perhaps the primary modeler only did the main cast and some interns had to do the NPCs.  There is no camera mode, and models go semi-transparent if you try to force the camera closer (this can be fixed with a mod, of course).Performance:I never encountered any heavy stuttering or crashes, but there were a few sidequests that wouldn't spawn objectives until I reloaded my save.  I also had to install an optimization mod to improve load times, which are just barely tolerable on my machine.  It's also somewhat annoying that it takes about 10~15 seconds to transition to the flying mount when in Trials it only took about 5~7 seconds, and it was already slightly annoying there.

_childDocuments_.review: Ouka Studios was sent as alms to the NetEase Tree. The developer has been shut down by the publisher, the day after the game released.In an era where there are a billion action jrpgs with interesting characters, and story's that keep you engaged and interested in the world they are set in, here comes Visions of Mana, which decided to shift the paradigm, and be completely unimpressive.Characters are poorly written, and decidedly lacking in introspection. From the Prologue, I was expecting the story to have a twist at some point, where some manner of unforeseen event happens, or the characters find a way to stop the cycle of sacrifice. Instead, the story, as provided in chapter one, stays consistently boring, and on track with what the characters wanted to do from the first moment you meet them. The story never evolves, or changes, at any time. The characters motivations never evolve or change, at any time. They simply are on a journey to a tree,  Realistically I didn't spoil anything because the game tells you the full story in the first hour. Whether you want to see the journey they embark on for $60 is up to you.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start off this review by expressing a few of my gripes with the game, because while it is a massive step up from its predecessor: Trial of Mana, in many ways, it's not without it's issue.The biggest problem this game faces is one it inherited from its predecessor, that being the awkwardness of the character models. Their lip sync is inconsistent, the idle and dialogue animations are repetitive and tend to get caught in loops and many of the facial expression can often come across as rather blank and even uncanny. Moments like these can tend to be very distracting and took me out of my immersion at times, but they're by no means deal breakers. I would also argue that the game's soundtrack does little to really stick in your mind. It serves its purpose fine during gameplay, but outside of play,  it's rather forgettable.Aside from what I mentioned above, this is still an overall solid RPG. The story and writing took a huge step up compared to Trials and the segmented, yet larger open world is just an absolute joy to explore. All the chests, items and interactables in the world, on top of the addition of sidequests, means that you rarely are just rushing from one story point to the next. The fact that interactables are marked on the map adds to the exploration, making it difficult to not want to just explore every inch of a new area. While I still wouldn't quite call this a top 10 RPG, Visions of Mana truly took several strides to improve upon the series and those strides show.

_childDocuments_.review: I did enjoy this game, the mechanics were fun and overall the story wasn't that bad, there have been certainly worse. The characters were interesting and the music is probably the best thing about this game. Some aspects of the game/story were rather predictable, however that isn't that bad. It's a pretty good beginner JRPG for someone who has not played a lot and wants to get into the series or JRPGs in general. The ending is however a bit blander than expected so don't go expecting something amazing.One issue I did have was the game constantly crashing. I have tried this game with 2 different graphics cards and still would get black screens then crashing. I don't know if this is an AMD issue (both cards were AMD, however I did use different cards/drivers from AMD) or just the game in general, however it would generally crash after playing for ~2 hours straight. So save often is my recommendation! I have beaten the game and likely will not return to it, but figured I'd write a review since I finished it.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely loved this game, probably my favorite Square Enix's RPG since DQXI. It's incredibly beautiful, each environement is a sight to behold. The music is great as usual, you can feel the Seiken 2 & 3 vibes. The story is pretty good- the most part is "classic" for a JRPG, I don't exactly expect the best stories in a Mana game to be honest, but this one had very likeable characters and a few plot twists to make it interesting enough.I liked the combat, although it's fair to say it takes 5-10 hours to become more interesting, but once it opens up with the jobs and characters, you can find very enjoyable and fast-paced way to play the game. Just don't use the lock, because honestly, it sucks lol. The exploration was also fun and enjoyable, you never spend too much time in the same place, the relics gimmicks are nothing complex but that's cool.In conclusion, if you like JRPGs, you'll most likely enjoy Visions of Mana. It's not a revolution of the genre, but it does great at what it wants to do, and you can tell the game was made with care and love for the series. In my opinion, it's the best Seiken Densetsu to date!

_childDocuments_.review: Secret of Mana was one of my favorite games when I was a little kid so I've always had a soft spot for the Mana series despite it constantly letting me down. While the story was the typically poorly written JRPG trash and the characters are just screaming to be punched in the face for begin annoying the rest of the game is actually fairly good. The game play loop kept me entertained enough to complete the game and the music was pretty solid even though the side quest where the standard boring fetch quest slop.It's nothing special but if you like the Mana series it's one the the best games they have released in a long time so if you have played Trials of Mana and are looking for more in the series play this game, if you haven't played Trials of Mana go play that first (it's better). _childDocuments_.review: I loved every single second! The story may be a bit generic here and there, and it does resemble Tales of Symphonia with the journey to the Mana Tree (even though it often gets sad), but the gameplay is what ultimately won me over. The class system is one of the strongest points in the game, and on 'Hard', the game can actually be quite challenging at times (especially the Aeries!).The game offers a lot of content, and if you're into collecting, you'll enjoy it even more!The only downside for me was that the animations in the cutscenes often felt lifeless, and the lip-syncing was really bad.I can definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoys the Mana series or good action RPGs!In my opinion, it's the best Mana game in the series, even though I was very biased towards the old/new Secret of Mana/Trials of Mana!Edit: I experienced many crashes, unfortunately, but to fix it, right-click the game in your Steam library, go to 'Properties,' then under 'Launch Options,' enter '-dx11'. After doing this, I had no further issues.

_childDocuments_.review: Visions of Mana is pretty good. It does have a nice art style, decent character designs and have vibrant and colorful over world to explore. And while I'm not that much in to love story plot I would very much have that over the nonsense I am seeing in the current modern day triple A and double A titles. Also am surprised that I have not heard any censorship on the scripts and whatnot considering that this is a Square-Enix published game and they have history of screwing with the scripts on their previous RPG titles.If there is one minor thing I would pick on this game is that whenever you're using Vuscav to travel around the sea you can't access menus and maps. I can't recall if you can in Trials of Mana but I vaguely remember it having at least a mini map to see where you're going when you're riding Vuscav but Visions of Mana didn't have any in that regard. It's nothing game breaking just a mild annoyance.All in all imo this is a high quality title. A shame about the Dev team that got axed a few days after they released Visions Mana because if they can produce a decent title like this I would like to see more of their future works.

_childDocuments_.review: Visions of Mana is not a horrible game, but I’d hesitate to recommend it to anyone other than people who straight up just want to play a mid-tier JRPG. The only aspect of this game that makes it stand out from its competitors are the stunning environments, and to be fair, the environments in this game are actually stunning; it’s the type of game where you look at a screenshot of it and say “I want to live there”. That doesn’t save Visions of Mana from having awful movement and gameplay though.Controlling a character somehow feels both stiff and floaty at the same time. You will also occasionally find yourself getting stuck on terrain for a moment, and it happens just frequently enough to annoy me. This carries over into combat where an otherwise decent action combat system is marred by the controls just feeling extremely off. The game does have some cool combat ideas as well, such as the ability to pause and issue commands to other party members. This can create a bit of strategizing as you have to cure status ailments, aid a party member that is being grappled by an enemy, etc. It is not enough however to save the simplistic hack and slash combat system, especially when said simplistic combat system controls awfully.The story is a pretty cliche JRPG affair, there’s some elemental stuff and some of your party members have to be sacrificed to stop a calamity from occurring. Long story short, it didn’t hook me and that is what matters. If there is some twist that is introduced 20 hours into the story, that is great and all, but it still failed to hook me from the beginning.In conclusion, I honestly don’t hate this game, but for me it feels like such a slog to play. If you are in the mood to just play a decent JRPG, it is alright. Don’t pay $60 for it though, wait for it to go on sale. I would probably just recommend I Am Setsuna over this game if you are just looking for a JRPG to waste some time with, as it is an overall less frustrating experience than this game was (and it’s not $60 DOLLARS).

_childDocuments_.review: Look, if you're a Mana Fan and you played Seiken Densetsu 3, when it was called that, and have also played the Trials of Mana remake: you're gonna like this game.  If you like real time combat JRPGs at all and just want a comfy game to sit down with for ~60 hours, you're gonna like this game.  If you're a nitpicker who is bothered by lack of polish in certain areas or games that are "good but flawed", you *might* like this game.  I loved my time with Visions of Mana and had pretty much non-stop fun, but even I understand where its flaws lie.Gameplay:This is not an open-world game: it's a mostly linear JRPG with some large areas that feel like little open worlds.  You can branch out and do certain things in these open areas in any order, and get bogged down by side-quests at your leisure, but the game is ultimately a straight shot from plot-point to mandatory place.  The core combat of the game is genuinely pretty fantastic.  It's real time with AI party members but you can quickswap to them as expected of a Mana game.  There's no co-op or multiplayer of any kind sadly, but that doesn't diminish the core fun.  It's limited initially, and the game is very careful to add new systems one at a time.  Eventually you have to make judgment calls on when to spend multiple sorts of "limit breaks" tied to 2 meters and how specifically to build in regards to each of those: with some interesting strategic trade-offs.  For example, you may want to equip the Vessel of Water onto a party member for the class they gain access to, but then you fight a boss that's immune to water and it makes the Vessel's combat utility completely nullified: now you could switch to a different class but that might come with other downsides that outweigh the upsides for you, lots of give-and-take systems with opportunity cost like that.  The accessorizing and general character building is also satisfying: and it opens up significantly in a cool way in the post-game. It's not all good though: the camera is atrocious at many points and you can't freely rotate the camera if you use lock-on... leading to some annoyance.  There's also some slight balance issues with the really strong stuff, and you'd need to self-impose limits to keep the game challenging.  Lastly there's definitely too many side-quests overall and most (but not all) of them are pretty repetitive and boring, but not so much that I didn't complete them all.Graphics:This is easily the best-looking game in the series and it has some jaw-dropping particle effects and attack animations in combat.  Field and environment graphics are mostly good, especially at a distance, but there are examples of pretty ugly and low-res textures on lots of things if you look hard enough.  All of the cutscenes are in-engine so they show your equipment and costumes, as well as the super-detailed character models, but this can contrast glaringly against the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ blurry brick texture on the castle wall behind you: Overall good but showing a distinct and distracting lack of polish,  Faces look great but facial animation has some weird misses, like certain bones (especially eyebrows) just aren't animated to move at all... making the character faces fail to convey the intended emotion at pivotal moments.  The disconnect between the faces and the voice acting can be jarring.Music:The soundtrack is outstanding, absolutely the best part of the game.  This game does justice to its predecessors with no fewer than 14 boss themes and tons of fun callbacks to prior Mana games.  The 3 composers are Hiroki Kikuta (THE Mana guy), Tsuyoshi Sekito, and Ryo Yamazaki.  The important thing to mention right away is that EVERY environment theme which can have enemies in it, has 2 versions of its background music.  There's a combat theme that changes some instrumentation and adds new drum tracks, sortof like a "Yoshi theme" from Sunshine.  Most of the environment themes are good, and most of the boss themes are great, but the real standouts in this game are the town themes.  Each town has such a distinct musical flair and the tracks are very long and masterfully done: Etaern's theme has been stuck in my head for weeks.Story:Some people play RPGs for story, and while that's never necessarily been the strongpoint of the Mana games (gameplay first), there's quite a lot going on here in terms of dialogue and cutscene action.  The writing is mostly fine, and the plot points are interesting if predictable.  The story inevitably treads some series staples like Mana Sword this, Goddess Tree that (it's right there in the thumbnail and title screen) but some of the locations in-between are new and pretty cool.  Some parts of this game are EXTREMELY SAD so maybe be warned if you don't necessarily like games that try to make you cry.  As is quite common these days, the English dub is not up to snuff relative to the Japanese voices.  Most of the main cast performances are fine, with absolute standout work by Morley and Aesh, but then there's Careena who is inexplicably a Texan kind o' guuuurl and whose performance has been memed on considerably.  The option to switch to Japanese is there for anyone who wants it (but I liked Careena and her VA grew on me).Conclusion:C'mon, real Mana fans already understand that most of us pre-ordered this game.  Every single person I know personally, who owns this game, pre-ordered it.  We were the target audience and we bought it.  If you're reading this review it might be because you are considering getting the game and aren't sure if you want it.  I got ~70 hours of very fun gameplay out of Visions of Mana on my quest to 100% achievements, and I did a lot of recording vids and just idling listening to the music as well.  I didn't need any convincing to get this game, so I'm not sure how to convince anyone else to get it... well except to ask "do you like having fun?"

_childDocuments_.review: Visions of Mana draws you into a beautifully crafted world with vibrant colors and stunning environments.The characters are so endearing that you quickly find yourself attached to them.The story itself is deeply engaging, challenging players to reflect on the fairness of the world’s customs and the moral choices the characters must navigate.There’s an underlying sense that something is off, and this tension drives much of the story’s appeal. The game makes you question the ethics of the world and its inhabitants, pushing you to consider how you feel about the setting and whether the rules of this world are just or flawed. Every chapter is packed with surprises, and kept me on edge and excited to see how the story would evolve and where it would ultimately lead. In terms of gameplay, Visions of Mana plays wonderfully.As someone who loves experimenting with different builds and strategies, I found the class system and the ability seed mechanic offered a ton of freedom to approach combat and character progression in my own way.The game offers a somewhat open world experience, but the sidequests and exploration provide optional rewards (that mostly add value for those who want more options for their builds), meaning players focused on the story won’t feel like they’re missing out on key items or upgrades. It strikes the perfect balance between offering depth for hardcore players and accessibility for those just following the main plot.As a longtime fan of the Seiken Densetsu series, Visions of Mana brought me back to the magical feeling of playing Secret of Mana and Seiken Densetsu 3 for the first time. The music, the visuals and the atmosphere all perfectly captures the nostalgic charm of those classic games while still feeling fresh and modern.If you, like me, hold a special place in your heart for the SNES-era Seiken Densetsu titles, this game will make you feel like a kid again, rediscovering the magic of those unforgettable adventures.Whether you’re a Seiken Densetsu veteran or a JRPG fan looking for something new, Visions of Mana is a game I highly recommend. It’s easily the best entry in the series since the SNES days, and I hope it draws in a new generation of fans to this beloved franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: EDITED:  I like this game however there are issues that I hope get resolved.1. Controls feel clunky on most characters.  As such combos just don't really work.  Commands where you hold down a button can be unreliable and I often have to repeat buttons before the move activates.  Attacks stop you in your tracks with most characters so melee can feel sluggish. That is not the case with Morley.  Use Morley! He's the only character where fighting doesn't feel slow. Note: Other characters get better as the game progresses.2.  Movement slower than I'd prefer.  You can enable 'auto-run' in the settings but the feature only works on the first dash and breaks after attacking pots or enemies.  Jumping disables running so you avoid jumping as much as possible.  You can change controls but only to approved buttons the game allows.  Running can only be set to L3 or R3 and constantly having to mash those buttons ever 3 seconds gets really old.  Mounts arent much of an improvement.  You have to manually dismount to engage in fights and movement feels very clunky making walking on foot feel preferable... If only auto run actually worked.3. Game performance seems decent however it pushes my PC much harder than I would expect.  My fans run at high settings constantly no matter the graphics settings.  I didn't expect my PC to be pushed from a game like this.On the positive, the characters are all likable and voice acting is great.  I have enjoyed the story and how the world opens up with time.  There are artistic themes that take me back to my younger years and the world is gorgeous.With the development team having been let go, I don't imagine this game will get much (if any) patching to fix minor bugs.  Be that as it may, I still find the game charming and worth my time.  if you're a gamer who enjoyed RPGs from the 90's I believe you'll enjoy the charm of this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Visions of Mana

_childDocuments_.review: As we grow older, we often find ourselves reminiscing about the past, cherishing the memories that have shaped us into the people we are today. Mana series was released in 1993 for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES), is a role-playing game developed and published by Square (now Square Enix). The game follows the story of Randi, a young hero on a quest to save the world of Mana from the clutches of an evil empire. Along the way, Randi meets a cast of memorable characters, each with their own unique abilities and backstories, who join him in his journey to restore the Mana Tree and bring peace to the land.Vision of Mana is MUST HAVE game that brings you down to the memory lane.
_childDocuments_.name: Visions of Mana

_childDocuments_.review: seiken densetsu 2 and seiken densetsu 3 had a love child and its called Visions of Mana. the story will be fairly predictable if youve played the others; but thats not necessarily a bad thing. the world feels massive; and that is about the biggest complaint i have as wellthe world feels massive cause it is massive. running around and exploring feels like less of a chore due to the fantastic art style, music, and collectables--but make no mistake; you are going to be doing A TON of running around. even with the ability to quickly teleport to locations; youll still be running and running and running and running.i wish the run speed was faster tbqh
