_childDocuments_.review: Very nice tower defence-slash-action game with great vibes. Very simple plot that doesn't ask much of you but fits the game perfectly and lets you just get on and play.If you played the demo and are wondering about much extra depth there is:1: The game does mix it up and not every stage is the same kind of thing. So far I've seen stages where you are unable to attack and need to rely on your villagers to do all the work, a stage where the opposite was true and you need to use traps/structures and yourself to clear it, and a stationary mission where you had limited room and had to wait for the enemy to approach and had to shift your dudes around constantly to cover all angles.2: Soh (you) DOES have an upgrade system of his own that you unlock after a handful of stages, which gives you access to various charge attacks, bow attacks (which includes a grapple) and a perfect parry/dodge retaliation system, and unlocks various in-stage buffs etc. There is also an entire second movement that trades away movement for more power. Nothing on the level of a proper character-action game but you get a lot more options once you play a while.3: Every stage can be entered after clearing it and that lets you use villagers to re-build structures and statues for rewards. Nothing important but it gives you a reason to visit the places when they aren't messed up from demons etc.4: Every stage has three extra objectives you can clear for rewards (totems or upgrade currency), some of the mutually exclusive, that force you to use more tools than just spamming loggers and archers, so you will have reasons to play stages multiple times.5: Every boss has a time-trial for extra rewards.6: Bosses from earlier in the game turn up in later stages as mob enemies.Also short missions and downtime mean it's perfect for the Deck. You need to mess with the graphics a bit to get an acceptable frame-rate though.

_childDocuments_.review: Weird game. It's a hack and slash tower defense game where the combat is based on...dancing. Art design and visuals are great. The actual tower defense gameplay is quite fun. The action bits are simplistic, yet solid. Boss and enemy design is quite good. The levels offer a variety of different challenges and forces you to switch up your tactics quite often.A few criticisms that I have are: 1) Each level has challenges to complete for currency or equipment that range from fun to beyond tedious. It forces replayability where unnecessary. 2) Difficulty spikes come at random. Some levels are really good, but others rely too heavily on gimmicks or seemingly random bursts of "challenge". Game would be much better if difficulty climbed more linearly. 3) Base building after finishing levels is tedious and another excuse for "replayability" as the only way to make progress on the base building is to replay levels (sometimes multiple times). 4) The purification of villagers and gathering resources at the beginning of each level gets quite old towards the end of the game. It's a neat gimmick that turns a bit tedious and feels like it's missing something especially with all the running around required to find everything. 5) Game crashes more frequently than it should and feels like it could use some general QoL updates. 6) Some of the bosses don't feel right. This is a personal taste thing, but some of the last few bosses aren't the most fun to fight and feels like they needed more time in the oven. Overall, this is almost a throwback to the weird games we'd see on the PS2 and all the good/bad that comes with it. It's a rock solid game that has a lot to offer in spite of it's shortcomings and worth at least trying.

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't expecting much from Kunitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess, but Capcom really knocked it out of the park with this one. It's a fantastic fusion of tower defense and hack and slash that kept me hooked from start to finish.You get to save villagers and assign them 11 different roles to help fend off nightly monster attacks. Whether you need melee and ranged attackers, healers, or debuffers, there's a role for every strategy. The control optimization is spot-on, letting you dive into the hack and slash action while effortlessly commanding your villagers to assist you.The boss stages are a highlight—some require teamwork with your villagers, while others are intense solo battles. Each encounter felt unique and challenging, making every fight memorable.The game’s artwork is fantastic, and the soundtrack is amazing—featuring classic Japanese music that fits perfectly with the game’s vibe.My only gripe is the lack of dialogue. The story seems intriguing with its two different endings, but without any spoken or written dialogue, it’s hard to fully grasp what’s going on. Despite this, the game has a lot of potential. I’m hoping for future updates or collaborations, like the Okami one we got at launch. It would be awesome to see more collabs where villagers could be transformed into characters from other Capcom titles, such as Vergil from Devil May Cry or Hunter from Monster Hunter.Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed every minute of it and can’t wait to see what’s next for this game. If you're into action-packed gameplay with strategic elements, definitely give this one a try!

_childDocuments_.review: Quite a nice little game. It was a bit weird at first as I'm not really familiar with Japanese myths and culture, but it was understandable nonetheless. Gameplay-wise, it's an interesting blend of almost tower-defense style stuff and an action game. The action game elements were somewhat half-baked at times, as you're mostly spamming the same combos over and over, but the rest of the game generally makes up for it. The units/villagers you can make are all distinct and have specific advantages and disadvantages, and in general the strategy aspect is pretty fun, although sometimes limited. My main complaint is that many of the bosses aren't fun fight, sometimes requiring micromanagement when your tools aren't really that well suited to it. Thankfully, only a couple of them (and the true final boss) are really bad, but it does put a damper on things somewhat.Visually it's sharp and interesting, the music is good (but the village theme gets incredibly repetitive), the UI is functional, and there are a lot of little collectible tidbits that don't do much but fit the game nicely.I'd recommend this to anyone interested in it. Despite no individual element really blowing me away, this is a game where the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.

_childDocuments_.review: kunitsu-gami is a special game. every single part is lovingly crafted, and the world it builds is captivating. there is beauty in both the grandiose and the minor, it brings joy in both its tension and its brevity. the developers of this game were committed to showing the player a reflection of japanese culture, and it oozes charm and heart from every orifice. i had my gripes. base-building, while a nice reprieve from the fast-paced action, begins to drag. some boss fights were poorly designed. not every level was a hit. but kunitsu gami provides the player with such a strong core premise, with such unique new ideas, and with such a heartful experience that these gripes begin to melt away. i will not remember kunitsu gami for a bad boss fight. i will remember it for the artistry that this game presents at every turn. if i had not played pyre in april, this would be the best game i played this year. i love it.(it got an update that increased cat and dog variety 10/10)

_childDocuments_.review: First thing, watch Skill Up's review because that's the reason I ended up buying this game and after finishing it, everything he said was 100% correct.This game is a throwback to a time when games were made because passionate people had cool ideas. Nowadays, more often than not, we get decisions being made by the guys in suits and publishers. It seems every other game is The Sequel 4, Game from 5 Years Ago: Remastered, Live Service Cash Grab.This is a focused, 15ish hour experience that focusing on engaging gameplay backed up by clever worldbuilding. Whether its the detailed models of Japanese snacks or the levels designed with rearl-world miniatures and then ported into the game, the heart and soul poured into this game by the developers is evident at every stage.Its a fun mix between Dynasty Warriors style hack-n-slash combat and tower defense. But the"towers" are villagers that you can assign different classes (called roles) to. Then you can level up those roles to make ones that you particularly like more powerful.Each level offers a unique enough twist on the formula to keep things interesting and the core gameplay loop is satisfying enough that you never get bored. That especially true because they didn't bloat the game too much with extra nonsense just to stretch it to 30+ hours.The only gameplay system that was underwhelming was the base repairing stuff. They probably included it for pacing reasons but it really didn't add anything other than a bunch of chores to do between levels so that you could get rewards to upgrade your character and your villagers. Could have done without that. Everything else is just fantastic and unique. It's what we all used to love about video games.

_childDocuments_.review: A refreshingly unique blend of tower defense and action RPG that is drenched in Japanese mythology. The first third of the game suffers from guiding the player's reins too tightly, but the game does an overall excellent job of opening up in the later stages and allowing the player to experiment with a wide tool kit. The only other complaint I have with the game is that missions lose a lot of the magic on subsequent re-clears for bonus objectives. Overall a wonderfully unique package that captivates with its visuals, challenges with interesting level design, and provides an ever expanding toolkit to experiment with.

_childDocuments_.review: The same joy I get from marching through my ranks of Pikmin and addressing each one the way Patton addressed the Third Army before storming Normandy do I now receive from playing Kunitsu-Gami. A sublime experience all around proving once more that Capcom are among the very finest working in the craft today. A supremely hang-outable game that cherishes details like the expert modeling of traditional Japanese  (Hideo Kojima scans actors, Capcom scans desserts) or the liberation of rabbits and deer from exquisitely-designed evils of folklore. It is a game that brims with life beyond its coding, feeling like the work of a genuine team of clever artists and designers who just love Video Games.Also hilariously reminds me of Bujingai, and I wish for an unlockable Gackt skin.

_childDocuments_.review: This feels like an old school experimental Capcom title, and I hope they keep making games like this.The game play loop is simple; collect resources and move the priestess toward the goal by day, then defend her by night.The game play mechanics are refreshingly simple. The villagers you recruit can be assigned one of many classes. Each class has a linear skill tree, and all upgrades apply to everyone in that class. In most combat situations, the only behavior villagers have is to stand there and wait for enemies to enter their radius before activating their ability. You can choose assign where they stand.The main character Soh handles beautifully. The vast majority of the time, you will be repeating the most basic of musou-style combos (LH, LLH, LLLH, etc.). You can also choose which specials and buffs to bring into combat.I can see how some folks might be disappointed by the lack of decision space. Villager behavior is not nuanced, and if you get excited about builds, this game doesn't offer much.All of these simple elements mesh beautifully, however. The game looks beautiful, sounds beautiful, and feels great to control. Please support AAA games like this.The first of my major criticisms is the menu/action control scheme. Confusingly, the developers decided that "A" (on an xbox controller) is sometimes confirm, but sometimes "A" backs you out of menus and "B" is now confirm. It is infuriating to enter a shop, then accidentally leave when making a selection.Second, some reviewers have complained about the town building feeling simple and like a mobile game. It doesn't really bother me, but jumping from base to base and waiting through loading screens to go in and grab a reward becomes a little aggravating. They should allow you to either grab rewards from the world map, or offered one large base that you slowly expand rather than multiple small bases.Despite these frustrations, it's a fantastic game.EDIT: After a few hours, you are given access to a bunch of upgrade trees for the main character, which opens up more game play options. It is welcome, however it is odd how all of it is dumped on your lap after many stages and bosses. It does rectify some of my comments above on "builds" and programming villager behavior, however most of the upgrades are straight forward attribute increases or simply selecting between options for attacks so I stand by my original statement for the most part.

_childDocuments_.review: This really reminds me of games from another era, just straightforward gameplay ideas but wrapped up in Japanese mythology, kagura dance, and beautiful visual design. _childDocuments_.review: It's fantastic for what it is. If you're unsure, play the demo.It's a comfy game. There's two cycles: tower defense and chilling. And within the tower defense you have day/night. Basically first you play a small portion of tower defense game and clean the towns. Then you repair them, go for a boss fight and collect sweets to give to the nice lady who purifies the land.While in the tower defense / cleaning portion, it's one of those games where you're kinda stressed out during the day/night cycle because you need to get ♥♥♥♥ done before the night falls or else you'll need to sweat during the night.Then you go back to the repair the town, pick sweets to give to the lady and enjoy the atmosphere. The game is also set up so that you'll most likely want to replay the tower defense sections, as it'll reveal secondary goals after you complete the tower defense portion of each location. Nothing is preventing you from mashing straight into the next tower defense level and blasting through all of the levels in a few hours.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a video game as an art form.It brings me joy to see that there are studios that are still allowed to fulfill their artistic vision in a way that feels alien in today's industry. And I bet Capcom knows this game won't be the financial success akin to Resident Evil or Monster Hunter, which makes me respect them even more, as it is clear that they chose this to be an experience rather than a money hit. Western companies must be on life support looking at this game.Every visual detail in the game is tailored in a way that evokes folklore, culture, spiritualism, respect and many other values that seem to be on the way to be forgotten in today's age. Every stage is colorful, with specific tones that let you know what's positive and what's negative, and once you purify the stage it comes back to life, with animals roaming around, villagers going about their day from cutting wood to scrubbing shrines clean each with their own detailed animation, making you feel as if they're living breathing beings. Even the costumes have layers interacting with each other, with collision physics applied so that each piece of clothing does not clip through. This on its own, in a project of this small scope is astonishing, again proof of the passion and time the developers put in. Not just a "screw it, including clothing collision is too time consuming, ship it as is", but a "let's take the time to polish these details".Even the enemy designs are cool yet grounded in folklore, inviting you to learn more about them and what they represent.Gameplay wise, this is a tower defense game with hack and slash mechanics. Simple, yet effective. The union of both is surprisingly enjoyable, to the point that you feel motivated to achieve the challenges each stage provides to get additional bonuses.There's also plenty of upgrades to look for and modifiers that help you through the tougher stages, giving a sense of improvement when compared to how did your character and the allies perform in earlier stages.There are boss fights, base management mini games after you beat each stage, cutscenes here and there, it's a pretty complete game, and I know in 2024 that's almost unheard of.Overall this is a game that you play for the visuals, and stay for the gameplay loop. Hope more studios would be willing to take a chance and experiment like this, as in the current stagnant gaming landscape, creative and unique ideas like this are just what we might need.

_childDocuments_.review: Kunitsu-Gami is a game that I feel personally conflicted about. If there was a TL;DR, it would be Kunitsu-Gami is a unique action combat tower defense RTS that ultimately has interesting aspects but falls short in truly being fleshed out or allowing adequate depth to have it stick out more.The game itself has strong points that combine in an a odd mesh, as it begins to get more interesting the game is basically done. There is an NG+ and it provides a true ending, but going off the achievement stats only 22% have finished NG and 6% have finished NG+ (which is insane, the true final boss is awesome) at the time of writing this.If there is anything I want to come out of this, is the hope that capcom doesn't shy from continuing to develop games like these or at least implement some aspects into other games. A decent amount of these mechanics I can see working well in either a different genre or another game altogether, and some sorta do exist outside of kunitsu-gami.The gameplay is not anything to run home about. It is cool though, when the game starts you're essentially greeted to a 10 minute basic tutorial for your character and a light introduction. Eventually the actual game starts, and then you're greeted to about a 5 hour tutorial. The game introduces new mechanics, more in-depth controls for your towers, and then it temporarily removes certain things.In a basic NG run the game tries to familiarize you with all features. Before saying "hey now complete this without this feature". Eventually you begin to upgrade your towers, and then your character. This would approximately be about 50% through the map or so, NG will still introduce new things. But 50% through the map, the game begins to feel a lot better.As for the gameplay loop, you enter a mission and the goddess dances her way to a gate. You spend orbs (you gather) to reveal the path to a gate. The objective is to cleanse the gates that have succumbed to a blight, all while protecting the goddess while she takes the path. In the morning you can purify smaller forms of corruption, and in nighttime the goddess stops moving and monsters invade. You can use your character to fight the monsters, or after cleansing corrupt villagers, use them as defense towers that protect the path. Like many RTS though, the monsters can navigate around in multiple different paths unlike your goddess, so you are incentivized to disperse your towers or help defend with your character + the towers. For your character there is the typical parry, counter, charge attacks, dance attacks, basic combos, and a bow (later on). As for the towers, they take on roles that have them do certain attacks, more roles unlock as you progress.Later on a variety of monsters pour in, some which can introduce new mechanics or types of attacks. Sometimes a breakdancing monster will start backflipping and kill your villagers, sometimes a giant comes in and slams them. The different roles of towers can take on different monsters more effectively, while some monsters maybe better for you to combat as they can corrupt your villagers again.The game sounds fairly simple, but after cleansing certain paths, you then rebuild the villages using the villagers you saved and do missions for this rebuilding to finish. It is fairly simple. Ever so often, theres a boss fight sometimes you can use towers, sometimes you do not. Along this to spice things up there are challenges in each mission. All in all the gameplay is fairly basic, theres no open world exploration or anything more enticing that you may desire. It is just missions and tiny villages you can rebuild and explore. But definitely do not forget to feed your goddess sweets!The Music is pretty good. Though sometimes you do not spend enough time in villages to really hear it out, sometimes bosses fly by so fast you never get to hear the whole song. In NG+ the music changes but you may not notice. At times there are songs that the visuals or effects match while feeling sort of trippy. The music is stylistic, and there are much tinier changes to the composition as you progress, but if you're just playing you may not notice some of the OST changing, until the much more apparent visuals match it. Which to say the least is a shame, because its pretty solid.This is probably my largest gripe with the game. Another reason to criticize either RE engine or Capcom's lack of will to create anything visually unique in this engine and aiming for realism. Realism isn't necessarily an issue, but this game probably needs the visual clarity because it lacks it. When you rebuild villages, there are fireworks, the village becomes more vibrant with colors, and the outfits of the villagers flourish with new colors. These overall, may never get noticed because it doesn't pop in the sort of semi-realism style the game has going. Where as Okami has the old japanese painting methods, all of it's effects stick out more, Kunitsu-Gami probably needs this sort of visual design or a more unique one. A lot of effects can be cool, but they feel out of place due to the semi-realism visuals.As previously mentioned, I am a bit conflicted. The good parts stick out for me personally, and the true final boss and music ends on such a high note. Personally, I would absolutely love more out of it or to see a new ARPG with the rebuilding gimmick. Is it worth approximately $49.99? I would say, 'ehhh' If you wish for Capcom to not be shy into branching into new IPs and experiences, have your money speak. Kunitsu-gami is pretty cool and interesting. But I think its a much easier to justify picking it up for about $20 or $30 and I would say even then, just make sure to fight the true final boss.

_childDocuments_.review: Kunitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess is the best game I've played this year. An experimental game from capcoms resident evil and devil may cry devs that's been described as feeling like an old school ps2 game in the best possible way, a successful risk that really sticks out as one of the most unique games of this year and something that will stick in my mind for many years to come. Kunitsu-gami is essentially a mash up of genres but mostly can be boiled down to a tower defence hack and slash. You play as Soh a warrior tasked with defending Yoshiro,  a maiden with the ability to cleanse the corruption that has spread through the mountains. The game takes place in a feudal Japanese setting with the monster you fight taking heavy inspiration from yokai.The gameplay is split into two stages which act as day and night, the day is spent gathering resources and clearing a path to a tori gate that needs to be purified by Yoshiro, and also freeing villagers who act as this games towers, you give the villagers roles that vary quite drastically from simple melee/range to spellcaster and tanks. Once night fall you are set upon by monster and it's up to you with your simple but affective hack and slash combat to take down the monster with the help of your villager army. What makes this game so special is not only it's fantastic gameplay but the presentation, the Japanese setting leans so heavily in it's ancient culture that it's hard not to love the style, from the dancing, the sweets that Yoshiro love and the environments. Everything is so polished.I want to make a special shout out to the amazing soundtrack as well. It's very easy to tell the devs worked on resi and dmc because that can really be felt in the soundtrack, it's not bombastic but it's very eerie and I loved it so much. Games like this is why I love capcom, they took a risk with this simplistic premise and it paid off massively, I love that they pay direct homage to other games in capcoms library like okami and to a lesser extent onimusha.This game is a genuine classic and if like me you've been struggling to find something truly unique this year then you need to give this game a go.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm normally not into tower defense games, but the way they implemented action into the game really appeals to me. The music, art style, and overall feel of the game is really good. You have high energy fights, followed by a slower rebuilding mechanic for villages. This allows you to visually see the impact you have as you progress through the game. I absolutely can't recommend this enough, especially if you're a big fan of Okami from PS2. They have a nifty costume that acts as a callback.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, I love tower defense but this game just doesn't hit the itch.My biggest issue with the game is the map design, the game desperately needs proper lanes or funnels where you can set up defenses, the later levels become an absolute mess of enemies spawning from 4 different directions with levels that are too open, so the winning strat is putting all your characters around the shrine maiden in a circle. It doesn't really feel like a tower defense game.Along with that there are a lot of (in my opinion) useless characters or classes that do the same thing with different flavor, the sumo wrestler is almost detrimental to you because he constantly pushes enemies out of range, the marksman is a more expensive archer that does more damage while shooting slower, to the point I can't tell if there's even any difference in their dps, especially since the archer is far cheaper to max out in the skill tree. Same exact thing with the lumberjack and the spearman.There are definitely things to like about this game and I hope it gets polished, it's just really not worth 50 euro and considering the peak player counts on steam I feel like this game will be abandoned fairly quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: It's the summer of 200X, you're at Blockbuster pacing back and forth in the PS2 section. You only have enough cash to rent one game for the week and you've spent the last 20 minutes listing pros and cons for each candidate. Then out of the corner of your eye, you see it, Kunitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess. You rent it, take it home, burn through it in a matter of days because ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, it's a GOOD video game.But it's not the summer of 200X, it's the summer of 2024 and Capcom just released a budget video game carried solely by its gameplay and presentation. This game came straight out of a time warp, it feels right at home with games from the PS2/3 era. All gameplay, story front loaded then drip fed to you through short cutscenes at the beginning of levels with no spoken dialogue. Game play is simple but complex, day/night cycles with defenses and armaments to be built. 11 classes of pikmi-, towe-, I mean villagers to choose between to survive the night. It's truly a beautiful game with a lot of heart and soul, I hope it exceeded Capcom's expectations so this team could continue making more games.Update: Steam Game of the Year baby! Let's gooo!

_childDocuments_.review: While I think the price-point of this game is taking a slight piss, it's definitively worth a purchase on sale. Granted, that is only true if the themes of the game is something that interests you (which I assume if you're already reading reviews).While the "story" feels a bit bare-bones, the game is accompanied by a brilliant hybrid of strategy/tower-defense and action/hack'n'slash. You rummage around looking for resources/units during daytime (as well as constructing your defense for the night), and you fight demons spawning from designated gates at night time. The enemy design is absolutely top-notch, and if you're someone with a slight interest in Japanese mythology this is definitively something you can appreciate.IN SUMMARY; While the price is a bit steep, at a sale this game is a solid recommend from me. The gameplay is solid, the design/theme of the game is exceptional, and it's not a demanding game to get into. °˖✧◝(⁰▿⁰)◜✧˖°

_childDocuments_.review: A breath of fresh air in the higher budget video game segment.It's kind of a "reverse tower-defense" with how you are the one pushing towards the gate while protecting the Maiden from "Seethe". I've played other action-oriented tower-defense titles like Dungeon Defenders, Orcs Must Die or Sanctum and yet this game somehow brings something entirely new to the table.The story isn't that engaging and there is no voice acting, but the presentation is so gorgeous that it's a delight just looking at the cutscenes.I like the variety of upgrades and villager roles, there's also a surprising amount of levels to go through but It's not a flawless game by any means as some of my pain points are:Overall it's a great and very unexpected game in today's market that is probably a bit overpriced, but I'd rather pay a bit extra if it meant that games weren't as homogenized as they are in the current climate.

_childDocuments_.review: A gorgeously distinct game which evokes the feeling of an underrated PS2/3 game. It’s unique gameplay loop, mixed with hack and slash gameplay and real-time strategy is addictive, if not slightly bit repetitive at times, but still very engaging. The game can be stressful at times but in a good way, which just encourages you more to make it to end of the path. The uniqueness of this game’s visual style is wonderfully realised through the use of the traditional Japanese setting, that is tainted by amazingly designed yokai, which is fused with some modern sensibilities, like a experimental soundtrack that’s layered with dread filled chanting war cries, mixed with upbeat techno. It’s a one of a kind game and very refreshing, happy to see that Capcom took the chance to make a smaller title and would love to see a sequel to explore this world more, but loved my time with it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a return to the old ways. There's a magic and a charm to it that I struggle to explain. The game has this stiffness to it that feels like it should be there. As if each swing of a blade was a ritual that you couldn't rush, canceling many of the animations would feel like speeding through a prayer. It's a strange friction that makes perfect sense to me.The game also has a good sense of progression. At the start it is incredibly simple. The growth from that point is done in a way that is easy to understand, but still gives you plenty to focus on. The game mechanics are used in a powerful way that gets a lot of mileage out of limited options.I think we need more of this in our games. Open worlds and dialogue trees are fine, but they shouldn't be required. This is a game that delivers exactly what it intends to.

_childDocuments_.review: In between juggernauts like Monster Hunter, Street Fighter and Resident Evil its nice to see Capcom taking a gamble off the beaten path. Kunitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess is an action-RTS tower defense game with a unique aesthetic that draws from Japanese folklore and theater.+ Gameplay: While it doesn't reinvent the wheel it throws enough new things to keep it engaging. You have your upgradeable army and hero to customize while the basic premise of getting Yoshiro from point A to B across the map is complexed by doing so while having to collect resources, setup defenses and being aware of bottlenecks and side trails that might let the monsters get to her while she makes her way to the end of the level under a day-night cycle.+ Aesthetics: Even from a distant third person view the game just looks great. From the levels, the monsters, the villagers and the various knick-nacks that pass for gear. You can tell the developers were quite passionate about this project as they put a lot of work into art assets which have no in-game value but contribute greatly to the feel and atmosphere of the game like Yoshiro's sweets, collectible woodblock prints and fire etchings.- Tedious: No two ways about it, this game is a time sink. To fully complete it and maximize the resource you'll need to fully upgrade yourself and your small army, you will have to play a level at least twice and, from what I hear, to complete ALL the equipment you'll have to replay the game a whopping 8 times! And to unlock the golden ending you need to play the whole game at least twice. This isn't helped by the fact that the bonus objectives are hidden from you the first time you play a level!-Bad UI: While the UI looks great its not very convenient. Clearly a lot of it was sacrificed in the name of style over substance. For example, to equip your Mazo Talismans you have to manually go through a nice looking scroll, entry-by-entry across 80 items. Also you can't save your talisman loadouts and many levels will require you to switch between them for optimal play. The same for changing classes, you get a nice woodblock print illustration of each class but you have to spin a entire wheel. And worst of all is the tacked-on base building where you have to run across the entire village and manually assign each job to your pool of villages, which could've been easily handled by a single menu, do a level, and then come back to individually collect the results.All told its a good AA game worth its 40 dollar asking price. If it ever goes on sale, grab it. You won't regret it. Now if only Capcom would make a sequel set in Onimusha, that would be one heck of a treat.
_childDocuments_.name: Kunitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess

_childDocuments_.review: I can't help it. You know I'm obsessed with it. The instant I see some dancing priestess throwing out the nastiest ass mudras to summon a floral ninja from the aether, I'm gonna be friction shining my prayer beads with that spiritual ecstasy only brought forth from the finest of concept-game vintages.They seldom make them like this now. Far more concerned with aesthetic and ambiance than narrative complexity, a niche cluster of genres coalesce into an experience that is so idiosyncratic it has dispelled the miasma of ennui induced by endless cozy farm games and stagnant retro throwbacks, the latter always seeming to superficially emulate their forebears without really capturing their spirit. They captured that jaun here.The adventurousness of the 90s and early 00s is absolutely bursting out this fat little gob of sixth gen goodness - before conventions were established in their full and developers could still subsist in the industry by throwing "cool ideas" at the suits instead of market-ready models.It's a simple array of gameplay concepts, tower-defense, nominal strategy elements, and a beat-em-up core. Nothing on its own is particularly complex, but the layered experience gives you a ton of moving parts that leads to a deceptive amount of depth. Weighing unit upgrades, searching for synergies with your Mazo talismans, making good use of resource management by judging time against the best course of action, and respecting the enemy composition along with the balling ass bosses. Also the art design is just phenomenal, the enemies have a ridiculous amount of personality. The very first boss shows up and it's some big-ass crusty monk-type (new Pokemon type please) who rolls out, rips his own face off so his bloody uvula is swanging like your grandpa's raisins, and proceeds to whip your ass with his prayer beads. Your dudes will dance and clap and rave as enemies barrel towards them. Animals will come to your priestess' feet as she performs the Snow White sutra after you dispel the cruelty of industry and greed from them. The frickin' barricades aren't some dumb jumble of bricks or something, they're magical glowing walls of moving fractals that make you feel like you're tripping balls. What a game - completely came out of nowhere. Capcom make more of these please. I love Resident Evil but I can only get so much out of seeing Chris progressively become more like an unhinged ape let loose in Dawn of the Dead.

_childDocuments_.review: I love and respect this game so much - it is a fun and engaging hybrid of multiple genres that is full of so many ideas. it seems like every level will introduce a new mechanic, enemy, or contraption. Originally i thought they would all be combining (like constantly having forks in maps when carving the spirit path), but the further I got, the more I realized every level was instead trying very hard to be unique (sometimes in very unexpected ways, such as a level where you're ambushed while riding boats). I don't want to spoil a ton of mechanics, but I feel like the snow level (4 or 5) is when my enjoyment went from "this game is ok" to "I love this game".the stages feel connected with the rest of the world because the villagers you rescue can then be used to repair the level you just cleared, unlocking rewards (like currency for upgrading classes), and later on there is a good chunk of customization available (more than just villager classes).my only real complaint is that, for most of the game, the difficulty is on the low side. level replayability is encouraged (and there are occasionally some tougher side objectives, such as not taking damage / not using rations to heal / not letting your shrine maiden take damage, and you can always try to go for all 3 of the stage's side objectives at the same time if applicable). i also kinda wish there was a pikmin mode - by that i mean, only being able to play each stage once, and having to go FAST, which also means you are prioritizing certain village repairs before others since you wouldnt be allowed to spam missions. maybe I'll have to come up with my own challenge run ideas, but this game is definitely worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: A blend of tower defense and action game with amazing art style and design. The art and story is based on Japanese folklore and reminds me a lot of Hell's Paradise. Each stages are very unique and comes with it's own twist: there are normal stages where you need to escort and defend the Waifu Yoshiro by assigning villagers which acts like move-able towers in tower defense game; there are also boss fights where it is more like an action game; and there are a few unique stages with special mechanics which I should not spoil too much. It's amazing that Capcom despite having multiple established IPs, they are still willing to try out new IPs. Also they released it as a full game with no microtransactions unlike a lot of games going towards the live service route.

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay, but gameplay too basic. I can't help but feel it could be more.Update: It too tedious. Far too many (boring) challenges that had me replay a stage simply because I didn't know objectives the first time around.I'm enjoying it, but if I pause to play another game, I am never coming back to it.It is a tower defense with action combat (not unlike orcs must die, dungeon defenders and many others) EXCEPT there's a little progression and very basic base building built in.The game has a lot of nice systems, but neither of them is developed to a degree that adds depth. Like there's at least 4 ways to become stronger (kinda) and over 75% of what I experienced feels like it's designed to pad playtime. Is there any reason I'd want to beat a stage without using contraptions? It actually makes no difference, except I have to play a 2nd time, because the first time the game concealed those challenges.You get access to a 3 move combo (+ 5 finishers 3 of which are combo finishers). You also get jump, which could be disabled and nobody would notice. You also get a dodge, which is actually worse than just running most of the time. Most enemies either die in 1 hit or don't flinch so combos are only as viable as you can make them safe (usually unpredictable).You also get a special attack that you can use like once/minute and bow that can later get upgrades. To put it bluntly, combat boring kind of technical. Even on bosses that require you dodge it feels more like a platformer boss, where you just have to know when or where to move.You get a limited amount of villagers and use somewhat limited resources to turn them into combat/support units.It starts VEEEERY slow and does a terrible job at selling it, but it does get better, as you eventually get access to more units, and enemy variety actually force you to use more units.There is one negative that's bugging me. Units can get upgraded (outside of run only) and upgraded units are just better than non-upgraded ones. This means that you might want to place an archer to deal with flying enemies, but if you don't have it upgraded it will not do much and you'll have to do more work than the archer. _childDocuments_.review: This is one of my favorite games this year - I love the aesthetic, the outfits, and I've always had a fondness for tower defense games. I found the gameplay challenging but not punishing (I did have to think about which units I created, where, and why), and there's so much variety in how you can approach each level and cycle! I also like the bosses (the centipede one kept kicking my ass though, haha!) and I like how there's such a detailed day/night cycle that you can make a strategy depending on what time of day it is. I thought the base building mechanics were well done, and it makes sense to have progression tied to having another level/boss completed.In case you're looking for tips: Ascetics are really versatile, make sure you upgrade your archers, and woodcutters are the best for making a little 'meatgrinder' that the Seethe have to traverse.I beat the centipede boss before the newest patch, so it might've gotten balanced, but here's some tips: Don't light all the lanterns, get a whole bunch of archers to take advantage of the weak points, and the bosswill always do their unblockable attack towards *you* (make sure you're away from Yoshiro when it starts up or run away)Hope that helps

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting mix of various genres. During day time you explore the small-ish map you're given, rescuing villagers that then during the night time serve as a way to defend the shrine-maiden you're escorting, while you control a character doing 3rd person action combat to help them out.The villagers gradually unlock new roles you can assign them, ranging from archers to sumo-wrestlers that will taunt enemies.You can press a button to pause the game and command the villagers to stand somewhere and they will attack enemies within their range, but they are not static towers, they may rush forward to combat someone and then go back to their assigned position, making them feel like actual people instead of static defense.The maps are well designed with various paths for the enemies to take, but trying to find everything in some of them can be a pain as you get a substantial reward for doing so. After finishing them for the first time you can view optional objectives for extra rewards, but you can accidentally complete them on your first time as well.Between stages you can assign villagers to repair the area you just finished which gives you currency needed to upgrade the villagers and eventually yourself. This is also gained from the bonus objectives for each stage, encouraging you to replay them. This can get a bit tedious after a while as you have to go back and collect the rewards from completed repairs and assign new repair jobs. Completely repairing an area takes 2-3 visits, repairs progressing every time you finish a stage.After finishing the game you unlock New Game+, which is mandatory for the actual ending of the game. You get to keep all your upgrades and stages get two additional objectives to earn more upgrade currency. They also get slightly harder with end game enemies appearing earlier.Overall the game is very fun and if the gameplay seems interesting I definitely recommend checking it out.

_childDocuments_.review: I received a review code from Capcom for Kunitsu-Gami.The game is close to being my 2024 game of the year, It uses a unique blend of Tower Defence with Action game elements and mixes the two together with a masterful blend of strategy.This game's unique world, combined with its beautiful graphics and art direction pulled me in everytime I booted it up! As a testament to his game's addictive nature, I've even got all of the acheivements and still left wanting to play it more.This game represents the era of gaming where creativity was top priority. This game feels like an old school Capcom classic from a previous generation. In a world full of staleness, Kunitsu-Gami proves that creativity is still possible in gaming.

_childDocuments_.review: OMFG, for the love of good games, please buy this.What an incredible title and such a shame it didn't receive the marketing it deserves. After reaching a certain part of the progression I had to leave a review, because this is so much more then a tower defence game.Gameplay (is king)So at it's core, yes, it acts like a tower defence, but you don't have fixed towers, instead you have villagers that you can command at all times. You can move them, fix them in place, or place them on strategic points (like a +dmg or +range zone). When you start the map you have a timer. Before the night comes, you need to explore the map, gather resourses, get as many villagers as possible and hopefully plan your defence. Then you move the sexy lady that you're defending along the path(s) and stop her where you have the best chance of not dying. After that the night starts and the FUN starts.So at first, your characters has a few set moves and you slowly get more and more types of soldiers you can upgrade your villagers into (melee, tank, archer etc),  build your bases to unlock new stuff, improve your soldier archetypes etc. But about 8h in, I unlocked the main characters upgrades....and ooooooh boi , the game just just went crazy. The amount of stuff you can do with your character is stupid now. (once upgraded) He becomes basically a monster hunter, with multiple combos, ranged attacks, perfect parry etc etc. Now this turned into an action game more then anything lol. Other then that, the bosses are really good and crazy looking, with superb animations.Visuals.Incredible. Just like most capcom games, it's not about the textures, who gives a Fk about that? It's about the ARTSTYLE. And man, this game looks amazing. So much Japanese inspired fantasy/religious art/creatures/monsters. If you've played nioh you will recognise a lot of them. But yeah, superb stuff.Animations are also PHENOMENAL. In typical Capcom fashion the animations have more effort put into them then all western games combined. I still don't understand how we have this floaty/robotic garbage in all western games, meanwhile I look at my character in this game and every 2 min I say "DAYUM that looked SO cool!". Also that one dance they do at the end of the mission is on the same level as a MonsterHunter cooking cutscene haha.MusicReally good, obviously, Japanese music, with a little metal in there at one boss which surprised me. Hope to hear more of that.No idea how much content the game has, but so far it's absolutely worth the price. Maybe the price is what scared so many people in the first place. Buy yeah, it's a ton of fun, no monetisation BS in sight, the attention to detail is insane, everything in the game just screams high quality/effort. I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really cool game that I'm positive is not going to do well in the West. It has a weird name, it has a weird art style, it has a weird marketing campaign, it a weird playstyle. However, all these things are what makes Kunitsu-Gami novel and special. It's a very Japanese game and no, not like Senran Kagura is Japanese. It's Japanese in ways that are inherent to hisotric culture and mythology. While players of games like Nioh are probably familiar with the spirts and demons presented in this game, the thematic focus on Kagura and Shinto Harae are what makes this game stand out in its art direction.If you only play a few missions, it's easy to think that Soh is rather overpowered and the game is too easy. Make it a bit further than this and you'll quickly find otherwise. While Soh is a great hero unit, he can't do this alone. That's where your villagers come in. The game has a very cool twist on tower defense in that instead of towers, you get moveable units all with their own niche roles. This helps as your defense point is constantly moving. Missions often have unique gimmicks which change up the usual formula, keeping each one fresh. As is tradition with Capcom titles, the game is big on being replayable with side objectives becoming unlocked after completion and the ability to farm up crystals and rations in easier missions if a more current one is giving you a hard time. I'd call this game a blend of character action and tower defense, something that plays really cool.This is the first game I've preordered in a long time and I rather pleasantly surprised at just how intent it seems to be on not letting me down. I'm always glad to see a new IP, especially something this cool. Also, you can give Yoshiro snacks. Game of the year.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; I HIGHLY recommend Kunitsu-Gami. Capcom combines it's amazing looking RE engine with superb motion capture to bring the beautiful and historically accurate Japanese settings and folklore to life. And most surprising of all, it's a bloody fantastic game as well.Kunitsu-Gami is beautiful. VERY beautiful. Each level feels like you are moving through a diorama set. Soh, your main character, fights with a style akin to a traditional Japanese stage dance. Yoshiro, your maiden, dances gracefully along the path while moving, and the villagers do a battle dance in sync with the traditional Japanese music during combat. After clearing a stage, you can return to it to admire and restore them to its former glory with the help of your villagers. You can also visit Yoshiro in her tent to upgrade or change your equipment, all the while she could be practicing her dance moves or fidgeting at her seat in the background. You can even unlock Japanese sweets for Yoshiro to happily eat them in front of you, with all the glorious high quality food rendering in most RE engine games like Monster Hunter. Everything in this game screams style and art so much so that I can't help but feel that the devs were having a blast making them.This is a also very well paced game. Almost every level introduces a new type of enemies or environmental danger, throwing curveballs at you to force you to adapt. I was initially worries it might get stale after a while, but I'm genuinely surprise how much fun I'm having even after 17 hours. Each new stage felt like a puzzle, having to decide the best spot to park my maiden for the night while frantically running around during the day to find everything I can use to give me an edge in battle like traps or choke points before night falls.I also really like the resource management aspect of the game, where everything from moving the maiden to changing your villagers job costs resources. Deciding how much I'm willing to spend on moving the maiden versus how many strong units I might need in every level is really fun and engaging, so much so that I kept finding myself replaying levels just to find the optimum strategy and complete optional challenges.What I absolutely loved about Kunitsu-Gami is the variety of customization available. There more than 10 job types for your villagers and many upgrades for your main character to unlock. You can also equip accessories you find from completing maps or challenges that will vastly change how you will play. For example, one of them will increase all villagers attack power while reducing yours, making it play more like an RTS than a character action game. There's so much build variety to be discovered I'm always excited to find new accessories or abilities to unlock.Not everything is positive though. While it runs smoothly in max settings most of the time with my 4070Ti, I do encounter a fair number of crashes. While it's not very frequent, it is significant enough that I'm mildly annoyed. I also do wish for more variety of music, as while they are fantastic, the battle music do get somewhat repetitive as there is only ONE battle music for the entire game. Management of villagers could also use an improvement, as the UI for it is kind of clunky and it's pretty hard trying to select the unit you want when they are all bunched up close together.Overall, Kunitsu-Gami is a must-buy for anyone looking to try something new and fresh. You can clearly feel the love and passion of the developers in every corner of this fantastic piece of art. This is truly a new golden standard for a AA game, and is quickly rising as my GOTY. Please make more games like this Capcom, and thank you for allowing gems like these to be made again.

_childDocuments_.name: Kunitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess

_childDocuments_.review: This game kind of came out of nowhere but it is likely going to be my favorite game of 2024. The more I take my time with it, the more I find incredible little details, such as examining the highly detailed tsuba (sword guard) while taking a rest in one of the villages. Or purifying corrupted animals, later to find them forming a small circle around Yoshiro (the shrine maiden) who gently tends to them.I agree with others that it feels exactly like a PS2-era Capcom game, but that is not a detriment. It's also an experience unlike anything I've ever played. It's a mix of hack and slash, Onimusha-style action with elements of tower defense and resource management. It's uniquely stylish. I've enjoyed watching Soh create airborne kaleidoscope ribbons with each elegant step in dance with his blade.Capcom just knows how to make a good, solid, chicken noodle soup video game. It just makes you feel all warm and fuzzy, and a bit nostalgic of times now gone. If you're looking at this game and caught even a slight interest, I highly recommend trying it out. The game takes a little bit of time before it really opens up, but once it does, the payoff is absolutely worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Kunitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful little game. It's got a great gameplay loop, is relaxed enough not to feel super stressful, and there's a nice sense of progression as you fix up the villages you save. Completionists will have a lot to do trying to beat all the stages with all their individual challenges as well, though the game is a respectable, achievable length without this from what I understand.The game's single downside is that it's not overly difficult. I'd love to see a hard mode update or DLC in the future to give an extra layer of challenges for the hardcore, but really just as an excuse to spend more time with what is a delightful and creative game with a warm and inviting world.
_childDocuments_.name: Kunitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess

_childDocuments_.review: Ceremony.This game is the very embodiment of that word. Nearly every interaction in Kanitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess feels like a ceremony:From its Möbius strip-like gameplay loop to the rhythmic, intense Taiko drum patterns during battles, the experience is steeped in a beautiful, ritualistic nuance. The village's music, which conveys hope and sweetness tinged with melancholy and uncertainty, adds a layer of perseverance. Navigating the menus resembles a tea ceremony (sadō/chadō) complete with desserts. The unique in-game model designs and artwork are also part of this immersive ceremony, all wrapped in a story told through dance and gestures—with little to no spoken words—centered on themes of community, environmentalism, tragedy, and sacrifice.The game is rich with cryptic metaphors, hidden details, folktales, and traditions that enhance the experience. However, I worry that many players might dismiss it as a “tower defense and hack 'n' slash” game and miss out on its deeper significance.-In Shinto rituals, Kunitsu-Gami are kami (Shinto deities) revered as intermediaries between the human and divine realms. They are believed to be connected to the land and possess spiritual powers often invoked in purification rituals (harae/harai) to remove impurity (kegare/seethe). These rituals aimed to maintain harmony and balance between humans and the natural world. Thus, the Kunitsu-Gami were worshiped as tutelary deities to ensure the land's prosperity and the community's well-being.The game’s story revolves around the Kunitsu-Gami residing on a mountain, providing blessings to the people living there. However, humanity's greed led to the desecration of the mountain for riches, causing a buildup of sin. As generations passed, this sin breached the barrier between the spirit and human worlds, unleashing defilement into the impermanent world.The sun that once warmed the villages is now cloaked in shadow. As humanity's sins transform into terror, the karma from those who killed and forsook the cycle of life has awakened the Seethe.The Kunitsu-Gami and the villagers, adorned in ceremonial masks and guided by the melodies of flutes and night-time wails, courageously bear the spirits of countless lives. They strive to purge fears and purify human sin so that one day the sky will once again be filled with heavenly light, bathing the world in a peaceful glow.None of this is directly conveyed to the player with dialogue (save from the brief prologue). Yet, by engaging with the game attentively—whether it's helping villagers rebuild, selecting upgrades and accessories (with the freedom to undo upgrades), petting the dogs, cats, deer, snakes, cattle, boars (the player can't pet the chickens and pheasants, sadly), or just adjusting the classes of your villagers during The Night Parade of One Hundred Demons—the moments of the final battle become all the more rewarding.-This is a game that made me feel pity for the bosses' backstories, a sense of relief when dawn approaches, and a bittersweet ending. For what it's worth, I find myself eagerly anticipating the chance to explore different play styles in New Game+.Enjoy the ceremony. This is, without a doubt, my game of the year for 2024.---Final Update:I absolutely loved New Game+, there were a few surprises in terms of content that enhanced the overall experience. I very highly recommend giving it a try when prompted <3My closing thoughts. Despite the redundancy of re-playing levels in order to complete their side-quests, I was having a really good time utilizing end-game equipment and abilities to challenge myself and seeing how many bosses I can defeat in a matter of seconds ^_^This was a game worth 100% completing. :D

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game quite a lot, though the rarity of cutscenes with voice acting or a lack of overtly clearly defined characters may turn some away. What can be inferred, from the text presented in game, and the wall scrolls you obtain do help paint a history your imagination can fill in the gaps on. _childDocuments_.review: An innovative mix of an action and strategy game. The combat is smooth, there are many classes for your villagers, enemy types and bosses. Getting upgrades and leveling up your villagers is fun. The whole package feels well designed and polished. I read somewhere that this game took over 4 years to make, and it shows in how much variety and polish there is. These days games try to be big and long, but with this game CAPCOM went for moment to moment fun and a nice tight package.

_childDocuments_.review: Really great, and surprisingly out of nowhere gem! I found the demo a day before it released, played the first two stages, and instantly preordered. I feel like this is a modern title with PS2 charm in terms of atmosphere, sound design, and how enjoyable it is to play. It starts out easy but seems to ramp and build upon itself. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Kunitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess

_childDocuments_.review: A very nice tower defense hybrid game. There's enough mechanics to not get too boring during its campaign. Plenty of tanky enemy types to worry about so that you can't just sit still while your units kill everything.Story is surprisingly decent too considering that there's no spoken dialogue. Lots of detail and lore to read up on, but not an overwhelming amount like a lot of JRPGs. There's slightly more strategy required to beat some of the later stages and the extra challenges per stage usually require multiple attempts at least. Though to be honest, my main strategies for nearly every stage and boss is to make almost every unit a marksman and the odd 1 or 2 a support/melee as backup.I beat this game at around 18 hours while replaying a bunch for challenge objectives but also not attempting some of the more annoying objectives.
_childDocuments_.name: Kunitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess

_childDocuments_.review: FEELS LIKE A GAME FROM MY CHILDHOOD.A surprise hit for me. Feels like a game that came out of that PS2 era experimental time of games. Lots of little charming things that don't directly effect game play, like having an upgrade you can equip in one of your slots that just makes your attacks more sparkly. Game is pretty relaxing and only got super hectic a couple times but I had a ton of fun. Game can have a lot of downtime running around and repairing the different levels but none of it is required to do and can be fun seeing all the places come back to life slowly. Almost every level has something that sets it apart and I almost wish each concept got another level or two to really flesh it out. Wish there was some challenge missions that were built to specifically show the strengths of each class or ones with weird restrictions like you can only use bowmen. If they put out a DLC of just challenge missions with different wacky gimmicks I'd say this game would be close to perfect. Not really any games that play just like this one and it really scratched a few spots simultaneously. BIG RECOMMEND
_childDocuments_.name: Kunitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess

_childDocuments_.review: As one of the few who finished this game, I recommend it (though I do recommend to buy it on sale, instead of full price.). It feels like a game from the ps2 era where they experiment more with game play but the budget is lower. This means the game has some interesting mechanics and game play, but there are noticiable flaws such as some jank, repetitious game play (they run out of budget so they have to repeat gimmics), and some mechanics that just aren't fleshed out (base repairing). The game also starts off way too easy, making for a boring first impression. It gets much better later on.Either way it's an interesting mixture between tower defence and action game.
_childDocuments_.name: Kunitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess

_childDocuments_.review: Capcom is back on their PS2/Gamecube era drugs, folks!Kunitsu-gami is a brawler/tower defense game in which a genderless spirit Soh escorts a priestess and she slowly purifies corrupted lands with the power of choreography.Action Strategy hybrids are always challenging to make and sell.  Only a few were successful.  If you make the player too powerful, strategy doesn't matter and you created Dynasty Warriors (Ninety Nine Nights, Fire Emblem Warriors.)  If you make the player weak, being weak needs to be fun (Pikmin.)  Brutal Legend got it right.In this, Soh is slow, but strong.  The game wants you know that you cannot be everywhere at once.  Instead, you rescue villagers and used divine masks to give them defensive roles to attack enemies and heal and support allies.  Like towers, they don't move: they can only be commanded to defend a small area.  Like all my favorite Action/RTS hybrids, this sometimes feels like a game of plate spinning, in which you figure out which area's deserve Soh's powerful blade and which can be defended by your allies.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is SO close to being incredible, but the simplicity of the combat and the ease of most levels betrays it. There's far, far too many levels where you can basically just camp in one spot and lazily do the same attack over and over when a guy walks by. The game is very afraid of throwing too many of the enemy types at you at once, and it results in a very action anemic experience where you spend more time waiting than anything.The downtime in this game is legitimately insane, I can't believe it got past the design phase. First off, you have preparations. So, ok, you have to run around a small level purifying sections of the map to gather villagers and upgrades. This isn't TOO bad, the animations get tiring and you don't have a sprint but if this was all I wouldn't mind. But for some godawful reason, they decided once you beat a level you have to go back into the map and run around it again so you can command the villagers to repair buildings. Some of these buildings give vital upgrades, and you get a unique piece of gear when all upgrades are done. So you set the villagers to do maybe a third of the building tasks, because there's a limited number of them.And then you go off and do a mission. And then you have to go back and run back to the spots again to claim the rewards. And then you have to run around to the other repair points, because you can't reassign villagers until you claim your reward. And then you have to do it again, and ALSO there will be some random planks of wood scattered around that you have to command the villagers to grab for some of the repairs. And then you do it one more time, and then you have to run into a tent on the map to claim the final prize. The end result is you're running around each map a half dozen times doing essentially nothing, because yes you have to do this for EVERY LEVEL.There's also brief boss arenas where you fight one big foe and don't have to do any of that. But they also have a time trial element, where you assign all your units before the fight and then go in. If you screw up the time trial? You're assigning 6+ guys individually again, because there's no option to restart from the fight. In one of these you have 12 guys and the time trial is extremely tight. All of this adds up WAY too much.Last note, you can't rebind a lot of buttons properly. The command button has to be on a bumper or trigger, even though it's not a button that needs to get pressed urgently basically ever. Because of this, the default control scheme has dodge on click left-stick and it's a big pain in the ass to find a configuration where you're not giving up something. If command could be set to up on the d-pad, problem would be solved. But that has to be taken up by the photo mode button that almost no one ever uses.Edit: I made it halfway into new game+ now and yeah, this game just never gets even remotely difficult. There's a small period of time in the last few levels where the game gets hectic enough to be fun (but still not challenging) and then new game+ just gets easier again despite you now having even more upgrades. The only semi-hard thing is doing some of the don't get hit / don't let Yoshiro get hit challenges but they're not actually difficult, they just encourage you to play super safe and lame. Maybe I'd recommend this game if they add some endgame DLC or crazy master levels or something, but as for now the monotony is not worth the few moments of fun it provides.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game that gets the mixture of tower defence and hack and slash combat just right.  The scope + ambition of Kunitsu-Gami will remind many of the Playstation 2's offerings, be it Monster Hunter, Okami or even Ico.  I hope to see more games from director Kawata (and maybe a port of Shinsekai: Into The Depths, pretty please).
_childDocuments_.name: Kunitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess

_childDocuments_.review: This is the game people want when they say 'I wish they made good games again'. I bet you've already heard the quote 'it's like a PS2-era Capcom game' but well, that's the most succinct way to describe it.A longer way is 'What if Onimusha but also some Okami vibes with Tower Defense spice' and this is kinda it. You fight demons (Seethe) with a lone samurai (who is a messenger from a god) together with a Magical Girl who can purge the demons. Along the way you save villages, rebuild them and recruit villagers as your Tower Defense Army. Every now and then you get some level gimmicks that refresh the gameplay and that's it. It's pretty fun.The downside is that it seems the game is prone to crashing if you keep alt-tabbing a lot. Another downside is that, personally, I feel it's 10 bucks too much for now. It's clearly a passion project of someone at Capcom, but I don't think the game is getting the advertisement it deserves; it seems to be disappointingly unnoticed. Thankfully it's a single player game, so it's just your enjoyment on the line. There's a demo, give it a try, if you like that kind of gameplay, consider a purchase.Psst - there's also Okami music available to switch the ingame tracks. Truly, the Okami sequel we all waited for, and Capcom totally did not forget about us!
_childDocuments_.name: Kunitsu-Gami: Path of the Goddess

_childDocuments_.review: A smaller-scale, fun game. At first I was impatient and just waiting for the hack n slash parts, but after I accepted the game for what it was, I started to really enjoy it. It has a simple formula, but level design stops it from feeling repetitive. Seeing the previous areas you've completed as they're restored to their previous state is peacefully satisfying and adds an emotion dynamic of chilling between more intense levels. To me, its main shortcoming is replayability. As much as I enjoyed my time with the game, I don't feel any need to keep playing after completing it. I got 18 hours of fun out of this game and it's up to you to decide what price that's worth paying for.
