_childDocuments_.review: It pains me to write this, but I can't in all good conscience recommended this package IF you already own Sonic Generations, however even then there are still some caveats.Shadow Generations is brilliant expansion in the same vein as Bowser's Fury to Super Mario 3D World. Apart from some questionable music remixes, it's definitely on par if not better than Sonic Generations in the boost series of games. It's really designed to be an introduction game for a lot of newcomers to the series in order to promote the next film and visa-versa.Shadow feels tight to control during segments where he needs to be. To have you in control in a Sonic game is already a plus but this is probably one of the tightest in the boost era if not the whole series. The attention to detail in these stages, despite you speeding past most of it shows a lot of passion and polish. Little details like the Doom Eyes constantly keeping track of you in the hub world. The Bosses are, if not a little too easy, but are pure gimmicky shounen-style kino.Story is great and a little moving at times but if you're a newcomer know there's a lot of borrowed elements that head writer Ian Flynn likes to use in his scripts. What, you thought the origin of Shadow's name was Flynn's idea?  He gets a lot more praise than he probably deserves.Also it's a real shame the prologue animation was not included in the Steam version, while not integral to the game it was wonderfully animated and points get deducted from SEGA for Playstation's exclusivity greed because they don't know how to sell their own games.Some cons being that in some precise platforming sections there is no shadow directly under Shadow (heh), this is fundamental 3D platform design 101 and it's annoying when devs ignore this very basic principle, you will over/underestimate your jumps at times.Thankfully these are far and few between and don't ruin the core experience.Doom morph has really finicky air control.And personally the remixes can be really hit or miss (but mostly miss) and make me pine for the original music more often then not. Maybe this is just me being old, but Sonic OSTs haven't really been as timeless or as memorable since the boost era started. Thankfully you can collect music from Shadow's past games as you can do in Sonic Generations.Plus it's too short; there are only 6 stages with 2 acts between them separated by 3D (Act 1) and 2D (Act 2) plains and as a result Doom powers are underutilised. One only hopes there might be some new levels added in the future.Now what to say about Sonic Generations. there are no improvements to it as far as I can tell, it's essentially a carbon copy, however something feels... different about it, little things that I noticed compared to the original (and I'm not talking about the script changes (as referential as they may be)).In what I would consider to be the best boost game out of the lot the controls don't feel as tight, weird camera angle changes just happen out of nowhere and I can't help but think that I've been duped into buying a slightly less good Generations for what now I realise probably should've been a standalone game for Shadow.I can't help but think what time and resources could've instead been used the make Shadow Generations a bigger game.And that's where it hurts the most, my wallet. Another issue being that the Original has also been delisted from Steam, if this is your first time playing Generations then this probably won't affect you in the slightest, in which case, buy away; have fun, but to those of you who have played before, I would recommend buying at a discount, half-price maybe.And while we're on the subject, Sega what the hell are you playing at removing all your Megadrive and Dreamcast games from here?oh and  denuvo, we don't like denuvo here.

_childDocuments_.review: No more "A step in the right direction". They actually did it.Shadow Generations is a triumph. A really, REALLY good Sonic-style platformer that iterates on both the skillful, multi-pathed platforming of Generations, and the addictive open-zone style of Frontiers. The main levels all bang, and the Doom Powers are a great additional wrinkle for Shadow's moveset (though Doom Morph took me a minute to understand, but once it clicks it's good.) For the first time in a while, I was replaying these stages over and over, trying to find new paths and cut down on my times. It's fun. REALLY fun!Heck, this is even the first game in the series where all the bosses are good! They scale back the scope of Frontiers' Titans for more focused spectacle, while allowing much more mechanical complexity so it doesn't feel mindless in the slightest. The story's good and heartbreaking, reflecting on the past while weaving it into something new, and the visuals are a frankly unbelievable leap from Frontiers. My only real complaint is that I wanted more of it.Now more than ever, I'm glad Sonic Team proved me right: the base of what we have in the open-zone format is fantastic, and iterating on it will only bring good things. Looking forward to the next mainline entry, I wanna see this level of quality on original level visuals! (Though I won't lie, it was very nice seeing these biomes again.)(Oh also there's a Sonic Generations rerelease in here too. It's fine, it rounds out the package nicely. Sonic Gens is a good game, and they avoid a Colors Ultimate situation with it. The script rewrites are strange but I don't mind them. Overall, really good bang for your buck, especially if you never played Sonic Generations.)

_childDocuments_.review: (This review contains light gameplay spoilers for Shadow Generations, proceed with caution)I want to preface this review with the fact that I was worried about this game and how it would turn out. Frontiers, although the boss fights were very fun, had a VERY repetitive gameplay loop, and the platforming segments in the open world areas definitely didn't fill me with hope regarding this game's levels. However, I must admit, I've never been so wrong about a game in my life. I was absolutely blown away by this game and how constantly action-packed and fun it was.The sense of constant momentum and action in Shadow Generations is absolutely INCREDIBLE. Unlike Sonic Generations, it doesn't feel like I have to constantly slow myself down just to do some platforming. Shadow's controls are incredibly satisfying and they feel much more refined compared to how it feels to move as Classic or Modern Sonic. On top of that, we got some beautifully animated cutscenes and amazing music, although that's to be expected with Sonic games. I loved all the Doom abilities (except for maybe the squid because slingshotting with those balls was really janky), and unlocking the wings in every level after beating the game was a really cool reward, and definitely made me experiment with the levels in brand new ways. Absolutely incredible job, Sonic Team. Also METAL OVERLORD BOSS FIGHT ♥♥♥♥ YEAH I LOVE SHADOW GENERATIONS!!!

_childDocuments_.review: Shadow's alien daddy issues: part 2. Love seeing Black Doom comeback after so long!The gameplay and level design in both campaigns is solid. I was a bit worried the new levels in Shadow Generations might be shorter and feel too on rails like in Sonic Forces, but thankfully that is not the case. There are lots of paths to take, each main level takes a good 4-5 minutes to complete and there's a good number of them like in Sonic Generations. The challenge missions are also decently fun to play through and there are lots of collectables to hunt down in the hub world. Completionists will have their fill getting all the S ranks and collecting all the extras. The use of the Frontiers control scheme is also a great choice: everything feels responsive and not janky at all.The plot in Shadow Generations is truly great. Both the prologue animations and the actual game's story offer lots of lore references and expansions for people who are looking for it. Those who have been playing Sonic games for years and love Shadow as a character will appreciate what has been done here.

_childDocuments_.review: This short review focuses on the Shadow Generations portion of this dual pack.After the disappointing Sonic Generations port, I began this game with low expectations. However, I quickly realized how much superior Shadow Generations is.Shadow Generations is a brand-new game starring Shadow the Hedgehog. Set during the events of Sonic Generations, this title follows Shadow's side of the story as he revisits past friends, enemies, and locations from his adventures.Built on the Hedgehog Engine 2, it benefits from additional graphical settings and improved visuals, but it also reuses a lot of assets from Sonic Frontiers, as well as the tweaked character controller from Sonic Lost World that Sonic Team has been re-purposing for a long time now. The character controller still has issues from losing momentum when double jumping, but the movement feels much more polished when compared to Sonic Frontiers. The addition of a free-roam 3D hub world jam-packed with collectibles and challenges is a welcome one, and the levels that were selected for this game were good picks. Although I was disappointed to find that there were no stages from Shadow's only game, Shadow the Hedgehog, instead, a level from Sonic Frontiers was put into the game. This could have simply been a cost-reducing or time-saving decision.Overall, I found myself really enjoying this game as I played through the various levels and explored the 3D hub world. I also really loved seeing how Shadow's story was expanded upon as it had been a long time since he and other characters connected to him had gotten any development.I definitely recommend getting this dual pack just for this game alone, especially if you're a Shadow fan. You'll have a blast!_____________________________________This short review focuses on the Sonic Generations portion of this dual pack. Unfortunately, something must have gone horribly wrong during the development of this port of Sonic Generations, which seemingly still runs on the same old Hedgehog Engine 1. The physics and character controllers for both Classic Sonic and Modern Sonic are familiar yet slightly off in how they feel and move, not to mention the inability to use the D-pad as Classic Sonic. Collision detection seems to be inconsistent in places, and the camera will sometimes malfunction in both 2D and 3D levels, leading Sonic to his doom as he is unable to follow his path. The game suffers from frequent stuttering and lag spikes, even on a high-end PC. Many of the changes to the writing, animations, and models were unnecessary, and more time should have been spent on quality control instead.Sadly, I feel that this is a far inferior experience to the original Sonic Generations, and I cannot recommend it at this time. If you are looking to play Sonic Generations, I urge you to seek out the original version, which is still available but unlisted, so you can enjoy a truly polished experience._____________________________________As much as I would like to turn this into a positive review after playing Shadow Generations, I can't bring myself to do so. The current state of Sonic Generations is unacceptable and brings down the value of the whole pack. Due to this, I will be keeping this as a negative review. However, do know that Shadow Generations is an excellent game worth playing!

_childDocuments_.review: They cooked hard with Shadow Generations. Separating full 3D levels and full 2D levels is a big improvement in my opinion, and the 2D ones this time around have good level design so I don't mind them. There was good effort put into the challenge stages too, often the level design feels varied enough that it's just like another normal act to play. There's some replayability with the Doom powers and a ton of faster alternate paths to find. Spent hours in the original generations grinding for better times and I can already feel Shadow will be the same. The open hub has some great Frontiers-esque timed challenges and a ton of collectables to extend the runtime a bit further. The story i still relatively limited in scope but that's still miles better than Sonic's side, and I enjoyed the long-awaited closure to Shadow's character arc. I do wish there was a few more levels since they pretty much showed everything in the trailers, but it's not a big deal considering the quality we got. Boost Sonic is back and the best it's ever been!Oh, and Sonic Generations is still Sonic Generations. Script changes range from good to inoffensive and I appreciate the limited new content.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone that has been a Sonic fan for 20 years, this package is everything I could ask for. I want to geek out so bad in this review, but for the sake of keeping it spoiler free, I'm just going to touch on the actual gameplay of the two games.Sonic Generations:----------------------------Not really much has changed here. It's Sonic Generations almost the same way you remember it, but with slightly better visuals, small gameplay tweaks (addition of the drop dash, chao to find in every stage, and improved controller support). Not sure if this is a result of how much better the game runs, but it seems like classic Sonic feels a little less weighty than the original release, which is actually a good thing to me, but could be jarring to others. To make the game's writing more consistent with Shadow's story and give it more substance overall, Sonic Team/SEGA had Ian Flynn rewrite a lot of the cutscenes and for the most part, they are a welcome change. They are going to be jarring for fans of the original Generations, but newcomers won't have an issue with them whatsoever. For the most part, they are perfectly fine and improves on where the original version of the game was lacking (they are no where near as offensive as politically charged reactionaries are trying to make them seem). The only problem I have with them is that some of the animations aren't updated to fit the new dialogue, but that's just a nitpick at worst (it brought us the Classic Sonic ate Angel Island joke, so I can't really complain about it). I have encountered a few bugs I've never scene in the original release, but only one resulted in a softlock. At the end of Metal Sonic's rival fight, I somehow died while I was landing the last hit on him and it resulted in his defeat animation playing with a static 2D camera, no assets other than classic, metal, and the background, and the two floating around the upper right part of the screen. Once the animation finished playing, the screen faded to white and the game froze up. Besides that goof, the game is very polished, which is to be expected from an overall very safe remaster. However, I do wish a little more was added to really spice it up beyond it's already good original PC release. Even though my time with it is shorter than the absurd amount of time I've already put into Shadow's story, I can easily say that this is the definitive way to play vanilla Sonic Generations. At least on PC. 8/10!Shadow Generations----------------------------There is a good reason Sonic Team was so confident in this game. Not only is it easily one of, if not THE, most polished games Sonic Team has put out in over a decade. It stands toe to toe with their best offerings, including Sonic Generations itself. The levels are very well designed and art a blast to speed through, the bosses are the best we've gotten in ages, and the open zone is an evolution of the ones present in Sonic Frontiers. The open zone isn't huge by any means, but it is big enough and there are A LOT of collectibles to find in it. Mostly music that you can play in levels and boss fights (functions the same way it did in Generations), concept art, and history/lore. There are only six levels total, which I can see being disappointing to some, but I think the level design and how many branching paths there are to take more than makes up for it. These levels are very beefy and your first casual run of them can easily exceed five or more minutes. There are quite a few 2D acts (with the exception of the final stage, every act 2 is a 2D stage) and at first they seemed like they were going to be similar to the ones in Forces, but I'm more than happy that I was wrong about that. They are very well designed and get the best out of Shadow's abilities without being too overbearing. Can say the same about the challenge levels you have to beat to get the keys you need to access the boss fights. They are pretty short and don't overstay their welcome. You do have to finish all of them to fight the second to last boss, but I had a fun time speeding through them as they are designed to be rushed through unlike most of Sonic Generation's challenges. As for the bosses, they are fantastic! They feel like a mashup of the spectacle of the Frontier's bosses with gameplay that surpasses their original encounters from the games they originate from. They aren't difficult all things considered, but they aren't pushovers and may take a lil bit of time to figure out. All of them go above and beyond, but one boss fight had me grinning ear to ear because of the dialogue and how well it was executed. The doom powers are very context sensitive, but with how many there are and how they work, it makes sense for them to be. They add a wonderful amount of variety to the game, but even without them, this game is more than strong enough to stand out on its own. All of this is boosted by how polished it is, the insanely good music, production value, and how open Sonic Team has been about this game. It is a must play for Sonic fans and newcomers alike. Only bugs I ran into was one of my abilities breaking after the second doom power cutscene, Shadow getting stuck floating the air for a few seconds while homing attacking a spring, and the second to last cutscene of the game freezing up (I fixed it by verifying the integrity of game files). Overall, Shadow Generations is just as, if not more polished than Sonic's story and surpasses it in almost every way. It is a must play for any Sonic fan! Easy 9/10!All hail Shadow!

_childDocuments_.review: I, like many people, was dubious at the thought of a remaster of Sonic Generations. My trust in Sega regarding this was also particularly low due to the disappointment that was  a few years back - shoddy remakes with technical issues not present in the original games, all the while delisting said original games from digital storefronts forever, alongside developer mistreatment.With Sonic X Shadow Generations, Sega seems to have learned their lesson, at least somewhat. First of all, the original Sonic Generations from 2011  While not the best solution to this, this is still a better compromise than what they did with Sonic 1, 2, CD, as well as 3 & Knuckles.Second - there is actually something new here for everyone. Sonic Generations, surprisingly enough, received new content in the form of re-animated cutscenes or brand new dubs to fit the series' continuity better. This is the first time I've seen them actually rewrite the story of an older game to make it make more sense within the confines of the series' universe canon. The one thing I do not like about the remaster of Sonic Generations here is the nerf to Classic Sonic's movement. The overpowered spindash from the old version of the game is completely gone, making Classic Sonic feel insanely sluggish to control due to years of muscle memory from the older version. Aside from that, if you wanna know what I think of Sonic Generations itself, Now, for Shadow Generations...okay, first of all - I find it very weird that they named it "Shadow Generations" to begin with. Shadow has had playable main story appearances in 4 games total - Sonic Adventure 2, Sonic Heroes, Shadow the Hedgehog and Sonic 06. What I really wish they did with the Shadow Generations portion is decouple it entirely from Sonic Generations & release it as its own separate game, with a longer, more detailed and fleshed out story, a few more levels - preferably with more original theming rather than revisiting ones from older games again - and name it "Shadow the Hedgehog 2".That's just the thing...playing this honest to god felt like a direct sequel to the infamous 2005 game - Shadow the Hedgehog. And you know what? I am so on-board with this idea. I am one of the rare few who actually loves that game, despite its glaring issues with structure, pacing & everything else. And I absolutely adore the ideas they toy around with in the game, be it the new powers for Shadow or fleshing out characters which we vaguely knew about regarding Shadow's past. That whole thing was AWESOME and I genuinely wish they just made it a full blown "Shadow the Hedgehog 2" with it instead.Granted, I understand why they didn't and felt the need to basically shoehorn it into a remaster of Sonic Generations - marketing. Because Shadow the Hedgehog was critically panned & overall receives mixed-to-negative feedback from the community even in 2024, close to 20 years after its original release, I understand that they don't want to make a sequel to Shadow the Hedgehog, at least not yet.What I'm hoping for is that Sonic X Shadow Generations is just the testing ground to see how receptive people are to the idea of Shadow starring in his own games again, and my honest opinion? Hell yeah! I've already mentioned that I love the original Shadow the Hedgehog. I love the Shadow Generations portion of this game so much, just wish there was more of it. And I want to see more dedicated Shadow the Hedgehog games in the future.The game itself is rather short. I completed Shadow Generations in around 3.5 hours - not much longer than Sonic Generations itself. Controls' wise I found it to be pretty much perfect. Aside from the final stage where it's centered around a new ability Shadow gets, everywhere else I found him controlling pretty much perfect. Did not encounter any bugs or anything of the sort in my time playing either. The length of the game though...again - really wish they made it its own separate game & had time to flesh it out, it's so good otherwise!From a technical standpoint, I ran this game start to finish on my Linux machine and it ran beautifully. Steam Deck & Linux people, you're in for a great OOTB experience with this one!Overall, yeah I do recommend Sonic X Shadow Generations. For both people who have never played Sonic Generations, and those who know it front to back. There are enough neat additions in Sonic Generations that will make you go "I wonder what else they changed", as well as a very enjoyable Shadow adventure to go through, albeit both games are rather short.I can't wait to see what the modding scene for this will look like.

_childDocuments_.review: Sonic Generations was already a standout title, celebrating decades of Sonic’s legacy with its fast-paced gameplay, nostalgic levels, and seamless blend of classic and modern Sonic styles. But this re-release, now featuring Shadow Generations, takes the experience to an entirely new level. It’s not just a rehash of an old favorite—it’s a revitalized love letter to the franchise that longtime fans will appreciate while being an excellent entry point for newcomers.The addition of Shadow Generations brings a fresh dynamic to the game. Shadow’s gameplay feels unique yet complementary, offering his signature chaos-fueled speed and darker tone to balance Sonic’s bright and upbeat energy. New stages and challenges designed specifically for Shadow expand the gameplay experience, making this version feel more like an enhanced sequel than a simple re-release. Visually, the game still shines, with vibrant, updated graphics that breathe life into both classic 2D levels and the modern 3D worlds. Combined with a remastered soundtrack that includes both Sonic’s and Shadow’s most iconic themes, the game feels both nostalgic and innovative.Whether you’re revisiting Sonic Generations or experiencing it for the first time, this edition is undoubtedly the best way to play. The added content, improved performance, and expanded storyline with Shadow make it a must-buy for Sonic fans and platforming enthusiasts alike. This isn’t just a game—it’s a celebration of everything that makes the Sonic universe unforgettable.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who's been extremely hit or miss on the "boost-centric" gameplay of the series starting with Unleashed, I think Shadow Generations is possibly my favorite overall iteration to date.As far as comparisons to the original Sonic Generations, easily the biggest upgrade to me was... how the levels are structured. The constant switching between 3D and 2D sections extremely bothered me making replays of Modern Sonic levels not always fun especially since 2D sections still feel overly stiff.In Shadow Generations, the change to having ALL Act 1s be full 3D means levels very much more consistently good. I still don't care for the full 2D levels in Act 2s but they are very slightly better than 2D sections in most boost-centric games but that's not saying much. But when 7/12 levels are full 3D they are MUCH more fun to replay consistently than even Sonic Generations Modern Sonic levels. The 3D levels feel the closest to a Adventure-era level AND a Boost-centric level combination which is what I've wanted if Sonic Team was never gonna do full Adventure era style levels anymore.One very interesting addition to levels are Shadow-specific powerups. Sonic technically had these through Colors and Generations but very limited. Shadow gets Chaos Control AND his stun lasers from Shadow/06 which I thought were VERY welcome as l actually liked the combat focus of those Shadow levels. Shadow also gets temp powers based on terrain and... really edgey wings that replace a Super form. I have mixed feelings on these BUT since replaying levels lets you turn off the wings in particular I'd say these are net positive to give people options to make Shadow feel POWERFUL. That said the Wings were a bit much for me so that specifically I avoided using outside the first go through the levels.The hub world is one of the better ones we've had since... Adventure 1? 2006s sucked, Unleashed was kind of a pain, and Generations was literally just walking left to right. Never played Frontiers because I really don't like open-world games. Shadow Generations hub world is a good mix of having platforming and ways to practice moves, find secrets, and just be big enough to find stuff but not full of empty space like so many terrible open-world games try to do these days.One of the biggest surprises is how FUN and EPIC the boss fights were. Many 3D sonic games, including the supposedly popular ones have lots hit or miss bosses, including Sonic Generations. In Shadow Generations, even if some are long they are so active and have cool setpieces, zoom-ins, well-placed quick time events and fitting dialogue that I enjoyed every one. They're not in the running for best boss fights ever, but they are in the upper tier of Sonic boss fights. This is how you do long boss fights well (looking at you Superstars).As Shadow Generations is the first "Ian Flynn" written Sonic game I played (didnt go to Frontiers)...  I can see the hype behind him. Long gone is the cringey dialogue Sonic had from Colors up to Forces. Shadow's dialogue with Maria, Gerald, Rogue, and Omega just felt... authentic and wholesome. Fitting for a game meant to celebrate every game Shadow was playable in.Outside some of the powers being too edgey, and not liking 2D levels much the only other flaw I have is... the music while OK is nowhere near as memorable as Sonic Generations. Most of it is because the levels they chose as a whole don't have music nearly as memorable or iconic as the one they chose for Sonic in their original games. Not a bad soundtrack by any means just overall more forgettable.Overall though I had a surprising blast with Shadow Generations. People are hyping this up as Sonic team BEING BACK but Sonic Team ALWAYS has the "cycle" meaning they'll probably go back to making mediocre to bad games soon after 1 or 2 good hits. That said with this game basically being a 2-in-1 I look forward to more 3D Speed levels to happily replay from time to time, as Sonic 3D levels are some of my favorite games to just replay on the fly.

_childDocuments_.review: When SEGA annouced they were making this game, I wasn't really looking forward to it. To me it seemed like a cheap way to sell old game for a ridiculous price tag with a sprinkle of new content. Holy smokes was I far from the truth.This brought me back to when I first played Sonic Generations as a kid. It was my first contact with Sonic the Hedgehog franchise and I loved every single bit of it. Even these days, I religiously replay the game until there's nothing left to collect or beat. I kept chasing that feeling of being able to experience it for the first time. While playing the Shadow campaign of this game, it absolutely delivered on that. It's fun just like it's predecessor, if not even better. One thing I gotta mention is that the hub (or the "white") world is very very reminescent of how Sonic Frontiers treated it's sandbox open world gameplay, except it's clustered and tightened to one smaller area. While it may sound like a bad thing, it's not. It is the perfected concept of what was Frontiers supposed to be and how I wanted it to feel.The way they handled the Sonic part of this game is also great. I can't really get into that remastered feeling of the gameplay since Generations always looked this beautiful to me, but I adore the feeling of spotting any slight little changes. The chao collection let's me replay all the levels while giving me something fresh to look out for. I know that it's just a minor gimmick, but I love it nonetheless. Overall, Sonic X Shadow Generations is a great game for old and new players alike. SEGA built upon a working concept and made it even better. 10/10, it's a great time to be a Sonic fan.

_childDocuments_.review: i have it on good authority that we are absolutely BACK folksI just rolled credits on Shadow's story, and I had an absolute blast. I will be upfront here - if you are just looking to do a run of the story and call it a day there, and you don't care about the remaster of Sonic's half of the game, there's not exactly a lot of content here - only a few hours worth. The content that is here, however, is fantastic, and the play time in this game (much like other sonic games) comes from repeated playthroughs of levels to discover more secrets and collectibles, mapping out optimal routes through the stages to achieve those S ranks and times beyond. The levels that they chose to bring back are pretty much all smash hits, and both the 2D and 3D stages are really enjoyable to race through. It's really cool to see some stages that aren't always the "greatest hits" get the Generations treatment here, and the stages themselves are also all tightly designed with Shadow's growing moveset through the course of the game kept squarely in mind, encouraging further replayability in old stages to discover previously impossible paths.The open world in Shadow's half also feels great to manoeuvre around in - when I played some of Frontiers I wasn't absolutely huge on its open world features, but the formula has definitely been a lot more refined here. One of the main issues with Frontiers is how out of place all the rails and platforms and such felt - it really felt like they took an island and gameified it, but that issue isn't present at all here due to the setting of White Space - there isn't any natural geography to gameify.Story-wise, Shadow's section is nice. It's not the most involved, much like original Generations' story, but it explores his past and how he has never truly gotten over those he lost and the manner of his own creation, and sees him coming face to face with the most important characters in his story previous to the game.Overall, the game is fantastic, and I had a ton of fun, but at the price point I'd only fully recommend it if you either plan on being a completionist in the game, or you want to do a full playthrough of Sonic's section in addition to Shadow's - those just looking for a basic playthrough of Shadow's section without all the bells and whistles or collectable hunting will find themselves a little shy on content and it may not be worth paying full price for.

_childDocuments_.review: Sonic X Shadow Generations is 2 games compiled into one.Sonic Generations is by and large the 2011 original, with some better support at higher resolutions and actually pillarboxes properly in ultrawide. The story's been rewritten and keeps the same beats, but makes things a little more grounded and I think better characterises the cast given the circumstance. The extra chao are a neat little thing to look for but I wish they'd been used to give us some extra concept art or background music as so far they don't seem to reward anything except a photo of where the Chao was found. The Drop Dash has been added as an optional skill for Classic Sonic and a base part of Modern Sonic's moveset, but it didn't feel like it ever really came up for me as being something to use, though that could just be because I'm so used to the 2011 original and it doesn't really harm anything by being here.Shadow Generations by comparison feels closer to Sonic Frontiers than it does to Sonic Generations, Shadow largely plays like Sonic but Chaos Control and Chaos Spear give him just enough extra "stuff" to do that the levels can be a little more experimental with things. Even simple interactions like having to hit a switch or enemy with chaos spear as you approach adds just a little extra dimension to be aware of that I think makes a good run of these stages very satisfying, and that's without the extra moves you unlock throughout the campaign that allow you to traverse water, or glide through the air, or become a squid, or knock certain enemies skyward and launch them away, before teleporting to where they landed. The latter move is very satisfying to experiment with, trying to find places they may not have expected you to aim for to try and skip things and the like.Compared to Frontiers, it's much more condensed and straightforward, you beat levels to progress, and the levels contain keys that let you open chests you find in the open zone to get concept art, music and the like. It's an extra step over Sonic Generations just giving you the stuff via Red Star Rings but I think it helps give the open zone a use that the white space in sonic generations kind of lacked due to how simple it was. In the open zone, you can also find entries from Gerald's journal that was offered as a physical bonus to view in-game, and spare parts which can be handed in to get some more concept art. I think it's done an excellent job of "trimming the fat" from Frontiers and it's got me excited to see where this gameplay style will go next. The port is locked to 16:9 and pillarboxes on ultrawide, but the framerate caps at 120 here compared to Sonic Generations' 60. You can see the bump in graphical quality going between the 2 games as Shadow is running on the Hedgehog Engine 2 whilst Generations runs on the original.Overall, a great package and a must-have for any Sonic fan. Maybe wait for a sale if money's tight as each game is only about 4 hours long going straight to credits. I only hope Sonic Team can keep the momentum for the next entry and beyond.

_childDocuments_.review: SONIC X SHADOW GENERATIONS? A Nostalgic Yet Modern Blast Through Time!SONIC X SHADOW GENERATIONS offers fans an impressive double feature, combining a new Shadow-focused campaign with an enhanced edition of the acclaimed Sonic Generations. In this reimagined adventure, players explore Shadow's darker journey as he faces off against his nemesis, Black Doom, while also reliving the classic, high-speed escapades of both Classic and Modern Sonic. Featuring fresh mechanics, a new hub world, and a wealth of unlockable content, this game delivers a celebration of the Sonic series that appeals to longtime fans and new players alike.The standout experience in SONIC X SHADOW GENERATIONS is undoubtedly Shadow’s fresh storyline, which fleshes out his mysterious past and expands on his unique "Doom Powers." These powers bring a thrilling gameplay twist, allowing Shadow to control time, surf across water, and traverse levels with a combination of stealth and aggression fitting of his Ultimate Life Form title. The new "White Space" hub world takes cues from Sonic Frontiers, giving players an open-zone setting to explore, where discovering collectibles, hidden secrets, and background lore adds depth and value to Shadow's side of the game.The remastered Sonic Generations campaign complements Shadow's adventure well. Fans of the 2011 original will find Sonic's levels as exhilarating as ever, now enhanced with HD graphics, optimized performance, and small gameplay tweaks, like the addition of a drop dash move and collectible Chao in every stage. While Sonic’s story remains mostly the same, small rewrites add context, giving both the Classic and Modern Sonic campaigns a fresh feel without detracting from what made the original a classic.On the technical side, Sonic X Shadow Generations delivers in spades. Running smoothly at high frame rates, even on mid-range PCs, the game shows marked improvements in performance over recent Sonic titles. Sonic Team has fine-tuned the graphical elements of both campaigns, with new animations, sharper textures, and improved lighting effects that make Shadow's journey through familiar stages visually engaging. The soundtrack is a nostalgic powerhouse, offering remixes of fan-favorite themes alongside iconic tracks that players can choose as background music for levels, adding a personalized touch.Players looking for a flawless technical experience will be pleased to know that the game has minimal issues. While some controller compatibility and ultrawide support complaints exist, they are minor compared to the game’s overall polish and stability. The game’s high optimization standards are especially notable given Sonic Team’s recent struggles with other titles.SONIC X SHADOW GENERATIONS offers a thrilling journey that celebrates the legacy of Sonic and Shadow. Shadow's campaign provides an emotional, action-packed storyline that gives longtime fans the in-depth character exploration they’ve been craving, while Sonic Generations continues to be an enjoyable romp through the best of the franchise’s past. For those who haven’t played the original Sonic Generations, this package is a must-have; and for longtime fans, Shadow's new story and the game’s quality-of-life upgrades make it a worthwhile addition to their collection.Are you a Sonic fan ready to dive back into the ultimate speed adventure? Be sure to follow our  for more Sonic and Shadow game reviews, discussions, and nostalgia-fueled content! Join our community to stay connected with the latest in Sonic’s world!

_childDocuments_.review: I've never felt more validated for being a Ride or Die for Shadow The Hedgehog (05) than after playing this.Shadow Generations builds on some of the gameplay ideas introduced in Frontiers & puts it into a more focused lens. With traditional 3D & 2.5D levels for Shadow, as well as introducing tons of new gameplay mechanics exclusive to him via his Doom powers. Sonic Team have clearly taken some of the lessons from Frontiers "Open Zone" format & applied it to the hub world. The hub world is not as large as the islands in Frontiers, however it is incredibly fun to traverse, as well as being much denser & filled with things to do & find. Shadow Generations has arguably some of the best gameplay & level design in the entire franchise. Along with a good story that helps flesh out & develop Shadow while getting first time fans up to speed on his story. Shadows characterisation & gameplay is literally the best it's ever been here & hopefully Sonic Team takes note of this for the future.This game is a love letter to Shadow fans. From the collectables that help build on the lore with Gerald, Maria, the ARK & the creation of Shadow. To the story that roots itself firmly in the history of Shadows Journey through SA2, Sonic Heroes, Shadow 05, Sonic 06 & even Sonic Forces. Everything that fans love about this character & his lore/story is here on full display proudly, & I couldn't be happier.Sonic Generations is mostly the same package with some minor upgrades here & there such as control options for classic or modern controls & a few visual tweaks. It also has the added collectable Chao in the main stages, which adds a nice extra layer of content, especially for completionists. Overall Sonic Generations is still the same great game it was back in 2011, with a couple of old issues here or there from the original release that stop it from being an all timer. Mainly the final boss that is arguably one of the worst in the series & is probably the only major negative for the game.Both of these games make a final product that is both a genuinely great starting point for newcomers to the series & a fresh experience for older fans with Shadow Generations. Which could honestly be one of the highest highs the franchise has seen in a while.Between Sonic Frontiers & now this game, I can't wait to see where Sonic Team goes next with the franchise. Especially for Shadow.

_childDocuments_.review: So I have just 100% Sonic X Shadow Generations. And here's my review. Tldr: Original og Gens is better for technical reasons. And Shadow Gens is really good, but not as good as Gens but it's still great. So first of, Gens remaster. While it's technically a remaster, it's definitely not what we want one to be. Texture and model pop in. Nothing that'll ruin the experience, arguably. But shouldn't be there. Especially in places where it wasn't in the original. The game also does not sync up to your refresh rate. Og PC port did. Drop Dash is a skill for classic, but is part of modern's basic kit... that's weird. New physic glitches that weren't in the original. It's not bad. But if you just wanna play Gens, play the original PC port. It's just better. Shadow is good. The physics work great for its level design. Not my favorite physics, way too slow for my liking, but they did well working with it. Tho it's lacking in the level design. Not how you play through it, just the visuals surrounding it. In OG Gens you can see the alt paths around you. And not because they look like paths, but because they organically fit in the level. They originally look like something you can't go to. BUT YOU CAN. That doesn't happen in Shadow. While it's better than Frontiers, it still feels fake. And most of the levels are only there cause they can reuse assets so there's that.... It's probably the reason there isn't a Shadow 05 level. They reuse assets from Shadows fight in og Gens for Space Colony. Rail Canyon is literally just rails and rocks. Kingdom Valley is honestly just generic ruins. Sunset Heights and Chaos Island are the Pinnacle of reuse from Forces and Frontiers respectively. And Radical Highway just reuses assets from the city stages in Frontiers. And they don't add anything to make them feel unique, unlike og Gens. I loved seeing robots selling ice cream in Rooftop Run. That doesn't happen here. It's a good game, a great one. But I gotta say Sonic gens is better. Still worth the asking price tho. Over 40 hours of content

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: This review will mostly cover the new Shadow Generations part of the game and the quality of the remaster here on PC (and Steam Deck). Also, I will not be covering the controversy of the rewrites in OG Generations because I never enjoyed the story there anyway. I will be covering Shadow Generations story a little (with as little spoilers as possible) as there is something to say there. Lastly, there will be spoilers for the stage roster in Shadow Generations so if you haven't seen the trailers and don't wanna be spoiled, I'd play the game and then come back.Also, before I begin, just as a quick summary of my thoughts on the original game (as I never reviewed the original despite owning it on PS3): I love Sonic Generations. While it is too short and too easy, the 18 stages it has is near infinitely replayable, the references are brilliantly done, the music has some of the strongest remixes in the series and the OG Generations modding scene was amazing (I sadly played the original on PS3 so I never got to play these mods but I won't deny how awesome they were). Revisting it after 10 years on pc was a joy as well.Onto the main attraction, Shadow Generations is an absolute joy to play and replay. While it only took 4 hours to beat, it's a four hours I don't regret.Starting with the stages: Shadow has 12 of them across 6 different zones. Not as many as OG Generations but that's not an issue as these 12 are incredible. Kingdom Valley is the MVP as the new visuals and lighting make the stage jaw-droppingly beautiful. The weakest stage visually is Sunset Heights (mainly because I think Forces sucks) despite the same beautiful lighting of the Hedgehog Engine 2. Onto the stages mechanically, Kingdom Valley is once again the best one for how the chaos powers unique to Shadow allow for some creative skips and shortcuts. Chaos Island is probably the weakest level to play because it doesn't make sense and the Chaos Morph is so slippery to control but it isn't a bottom tier Sonic level. The rest of them are very well designed and have a surprising amount of spectacle to them via dynamic camera and animations.The Open Zone from Frontiers returns as the hub world and they made some drastic improvements, focusing on a single, smaller yet more dense hub world to get around in. It still feels very game-esqe when traversing it but the improved controls and faster movement helps to make it fun to run around and complete the challenges. Open Zone still isn't at its fullest potential but this shows it does have potential.Briefly mentioning the Doom and Chaos Abilities Shadow has, they're all very fun to use and are not pace breakers... except the Doom Morph. That one is by far the worst. The others like the Doom Spears have a lot of usage and using them while running is super nice. Chaos Control has much more usage than I thought it would with how freezing time opens up shortcuts in stages like Space Colony, Sunset Heights and Kingdom Valley.The music is great. Not that its surprising because Sonic has pretty much always had excellent music. Shadow Generations remixes didn't sit with me until I heard them in game where they grew on me and I even prefer the new Kingdom Valley mix over the original from 06. Won't spoil the boss themes but they all slap hard and really add to the epicness of the fights.Bosses are... okay. They're cool and feel climatic for sure but like OG Generations, they can be too easy, even on the post game hard mode if you know what you're doing (though, this hard mode is a legit challenge at times with how you have no rings). The Biolizard is my favourite one by far. Apology accepted for the awful one in Generations 3ds, Sega. But please make bosses more challenging without the need for hard mode going forward.The story itself isn't very long but from a longtime fans perspective, it was excellent. I loved it. Shadow got some great development and seeing him humanised in the way Ian Flynn did it made me legit cry. For newcomers, I recommend watching the Dark Beginnings videos if you don't wanna play prior games but still want to understand the basics of who Shadow is and his connection to certain characters.To wrap up on the quality of the remaster and it's performance, I'm quite surprised. While visual updates are mirror, there were some as OG Gens is in Hedgehog Engine 2 now, which has much better lighting and shadows than the first Hedgehog Engine. This makes the stages in both OG and Shadow Gen look beautiful and eye popping. With performance, despite the game having Denuvo (which can impact performance), it runs very well on PC with me experiencing more frame drops on Shadow Gen that OG Gen, especially on Steam Deck. On Deck, OG Gen has no lag in gameplay but Shadow Gen can drop to as low as 40 fps but averages around 50-60 fps so performance is generally good. Cutscenes in OG Gen can lag and stutter as they were optimised for 30 fps so playing anything higher can cause issues. Shadow Gen's cutscenes are not pre rendered to my knowledge so they can lag more if you don't have good specs.Overall, as a complete and expanded package, this was a fantastic Sonic game back in 2011 with just Sonic Generations but with Shadow Generations, it's even better now. Sonic Team have clearly listened to all the feedback from the 2010's games and Frontiers with this one. I'm rooting for them to take everything that worked here and use it in a new game that doesn't reuse assets. As a final word to the developers and publisher: Sega, let Sonic Team cook for as long as they need for the next game. They're really onto something with the Open Zone style and having boost formula traditional stages as part of the games progression. Frontiers laid a groundwork, Shadow Generations showed it was solid via many improvements I and many others have highlighted. Do not screw up the Sonic series going forward. Oh, and give us an Unleashed remaster next.

_childDocuments_.review: If you haven't played Sonic Generations before, this might be worth it. Otherwise it's really hard to recommend. It's not really that the game is bad: it's not. It's just....disappointingly fine. It's a C for a student who got an A last time and failed to take into account any of the feedback they got on the last assignment, and worse, fell back on bad habits and didn't put in the same effort. The levels are shorter and less polished, with an overreliance on the abstract floating platform theme of frontiers. The mechanics are interesting but shallowly explored and poorly integrated into the levels. Instead, you're railroaded into "mini-stages" to play with them in isolation, copying the worst part of Sonic Generations design. The overworld is lifted directly from frontiers, and while it's significantly denser, it feels cluttered and nonsensical when compared with the clean, segmented 2d version in the original. Shadow controls like he's on ice, and while it's manageable, he's still significantly harder to control than sonic, and stages don't feel designed around it at all. It's therefore unfortunate that there are no more "skills" that could alter his movement. There are also technical issues. The Shadow story had significant laggyness, even during cutscenes. A driver update helped but didn't fix the issue. And no, I don't game on a potato. The Generations remake included runs fine, but the anti-aliasing looks like it's broken. This is not on anyone who actually worked on the game. The entire package stinks of ""business"" and lack of budget. Where generations felt like a sincere celebration with an appropriate level of dedicated resources, this feels like a product, ripped out of DLC plans for the original game, put on a tight deadline to push a movie release, marked as a sequel even though it's barely longer than the steam refund limit. The game didn't deserve that, and it suffers for it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is no doubt the best 3D Sonic game in YEARS no competition.SHADOW GENERATIONS being the main selling point, has a great story, with beautiful animations, graphics, and attention to detail that casual and especially hardcore Sonic fans will be able to enjoy.The gameplay feels like a cross between the boost games and Adventure era games, with a high emphasis on speed and being as fast as possible, while still feeling WONDERFUL to control and MORE than playable most of the time without boosting if you REALLY don't want/have to.The music, both originals and remixes are all wonderful. Shadow's character has been done SERIOUS justice, since the days of "edgy the hedgy" and the "I hate everyone" attitude he had from 2012 onwards. Now, Shadow feels real. LIKE HE SHOULD FOR THE CHARACTER THEY ENDED WITH BY THE END OF 06. He is traumatised and in turn quiet, but not a dark, brooding edgelord that hates everything and everyone. Instead, Shadow does things his way before asking others opinions, but still considers the feelings of others and CARES about his close friends in Rouge and Omega.The levels are all well designed and feel expansive, even if all alternate paths put you back on the main path quickly, they FEEL bigger than they are and that's great. The white space hub is FULLY 3D meaning, again, for the first time in YEARS a 3D Sonic game has more 3D than 2D (Yes I know Frontiers but in the greater scale)There are plenty of optional collectables around the white space to unlock music, art and lore, with the hub feeling small compared to Frontiers HOWEVER it is FAR more focused, with each area fitting the theme of the level it surrounds and some new rail, ramp, spring, or loop every few feet makes it feel dense and FUN to roam in.The story is simple, yet interesting, and doesn't feel like a cringe Saturday morning cartoon for Gen Z, and rather an anime style plot in the vein of Dragon Ball or My Hero Academia, with power ups, screams, teleporting, beating big powerful bad guys with a genuinely heartfelt and well written story between the action.Ask any SENSIBLE person online (not children) who has played the game they will probably agree with me.SONIC GENERATIONS is very... Flaccid in comparison. Sonic Gens is Sonic Gens, it's a great game, bit of a flat story etc, it's an older game you know the drill. But this remaster... Kind of ruins it a bit.The cutscenes have been reworked to not only feature a COMPLETE REDUB, but also some minor animation edits to better fit the "modern" interpretation of the characters. Which in itself is fine, and the redub WRITING, while unnecessary, is decent, adds some context to certain scenes or character interactions, but then other times the line delivery is AWFUL, with dead space between lines. In some cases, the original animation is left untouched while the dialogue is changed. The worst example of his is early on when Knuckles is rescued. In the original, he comments that he didn't NEED (Classic) Sonic's help, and then asks "Did you gain weight?" to which Classic looks down and rubs his belly in a "Huh? You think I'm fat?" Kind of way. In the REDUB, Knuckles (more in character) shows concern for his missing island... As Classic Sonic looks down and rubs his belly... DID HE EAT THE ISLAND?!Overall Sonic Generations is basically the same as it was before with some of the lower res textures and models being upscaled or retouched to look nicer on modern monitors, but with a redub that feels rushed, not quite needed, and animations that feel forced in for no REAL good reason.I played SONIC GENS to death on PC, mods added way more life to it. But I bought THIS package for the SHADOW portion, and I was NOT dissapointed.PROS:-FANTASTIC Shadow portion, pushing to be one of the best 3D Sonic games ever-2 brilliant games for the price of 1 full priced game-PLENTY of content and things to do-Shadow Generations... That whole thing is a proCONS:-Nonsense changes to SONIC GENS-Shadow Gens being a little too short, but as good as it is, I'd rather it be short and fun, than long and boring-Awfully rushed redubbing and animating of Sonic Gens-Not enough Shadow Gens for my liking, I want more, it was too good, Sonic Team cooked, now make other characters have games (BLAZE THE CAT GAME PLEASEEEE???????)

This is odd when you consider that Sonic Frontiers also had a mini soundtrack and that included some of the songs featured in the game (even if it wasn't all of them). It was pretty disappointing to not see anything new in this game's mini soundtrack, then again I might have missed something and if so, that's news to me.The second thing I didn't like that much was the Terios skin for Shadow. I'm primarily referring to his running and boosting animations and how weird they look when equipping the skin. Unlike Shadow where he wears roller skates, (no wait sorry "Air Shoes" as Shadow calls them), Terios' design doesn't have him wear anything that could justify him using Shadow's skating animations. Also yea Terios' quills do look weird, but I don't mind them that much.Overall, this is a very solid game and if you didn't try the original Sonic Generations either, I'd say this is worth getting given that, at least to my knowledge, there are barely any differences between the original steam release and this version.

_childDocuments_.review: In short, this is a fantastic compilation of a beloved series classic alongside a brand new Shadow game of even higher quality. A perfect game for fans and newcomers alike.On one hand, you have a remaster of Sonic Generations, one of the best 3D Sonic games with great levels, music, and gameplay that covers the history of the series up to 2011. The remaster brings the game to a more modern standard with a bit of added content mainly through Chao Rescue. The rewritten dialogue aims to reduce the meta dialogue and write the characters more in-line with the rest of the series.On the other hand, you have a brand new game in Shadow Generations. Gameplay-wise, Shadow feels like an in-between of Frontiers and Generations, which is good. The controls are tight where they need to be to make the game feel great in both levels and in the open-zone hub world, in a way that reminds me of Adventure 1. Level designs are varied, with lots of branching paths to take and shortcuts to find, which makes it satisfying to replay levels and nab the collectibles. Something I'd also like to highlight is the writing. The game has a great story that shows that, when allowed to, Ian Flynn can still write an amazing Shadow story. It also fits in several beloved characters that were notably not in Sonic Gens and the overall writing feels perfect for an emotional Shadow story that takes place during Sonic Generations. The biggest catch I would say is that the mini artbook and soundtrack that come with the digital deluxe edition were pretty disappointing. So if those are what was selling you on the digital deluxe, maybe hold off. The soundtrack does not contain any of the new remixes.TLDR: Sonic Gens is still Sonic Gens, but no janky launcher, an improved script (in my opinion) and cinematics, with a bunch of adorable Chao added as collectibles. Shadow Gens is a great evolution of the series formula with great controls, story, visuals, levels, and style.

_childDocuments_.review: An overall excellent package with two of the best entries in the entire series. Sonic Generations has admittedly aged less agreeably in some areas, but while the physics aren't perfect the game still manages to be a great time with boundless speedrun potential. The original release was very light on narrative, and the remaster here is no different, though many scenes have been altered, it ultimately doesn't contribute to much other then highlighting how some of the legacy voice cast is starting to show their age, namely Dr. Eggman's VA Mike Pollock.These issues don't however contribute to any less of an outstanding game experience. For every flaw the game has, it's outweighed by the still gorgeous presentation, excellent level design, exciting set pieces, and near endless replayability and side content to keep you occupied. The finale of the game leaves a bit to be desired, but the experience is still DEFINITELY worth a first go. ----------------Shadow Generations is the real star of the package, which is saying a lot considering the other half is one of the most beloved entries in the series. Shadow Generations builds itself on Hedgehog Engine 2, which is the same engine used for the likes of Sonic Frontiers, and you'll find a lot of familiar elements from that entry, largely for better. The controls feel like they perfected what was previously attempted in Frontiers, though like that game, mid-air control still leaves a bit to be designed when turning. Gone are the many custom sliders and toggles for control that Frontiers introduced, with the only one remaining being deceloration. This ultimately isn't a negative however as despite my qualms the game might be one of the best feeling games in the series to control in 3D. Everything feels finely tuned, and the more open hub-world gives you plenty of opportunities to refine your skills and abilities for the masterfully crafted main levels. The level design in the original Sonic Generations was already brilliant in many ways, and Shadow Generations in no different, I'd even argue in many ways they're better. These levels are all perfectly paced, and despite being longer than Sonic's they never feel like they drag out, they never feel padded, they always end exactly when they feel they should. There are many alternative routes you can take during your play experience that can give you short cuts to improve your time by the levels end, though unlike Sonic Generations, passing checkpoints no longer tells the player how much faster or slower they were at hitting said checkpoint, which is a big shame as that was a really nice feature. However it's made up for by the absolutely PLETHORA of new abilities at your disposal that can be used to open up more options within the levels, the Doom Powers. Levels typically are designed with your latest Doom Power in mind, though it would've been nice to see a few extra options in previous levels for them as well, but this is only a minor grievance as the hub world still has A LOT of opportunities for use of each and every one, and the levels still aren't shy of using them either. I was not fond of the "Doom Morph" ability at first, seems like a more finicky context sensitive version of the Doom Surf, however I quickly learned just how cool it could be, and the hub challenges near Chaos Island made me realize just how many uses there could be for it. While saying Sonic Generations has a story is a bit of a generous stretch, Shadow Generations thrives off of it, no doubt helped by the brilliant writing talents on board. The story has heart, and towards the end will have you feeling very emotional. Shadow is a far more nuanced character than others in the franchise, and this narrative furthers that in ways touched upon by previous entries, but in a fresh and touching way, all helped out by the huge upgrade in animation quality. Characters feel more expressive and lively, scenes are framed in very good ways, blocking is excellent, and the voice actors with one major exception (Karen Strassman as Rouge) all come together to create a very good story.Few things can be said except THIS is the kind of thing fans want to see going forward, a masterfully crafted open world, brilliant level design, cool set pieces and a story that has depth. Here's hoping Frontiers 2 takes what was learned here and applies it going forward. AMAZING experience all around.

_childDocuments_.review: It's his year.-   -Running on the Hedgehog Engine 2 (same as Sonic Frontiers), this game is not only visually impressive, but is probably the most innovative gameplay-wise. I mention the engine, because it allows for this game to have awesome detail and still run at a smooth 120 FPS.The story was more than I was expecting. Written by Ian Flynn (writer of the Sonic Comics), the story takes a comprehensive yet brief look at Shadow's character, and even partially expands the story. I personally believe the story was excellent, because the only criticism I have is that it ends. You won't get an experience that's as long as Sonic Generations, but it's a great addition if you're new to Sonic Generations already.That's not to say there aren't issues, but the ones that I have are more fundamental - such as Sonic Team/ SEGA's choice of levels. The game starts off  strong, but it runs out of steam towards the end. For a game that's a celebration of Shadow, there's one particular stage that doesn't fit him whatsoever. Ironically, it might be also be the weakest stage in the game.Overall, it was a great story that I was keen to experience myself, and I'm very glad that I did.-   -It pains me to say there aren't any massive changes in this re-release of Sonic Generations almost 13 years later. I played a lot of Sonic Generations on Xbox 360 and PC prior to this game's release, so I started with Shadow Generations - and now that I have, I'm very sad to say that none of the unique aspects of Shadow's campaign make it to Sonic's.Sonic Generations is, except for a handful of small changes, a 1:1 of the 2011 version.The single-most glaring issue for me is that Sonic Generations runs only from 30-60 FPS. After 13 years, I was really hoping Sonic Team could manage 120-144 FPS to accommodate modern hardware and modernize the game a bit more. You might think it's nit-picky, but I don't think that was a huge ask for $60.In the end, it's still Sonic Generations. It's not bad at all (in fact, it's arguably one of the best), but If you were hoping they threw in some more levels or content besides the Casino Night DLC, I've got some bad news for you.In short, I don't recommend you buy this game at $50-60. I recommend waiting for $30 or less.But Shadow Generations does have Big the Cat, so I might have to put my bias aside and give it the 1,000/10 it deserves, it's just that peak.

_childDocuments_.review: It's just like the olden days really.THIS WILL BE SPOILER FREE RELAX ALL READERSGonna start with the new stuff here, all of the Shadow side of the game is entirely new and that is what the bread and butter of this game is and what most people will buy it for if they owned Generations before. The story is decent enough for very short stories, both take around 5-6 hours give or take. (I didn't 100% Shadow's side but I did beat every level and boss, I didn't play the Sonic Side besides the 1st level). This length is however a lot shorter then many probably hoped for as it's easy to wrap up each story in a single play session espescially if you skip cutscenes and I STRONGLY URGE people to take they're time with it and space it out among other games. There is only 6 levels (and 4 bosses) in the Shadow side, 2 of which honestly don't make any sense in the context of the game, as they come from games that existed long after the time-frame Generations takes place in and both the Sonic and Shadow sides take place at the same time. Sega dropped the ball here however as in all the promotional stuff we already knew basically everything that Shadow's story was bringing stage and boss wise before the game even came out just not the order. Shadow's levels also all take longer then most of what the Sonic side has, 1st level Sonic side easy to clear under 3 min both sides, Shadow's first level will take between 4.5-5 min on a first run through for Act 1 alone. This stuff isn't a negative per-say it just sucks that people who followed the marketing got spoiled for a lot of stuff. What is a negative though is any collectables obtained through the Shadow Story do not Carry over into the Sonic one as, judging by what the game does when you click the Sonic side, plus there being 2 exe's in the folder, it runs an entirely separate game. Another obvious negative is Denuvo, nuf said. I haven't really experienced any performance issues except frame drops in a few places, and only in cutscenes, but what drops I have seen are VERY noticable, and I have a 3070TI and more then enough RAM to run the game so it might not like systems on thee minimum requirements spectrum. The Sonic side from what I can tell from just after the first level (and 100% the original Generations ages ago) is the same thing mainly. The story DOES have some rewrites and its been re-dubbed from what I can tell. Sadly the funny stuff in the birthday scene at the beginning where Amy gets held back by Sonic as she's fangirling, and her sending Knuckles into a tree are both gone in this version, as well as the first conversation between Sonic and Tails after clearing Act 2 of the first level is also changed a little bit. I do not know the level of rewriting and redubbing that's actually in the game fully yet but I assume there will be more in the later stages of the story. The new controls are also somewhat annoying to get used to but you can switch it back to the og Generations scheme if you wish so its not a problem. The game also makes Red Rings unobtainable on the first clear of a stage ACT (least with the 1st level) and there are new Chao to find, hints for them are actually available in the Collections Room which you get access to after clearing Act 2 of the first stage by going left instead of right. The "HD" textures of Sonic Generations is BARELY noticable so there is a chance returning players will not be able to tell unless they look closely. Aside from what I said in this paragraph however, the Sonic Side is the same game that came out all those years ago.The Deluxe edition really only comes with a beta Shadow design which is mid, a Modern Sonic skin that looks off, the early access is nice but again you CAN beat one of the 2 stories very easily in one sitting if you have the time to burn. The extra BGM's are only available in the Shadow side and they are all songs from like Sonic Riders and up in the timeline. The DLC is known to be a movie tie-in with Sonic the Hedgehog 3 and comes out before the movie does in theatres so I can't rate it at all. And yes the Gerald Robotnik notebook they were advertising is in the Shadow collection room fully accessable you just gotta get its pages.All in all this game is a very Solid revisiting of an old 3D classic with a bunch of new flair in the form of a sister game accessed from the same launch. If Denuvo doesn't mess with your experience cause you have a stronger gaming rig or get lucky this game is well worth it as it is effectively a 2 in 1 special. However if you have a computer on the weaker side of the spectrum this may struggle to run at times cause of that dumb DRM. There is no info on how modding this game is gonna go, Sega seems to be ok with it yet they use a DRM that makes it harder to do so I dunno what is going on in they're heads.Is the game worth its asking price? The standard edition is most certainly worth it long as Denuvo doesn't cause too many issues, the deluxe depends on your opinions on what it comes with. Keep in mind there is no longer a way to purchase the original Sonic Generations outside of bundles now. If you have never played the original Generations game treat yourself with this game, espescially if your a long time Sonic fan there is a ton to like in this game, even more if your a huge Shadow fan as that is by far the superior game out of the 2 in this purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: I've already played the original Sonic Generations way back in 2011 on the 360, so my focus wasn't really on that. Don't get me wrong, the levels are still fun for what they are. Beyond some daytime Sonic Unleashed stages, they were the best modern Sonic had to offer in terms of level design. However, it's pretty apparent that its gameplay is dated. Sonic is still incredibly awkward to handle when he's not going 999 mph, Classic Sonic still has a momentum bug here and there when it comes to slopes and curves, and there's a large dependence on having skills make the gameplay tolerable when it should be tolerable from the start. Beyond this it's still a really good time. Shadow Generations? Amazing. Level design is incredible. Shortcuts are just visible enough to notice, but just out of the way where you have to think on your feet to figure out how to get there. The new abilities are varied and all useful in their own way. Shadow controls almost like his Adventure counterpart (can't state enough how good this is.). Bosses are actually fun to fight. And there's just enough side content to keep you busy, even after beating the final boss. My only issue is that, compared to Sonic Generations, there aren't as many stages, acts, and bosses. I honestly wish there was more.

_childDocuments_.review: They've achieved almost unbelievable.The Sonic part is virtually unchanged in terms of the content. Re-written and re-voiced dialogues and cutscenes don't change the meaning at all, but make everything more sensible. The graphics is mostly the same, but the engine was updated to support modern resolutions and there are some very minor, subtle improvements with things like LOD. All the cutscenes, the most age-showing part of the original Generations, were re-rendered (or maybe run in the engine, I can't really tell), so they look as sharp and smooth as the rest of the game, even at 2560x1440@60FPS.The Shadow part is just a masterpiece, making use of the best parts of Frontiers and Generations and re-imagining classic level design into something entirely new. It's a bit more demanding in terms of hardware obviously, but because if that it looks absolutely stunning and runs at perfect 120FPS on my hardware (Laptop with a 12th gen i9 and RTX 3080 Ti). And the story is very carefully weaved into the original Generations and covers a lot of plot holes.Thank you, Sonic Team. You've done everything right.

_childDocuments_.review: I think the best way to summarize this entry into the Sonic franchise is "quality over quantity."Shadow's portion of the game is fairly short if you simply blast through the story, but everything about it is excellent. Everything here just feels so GOOD.Everything feels polished, the presentation is stellar, and the performance is smooth as could be. This game was truly a joy to jump into and play through- though I plan to 100% it because of how fun it is!Each stage is a visual treat, with interesting "stage gimmicks," really cool set pieces and fun side paths to discover, and Shadow's new abilities are a TON of fun to learn and master.The story is short and sweet, with its length being the only real negative. The cutscenes are excellent, you can tell the animators had a lot of fun with this one, and there's a lot of heart in what story there is.One small criticism: the default controls for mouse+keyboard are a little clunky, requiring reaching for unusual keys, and boost not being on shift is kind of criminal. The keybind interface doesn't even seem to recognize shift as a button to bind to. I recommend using a controller and adjusting the bindings to your comfort.Of course, there's the Sonic half of the game as well, though it isn't new. Sonic Generations is generally considered one of the better 3D Sonic games, but might show its age if played after Shadow Generations. Still, as the standalone version was delisted and Shadow Generations is so good, if you've never played the original Generations game, it's hard to say no to two great games bundled into one.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is split into two:* The Remaster for Sonic Generations which almost the same. It has new dialogues and new voice lines that change the story and characters a bit. Yes they suck, but the original suck as well, and nobody plays Sonic Generations for the story otherwise. Gameplay-wise it's the same without lives and with the addition of the dropdash, which does a bit difference in Classic Sonic.* Shadow Generations which is a brand new experience and perhaps the best Sonic game in a long while. The stages last more than 1 minute, it's amazing! Also Shadow is not a Sonic re-skin (thank god), and he has unique abilities and some missing ones from his counter-part. The story was typical EDGINESS you would expect from a Sonic story. Not too bad, but nothing too notable. I got this remaster for this portion and I was left really happy.

_childDocuments_.review: When you buy this you get two things, Shadow Generations and a launcher to play Sonic Generations.What you get out of the sonic generations portion is a nice no hassle no 2011 launcher jank, your options are in-game and you get a bunch of nice bonuses with the Digital Deluxe. You lose (assuming you didn't already have Gens), easy access to modding (for now) and the time to regain all achievements and beat the game again.What you get out of Shadow Generations is about 4 hours of the most well polished and presented sonic levels and hub area they've ever made, with just the right amount of gimmicks, set pieces, and challenges to keep you engaged. (6 Stages, 2 acts each, 4 bosses)The gamefeel in Shadow Gens feels more like an updated Frontiers than an updated generations, the game feel is very similar to frontiers (the way the camera locks, the way boost behaves, enemy and rail lock on, how momentum carries, and how acceleration works). I'm of the opinion this is a test drive for what Frontiers 2 will bring us. Overall, a fun but criminally short ride with Shadow Gens and another run at a QoL improved Sonic Gens. Once modding catches up, you'll have one of if not *THE* best sonic title to own on PC.

_childDocuments_.review: I was pretty hyped for this game in the run up till its release, and while I am disappointed by one or two things about Shadow Gens. Story while short is very good, seeing a modern day Shadow interact with Maria and Gerald before the events of SA2 is heartwarming and at times heartbreaking. Gameplay while a little slower and stiffer then Frontiers is still really good. Levels are fun with a good amount of multiple pathways. Boss fights for me are a mixed bag, they're fun but a little too easy imo, they last a little longer in hard mode but there isn't a whole lot that changes with the hard mode version. As for the Sonic Generations remaster, it is very similar to the original, the biggest change is that the entire script is rewritten. For the most part I am ok with the new script but there are a few moments where I prefer the original script (examples being the cutscnes with modern sonic and tails after green hill and chemical plant). Gameplay is exactly the same as the orignal with the stellar level design you know and love. Albeit the controls of boost Sonic haven't aged all that well, he feels very stiff when not boosting and when hes in the air.Overall I'd say the package as a whole is worth the asking price as you get 2 great games for the price of one. Hoping that Frontiers 2 takes what this game did great and runs with it.
